parts.overview: Ostra is a local server that runs an engineering pipeline on a workspace of projects. A user opens the React console in a browser, enters a request, and approves gates. The Rust engine then runs agents through research, spec, plan, implement, review, test, and docs stages. Each session is an append-only event log, and a pure planner decides the next step from the folded state. Agents run on a native API loop or inside installed harness CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Antigravity). A policy engine checks every tool call, and a sandbox enforces the boundary in the kernel. The server also gives the console file browsing, code navigation, a Git dock, external MCP servers, documentation books, lesson memory, and Web Push. The repository holds 15 crates, the console in `web/`, the design system in `design/`, the agent assets in `assets/`, and the tests in `tests/`.

sections.title: Ostra overview and first run
sections.summary: What Ostra does, how to build, install, and start the `ostra` binary, which subcommands and flags it has, how the Docker files work, and how the binary serves the web console.
sections.body:
## What Ostra solves

Ostra is a local server that runs an engineering pipeline on your own projects and shows it in a browser console. Without it, you start each coding agent by hand, track each run yourself, and decide alone what each agent can do. Ostra starts the agents, records each run, asks you at the gates of the pipeline, and applies guards and a sandbox to the commands that the agents run.

The `ostra` binary is the whole product. It contains the server, the engine for the pipeline, the executors, and the web console. You build one binary, start it, and open one URL in a browser.

This page covers these topics:

- How to build the binary.
- How to start it with `run.sh`, as a service, or in Docker.
- The `ostra` command and its subcommands.
- The flags for the port, the browser, and frontend work.
- How the binary serves the embedded web build.

This page stops before the settings files, the sign-in rules, and the internals. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) for the settings files, [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md) for the sign-in rules, and [Architecture and crate map](architecture.md) for the crates.

## Build the binary

The release binary embeds the web build, so you build the web UI first and then the Rust server. The script `build.sh` does both steps. It stops on the first error.

The build needs these tools:

- Rust `1.98.1` with `rustfmt` and `clippy`. The file `rust-toolchain.toml` pins this version, and `rustup` installs it.
- Node.js 24 and `npm`. The `Dockerfile` and `install.ps1` both use Node.js 24.

The script `build.sh` runs these steps in the repository root:

1. If the folder `node_modules` is missing, run `npm ci --no-audit --no-fund`. The root `package.json` lists `design`, `web`, and `site` as npm workspaces, so one install covers all of them.
2. If `web/dist/index.html` is missing, or any file in `web/src`, `web/public`, `web/index.html`, `web/package.json`, `design/src`, or `design/package.json` is newer than it, run `npm run -s build` in `web/`. Otherwise the script prints `Web UI is up to date` and skips the step.
3. Run `cargo build --release -p ostra-server`. The result is `target/release/ostra`.

The script builds the web UI first because the Rust compiler embeds the folder `web/dist` into the binary. The folder `web/dist` is in `.gitignore`, so a new clone has no web build until you run the script.

Note: the root `package.json` lists `site` as a workspace, but the folder `site/` does not exist in the repository. The `Dockerfile` also copies `site/package.json`. Add a `site/` folder with a `package.json` before you build the image or run a fresh `npm ci`, or remove `site` from the workspace list.

For development, use the commands of the project profile:

| Purpose | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Compile every crate | `cargo build --workspace` |
| Run the Rust tests | `cargo test --workspace` |
| Format the Rust code | `cargo fmt --all` |

See [Testing and evals](testing.md) for the web tests, the browser tests, and the live-model evals.

### What happens when

- If `web/dist/index.html` is missing in the compiled binary, the server still starts. Every page request returns status 200 with the text `The web build is missing. Run `npm run build` in web/ and rebuild ostra.`
- If you change a file in `web/src` but do not run `build.sh` again, the binary keeps the old web build, because the compiler embeds the web build.

## Start the server with run.sh

The script `run.sh` builds the binary and starts it. It passes every argument to `ostra`. For example, `./run.sh --port 8080` starts the server on port `8080`.

The script has these steps:

1. Run `./build.sh`, unless the variable `SKIP_BUILD` is `1`.
2. If the file named by `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` exists, apply its credential lines. The script applies only the lines of the form `export NAME=value`, so no other line in the file runs.
3. Run `exec ./target/release/ostra` with your arguments.

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` | Path of a file with `export NAME=value` lines, for example provider keys. |
| `SKIP_BUILD` | When `1`, start the existing binary and do not build. |

After the server starts, it prints the sign-in URL and, unless you disable it, opens your browser. See [Start the server and choose the port](#start-the-server-and-choose-the-port).

## The ostra command and its subcommands

The `ostra` command has one default action, which is to start the server, and several subcommands. The `clap` parser in `crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs` defines them. The serve flags are also top-level flags, so `ostra --port 8080` and `ostra serve --port 8080` do the same.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ostra` or `ostra serve` | Starts the server. This is the default. |
| `ostra config` | Prints the path of the global config file. It writes the default file first if none exists. |
| `ostra url` | Prints a fresh sign-in URL for a running server. |
| `ostra sessions` | Lists the browsers that are signed in. |
| `ostra sessions revoke <id>` or `ostra sessions revoke --all` | Revokes one sign-in, or every sign-in. |
| `ostra signout` | Signs out every browser. It does the same as `ostra sessions revoke --all`. |
| `ostra stop <session>` | Stops a session when the server does not run. |
| `ostra hook` | The hook bridge for harness executions. A harness calls it. You do not. |
| `ostra mcp-stdio` | The MCP stdio shim for harness executions. A harness calls it. You do not. |

A harness is a coding agent program that Ostra runs in a terminal, such as Claude Code. See [Harness executors](harness-executors.md) for the hook bridge and the shim.

The binary also accepts the hidden argument `sandbox-init` as its first argument. Ostra uses it inside a sandbox, and `--help` does not list it. The binary checks for it before it starts a runtime or logging.

The commands `url`, `sessions`, and `signout` belong to the sign-in system. See [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md) for the token, the cookie, and the lifetimes.

### What happens when

- If you run `ostra stop <session>` when the server runs, the command fails. It tells you to stop the session from its board, or to stop the server first. The running server owns the session, and a second writer conflicts with it.
- If you run `ostra stop <session>` when the server does not run, the command cancels the running executions of that session. The next start does not recover and run them again. It prints `Stopped <session>; <n> running executions were cancelled.`
- If no registered workspace has the session, `ostra stop` fails with `No registered workspace has a session <session>.`
- `ostra sessions` and `ostra signout` work when the server runs and when it does not run. A running server refuses a revoked browser within 5 seconds.

## Start the server and choose the port

The server listens on port `7878` by default. The constant `DEFAULT_PORT` in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` holds this value. The function `run` in the same file starts the server.

The server chooses its port in this order:

1. The flag `--port`, if you set it.
2. The setting `server.port` in the global config, if it exists.
3. Port `7878`. If it is busy, the server tries each of the next 19 ports, up to `7897`.
4. A free port that the operating system chooses, if all 20 ports are busy.

If you set a port with the flag or the setting, the server binds exactly that port and does not try another. If the port is busy, the server exits with the bind error.

```rust
async fn bind(ip: std::net::IpAddr, port: Option<u16>) -> anyhow::Result<tokio::net::TcpListener> {
    let start = port.unwrap_or(DEFAULT_PORT);
    if port.is_some() {
        return Ok(tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(SocketAddr::new(ip, start)).await?);
    }
    for p in start..start + 20 {
        if let Ok(l) = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(SocketAddr::new(ip, p)).await {
            return Ok(l);
        }
    }
    Ok(tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(SocketAddr::new(ip, 0)).await?)
}
```

The server uses the port that it really bound for the sign-in URL and for the harness callback address. A scan that lands on another port therefore does not break the sign-in link.

### Startup order

The function `run` does these steps in order:

1. Write the default global config if it does not exist, then read it.
2. Resolve the listen address and bind the port.
3. If no other server runs, stop the processes that an earlier sandbox left, and remove stale egress sockets and decoy files. The code does this before recovery because on macOS nothing ends those processes with their parent.
4. Call `build`. It does these actions in order:
    1. Check the sandbox section of the config.
    2. Open the registry and unlock the master key.
    3. Write the embedded agent assets to the `assets` folder of the data directory.
    4. Create the providers, the executors, the notifier, and the shared state.
    5. At the end of `build`, before it returns, open each registered workspace and call `app.attach` for it. `app.attach` runs `recover()` to recover the sessions of the workspace. A workspace whose folder is missing is skipped with a warning. A workspace that fails to open is logged and skipped.
5. Write `server.json` in the data directory, and print the sign-in URL.
6. Open the browser, unless you disabled it.
7. Serve the REST routes, the WebSocket route, and the web build.

The server exits with an error before it writes `server.json` if the `[sandbox]` section of the global config is invalid. If the sandbox is unavailable, the server still starts with the default mode, but it prints a warning that agent commands run without a sandbox and with your full user rights. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md) for the modes.

### Stop the server

The server shuts down gracefully when it receives `SIGINT` (Ctrl+C). It then removes the hook bridge socket and `server.json`. The `Dockerfile` sets `STOPSIGNAL SIGINT`, and the systemd unit sets `KillSignal=SIGINT`, for the same reason. The server handles only this signal. The `install.sh` comment says that `SIGTERM` kills the server in the middle of a write.

### Where the files are

The server keeps its config file, its data directory, `server.log`, and `server.json` in default folders. See [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) for every path and the variables that override them, and [Storage](storage.md) for the databases in the data directory.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to change or stop it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--port <number>` | Not set. The server uses `server.port`, then `7878`. | Command line only. | At the next start. | The line `Ostra is running on <address>` in the terminal. | Start the server again with another number. |
| `server.port` | Not set. | Section `[server]` of the global config file. Run `ostra config` to print its path. | At the next start. | The same line, and the sign-in URL. | Delete the key to use the scan from `7878`. The flag `--port` overrides it. |
| `--no-open` | Off. The server opens the browser. | Command line only. | At the next start. | The server prints `Could not open a browser; copy the URL above.` when the open fails. | Add the flag to stop the browser from opening. The Docker image and the installed service both use it. |

The flag `--no-open` only stops the browser from opening. The server still prints the sign-in URL. The bind address and the allowed hosts control who can reach the server. See [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md) for the flags and settings.

## Work on the web console with the dev flag

The flag `--dev` lets the server accept requests from the Vite dev server. Vite listens on port `5173` and proxies `/api`, `/ws`, and `/mcp/oauth` to the Ostra server. The proxy target is `http://127.0.0.1:7878`, and the variable `OSTRA_DEV_SERVER` in `web/vite.config.ts` changes it.

With `--dev`, the allowed host list of the server gets two more entries: `localhost:5173` and `127.0.0.1:5173`. The code is in the host list function of `crates/ostra-server/src/auth.rs`. Without the flag, the server refuses a request that has another host name. The server checks the host name on each request, so the browser at port 5173 needs the entries.

Use this procedure:

1. Start the server: `ostra --dev --no-open`. Use the sign-in URL that it prints.
2. In `web/`, run `npm run dev`. To work without a server, run `npm run dev:mock` instead. It uses a mock API.
3. Open `http://localhost:5173` in the browser.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to change or stop it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--dev` | Off. | Command line only. | At the next start. | A request from `localhost:5173` fails the host check when the flag is off. | Start the server without the flag. Do not use the flag in a production run, because it widens the host list. |

## Install Ostra as a service

The scripts `install.sh` and `install.ps1` build Ostra, copy the binary to a user folder, and run it as a per-user service that starts at login. They need no administrator rights.

Both scripts accept the same commands:

| Command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `install` (default) | Build, install, and start or restart the service. Flags after it go to `ostra`, for example `--port 8080`. |
| `restart` | Restart the service with the installed binary. |
| `status` | Show whether the service runs. |
| `url` | Print a fresh sign-in URL. |
| `uninstall` | Stop and remove the service and the installed binary. The config file and the data directory stay. |

A command that starts with `-` counts as `install`. Each script prints the sign-in URL after the server reports that it runs. The wait limit is 15 seconds in `install.sh`. If the server does not report in that time, the script prints where to look for the logs and exits with an error.

### Install on macOS and Linux

The script `install.sh` supports macOS and Linux. On another system it prints `Unsupported system <name>. Use ./run.sh instead.` and exits with status 1. The `<name>` is the output of `uname -s`.

- The binary goes to `$OSTRA_PREFIX/bin/ostra`. The default prefix is `~/.local`.
- The script writes a launcher, `ostra-service`, in the same folder. It runs `ostra serve --no-open` and binds to the loopback address by default.
- On macOS, the service is a launchd agent with the label `dev.ostra.server`. The agent restarts the server after it fails.
- On Linux, the service is the systemd user unit `ostra.service`. It uses `Restart=on-failure` and `KillSignal=SIGINT`.
- The launcher applies the `export` lines of `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` at each start. A changed key therefore needs only `./install.sh restart`, and the secrets stay out of the plist or the unit file.
- The script records your config path and data folder overrides in the launcher when you set them.
- The script replaces the binary by rename. A running server keeps its old binary, and macOS does not stop it because its image changed.

On Linux, the service runs when you are logged in. To keep it running after you log out, run `loginctl enable-linger $USER`. The script prints this advice when linger is off.

Caution: do not install with a bind address that is not loopback on a network that you do not trust. The server uses plain HTTP, and anyone who reaches the port with a sign-in link can run commands as you. The script prints a warning when the bind address is not a loopback address. Use an SSH tunnel or a TLS reverse proxy. See [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md) for the bind address and the allowed hosts.

### Install on Windows

The script `install.ps1` builds `ostra.exe` and registers a Task Scheduler task with the name `dev.ostra.server`. The task starts at logon, runs at the limited run level, and repeats every 5 minutes. A repeat starts the server again when it has stopped.

- The task starts with your saved environment, not with the environment of the shell that runs the script. The script stops with an error if the config path variable or the data folder variable in the shell differs from the saved user value. Save the value with `setx` or unset it.
- The script does not support `OSTRA_ENV_FILE`. It stops with an error if you set it. Save the provider keys in the setup screen or as user environment variables.
- The script stops with an error if another Ostra server already runs, because two servers must not share one data folder.

## Run Ostra in Docker

The files `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` run Ostra in a container. The `Dockerfile` has three stages in total: `web`, `rust`, and `runtime`. The first two are build stages and the last is the runtime stage.

| Stage | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `web` | Installs Node.js 24 on Ubuntu 26.04, runs `npm ci`, and builds `web/dist`. |
| `rust` | Installs the toolchain from `rust-toolchain.toml` and runs `cargo build --release -p ostra-server`. It copies the binary out of the cache mount to `/usr/local/bin/ostra`, because the cache mount vanishes after the step. |
| `runtime` | Installs `ca-certificates`, `git`, `openssh-client`, `curl`, and `bubblewrap`. It copies the binary and runs it as the user `ostra`. |

The runtime stage sets these values:

- The user `ostra` has UID and GID `1000`. A bind-mounted host folder that the first non-root Linux user owns is then writable without a `chown`.
- `OSTRA_DATA_DIR=/data` and `OSTRA_CONFIG=/config/config.toml`. These two variables set the data directory and the config file. See [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) for both variables.
- `EXPOSE 7878` and `STOPSIGNAL SIGINT`.
- `ENTRYPOINT ["ostra"]` and `CMD ["--bind", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "7878", "--no-open"]`. The flag `--bind` sets the listen address. See [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md) for `--bind` and the allowed hosts.

Inside the container, the server listens on every interface so that Docker can forward the port. The `docker-compose.yml` file publishes the port as `127.0.0.1:7878:7878`, so only the host can reach it. Reach it from another machine through an SSH tunnel or a TLS reverse proxy.

The compose file mounts four paths:

| Mount | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `ostra-data:/data` | The data directory. |
| `ostra-home:/home/ostra` | The home folder. Harness programs that you install from the setup check, and their logins, stay after the container ends. |
| `./config:/config` | The global config file. |
| `/srv/ostra/projects:/srv/ostra/projects` | Your projects and workspaces. |

Follow these steps before the first start:

1. Create the folder `./config` next to `docker-compose.yml`: `mkdir -p config`.
2. Give it to UID 1000: `sudo chown 1000:1000 config`. A folder that the Docker daemon creates is owned by root, and Ostra cannot write `/config/config.toml` there. The server then exits at start.
3. Replace `/srv/ostra/projects` on both sides of the projects mount with one absolute host folder that UID 1000 can write. Ostra stores workspace and project paths literally, so both sides must be the same path.
4. Run `docker compose up -d`.
5. Open `http://localhost:7878`, and use the sign-in URL that the server prints in `docker compose logs ostra`.

The build context excludes `target/`, `node_modules/`, `web/dist/`, and `.ostra/` through `.dockerignore`, because the `Dockerfile` builds the web UI and the binary itself.

## Embedded web build and the service worker route

The server serves the web console from files that the binary contains. The `RustEmbed` type `Web` in `crates/ostra-server/src/assets.rs` embeds the folder `web/dist`. The router in `crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs` uses `static_handler` as its fallback, so any request that no API route handles goes to it.

The handler follows these rules:

- If the path names an embedded file, the handler returns the file with a content type that it guesses from the name.
- A file under `assets/` gets the header `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. Every other file gets `Cache-Control: no-cache`.
- A path that starts with `api/`, `internal/`, or `assets/` returns 404 if no file matches. A root-level path with a dot, such as `/favicon.ico`, also returns 404 unless it ends in `.html`.
- Any other unknown path returns `index.html`, so the React router loads a client route directly.

The reason for the last two rules is in the code comment. A client route can end in a file name, for example `/w/{ws}/f/{key}/src/main.rs`. Only paths that have the shape of an asset can return 404.

```rust
pub async fn static_handler(uri: Uri) -> Response {
    let path = uri.path().trim_start_matches('/');
    if !path.is_empty()
        && let Some(res) = file(path)
    {
        return res;
    }
    if path.starts_with("api/")
        || path.starts_with("internal/")
        || path.starts_with("assets/")
        || !path.contains('/') && path.contains('.') && !path.ends_with(".html")
    {
        return StatusCode::NOT_FOUND.into_response();
    }
    file("index.html").unwrap_or_else(|| ...)
}
```

The service worker is the file `web/public/sw.js`. The Vite build copies it to the root of `web/dist`, so the server serves it at `/sw.js`. The code comment gives the reason: the server serves it from the root so that the service worker covers the whole app. The file gets `Cache-Control: no-cache`, because it is not under `assets/`. The worker shows push notifications and opens their deep link when you click one. See [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md) for the push code and [Web console shell](web-console.md) for the client side.

The test `client_routes_load_the_app_and_missing_assets_404` in `assets.rs` checks the cases. Paths `/w/ws_1/settings` and `/w/ws_1/f/app/src/main.rs` return 200. Paths `/assets/gone-1234.js`, `/favicon.ico`, and `/api/nope` return 404.

## Where to read next

- [Architecture and crate map](architecture.md): the crates, and the path of a request from the browser to an execution.
- [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md): the settings files and the first workspace.
- [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md): the sign-in URL, the cookie, and remote access.
- [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md): every setting key, flag, and variable.

The `ostra sessions` action enum, with the `revoke` subcommand.
The serve flags: `--port`, `--no-open`, `--dev`, `--bind`, and `--allow-host`.
Port binding, the startup order, the printed sign-in URL, and graceful shutdown.

sections.title: Workspaces, settings, and routing
sections.summary: How Ostra stores settings in three files and a registry, resolves a route for executor, model, and effort, validates a save, approves commands from folder files, and creates and opens a workspace.
sections.body:
Ostra must answer four questions for every agent execution: which executor runs it, which model it uses, how much reasoning effort it gets, and which commands from the repository it can start. A repository can change its own `.ostra` files with a `git pull`. Therefore Ostra splits its settings into three files and one registry. It validates a route when the user saves it. It starts a program from a folder file only after the user approves that exact content.

This page covers:

- the three settings files and the registry
- the workspace and project model
- the timeout of code providers and language servers (`MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT`)
- instructions (`instructions.all` and `instructions.agents`)
- tiers and providers, and the credential variables that agents never receive (`DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV`)
- route resolution for executor, model, and effort
- save-time validation
- the list of setting keys (`SETTING_KEYS`)
- approval of commands from folder files
- workspace creation and the runtime of an open workspace
- the console layout state

The limits, the sandbox settings, and the permission rules have their own pages: [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md), [Sandbox](sandbox.md), and [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).

## The three settings files and the registry

Ostra reads settings from three TOML files. A fourth store, the registry, holds the values that a folder file must never set. The code that defines the file structures is in [`crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs).

| File | Path | Scope | Main contents |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Global config | `config.toml` in the `ostra` folder of the OS config directory, `~/.config/ostra/config.toml` on Linux | The machine | `tiers`, `providers`, `harness`, `server`, and the safety tables that other pages own |
| Workspace settings | `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.toml` | One workspace | `name`, `projects`, `routing`, `instructions`, and the tables that other pages own |
| Project profile | `<project>/.ostra/project.toml` | One project | stack, commands, module map, skills, review rules |

The registry is a database on the machine. It holds the approvals, the permission mode, YOLO, the limits, and the sealed secrets. The [Storage: databases and lesson memory](storage.md) page owns its schema. The [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) and [Sandbox](sandbox.md) pages own the safety tables.

### How each file loads

- `Shared::global` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs) reads the global config again on every call. `WorkspaceHost::global` forwards to it. Edits apply without a restart.
- If the global config does not parse, the server logs a warning and keeps the last good copy.
- At startup, the server calls `ensure_global_config`. It writes the default file when the file is missing.
- If the file is deleted while the server runs, `load_toml` returns the defaults of `GlobalConfig`.
- `WorkspaceRt::settings` reads `workspace.toml` on every call. If the file does not parse, it logs a warning and returns `WorkspaceSettings::seeded("workspace")`.
- A workspace file never sets the permission mode, YOLO, the limits, or the sandbox choices. See [Values that live in the registry](#values-that-live-in-the-registry).

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_CONFIG` (environment variable) | Unset, so the OS config path above applies | The environment of the `ostra` process | After a restart | The `ostra config` subcommand prints the path | Set the variable to another `config.toml` path |
| Global config edits | The server writes the defaults of `GlobalConfig` at startup when the file is missing | `config.toml` | At the next call that reads the global config | The Workspace page | Edit the file with a text editor |
| Workspace settings edits | Seeded settings | `workspace.toml` | At the next read of the file | The settings editor in the console | Edit in the console, or edit the file and approve the commands |

The [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) lists every key of the three files.

## The workspace and project model

A workspace is a folder with a `.ostra` folder inside it. The `.ostra` folder holds `workspace.toml` and `workspace.db`. A project is a code folder that the workspace lists under `projects`. Sessions, agents, and the console all work inside one workspace.

The `WorkspaceSettings` struct holds the workspace file. These fields belong to this page:

- `name`: the workspace name. Validation refuses an empty name.
- `projects`: a list of `ProjectEntry` values.
- `routing`: the executor, model, and effort routes. See [Route resolution](#route-resolution).
- `instructions`: the custom text that agents receive. See [Instructions for agents](#instructions-for-agents).

Other pages own the rest of the fields: the YOLO, permission, notification, limit, sandbox, tool enforcement, and MCP server fields. See [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md), [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md), [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md), [Sandbox](sandbox.md), and [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md).

### Project entries

Each `ProjectEntry` has these fields:

| Field | Meaning | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | The short name of the project | Lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. The first character is a letter or digit. Each key is unique in the workspace. |
| `path` | The project folder | An absolute path. A path with a root and no Windows drive also counts as absolute, so configs stay portable across systems. |
| `stack` | The stack that seeds skills for an empty folder | Optional free text of at most 64 characters (`MAX_STACK_LEN`) with no control character. |
| `code_provider` | A program that answers code navigation | Timeout rule: see [Timeout of code providers and language servers](#timeout-of-code-providers-and-language-servers). Other rules: [Code navigation](code-navigation.md). |
| `language_servers` | LSP servers for code navigation | Timeout rule: see the same part. Other rules: [Code navigation](code-navigation.md). |

The stack is free text because the set of real stacks has no fixed list. An empty stack lets the initializer detect the stack from the code. The [Project init and skills](init-and-skills.md) page owns the stack reference files and the stack slug (`STACK_REFERENCE_NAME`).

The `.ostra` folder of a workspace is not a place for a project. Both workspace creation and project import refuse a project inside `<workspace>/.ostra`.

## Timeout of code providers and language servers

A code provider or a language server must answer a request in a fixed time. If it does not, Ostra answers the request with the built-in provider. The field `timeout_secs` sets this time, in seconds. `MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs) is the upper bound. Its value is `120` seconds, and Ostra refuses a larger value.

These rules apply to `[projects.code_provider]` and to each `[[projects.language_servers]]` entry:

- The default is `10` seconds. The default function `default_provider_timeout` supplies it when the file has no `timeout_secs`.
- A valid value is from `1` to `120` seconds. Validation refuses `0` and any value above `120`.
- The refusal message is "Use a timeout from 1 to 120 seconds."
- The issue path is `projects[i].code_provider.timeout_secs` for a code provider. It is `projects[i].language_servers[j].timeout_secs` for a language server.
- The first item of `command` must name a program. An empty first item is a separate issue at the `command` path.
- A language server lists known language ids in `languages`. Each language belongs to one server, because each file asks one server.

The tests show that `timeout_secs = 0` and `timeout_secs = 500` both produce an issue, and that a missing value reads as `10`.

A folder file can change `code_provider` and `language_servers`. Both start a program, so Ostra holds them back until the user approves them. See [Approval of commands from folder files](#approval-of-commands-from-folder-files). The [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) page owns what the program receives and returns.

Maximum `120`. | `workspace.toml`, table `[projects.code_provider]` | At the next read of `workspace.toml`, after approval | An issue next to the field in the settings editor | Set a value from `1` to `120`, or remove the key to return to `10` |
| `projects[].language_servers[].timeout_secs` | `10` seconds. Maximum `120`. | `workspace.toml`, table `[[projects.language_servers]]` | At the next read of `workspace.toml`, after approval | The same issue list | Set a value from `1` to `120`, or remove the key to return to `10` |

## Instructions for agents

Instructions are custom text that Ostra adds to the prompt of an agent. `instructions.all` goes to every agent. `instructions.agents` is a table of agent name to text, and each text goes only to that agent. Both live in the `[instructions]` table of `workspace.toml`. The `Instructions` struct has the fields `all` (an optional string) and `agents` (a table of strings).

### How Ostra builds the list for one agent

`WorkspaceSettings::instructions_for` builds the list for one agent. It follows these rules:

1. It adds `instructions.all` first.
2. It adds the text of `instructions.agents.<agent>` second.
3. It skips a text that is empty or has only spaces.

So an agent receives 0, 1, or 2 texts, and the text for the agent comes last. The spawn factory in `ostra-engine` calls `instructions_for` for each spawn. The result is the same each time the settings are the same, because the method reads only the settings. The [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md) page owns the prompt layout.

An entry in `instructions.agents` for a name that is not an agent never reaches an agent. Validation does not check the names in this table.

### Artifact tags in instructions

An instruction can name a workspace artifact with the tag `@_artifacts/<path>` (`TAG_ROOT`). The spawn factory then adds the absolute path of each tagged file to the instruction, so every executor can read it. A tag for a hidden or missing artifact resolves to nothing, and the agent gets no file. Therefore `WorkspaceRt::validate` checks each tag when the user saves (Rule W3). It reports one issue for each bad tag:

- If the artifact is hidden, the message says to unhide it, because agents never see a hidden artifact.
- If the artifact does not exist, the message says to add it on the Artifacts page or remove the tag.

The issue path is `instructions.all` or `instructions.agents.<agent>`. A refused save returns status 422 with these issues. The [Workspace artifacts and uploads](artifacts-and-uploads.md) page owns artifact rules.

| `instructions.all` | None | `workspace.toml`, table `[instructions]` | At the next execution spawn | The Instructions tab of the settings editor | Clear the text and save |
| `instructions.agents` | Empty table | `workspace.toml`, table `[instructions.agents]` | At the next execution spawn | The same tab | Remove the entry and save |

## Tiers and providers in the global config

A tier is a level of model capability. The four tiers are `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, and `frontier`. A tier table maps each tier to a concrete model for one executor. A workspace route usually names a tier, not a model. Therefore one workspace file works with every executor, and the global config decides which model each tier means.

`[tiers.<table>]` in the global config has one table for each executor: `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. A harness executor uses the table with its own name. The `native` table uses `provider:model` names. A harness table uses the model name of its own CLI. The struct `TierTable` has the four optional fields `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, and `frontier`.

### Default tier tables

| Table | `fast` | `balanced` | `advanced` | `frontier` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `native` | `anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` | `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-fable-5-1` |
| `claude` | `haiku` | `sonnet` | `opus` | `fable` |
| `codex` | `gpt-5.6-luna` | `gpt-5.6-terra` | `gpt-5.6-sol` | `gpt-5.6-sol` |
| `grok` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` |
| `agy` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` |

A table can leave a tier empty. If a route needs an empty tier, resolution fails with an error that names the missing `[tiers.<table>]` entry. The error text has this form: `` `plan` routes to tier `advanced` on `native`, but `[tiers.native]` in the global config has no `advanced` entry``.

### Providers

`[providers.<name>]` describes how Ostra finds the credentials of a native provider. The defaults define `anthropic` and `openai`. Each `ProviderConfig` has these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `api_key_env` | The environment variable that holds the API key. |
| `auth_token_env` | The variable that holds a bearer token. Ostra sends it as `Authorization: Bearer` when no API key is set. |
| `keychain_service` | The OS keychain service to read the key from when the variables are unset. |
| `base_url` | An override of the API base URL. It wins over the variable and over the saved URL. |
| `base_url_env` | The variable that holds the base URL, used when `base_url` is unset. It wins over the URL saved from the browser. |

The default `anthropic` provider sets `api_key_env`, `auth_token_env`, and `base_url_env`. The default `openai` provider sets `api_key_env` and `base_url_env`. Neither default sets `keychain_service` or `base_url`.

Credentials that the user enters in the browser are not in `config.toml`. Ostra keeps them in the registry as `SavedCredentials` with the fields `base_url`, `api_key`, and `auth_token`. The variables in `ProviderConfig` override them. The [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md) page owns the sealing and the form. The [Model providers and pricing](providers-and-pricing.md) page owns the provider calls.

### Credential variables that agents never receive

Ostra must not pass credentials to agent processes or MCP servers. `credential_env_names` builds the full set of names as a sorted set without duplicates. It skips an empty name. The set has these members:

- `DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV`: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `OPENAI_BASE_URL`. These are the variables that the default providers read.
- `BRIDGE_ENV`: `OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_URL`, and `OSTRA_HARNESS`. A child can inherit these from the environment of Ostra only by accident. Ostra drops them and sets them again for each child, so a child never gets an identity by accident.
- Each variable that a `providers.*` entry names in `api_key_env`, `auth_token_env`, or `base_url_env`.
- Each `oauth.client_secret_env` of an MCP server.

The set grows when the user adds a provider to `config.toml`, because the function reads every `providers.*` entry. The code that starts a child process calls `credential_env_names` and removes each name from the environment of the child. These callers use it: the harness launch in `ostra-exec-harness`, `mcp_secret_vars` in `ostra-exec-native`, `host_command` in `ostra-sandbox`, the MCP gateway in `ostra-server`, and `configured_secret_vars` in the Bash tool of `ostra-tools`.

```rust
pub fn credential_env_names(
    global: &GlobalConfig,
    mcp_servers: &[McpServerConfig],
) -> BTreeSet<String> {
    let mut names: BTreeSet<String> = DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV
        .iter().chain(BRIDGE_ENV).map(|s| s.to_string()).collect();
    for p in global.providers.values() {
        names.extend([&p.api_key_env, &p.auth_token_env, &p.base_url_env]
            .into_iter().flatten().filter(|n| !n.is_empty()).cloned());
    }
    ...
}
```

A missing entry makes each route that uses it fail validation. |
| `providers` | `anthropic` with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`. `openai` with `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_BASE_URL`. | `config.toml`, tables `[providers.<name>]` | At the next call that reads the global config | The provider list in the workspace detail | Edit `config.toml`, or enter credentials in the browser form |
| Credential variable set (`DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV`, `BRIDGE_ENV`) | Fixed in code. Not a setting. | Not stored | Each child process gets the filtered environment at its start | Not shown | Add a variable name to a `providers.*` entry to add it to the set. The built-in names cannot be removed. |

## Route resolution

A route answers one question: where does this execution run? Ostra resolves a route from the workspace settings and the global config. It does this when it spawns an execution, and again for each validation. The code is `resolve_route` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs).

### The route key and the query

The route key is an agent name, or `judge`. `route_keys` returns the 14 agent names and `judge`. A `RouteQuery` carries these inputs:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `key` | The agent name or `judge`. |
| `default_tier` | The default tier of the agent from its definition. A model route of `default` uses it. |
| `complexity` | The phase complexity: `low`, `medium`, or `high`. `None` counts as `low`. |
| `tier_override` | Forces a tier regardless of the model route. The runner sets `advanced` for the initializer in `generate-skill` mode. |
| `executor_override` | Forces an executor. The runner takes it from `SessionState::forced_executor` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs). The method forces `native` after a harness failure, for a quick-change session, and for the quick-answer agent. |

Only `implementer` and `write-test` receive a phase complexity (`routes_by_complexity`). The `**Complexity:**` line of the plan phase supplies it. For every other agent the complexity is `low`.

### Resolution order

The result is a `ResolvedRoute` with the fields `executor`, `model`, and `tier`. For a native route the model is `provider:model`. For a harness route it is the model name of the CLI.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["RouteQuery: key, complexity"] --> B{"executor_override set?"}
    B -- yes --> D["executor = override"]
    B -- no --> C["resolve_executor"]
    C --> D
    D --> E{"tier_override set?"}
    E -- yes --> I["model from tier table of the executor"]
    E -- no --> G{"model route found?"}
    G -- no --> X["RouteError"]
    G -- yes --> H{"kind of value"}
    H -- "default or tier name" --> I
    H -- "concrete model" --> J["check_model"]
    I --> J
    J -- "fails" --> X
    J -- "passes" --> K["ResolvedRoute"]
```

### What happens when

- If the key is `judge`, `resolve_executor` returns `native`. A judge call is an engine call, not an agent execution.
- If the settings have no model route for the key, resolution returns a `RouteError` that tells the user to add the key under `[routing.model.byAgent]`.
- If the value is `default`, Ostra uses `default_tier` from the query.
- If the value is a tier name, Ostra reads the tier table of the executor. A missing tier entry is a `RouteError`.
- If the value is a concrete model, `check_model` tests it. An empty model is an error. A native model must start with `anthropic:`, `openai:`, or `mock:` and must have a name after the colon.
- If the value is a per-executor table, Ostra reads the entry for the table name of the executor. A missing entry is a `RouteError`. If the entry is a tier name, Ostra reads the tier table.
- If the route fails when the runner spawns an execution, the runner records a denied execution with the reason `route: <message>`. It does not start the executor.
- If a conversation continues or resumes, the runner keeps the executor and model that the conversation started on. This also keeps the prompt cache.

```rust
pub fn resolve_executor(ws: &WorkspaceSettings, key: &str, complexity: Option<Complexity>) -> ExecutorKind {
    if key == JUDGE_ROUTE {
        return ExecutorKind::Native;
    }
    let complexity = complexity.unwrap_or_default();
    if let Some(e) = ws.routing.executor.by_phase_complexity
        .get(key).and_then(|m| m.get(&complexity)) {
        return *e;
    }
    ws.routing.executor.by_agent.get(key).copied().unwrap_or(ExecutorKind::Native)
}
```

The rule for all three route kinds is the same: the entry in `byPhaseComplexity` wins over the entry in `byAgent`.

## Executor routing

`routing.executor` decides which executor runs an agent. The value is `native` or `harness:<name>`, where the name is `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`. If no entry matches, the agent runs on `native`.

- `routing.executor.byAgent` maps an agent name to an executor.
- `routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity` maps an agent name, then a complexity, to an executor. The sample in the tests runs `implementer` on `harness:codex` for `low` and `medium`, and on `native` for `high`.

Two rules limit executor routes. Validation reports both:

- A `judge` entry in `routing.executor.byAgent` is an error, because judge calls always run natively.
- A `quick-answer` entry that is not `native` is an error, because quick answers run on the native executor only.

A workspace can start from a preset. `RoutingPreset` has three values: `native` (the default), `codex`, and `claude`. A harness preset puts `implementer` and `write-test` on that harness and keeps the model routes. Tiers resolve for each executor, so the model routes stay valid.

| `routing.executor.byAgent` | Empty | `[routing.executor.byAgent]` | At the next execution spawn | The Routing tab of the settings editor | Remove the entry and save |
| `routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity` | Empty | `[routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity.<agent>]` | At the next execution spawn | The same tab | Remove the entry and save |

## Model routing

`routing.model` decides which model an agent uses. A value has one of four forms:

- A tier name: `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, or `frontier`.
- The word `default`, which means the default tier of the agent.
- A concrete model, such as `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5` for the native executor.
- A per-executor table, such as `{ native = "anthropic:x", codex = "gpt-y" }`. The keys are tier-table names. This form fits an agent that can run on more than one executor.

The tests use a native model without a provider prefix, `claude-opus-5-5`. Resolution refuses it, because a native model needs the form `anthropic:<model>` or `openai:<model>`.

### Seeded model routes

`WorkspaceSettings::seeded` gives every new workspace a route for every agent:

| Tier | Agents |
| --- | --- |
| `advanced` | `explore`, `generate-spec`, `plan`, `fact-check`, `documentation`, `system-architecture`, `prompt-generation`, `judge`, `advisor` |
| `balanced` | `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `initializer`, `quick-answer` |

The phase agents `implementer` and `write-test` have no `byAgent` entry. Their `byPhaseComplexity` entries are `fast` for `low`, `fast` for `medium`, and `balanced` for `high`.

### What happens when a new agent ships

A new Ostra version can add an agent. A workspace saved before that version has no route for it. `keys_without_route` finds each key that lacks a model route. For a phase agent it checks all three complexities, and a `byAgent` entry covers all of them. Each such key is a validation error. The fix is the value `default`, because every agent has a default tier.

`settings_fixes` lists one fix for each key. `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/settings/fix` runs `WorkspaceRt::apply_fixes`. It writes all fixes without validating the rest, because an unrelated problem must not block a fix.

| `routing.model.byAgent` | One entry per agent except the two phase agents | `[routing.model.byAgent]` | At the next execution spawn | The Routing tab | Use the fix button, or set the value `default` |

## Effort routing

`routing.effort` sets the reasoning effort of an agent. The values are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, and `max`. `resolve_effort` returns the effort that the settings ask for, or `None`. When it returns `None`, the spawn factory uses the default effort of the agent definition for the executor.

The table has two forms:

- The split form has `byAgent` and `byPhaseComplexity` tables. The entry in `byPhaseComplexity` wins.
- The flat form is a plain table of agent name to effort. It is the older form, and Ostra reads it as `byAgent`.

If a value is not an effort, parsing fails with the message ``routing.effort takes `byAgent` and `byPhaseComplexity` tables of low, medium, high, xhigh, or max``. The split form refuses unknown fields. Therefore a typo such as `byagent` does not pass silently as a flat table of agents with a table value.

Validation reports an effort entry for an unknown agent. An entry in `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity` for an agent other than `implementer` or `write-test` is an error. The issue path is `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity.<key>`. `validate_workspace` writes the message with the agent key in backticks, then the text `does not run per plan phase; set its effort under` and `byAgent` in backticks, then a period.

## Save-time validation

A route that does not resolve is a settings error that the user sees at save time. It does not stop an execution later. Therefore `validate_workspace` in `ostra-core` and `validate_settings` in `ostra-workspace` run the full resolution for every route key. They return every problem in one list, not only the first. Each `ValidationIssue` has a dotted `path`, such as `routing.model.byAgent.plan`, and a `message` that tells the user what to do. Ostra sorts the list by path and message and removes duplicates.

### What validation checks

- The workspace name is not empty.
- Each project key has the right form and is unique. Each project path is absolute and, in `validate_settings`, names an existing folder.
- Each project stack is valid text.
- Each `code_provider` and each language server passes the rules of [Timeout of code providers and language servers](#timeout-of-code-providers-and-language-servers).
- Each key in `routing.executor.byAgent`, `routing.model.byAgent`, and `routing.effort.byAgent` is an agent or a retired agent name. A retired name does not make the file invalid.
- The two executor rules for `judge` and `quick-answer`.
- Every route key resolves on every complexity that applies to it. A route error appears at the path `routing.model.byAgent.<key>`, with the complexity in parentheses for a phase agent.
- If a route points to a harness that is not installed, the issue appears at `routing.executor.byAgent.<key>` and names the harness.
- If a native route names a provider that has no usable API key, the issue appears at `routing.model.byAgent.<key>`. The `mock` provider is exempt.
- The instruction tags of Rule W3.
- The limits: the parallel execution count is at least 1, and the session budget is a finite number of 0 or more. See [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md).
- The MCP server entries, the sandbox entries, and the permission rules. See [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md), [Sandbox](sandbox.md), and [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).

### Which agent keys pass

`validate_workspace` checks the executor and model keys against `route_keys()`. That list includes `judge`, so the first check also accepts `judge` for the executor. A separate check then reports the `judge` executor entry. Only the effort check uses `AgentName::ALL`, which excludes `judge`. The [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md) page owns the agent registry and the retired agent names (`RETIRED_AGENTS`, which holds `module-documentation`). It also owns the tool lists `CODE_TOOLS` and `HARNESS_AGENTS`.

The machine facts come from the `Environment` value: the installed harnesses and the providers with a usable key. The host supplies them through `WorkspaceHost::environment`.

### Where validation runs

| Route | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}` | Validates, then saves. If any issue exists, nothing is written and the request fails with status 422. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/validate` | Returns the issues for a settings body without saving. The settings editor calls it while the user types. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/validate` | Validates a create request. See [Workspace creation](#workspace-creation). |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}` | Returns `validation` and `fixes` for the saved settings. |

The [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) page owns the route groups.

| Validation of `workspace.toml` | Always on | Not a setting | At each save | Issue messages next to each field in the settings editor, and `validation` in the workspace detail | Fix each issue, or use a listed fix |

## The list of setting keys

`SETTING_KEYS` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs) is a list of 29 pairs. Each pair has a dotted key of `WorkspaceSettings` and a one-line description. The nav search uses the list so that a user can find a setting by name or by topic. The list is not a schema, and it does not validate a file.

### How the search uses the list

`nav/search.rs` in `ostra-server` reads `SETTING_KEYS` for each search. For each pair it computes three scores and keeps the best one:

- the score of the full key
- the score of the last part of the key, multiplied by 0.95
- the score of the description, multiplied by 0.85

A pair with a score becomes a hit of the kind `Setting` with the id `setting:<key>`. The hit label is the key, and its detail is the description.

### The rule that keeps the list correct

The test `setting_keys_name_fields` serializes `WorkspaceSettings::seeded("x")` to JSON. It splits each key at the dots and walks the JSON. The test fails if a key does not name a field. Therefore a rename of a settings field must change the list in the same commit. The test does not check the reverse: a new field has no key until a developer adds one.

### The 29 keys

The table has 26 rows, because one row stands for the four permission keys. The [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) page owns those four keys.

| Key | Description in the list | Page that owns the behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | Workspace name | This page |
| `projects` | Projects in this workspace | This page |
| `routing.executor` | Which executor runs each agent | This page |
| `routing.executor.byAgent` | Executor per agent | This page |
| `routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity` | Executor per agent and phase complexity | This page |
| `routing.model` | Which model or tier each agent uses | This page |
| `routing.model.byAgent` | Model or tier per agent | This page |
| `routing.model.byPhaseComplexity` | Model or tier per agent and phase complexity | This page |
| `routing.effort` | Reasoning effort for each agent | This page |
| `routing.effort.byAgent` | Reasoning effort per agent | This page |
| `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity` | Reasoning effort per agent and phase complexity | This page |
| `instructions.all` | Instructions every agent receives | This page |
| `instructions.agents` | Instructions per agent | This page |
| `yolo.default` | Start new sessions in YOLO mode | [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md) |
| Four `permissions.*` keys | Permission mode and the rules for tool calls | [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) |
| `notifications.push` | Push notifications for gates and finished sessions | [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md) |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | Executions that may run at once | [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | Dollars one session may spend before it pauses | [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) |
| `sandbox_mode` | Sandbox mode for agent commands, in place of the global one | [Sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| `tool_enforcement` | Whether guards check where tool calls read and write, in place of the global choice | [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) |
| `sandbox_network` | What sandboxed commands may reach, in place of the global choice | [Sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| `sandbox_allowed_hosts` | More hosts sandboxed commands may reach, added to the global list | [Sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| `sandbox_decoys` | More decoy credential files in agent sandboxes, added to the built-in ones | [Sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| `sandbox_loopback` | Which loopback ports sandboxed commands on macOS may connect to | [Sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` | Loopback ports sandboxed commands on macOS never connect to | [Sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| `mcp_servers` | External MCP servers whose tools agents can use | [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md) |

The list has no key for the fields inside a project entry, such as `projects[].stack`, and no key for the global config.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SETTING_KEYS` | Fixed in code. Not a setting. | Source code | After a new build | Setting hits in the nav search | Not changeable by a user |

## Approval of commands from folder files

The files `.ostra/workspace.toml` and `.ostra/project.toml` can arrive with a repository, a `git pull`, or an edit by an agent. Such a file can name programs: MCP servers, language servers, code providers, and a format command. Therefore a program starts only after the user approves exactly that content (Rule A1). The code is in [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/trust.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/trust.rs).

### What counts as a command

`workspace_hash` computes a SHA-256 hash of everything in `workspace.toml` that starts a program or loosens a check. The hash covers these items:

- Each MCP server: name, `enabled`, `command`, `env`, `url`, `headers`, and `oauth`.
- Each project that has a `code_provider` or `language_servers`: key, path, and those two fields.
- The permission allow rules.
- Each project folder outside the workspace folder (`ProjectOutside`). Agents can write in their project, so a folder file that points a project at `$HOME` widens what they can change.

If the file has none of these items, the hash is `None`, and the file needs no approval. The hash of a project format command is separate. `format_hash` hashes `commands.format` of `project.toml`, the one project command that Ostra runs itself.

### What an unapproved file does

`effective` builds the settings that programs run with. It is the registry overlay, plus these removals when the file waits for approval:

- Every MCP server has `enabled = false`.
- Every project loses its `code_provider` and `language_servers`.
- The permission allow rules are empty. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) for what the rules do.
- Every project outside the workspace folder is dropped.

```rust
pub fn effective(registry: &RegistryDb, root: &Path, mut s: WorkspaceSettings) -> WorkspaceSettings {
    overlay(registry, root, &mut s);
    if !workspace_approved(registry, root, &s) {
        for m in &mut s.mcp_servers { m.enabled = false; }
        for p in &mut s.projects {
            p.code_provider = None;
            p.language_servers.clear();
        }
        s.permissions.allow.clear();
        s.projects.retain(|p| !outside(root, &p.path));
    }
    s
}
```

If a program does not start for this reason, the message is `PENDING_MESSAGE`: "Approve the changed commands in settings, because they changed outside Ostra." The MCP gateway returns it, for example. The engine runs from the `effective` copy. `approved_workspace_file` returns the one copy of the file that Ostra checked, because a second read can see a file that changed after the check.

### How approval works

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Repo as Folder file
    participant Trust as trust.rs
    participant Reg as Registry
    participant UI as Console
    Repo->>Trust: git pull changes workspace.toml
    Trust->>Reg: kv_get trust:workspace:<root>
    Reg-->>Trust: stored hash differs
    Trust-->>UI: pending_commands with hash
    UI->>Trust: POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/approve with hash
    Trust->>Trust: recompute hash of the file
    Trust->>Reg: kv_set trust:workspace:<root>
```

- The registry key is `trust:workspace:<canonical root>` for the workspace file and `trust:format:<canonical project path>` for a format command.
- `pending` lists each file that waits. Each item has a `kind` (`mcpServer`, `languageServer`, `codeProvider`, `formatCommand`, `allowRule`, or `projectOutside`), a shell-quoted command, and the file hash.
- Ostra never sends the values of `env` and `headers`, because they can hold secrets. It sends the key names and the names of the `${VAR}` variables that they read.
- `approve` refuses with `ApproveError::Changed` when the hash from the browser is not the hash of the file now. The API answers 409 with the text "Review the commands again, because the file changed after they were shown." Therefore Ostra never approves a file that changed again without the user seeing it.
- `approve` refuses with `ApproveError::NoProject` when the project key is not in the workspace.

### What happens when

- If the user saves in the console and the file was approved before, `save_workspace` records the hash of the new content. Edits in the console never ask again.
- If the file waits for approval, a save keeps it waiting, so a save cannot approve commands that the user did not see.
- If an edit happens outside Ostra, the stored hash no longer matches, and the file waits.
- If a user registers a folder that already holds a `workspace.toml`, Ostra adopts the workspace. It records no approval, and it ignores the permission mode and YOLO of the file.
- If the user deletes a workspace, `forget` removes its approvals, so registering the folder again starts fresh.
- If a workspace was registered before approvals existed, `migrate` approves the files that it had at that time. It also moves the mode and YOLO from the file to the registry.
- `migrate_paths` does the same one time for approvals that Ostra recorded before project paths counted. A later change needs approval.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Approval of folder-file commands | Not approved, unless Ostra wrote the file | The registry, keys `trust:workspace:*` and `trust:format:*` | At once, when the user approves | `pending_commands` in the workspace detail | Review the list in the console and approve it. To revoke, edit the file so the content changes, or delete the workspace. |

## Values that live in the registry

A repository must not lift its own budget, turn off its own guards, open its own sandbox, or plant decoys that pause every session (Rule A2). Therefore `overlay` replaces the permission mode, YOLO, limits, tool enforcement, and sandbox fields with the values from the registry every time Ostra reads the settings. `write_file` removes the same fields from `workspace.toml` on every save. The registry holds them in one record, `workspace_access:<canonical root>`. A record that Ostra saved before the limits moved there has no limits, and the defaults apply.

Each owner page explains one group of these fields:

- [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md): the permission mode and tool enforcement.
- [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md): YOLO.
- [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md): the limits.
- [Sandbox](sandbox.md): the sandbox fields.

### Literal values in MCP entries

Ostra moves each literal `env` or `headers` value of an MCP entry into the encrypted registry and writes the marker `${ostra_secret}` in the file. Therefore a committed file holds no secret. The [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md) page documents the binding of a value to a server name and to a hash of its URL and command, and the deletion of values that no server names.

## Workspace creation

The create call builds complete settings from one request, validates them as a whole, and writes nothing while any issue remains. The code is in [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/create.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/create.rs). A half-created workspace leaves a folder and a registry entry that disagree. The all-or-nothing rule prevents this.

### The steps

1. `draft` checks `root`. It must be present, absolute, not a file, and not already registered.
2. If the folder already has a `.ostra/workspace.toml`, `draft` loads it and the request applies on top of it. Otherwise, it uses `WorkspaceSettings::seeded(name)`. A file that does not parse is an issue on `root`.
3. `draft` adds each project of the request. It refuses a folder that is already a project and a folder inside the `.ostra` folder of the workspace.
4. `draft` applies the request choices: the permission mode, the YOLO default, push notifications, and the routing preset. A bad value is an issue on that field.
5. `draft` runs `validate_settings` on the result. It maps the issue paths back to the request, so `projects[n]` points at the entry of the request. An issue with an older project from an existing file moves to `root`.
6. `register` returns the issues. Otherwise, it creates the folder, calls `trust::create_workspace`, and adds the workspace to the registry with a new `WorkspaceId`.

`POST /api/workspaces/validate` runs steps 1 to 5 and writes nothing.

Other pages own the behavior of the request choices: [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) for the permission mode, [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md) for YOLO, and [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md) for push delivery.

### What happens when

- If the folder already has a valid `workspace.toml`, the draft is `adopted`. Ostra resets the mode, YOLO, limits, tool enforcement, and sandbox fields of the file, because only the request sets them. `create_workspace` then records no approval.
- If the folder is a registered workspace, the issue is "That folder is already a registered workspace."
- If `register` finds the folder registered after it created the folder, it returns the same issue and writes nothing more.
- If the request has no `projects`, `permissions`, `yolo`, `notifications`, or `routing_preset`, the settings equal the seeded settings.

### For the user

| Request field | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name`, `root` | None. Both are required. | `workspace.toml` and the registry | At creation | The workspace list | Rename in the settings editor |
| `projects` | Empty | `workspace.toml` | At creation | The project list | Import or remove a project later |
| `permissions.mode` | `default` | The registry | At creation | The settings editor | Change the mode in the settings editor |
| `yolo.default` | `false` | The registry | At creation | The settings editor | Change it in the settings editor |
| `notifications.push` | `true` | `workspace.toml` | At creation | The settings editor | Change it in the settings editor |
| `routing_preset` | `native` (also `codex`, `claude`) | `workspace.toml`, as executor routes | At creation | The Routing tab | Edit `routing.executor` |

## The runtime of an open workspace

`WorkspaceRt` is one open workspace: its id, root, database, engine, and host. `WorkspaceRt::open` runs `trust::migrate` and `trust::seal_file_secrets`, opens `workspace.db`, builds the engine from the host services, and calls `sync_projects`. `sync_projects` makes the project rows of the database equal to `workspace.toml`. It deletes rows for removed projects and upserts the others.

### What the host provides

The `WorkspaceHost` trait is what a workspace needs from the process that opens it:

- `registry`: the registry, which holds approvals, the permission mode, YOLO, and sealed secrets.
- `global`: the global config, read again on every call. `Shared::global` implements it.
- `environment`, `providers`, and `harnesses`: the machine facts for validation and the workspace detail.
- `services`: the engine services for the workspace.

### Project status and project changes

`project_views` computes the status of each project:

- `Missing`: the folder does not exist.
- `Initializing`: an `Init` session for the project is `Running`, `Waiting`, or `Paused`.
- `Initialized`: `.ostra/INVENTORY.md` exists.
- `NotInitialized`: none of the other cases applies.

`project_views` also reads the git branch directly from `.git/HEAD`, because a git process for each project on each read is too slow. The [Project init and skills](init-and-skills.md) page owns the init flow.

`import_project` adds a project and refuses with an issue on `key`, `path`, or `stack`. `remove_project` removes a project from the settings and deletes nothing on disk.

### What happens when

- If a session works on the project, `project_busy` refuses removal. A session counts when it is `Running`, `Waiting`, or `Paused` and can use the project. A session that has no scope yet can use every project that it started with.
- If an execution runs in the project, or a clone or pull runs for it, removal is refused with a message that names the cause.
- If a request starts work at the same time, removal returns `STARTING`: "Wait a moment and try again, because Ostra is starting work in this workspace." The `work` lock is shared when a request starts work and exclusive when a removal runs. Therefore no work starts between the busy check and the removal.
- If any session, execution, or clone is live, `retire` refuses to delete the workspace. The API answers 409.
- If deletion is allowed, `unregister` removes the registry entry, the approvals, `workspace.toml`, `workspace.db`, and the `-wal` and `-shm` files. Project folders, session artifact folders, and the `.ostra` files of projects stay on disk.

## Console layout state

The console keeps its layout for each workspace on the server, so another browser restores it. The state is JSON in the `meta` table of the workspace database under the key `ui_state` (`META_KEY`). The routes are `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/ui` and `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}/ui`. The code is in [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/ui_state.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/ui_state.rs). The [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) page owns the route groups and the size cap `UI_STATE_MAX_BYTES`.

`WorkspaceUiState` has these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `tabs` | The open tabs in order. Each `UiTab` has `id`, `pinned`, and `preview`. |
| `active` | The id of the focused tab. |
| `left_tab` | The left dock tab: `sessions` or `files`. |
| `files_project` | The project key that the Files tab shows. |
| `sidebar_open` | `null` means the default of the console. |
| `dock_open` | Whether the quick-question dock is open. |
| `theme` | `light` or `dark`. `null` follows the system. |

### How a PATCH merges

`merge` takes the top-level fields of the body and writes them over the current state. A field that the body leaves out stays as it was. A field that the body sets to `null` is cleared. `merge` drops fields that the state does not know. After the merge, `merge` fixes the tabs:

1. A pinned tab is never the preview tab.
2. Pinned tabs come first. The order inside each group stays the same.

The pinned rule keeps the preview slot free for the next preview open and makes bulk close keep pinned tabs.

### What happens when

- If the body is larger than 64 KiB (`UI_STATE_MAX_BYTES`, 65,536 bytes), the answer is 413 with the text "Keep the UI state under 64 KiB of JSON."
- If the merged state is larger than 64 KiB, the answer is also 413.
- If the body is not a JSON object, or a field has the wrong type, the answer is 400.
- If the database write fails, the answer is 500.
- If the stored text no longer parses, `ui_state` returns the default state.

### For the user

The console saves the layout on its own. No setting turns it off. The [Web console shell](web-console.md) page owns the UI preferences that the browser keeps.

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Console layout (`ui_state`) | Empty state: no tabs, theme from the system | `meta` table of `workspace.db` | At each PATCH | The console layout after a reload in any browser | Change the layout in the console, or send `{"tabs": []}` to `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}/ui` |
