sections.title: Architecture and crate map
sections.summary: The 15 crates and how they depend on each other, how a browser request becomes an execution and comes back, the executor contract, typed IDs, where state lives on disk, and the platform helpers.
sections.body:
## Why Ostra uses crates with traits between them

A server that runs many workspaces, many sessions, and five kinds of executor has one risk. If the engine imported each executor, and each executor imported the engine, no crate could compile alone. No test could replace a part. Ostra avoids this with one rule: the crate `ostra-core` holds the shared types and traits, and the engine reaches the rest of Ostra only through traits that the server implements.

This page covers these topics:

- The 15 crates and their dependencies.
- The path of one request from the browser to an execution, and the path of the results back.
- The traits that connect the layers.
- The executor contract and the typed IDs.
- The place of each kind of state on disk.
- The platform helpers for paths, process trees, and shells.

Each subsystem has its own page. For example, [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md) explains the planner, and [Storage: databases and lesson memory](storage.md) explains the databases.

## The crates and their dependencies

The Cargo workspace has 15 member crates in `crates/` (`members = ["crates/*"]` in [Cargo.toml](Cargo.toml)). The folder `tests/windows-probes` is outside the workspace on purpose, because it has no Ostra code and its own build. All crates share the version `0.1.0`, the edition `2024`, the license `MIT`, and `rust-version = "1.98"` from `[workspace.package]`. The crate `ostra-server` builds the binary `ostra`. For the build commands, see [Ostra overview and first run](overview.md).

| Crate | What it holds | Other Ostra crates it uses | Page |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra-core` | Shared types, the executor contract, typed IDs, settings types, event types, path helpers, process-tree and shell helpers | none | this page |
| `ostra-store` | The SQLite databases: registry, workspace database, lesson memory, sealed secrets | `ostra-core` | [storage](storage.md) |
| `ostra-sandbox` | The kernel boundary around agent commands | `ostra-core` | [sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| `ostra-policy` | The guards and permission rules that check each tool call | `ostra-core` | [policy-engine](policy-engine.md) |
| `ostra-providers` | The chat interface and the Anthropic and OpenAI providers | `ostra-core` | [providers-and-pricing](providers-and-pricing.md) |
| `ostra-tools` | The native tools, such as Read, Write, Edit, and Bash | `ostra-core`, `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store` | [tools](tools.md) |
| `ostra-agents` | The agent registry and the prompt assets | `ostra-core` | [agents-and-prompts](agents-and-prompts.md) |
| `ostra-engine` | Sessions as event logs, the planner, the judge calls, the runner | `ostra-core`, `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store`, `ostra-agents` | [session-pipeline](session-pipeline.md), [event-log-and-runner](event-log-and-runner.md) |
| `ostra-exec-native` | The executor that runs an agent on an API key | `ostra-core`, `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-providers`, `ostra-tools`, `ostra-policy`, `ostra-store` | [native-executor](native-executor.md) |
| `ostra-exec-harness` | The executor that runs an agent inside a harness CLI under a PTY | `ostra-core`, `ostra-sandbox` | [harness-executors](harness-executors.md) |
| `ostra-code` | The code index, the dependency graph, and the LSP clients | `ostra-core`, `ostra-sandbox` | [code-navigation](code-navigation.md) |
| `ostra-mcp` | The MCP client for external servers | `ostra-core` | [mcp-gateway](mcp-gateway.md) |
| `ostra-notify` | Web Push, with the RFC 8291 and RFC 8292 code | `ostra-core` | [secrets-and-push](secrets-and-push.md) |
| `ostra-workspace` | Workspace settings, projects, approvals, and the runtime of an open workspace | `ostra-core`, `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store`, `ostra-engine`, `ostra-agents`, `ostra-policy` | [workspaces-and-settings](workspaces-and-settings.md) |
| `ostra-server` | The binary `ostra`: sign-in, the REST and WebSocket API, and the code that gives each workspace its engine | the 14 other crates | [server-api](server-api.md), [overview](overview.md) |

### Direct dependencies between crates

The diagram shows most direct dependencies. The table above lists every edge. The diagram omits two kinds of edge, and both are in the table:

- Each crate except `ostra-core` depends directly on `ostra-core`.
- `ostra-server` depends directly on `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store`, `ostra-agents`, `ostra-providers`, `ostra-tools`, and `ostra-policy`. The diagram reaches these crates through other crates.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  server[ostra-server] --> workspace[ostra-workspace]
  server --> engine[ostra-engine]
  server --> native[ostra-exec-native]
  server --> harness[ostra-exec-harness]
  server --> code[ostra-code]
  server --> mcp[ostra-mcp]
  server --> notify[ostra-notify]
  workspace --> engine
  workspace --> policy[ostra-policy]
  workspace --> agents[ostra-agents]
  workspace --> store[ostra-store]
  workspace --> sandbox[ostra-sandbox]
  engine --> agents
  engine --> store
  engine --> sandbox
  native --> providers[ostra-providers]
  native --> tools[ostra-tools]
  native --> policy
  native --> store
  native --> sandbox
  tools --> store
  tools --> sandbox
  harness --> sandbox
  code --> sandbox
  agents --> core[ostra-core]
  store --> core
  sandbox --> core
```

### Dependency rules

- **`ostra-core` uses no other Ostra crate.** Its module comment calls it the home of "the contracts between the engine, the executors, the policy layer, and the browser". Every other crate uses it.
- **`ostra-engine` does not use an executor, the policy, the providers, or the tools.** The engine gets these through the `Services` trait in [crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs](crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs). The module comment says that the server implements these methods and that tests use fakes. The tests in `crates/ostra-engine/tests/` define a `Fake` for `Services` and a `Scripted` `Executor`.
- **`ostra-workspace` uses the engine, not the server.** It defines the `WorkspaceHost` trait, and the server implements it with the `Shared` struct. This keeps the dependency pointing from the server to the workspace crate.
- **The server supplies the policy and the tools to a harness run.** `ostra-exec-harness` uses only `ostra-core` and `ostra-sandbox`. The type `Wrapped` in [crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs) builds the `ExecutionPolicy` and the `ToolEnv` for each harness execution, then runs the harness inside them.
- **`ostra-server` is the only crate that uses all the others.** It wires the parts in `app::build`.

Rust types in `ostra-core` that carry `#[ts(export)]` become TypeScript types for the browser. The file `.cargo/config.toml` sets `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` to `web/src/api/gen` and `TS_RS_LARGE_INT` to `number`. For the shared request and response shapes, see [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md).

## How one request travels from the browser to an execution and back

A request enters through the HTTP router of `ostra-server`, reaches the engine of one workspace, and ends in an executor. The results return through the database and a broadcast channel. The diagram follows one new session. The engine forwards each notice to the hub in `App::attach`, and the diagram shows that step as one message.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Browser
  participant API as Server API (api.rs)
  participant Engine
  participant Store as WorkspaceDb
  participant Services as ServerServices
  participant Executor
  participant Hub as App.hub
  participant Socket as Socket (ws.rs)
  Browser->>API: POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/sessions
  API->>Engine: create_session(CreateSession)
  Engine->>Store: append_event(SessionCreated)
  Engine-->>API: SessionSummary
  API-->>Browser: 200 SessionSummary
  Engine->>Engine: drive loop calls next_steps(state, ctx)
  Engine->>Services: global(), workspace(), executor(kind)
  Engine->>Executor: run(ExecutionSpec, host, cancel)
  Executor->>Engine: host.emit(ExecutionDelta)
  Engine->>Store: append_activity(delta)
  Engine->>Hub: EngineNotice::Delta
  Hub->>Socket: HubMsg
  Socket->>Browser: ServerMsg::ExecutionDelta on execution:ID
  Executor-->>Engine: ExecutionResult
  Engine->>Store: append_event(ExecutionFinished)
  Engine->>Hub: EngineNotice::Event
  Socket->>Browser: ServerMsg::SessionEvent on session:ID
```

### The steps in order

1. **The guard.** The `guard` middleware in [crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs) checks the `Host` header, the `Origin` and `Sec-Fetch-*` headers, and the sign-in cookie before any handler runs. For the rules, see [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md).
2. **The handler.** `create_session` finds the workspace with `ws(&app, &id)` and calls `start_work`. This call takes a shared lock on the workspace. A removal of the workspace takes the same lock exclusively, so no work can start between the busy check of the removal and the removal itself.
3. **The session.** `Engine::create_session` calls `start_session`. It checks the request, makes a `SessionId`, creates the session root folder, writes `sessions/.gitignore` with the line `*` if the file is missing, inserts the session row, and appends the `SessionCreated` event.
4. **The append.** `Inner::append` holds the session state lock. It stores the event in `WorkspaceDb`, writes the gate and decision rows, folds the event into `SessionState`, updates the session row, broadcasts an `EngineNotice`, and wakes the driver. [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) explains the log and the fold.
5. **The driver.** `Inner::drive` loops. Each time it calls the pure planner `next_steps` with the folded state. It starts each new step as a task, and it keeps a key for each step in the `inflight` set, so the same step does not run twice. [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md) explains the steps.
6. **The spawn.** `perform_spawn` waits for an execution slot, resolves the route, and asks `Services::executor` for the executor. It builds the prompt with `SpawnFactory::build`, builds the `ExecContext`, appends `ExecutionStarted`, and inserts the execution row. Then it calls `Executor::run`. The slot limit is explained in [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md).
7. **The deltas.** The executor sends each event of the run to `ExecutionHost::emit`. `EngineHost::emit` stores it as an activity row and broadcasts it as `EngineNotice::Delta`.
8. **The result.** When `run` returns, the engine adds the earlier usage, stores the result with `finish_execution`, appends `ExecutionFinished`, and frees the slot. The append wakes the driver, and the planner plans the next step.
9. **The way back.** `App::attach` starts one forwarding task for each workspace. The task reads `Engine::subscribe`, calls `files.observe` and `nav.observe`, and sends a `HubMsg` to `App.hub`. Each open WebSocket in [crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs) reads the hub and sends a notice only if the socket subscribed to a channel of that notice.

### How notices map to channels

| `EngineNotice` | Channels | `ServerMsg` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Event` | `session:<id>` | `SessionEvent` |
| `Delta` | `execution:<id>` | `ExecutionDelta` |
| `ExecutionStatus` | `execution:<id>` | `ExecutionStatus` |
| `SessionUpdated` | `session:<id>`, `workspace:<id>`, `home` | `SessionUpdated` |
| `ProjectsChanged` | `workspace:<id>` | `WorkspaceUpdated` |

The terminal bytes of a harness execution do not use the hub. The channel `term:<id>` streams them as binary frames from the PTY registry. [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) explains the channels and their limits.

### What happens when

- **A user answers a gate.** The route `POST /api/gates/{id}/answer` calls `Engine::answer_gate`. The engine rejects a gate that already has an answer. It appends `GateAnswered` and wakes the driver. For a permission ask, it also sends the answer through a `oneshot` channel, and the waiting `ask_permission` call returns.
- **A session ends while a step starts.** `append` refuses `ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionResumed`, and `CommandStarted` on an ended session and returns `EngineError::Ended`. The check sits under the state lock, so a stop cannot race it.
- **The session is paused or ended when the slot is free.** `perform_spawn` returns without a spawn.
- **The route does not resolve, or the executor is missing.** The engine records the execution as denied with the reason `route: ...` or `The <executor> executor is not available.`
- **The server restarts.** `Engine::recover` marks each running execution `Interrupted` with the error "The server restarted while this execution ran." A run that waited for a subagent answer keeps the status `Waiting`. The engine denies open permission asks, then starts the driver of each session that did not end.
- **A WebSocket falls behind.** The hub holds 8192 notices and the engine channel holds 4096. A socket that lags gets the error `lagged`, and the page fetches its REST snapshot again.
- **The workspace is removed.** `start_work` returns the error `No workspace <id>.` after the removal sets the `work` flag.

## The traits that connect the layers

Five traits connect the layers. Each trait has one real implementation and, in tests, fakes.

| Trait | Defined in | Real implementation | What it gives |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Executor` | [crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs](crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs) | `NativeExecutor`, and `HarnessExecutor` inside `Wrapped` | Runs one execution |
| `ExecutionHost` | `ostra-core` `exec.rs` | `EngineHost` in the engine | The callbacks that an executor uses while it runs |
| `Services` | [crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs](crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs) | `ServerServices` in [crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs) | What the engine needs from the rest of Ostra |
| `SpawnFactory` | `ostra-engine` `services.rs` | `AgentsFactory` | Renders a spawn for one executor and gives the judge prompts |
| `WorkspaceHost` | [crates/ostra-workspace/src/host.rs](crates/ostra-workspace/src/host.rs) | `Shared` in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` | What a workspace needs from the process that opens it |

### The `Services` trait

`Services` has nine methods. `ServerServices` holds the `Shared` state, the workspace root, and the `WorkspaceId`.

- `global()` returns the global config. The trait comment says that the engine reads it on every execution, so an edit applies to the next one without a restart.
- `workspace()` returns the effective workspace settings. `ServerServices` reads `workspace.toml` and passes it through `trust::effective`, which adds the values that come from the registry. If the file cannot be read, it uses `WorkspaceSettings::seeded("workspace")`.
- `executor(kind)` returns the shared `NativeExecutor` for `ExecutorKind::Native`. For a harness it returns the harness executor from `HarnessRuntime`.
- `factory()` returns `AgentsFactory`.
- `judge(route, system, user, schema, effort)` looks up the provider for the model of the route and calls `ostra_providers::structured`. It returns the JSON value and the `Usage`, or an error text. [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md) explains the calls.
- `notify(notice)` sends a Web Push for a notice when `notifications.push` is on. [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md) explains the sending, the encryption, and the keys.
- `protected_paths()` returns the paths of `Shared` plus `workspace.toml` and `workspace.db` of this workspace. `Shared` lists the `ostra` binary, the global config file, the data dir, and the assets dir.
- `command_approved(project, command)` asks `trust::format_approved` whether the user approved the format command.
- `add_allow_rule(rule)` adds the rule to the workspace allow list. It does nothing if the rule exists, and it logs a warning if the save fails.

The `WorkspaceHost` comment gives the reason for the split: the registry holds "approvals, the permission mode, YOLO, and sealed secrets, which never come from a folder file". A file in a project folder cannot grant itself a permission.

### The global config read

`Shared::global` reads the global config file on every call. If the file does not parse, or the `[sandbox]` section has an issue that `ostra_sandbox::validate::global` reports, it logs a warning and returns the last good copy. At start, an issue in the `[sandbox]` section stops the server with an error that names the file.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored | Change takes effect | What shows the state | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The global config file `config.toml` | `ensure_global_config` writes the default values if the file is missing | The platform config folder. [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) gives the path and the override | At the next execution for most keys. After a restart for keys that the server reads once at start, such as the port and the bind address | `ostra config` prints the path. The server log shows the warning `using the last good global config` | Edit the file |

For the keys, see [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md).

## The executor contract

The engine must run an agent on five different runners and treat the results in one way. The contract in [crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs](crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs) gives this. The engine builds an `ExecutionSpec`, gives the executor an `ExecutionHost` and a `CancellationToken`, and gets an `ExecutionResult`.

```rust
#[async_trait::async_trait]
pub trait Executor: Send + Sync {
    async fn run(
        &self,
        spec: ExecutionSpec,
        host: Arc<dyn ExecutionHost>,
        cancel: CancellationToken,
    ) -> ExecutionResult;
}

pub trait ExecutionHost: Send + Sync {
    fn emit(&self, delta: ExecutionDelta);
    async fn ask_permission(&self, call: &ToolCall, reason: &str, rule: &RuleRef) -> PermissionAnswer;
    async fn wait_for_wake(&self) -> Option<Wake> { None }
    // record_message, transcript, yolo: default no-ops
}
```

`run` returns an `ExecutionResult` and never an `Err`. An executor reports a failure as `ExecutionResult::error(message)`, which has the status `Error` and the `error` text.

The engine resolves the route of an execution before it builds the spec. [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) owns route resolution, its errors, and its settings.

### The execution spec

`ExecutionSpec` holds everything that one execution needs.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | The `ExecutionId` |
| `agent` | The `AgentName` |
| `route` | The `ResolvedRoute`: the executor and the model |
| `effort` | The `Effort` level |
| `system_prompt` | The agent prompt, rendered for the tool names of this executor |
| `first_message` | The spawn block plus the repo brief and the custom instructions |
| `capabilities` | The `Capability` list of the agent |
| `submit_schema` | The input schema of the tool `submit_<agent>` |
| `timeout_secs` | The timeout from the agent metadata |
| `ctx` | The `ExecContext` |
| `resume` | The `ResumeInfo`, present when the run continues an earlier execution |
| `harness_session_id` | A session ID that the engine chooses up front. The engine sets it for Claude Code and Grok Build, which accept one. It reuses the `native_session_id` of a resumed run, or makes a new UUID |

`ResumeInfo` has four fields: `from` (the execution that resumes), `native_session_id` (for harness resume commands), `note` (the first message of the resumed run, in place of the interruption notice), and `inspect`. When `inspect` is true, the run reopens only for the user to read and ask about. It has no first prompt, no tools, and no submit. It ends when the user leaves or stops it.

### The execution context

`ExecContext` holds what the policy layer needs to judge one tool call. The engine builds it for each execution in `perform_spawn`.

| Group | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| Identity | `execution_id`, `session_id`, `agent`, `initializer_mode`, `executor`, `project_key`, `phase` |
| Paths | `workspace_root`, `repo_root`, `session_dir`, `session_root`, `report_file`, `memory_db`, `protected_paths` |
| Permissions | `permission_mode`, `permissions` (the merged rules of the global config and the workspace settings), `yolo`, `enforce_tool_calls` |
| Sandbox | `sandbox_mode`, `sandbox_network`, `sandbox_allowed_hosts`, `sandbox_decoys`, `sandbox_loopback`, `sandbox_blocked_ports` |
| Run mode | `creates_project`, `answer_only`, `owes_reply` |

These rules apply to the fields:

- `protected_paths` lists the paths that no agent can write, delete, or execute from: Ostra's binary, its config, its databases, and every engine state folder.
- `repo_root` is the folder where the agent works. If `creates_project` is true (Rule O2), the engine sets `repo_root` to the session dir, because the project that the phase needs does not exist yet. The run must create that project first.
- `answer_only` is true for a consult run. A consult run answers a question and writes no file (Rule H3).
- `owes_reply` is true when the run starts with a question from another subagent. The run answers with `SubagentReply` and submits nothing before that (Rule H3).
- `enforce_tool_calls` is resolved from the workspace and global `tool_enforcement` when the execution starts (Rule G1).
- `ExecContext::sandbox()` gathers the five sandbox fields into a `WorkspaceSandbox`.

For the permission rules, see [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md). For the sandbox fields, see [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

### The result and its statuses

`ExecutionResult` has the fields `status`, `submit` (the `submit_<agent>` payload, if the agent called it), `final_text` (the last assistant text), `usage`, `native_session_id`, and `error`.

| `ExecutionStatus` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Running` | The only status that is not terminal. `is_terminal()` is false only for this status |
| `Ok` | The run ended normally. The `submit` input had no `stuck` or `handoff` status |
| `Stuck` | The `status` field of the `submit_<agent>` input was `stuck` |
| `Handoff` | The `status` field of the `submit_<agent>` input was `handoff` |
| `Waiting` | The run asked another subagent and waits for the answer (Rule H2) |
| `Error` | The executor failed. `error` has the text |
| `Denied` | The engine did not start the run, for example because the route did not resolve |
| `Interrupted` | A pause, a server restart, or another interrupt ended the run |
| `Cancelled` | The `CancellationToken` ended the run |

The engine changes `Cancelled` to `Interrupted` when the session state marks the execution as interrupting. The error text then names the reason.

`Usage` counts `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens`, `cache_write_tokens`, `cache_write_1h_tokens` (the part of the cache writes with the 1-hour TTL, which costs more), `cost_usd`, `tool_calls`, and `build_ms` (the wall time of build and test commands). `context_tokens` is the size of the latest request, not a sum. `Usage::add` sums every field except `context_tokens`. It replaces `context_tokens` when the other value is above zero. The engine adds the usage of an earlier part of a resumed execution, because an executor counts from zero.

### The deltas that an executor emits

`ExecutionDelta` is a tagged enum with the tag `kind` in snake case. The Activity view shows the deltas, and the database stores them.

| Variant | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `Text`, `Thinking` | Assistant text and thinking text |
| `ToolCall` | A tool call with its `call_id` |
| `Policy` | The `PolicyDecision` for a call |
| `ToolOutput` | Live output of a running shell command |
| `ToolResult` | The output, the `is_error` flag, and the `duration_ms` of a call |
| `Usage` | The running total of the usage |
| `Turn` | One model response of a native run: its own usage and cost, and the IDs of its tool calls |
| `Status` | A status message |
| `NativeSessionId` | The session ID of the harness or provider |
| `Egress` | The first answer of the egress proxy for a host and port, with the reason and a `local` flag |
| `Decoy` | A process in the sandbox opened a decoy credential file (Rule P3) |

`EngineHost::emit` does these steps for each delta:

1. It saves a summary line for a `ToolCall` (except `submit_` calls) and for a `Status`.
2. It stores the ID of a `NativeSessionId` delta.
3. It adds the earlier usage to a `Usage` delta, stores the total, and refreshes the cost of the session.
4. It appends the delta to the activity table and broadcasts `EngineNotice::Delta`.
5. It classifies the delta as a containment signal. It records at most `PAUSE_AFTER` signals for each execution, so a retry loop cannot flood the log. The signal that reaches the count pauses the session. [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) explains the signals.

### The host callbacks

- `emit(delta)` sends a delta to the engine.
- `ask_permission(call, reason, rule)` waits for the browser answer. Under YOLO it answers `AllowOnce` at once and records the gate with the source `Yolo`. A run without a session, such as a side-panel run, gets `Deny`, because those runs are read-only and never ask.
- `record_message(role, content)` stores one transcript message of a native run, so a resume can continue from it.
- `transcript(execution)` returns the stored messages of an earlier execution, oldest first.
- `yolo()` tells whether the session is under YOLO now. A user can change this during an execution.
- `wait_for_wake()` is for a harness run that asked another subagent (Rule H2). Ask and reply are tools: `SubagentAsk` and `SubagentReply`. Wake is a message that the engine delivers as a `Wake`. The run waits in `wait_for_wake()`, and the engine frees its execution slot. When a `Wake` arrives, the engine gives the slot back before the call returns. `None` means that no message will come. [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md) explains ask, reply, and wake.

A `Wake` has a `note` and an `owes_reply` flag. The flag is true when the message is a question that the run must answer with `SubagentReply` (Rule H3).

### Cancellation

`CancellationToken` comes from `tokio_util` and the module re-exports it. The engine keeps one token for each running execution. `Inner::interrupt` cancels the tokens of the executions that the session state marks as interrupting, and it denies their open permission asks. The executor must end the run when the token fires. For the loop of the native executor, see [Native executor loop](native-executor.md). For the harness, see [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).

## Executor kinds and streams

The type `ExecutorKind` in [crates/ostra-core/src/executor.rs](crates/ostra-core/src/executor.rs) names what runs an execution. It is `Native` or `Harness(HarnessKind)`. `HarnessKind` has four values: `Claude`, `Codex`, `Grok`, and `Agy`.

| `ExecutorKind` | String form | Display name | Live view (`ExecStream`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Native` | `native` | none | `Activity` |
| `Harness(Claude)` | `harness:claude` | Claude Code | `Terminal` |
| `Harness(Codex)` | `harness:codex` | Codex | `Terminal` |
| `Harness(Grok)` | `harness:grok` | Grok Build | `Terminal` |
| `Harness(Agy)` | `harness:agy` | Antigravity | `Terminal` |

- `ExecutorKind` serializes as a string with `Display`, and the TypeScript type is `string`. It parses with `FromStr`.
- The parser also accepts `harness:antigravity` as a name for `agy`.
- An unknown value gives the error ``unknown executor `<value>`: use `native` or `harness:<claude|codex|grok|agy>` ``. An unknown harness name gives ``unknown harness `<name>` ``.
- `tier_table()` returns the key into `[tiers.<table>]` of the global config: `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`.
- `ExecutorKind::all()` returns the five kinds, and `HarnessKind::ALL` returns the four harnesses.
- `stream()` returns `ExecStream::Activity` for the native executor and `ExecStream::Terminal` for every harness. The browser shows an Activity feed or a terminal because of this value.

For how a route chooses the executor, see [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md).

## Typed IDs

Six ID types in [crates/ostra-core/src/ids.rs](crates/ostra-core/src/ids.rs) name the main objects of Ostra. The macro `id_type!` makes each one as a newtype around a `String`. Each ID is its own type, so a function that takes a `SessionId` does not accept a `GateId`.

| Type | Prefix | Names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WorkspaceId` | `ws_` | A registered workspace |
| `SessionId` | `s_` | A session. It is also the folder name of the session root |
| `ExecutionId` | `x_` | One execution of an agent |
| `GateId` | `g_` | A gate, which is a question for the user |
| `DecisionId` | `d_` | A stored judge decision |
| `MessageId` | `m_` | A message |

```rust
macro_rules! id_type {
    ($name:ident, $prefix:literal) => {
        pub struct $name(pub String);
        impl $name {
            /// Time-ordered id, so lexical order matches creation order.
            pub fn new() -> Self {
                Self(format!("{}{}", $prefix, uuid::Uuid::now_v7().simple()))
            }
        }
        // Default, Display, From<String>, From<&str>
    };
}
id_type!(SessionId, "s_");
```

- **The form.** An ID is the prefix plus a UUID version 7 in the simple form: 32 hexadecimal digits without dashes.
- **The order.** A UUID version 7 starts with a timestamp. Thus the text order of the IDs matches the order of creation, and the types derive `Ord`.
- **The derives.** Each type derives `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord`, `Serialize`, `Deserialize`, and `TS`. The TypeScript type is `string`.
- **The conversions.** `Default` calls `new()`. `From<String>` and `From<&str>` wrap the text and do not check the prefix or the length.

Call `new()` only to make a new object. To read an ID from a path, a request, or a database row, use `From`. `From` accepts any text, so a wrong text becomes an ID that no object has, and a lookup then returns `NotFound`.

The crate root [crates/ostra-core/src/lib.rs](crates/ostra-core/src/lib.rs) re-exports the six ID types, `AgentName`, `Capability`, `InitializerMode`, `ExecutorKind`, `HarnessKind`, `Complexity`, `Effort`, and `Tier`. The sign-in IDs in the CLI (for example `si_...`) are not typed IDs.

## Where state lives on disk

All path derivations live in [crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs](crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs). Its module comment gives the reason: state is addressed by the session and the project key, and every reader and writer must resolve it in the same way. There are four levels: the global config, the data dir, the workspace, and the project. [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) owns the full list of paths, folder names, and environment variables.

### Data dir and global config

The data dir is the folder that `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` names. If the variable is not set, it is `ostra` inside the platform local data folder. The global config file is outside the data dir. Its path comes from `OSTRA_CONFIG`, or it is `ostra/config.toml` inside the platform config folder.

| Path | Content | Page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `registry.db`, `registry.db-wal`, `registry.db-shm` | The machine registry: workspaces, approvals, the permission mode, YOLO, sealed secrets, push subscriptions, and browser sign-ins | [storage](storage.md) |
| `master.key` | The master key file, when the key is not in the system keychain | [secrets-and-push](secrets-and-push.md) |
| `server.json` | The record of a running server. Start writes it and exit removes it | [browser-auth](browser-auth.md) |
| `server.log` | The server log, appended | none |
| `assets/` | The agent prompt assets that the server writes at start | [agents-and-prompts](agents-and-prompts.md) |
| `models-dev.json` | The cache of the price catalog | [providers-and-pricing](providers-and-pricing.md) |
| `decoys/`, `egress/` | Runtime files of the sandbox | [sandbox](sandbox.md) |

### Workspace folder

The folder `<workspace>/.ostra/` holds these items:

- `workspace.toml`: the workspace settings.
- `workspace.db`: the workspace database with the event log. [Storage](storage.md) explains it.
- `sessions/<session id>/`: the root of one session. The file `sessions/.gitignore` has the line `*`, so Git ignores all sessions.
- `uploads/`: files that the user uploaded and that no session claimed yet.

### Session root

| Path under `sessions/<session id>/` | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Files in the root | The cross-project artifacts, such as the spec and the plan, and the session context file |
| `<project key>/` | The per-project reports |
| `uploads/` | The uploads that the session claimed |
| `.state/` | The state of the engine. No agent can write here |
| `.state/harness/<execution id>/` | The hook config, the MCP registration, and `terminal.log` with the raw PTY bytes of a harness execution. Ostra keeps the log so that it can replay an ended run |

| `implementer(phase)` | `ostra-implementer-phase-<phase>.md` |

| `epa(phase)` | `ostra-epa-phase-<phase>.md` |
| `write_test(phase)` | `ostra-write-test-phase-<phase>.md` |

| `prompt_gen(n)` | `ostra-prompt-gen-<n>.md` |

### Project folder

The project folder holds `.ostra/INVENTORY.md`, `.ostra/project.toml`, and the lesson memory `.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3`. Ostra writes every new skill to `.agents/skills/` in the project. The agents also read the instruction file of the project root. [Project init and skills](init-and-skills.md) explains the inventory, the profile, and the skills. [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) lists the skill folders and the instruction file names.

### Permissions and secret paths

`ensure_data_dir` creates the data dir, or tightens an existing one, to the mode `0700` on Unix. The reason is in the code: the folder holds the registry with saved credentials, and SQLite creates its `-wal` and `-shm` files readable by everyone. `open_registry` in the server also sets the mode `0600` on `registry.db` and its two side files. The helpers `create_private_dir_all`, `create_private_dir`, `private_file_options`, and `restrict_to_owner` use the modes `0700` for folders and `0600` for files. On Windows a new folder inherits the access list of its parent.

`secret_paths(home)` returns every path that no agent can read: the data dir, the file in `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` if set, and each entry of `HOME_CREDENTIALS` under the home folder. `HOME_CREDENTIALS` has 56 entries, such as `.ssh`, `.aws`, `.netrc`, and browser profile folders. Five of the entries come from `cli_cred` and cover the sign-in files of the four harnesses. Two of the five name `Agy`: `.gemini/oauth_creds.json` and `.gemini/google_accounts.json`. The harness of such an entry is the one program that can see its file. The policy refuses tool calls that name these paths, the sandbox hides them, and Grep and Glob skip them. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) and [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

Move the files of the old data dir before you set a new data dir. The new folder has no `registry.db`, so Ostra starts with no registered workspaces and no saved credentials.

## The order of the server start

`app::build` in [crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs) wires the crates in this order:

1. It sets the server port for the sandbox, loads the global config, and stops with an error if the `[sandbox]` section has an issue.
2. It logs the state of the sandbox. The `WARNING` block on stderr appears only when `sandbox.message` is `Some`. That is the case when mode `auto` or mode `required` finds no backend. If mode is `off`, `decide` returns `Unsandboxed(None)`. Then the server only calls `tracing::warn!` and prints nothing on stderr.
3. It creates the data dir, starts the price refresh, opens the registry, and unlocks the master key.
4. It writes the prompt assets to `assets/` in the data dir.
5. It makes the providers, the code tools, the MCP gateway, the management and coordination connectors, and the `NativeExecutor`.
6. It makes the `Notifier` with the VAPID keys from the registry. It makes new keys and stores them if none exist.
7. It detects the installed harnesses and the access rules. It makes the `HarnessRuntime` with a callback address for the hooks: `127.0.0.1:<port>` if the bind address is loopback or unspecified, otherwise the bind address.
8. It makes `Shared` and `App`, the hub channel (8192 notices), and the push channel (1024 messages). It then binds the code tools, the management connector, and the coordination connector to the `App`.
9. On Unix, it creates the Unix socket of the hook bridge.
10. It starts the file-touch task and the navigation task.
11. It opens each registered workspace through `App::attach`. A workspace without `workspace.toml` gets a warning and is skipped. A workspace that fails to open gets an error in the log, and the others still open. `attach` calls `Engine::recover` for each workspace.
12. It removes the tool caches of sessions that ended, by `sweep_session_caches`.

For the port, the bind address, and the sign-in link, see [Ostra overview and first run](overview.md) and [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md).

## Platform helpers for paths, process trees, and shells

Three groups of helpers in `ostra-core` hide the differences between Unix and Windows. Each group is small, and a subsystem page explains how it uses them.

### Path comparison

The guards compare paths, so the helpers make each path one plain form first. `resolve(cwd, target)` follows each symlink, also a dangling one, before a later `..` applies. The reason is in the code: a link must not make a path look inside a root when the write lands outside it. `normalize` cleans `.` and `..` without file access. `is_inside(outer, inner)` compares the folded forms. On Windows `fold` makes two names that NTFS treats as one name equal.

Several helpers handle Windows paths. `canonical` removes the `\\?\` prefix on Windows, because Git, shells, and most programs refuse a verbatim path, and the guards compare plain paths. `from_msys` turns a Git Bash path such as `/c/Users/me` into `C:\Users\me`. `windows_path_problem` names a path that is not a plain file path, such as a network share, a device path, or an alternate data stream. `is_reserved_device` finds a device name such as `CON` or `COM1`. `dot_dot_after_link` finds a `..` after a link, because Win32 programs and Git Bash apply it to different folders.

### Process trees and shells

The module `proctree` stops a child process and everything that it started as one unit. On Unix the child leads its own process group, `terminate` sends SIGTERM to the group, and `kill` sends SIGKILL. On Windows the child runs in a Job Object with kill-on-close and no breakaway, so closing the job or exiting Ostra ends the whole tree. The child starts suspended, because a child that is not yet in its job can start children that escape it. The Bash tool, the Windows shell tools, the MCP stdio client, and the PTY of a harness use this helper.

The module `shells` finds the program that the Bash tool runs. On Windows it uses the Git for Windows `bash.exe` by absolute path, because the first `bash` on `PATH` is often the WSL launcher, which sees different files. It finds `powershell.exe` and `cmd.exe` under the system folder in the same way. [Native tools](tools.md) explains the Bash and Windows shell tools and the failure text when Git Bash is missing.
