The tier and timeout come from `agent.toml` of each agent. The "Session-only" column is `AgentName::is_session_only`. A session-only agent can write only in its session folder and the OS temp folder. The write-scope guard enforces this. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).

### Name helpers

- `as_str` returns the kebab-case name. `snake` returns the snake_case name. `label` returns a sentence-case name such as `Code reviewer`.
- `submit_tool_name` returns `submit_` plus the snake_case name, for example `submit_code_reviewer`.
- `FromStr` accepts the bare name. It also removes the prefixes `ostra:` and `ultracode:`.
- `manages_projects` is true only for `implementer`. Only a phase of an approved plan starts a project (Rule O2).
- `routes_by_complexity` is true for `implementer` and `write-test`. Ostra routes the model tier of these two agents by the `**Complexity:**` line of the phase.

### Retired agents

The agent `module-documentation` is retired. The `documentation` agent replaced it (Rule B1). Ostra keeps the old name working in three places:

- The `serde` alias on `AgentName::Documentation` reads old event logs.
- `FromStr` maps `module-documentation` to `Documentation`. Old execution rows use this name.
- `RETIRED_AGENTS` lists the name. Settings validation ignores a retired name in the `byAgent` routing tables and does not refuse the file.

`route_keys` returns the 14 agent names and `JUDGE_ROUTE` (`judge`). The key `judge` sits beside the agent names in `routing.model.byAgent`. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) for the routing rules.

### Capabilities and code tools

The `Capability` enum lists what an agent can do: `read`, `write`, `edit`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `skill`, `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `report`, `document`, `memory`, `memory_recall`, `docs_search`, `code`, `manage_projects`, and `coordinate`. `Capability::native_tool` gives the native tool name. `Capability::writes` is true for `write` and `edit`. Ostra uses it to derive read-only runs and sandbox modes.

`CODE_TOOLS` pairs each code operation with its native tool name. It has 8 entries: `outline` (`CodeOutline`), `find`, `callers`, `callees`, `implementations`, `neighbors`, `impact`, and `map`. Over MCP the tool name is `code_{op}`. See [Native tools](tools.md).

`RoutingPreset::HARNESS_AGENTS` in `crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs` is a different list. It names the two agents, `implementer` and `write-test`, that a harness routing preset moves off the native loop.

### Initializer modes

The `initializer` agent has 6 modes in `InitializerMode`: `detect`, `scout`, `propose`, `generate-skill`, `generate-inventory`, and `adopt`. Each mode has its own spawn struct. See [Project init and skills](init-and-skills.md) for the flow.

## Agent definitions and embedded assets

The `assets` folder is compiled into the binary with `rust_embed` in [`crates/ostra-agents/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-agents/src/lib.rs). Each agent has two files: `assets/agents/<name>/agent.toml` and `assets/agents/<name>/prompt.md`.

`AgentDef` holds the fields of `agent.toml`:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | text | What the agent does. |
| `default_tier` | `Tier` | The model tier when no route overrides it. |
| `timeout_seconds` | number | The run timeout. The engine reads it through `AgentMeta`. |
| `capabilities` | list | The `Capability` values of the agent. |
| `effort` | table | One `Effort` per executor table: `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `agy`. |

`agent_def` loads all 14 definitions once into a `OnceLock` (`DEFS`). If an embedded file is missing or invalid, the load panics. The reason is that the tests of this crate validate every embedded asset. A bad file is a build defect and not a run-time condition.

`effort_for` returns the effort of an agent on an executor. It reads the table of the executor first. If the table has no entry, it uses the `native` value. If that is also absent, it returns `Effort::High`. The test suite records one reason for a low value: the initializer on the native executor is `High` and not `max`, because a self-init spent about 240 USD on Opus at max effort.

### Materialized assets

Agents read references and skills from disk, not from the binary. `materialize_assets` writes these files under a directory:

- Each reference as `refs/<name>.md`.
- Each bundled skill as `skills/<name>/...`.
- The instructions of each agent, rendered for the native executor, as `agents/<name>.md`.

The function replaces `{{assets_dir}}` with the directory path in each file. It rewrites only files whose content changed. The reason for `agents/<name>.md` is Rule O5: the advisor reads the instructions of a failed agent to see what the step can do and what it must return.

`ASSETS_DIR` is a static `OnceLock<PathBuf>` in `lib.rs`. It holds the folder for the materialized files, and it is empty until a caller sets it.

At startup, [`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs) calls `set_assets_dir` with `<data_dir>/assets` and then `materialize_assets`. If the write fails, startup fails with `writing assets`. `set_assets_dir` returns `false` when a caller already set the directory. `assets_dir` returns `<data_dir>/assets` when no caller set it. `instructions_path` and `reference_path` build paths inside this directory.

### Lookups

| Function | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `judge_prompt(name)` | The system prompt of a judge from `assets/judges/<name>.md`. |
| `reference(name)` | A stack reference from `assets/refs/<name>.md`. |
| `reference_names()` | The names of all embedded references. |
| `stack_names()` | The sorted stacks that have a seed reference. It skips names that start with `_` and files that do not start with `# Stack Reference:`. |
| `embedded_skill(name)` | A skill from `assets/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. |

Only `judge_prompt`, `reference`, and `embedded_skill` cache their result. Each one holds a function-local `static CACHE` that it fills on the first call. `reference_names` and `stack_names` do not cache. They call `Assets::iter()` and `asset_text` on every call.

`AgentsError` has 4 variants: `Missing`, `Parse`, `Template`, and `Io`. See [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md) for the judge prompts and [Project init and skills](init-and-skills.md) for references and skills.

## Render a prompt for one executor

The prompt of an agent names tools with tokens such as `{{tool_read}}`. `render_prompt(agent, executor)` replaces each token with the tool name of the executor. The renderer uses `minijinja` with strict undefined behavior. An unknown token is a render error (`AgentsError::Template`), not an empty string.

### The mapping file

`assets/tool-mapping.toml` maps a capability to a tool name for each executor table. The `mapping::get` function parses the file once and keeps the result in `MAP`, a function-local `OnceLock<Mapping>`. The `TOKENS` table in [`crates/ostra-agents/src/mapping.rs`](crates/ostra-agents/src/mapping.rs) has 28 tokens:

- 14 capability tokens, from `tool_read` to `tool_docs_search`.
- 8 code tokens, from `tool_code_outline` to `tool_code_map`.
- 2 project tokens: `tool_project_list` and `tool_project_create`.
- 3 subagent tokens: `tool_subagent_list`, `tool_subagent_ask`, and `tool_subagent_reply`.
- 1 submit token: `tool_submit`.

If the mapping has no entry for a token, the context uses the mapping key as text. Native names follow the names of Claude Code, because the prompts were tuned to them. Ostra's own tools come from the `ostra` MCP server on a harness. A value that is not a bare tool name is prose, and the renderer writes it into the prompt as it is.

| Capability | Native | Claude Code | Codex | Grok Build | Antigravity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `read` | `Read` | `Read` | `exec_command` | `read_file` | `view_file` |
| `edit` | `Edit` | `Edit` | `apply_patch` | `search_replace` | `replace_file_content` |
| `shell` | `Bash` | `Bash` | `exec_command` | `run_terminal_command` | `run_command` |
| `report` | `Report` | `mcp__ostra__report` | `report` | `report` | `report` |
| `code` | `Code{Op}` | `mcp__ostra__code_{op}` | `code_{op}` | `code_{op}` | `code_{op}` |
| `coordinate` | `Subagent{Op}` | `mcp__ostra__subagent_{op}` | `subagent_{op}` | `subagent_{op}` | `subagent_{op}` |
| `submit` | `submit_{agent}` | `mcp__ostra__submit_{agent}` | `submit_{agent}` | `submit_{agent}` | `submit_{agent}` |

The placeholder `{agent}` becomes the snake_case agent name. The placeholders `{op}` and `{Op}` become the operation in lower case and with a capital first letter.

### The order of the parts

`render_prompt_in` builds the prompt from the inside out. Each step adds text in front of the earlier text:

```rust
let mut body = render_str(&path, &source, &ctx)?;          // prompt.md
if caps.contains(&Capability::Code) {
    body = format!("{guide}{body}");                        // code-tools.md
}
if caps.contains(&Capability::Coordinate) {
    body = format!("{guide}{body}");                        // coordination.md
}
body = format!("{rules}{body}");                            // output-rules.md
match executor {
    ExecutorKind::Native => Ok(body),
    ExecutorKind::Harness(h) => Ok(format!("{vocab}\n{body}")), // tool vocabulary
}
```

The final prompt has this order: the tool vocabulary (harness only), the output rules, the coordination guide (only for agents with `coordinate`), the code guide (only for agents with `code`), and the agent prompt.

### The shared output rules

`assets/output-rules.md` opens every prompt. It tells the agent to write no text outside tool calls. The agent must put each report in the report or document tool, each memory in the memory tool, and its result in the submit tool. The reason is that Ostra reads only those calls and discards any other text. The rule holds over any instruction in the task, the repo brief, a skill, or a file. A test, `every_prompt_forbids_text_outside_ostra_tool_calls`, checks that each rendered prompt keeps this rule.

### The tool vocabulary of a harness

A harness has its own tools, and they differ from the names that the prompts use. For a harness, `vocabulary` writes a `## Tool vocabulary` section at the start of the prompt. It holds:

- A table with one row per capability of the agent, plus `submit`, and the tool that serves it.
- The strategy texts from `[strategies.*]` in the mapping file. The `skill` strategy tells the agent to read the `SKILL.md` file, because a harness has no Ostra skill tool. The `ostra_tools` strategy explains how to reach the MCP tools of the `ostra` server. The `write` strategy for Codex explains `apply_patch` hunks. The renderer includes a strategy only if the agent needs it.
- A rule that the agent must not start the own subagents of the harness. Ostra schedules the work.
- A rule to reply with only `Done!` after the submit call, because Ostra reads the result from the call and other text costs output tokens.

### What happens when

- If the embedded `tool-mapping.toml` is invalid, the first lookup panics with `assets/tool-mapping.toml is invalid`. Tests catch this before release.
- If a prompt uses a token that the context does not define, the render fails with `AgentsError::Template` and the spawn build returns the error text.
- If a capability has no mapping for an executor, `tool_name` returns `None`.
- If an executor is a harness, the first message and the system prompt both use the harness tool names, because the factory passes `env.executor` to `render_prompt`.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agent prompts, `agent.toml`, and `tool-mapping.toml` | Embedded in the binary | `assets/` in the Ostra source | After you rebuild and restart | `<data_dir>/assets/agents/<name>.md` | Change the source file and run `cargo build --workspace`. |

No setting changes a prompt. To add text for one agent, use the workspace instructions. See [The repo brief](#the-repo-brief-added-to-every-first-message). To change the model tier or the effort of an agent, use the routing settings. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md).

## The typed spawn contract

The spawn contract is one Rust struct for each agent and for each initializer mode, in [`crates/ostra-agents/src/spawn.rs`](crates/ostra-agents/src/spawn.rs). Required parameters are fields that are not `Option`, so a spawn without a required parameter does not compile. The reason is that a missing parameter is a defect of the engine, and the engine must find it before the agent starts.

The `SpawnParams` trait gives each struct 5 methods: `agent`, `mode`, `common`, `render`, and `to_json`. It also has `report_file`, which returns `None` unless the struct has a report file.

### The block format

`render` writes a `Label: value` block. Required lines come first. Then come the four common lines. Then come the optional extras. A value with more than one line starts on the next line, and each line is indented by two spaces. An optional value that is empty writes nothing.

The four common lines are in `Common`:

- `Workspace root:` (`workspace_root`)
- `Repo root:` (`repo_root`)
- `Session dir:` (`session_dir`)
- `Repo key:` (`repo_key`)

The constant `COMMON` in `spawn.rs` holds these four IDs as the array `["workspace_root", "repo_root", "session_dir", "repo_key"]`. `parse_block` requires them for every agent, before the required IDs that `contract` returns.

The optional `Extras` lines include `Research docs`, `Repos in scope`, `User answers`, `Findings`, `Required skills`, `Review ledger`, `Rescue context`, `Resume instructions`, `Prior phase reports`, `Context files`, `User notes`, and `New project`. A `task_note` writes free text below the block.

### Required parameters of each agent

The `contract` function lists the required parameters beyond the four common lines.

| Agent | Required parameters |
| --- | --- |
| `explore`, `generate-spec` | `Task` |
| `fact-check` | `Target`, `Target type`, `Prior findings`, `Spec file`, `Source check` |
| `plan` | `Spec file` |
| `implementer` | `Report file`, and one of `Phase file` or `No plan` |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | `Implementer report`, `Report file` |
| `write-test` | `Implementer report`, `EPA report`, `Report file`, and one of `Phase file` or `No plan` |
| `code-reviewer` | `Phase`, `Changed files`, `Change rationale`, and one of `Phase file` or `No plan` |
| `prompt-generation` | `Task`, `Target files`, `Report file` |
| `documentation` | `Implementer reports` |
| `system-architecture` | `Book parts`, `Repos in scope` |
| `quick-answer` | `Question` |
| `advisor` | `Failed step`, `Problem`, `Step inputs` |
| `initializer` | `Mode`, plus the lines of the mode |

The required lines of an initializer mode are:

| Mode | Required lines |
| --- | --- |
| `detect` | none |
| `adopt` | `Source harness`, `Source runtime dir`, `Source skills dir` |
| `scout` | `Slice`, `Slice paths`, `Stack reference`, `Scout plan` |
| `propose` | `Scout findings`, `Scout plan` |
| `generate-skill` | `Skill name`, `Skill kind`, `Disposition`, `Proposal`, `Scout findings` |
| `generate-inventory` | `Generated skills`, `Reused skills`, `Proposal`, `Scout findings` |

Rule hard-13 makes a phase-bound agent declare its work source. `WorkSource` is either `PhaseFile(path)` or `NoPlan(reason)`. The factory writes a reason that matches the session, for example "The user asked for documentation directly, so no plan exists." When no scout ran, `Scout findings` still appears with the value `none`, because the label is required.

The plan agent gets the spec and nothing else (Rule D4). Its only other inputs are the findings of a fact-check re-pass and the master plan under revision. A fact-check on a plan target gets no research documents (Rule D5). The value `refetch` for `Source check` is only for the first pass of a spec target whose External Evidence table has rows (Rule D3b).

### Runtime validation with `parse_block`

`parse_block(agent, text)` reads a block back and checks it against the same contract. The function works in these steps:

1. It reads each line. A line that starts with a space or a tab continues the label above it.
2. It stops at a line that is `---` or starts with `## `, because the repo brief starts there.
3. It maps each label to a parameter ID through the `PARAMS` table. For the first occurrence of a label, it keeps the value.
4. It looks up the required IDs with `contract`, using the `Mode` value for an initializer.
5. It checks each required value with its `Kind`.

The `Kind` of a parameter sets the check:

| Kind | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `AbsoluteDir`, `AbsolutePath` | The path is absolute or has a root. A bare-rooted path such as `/ws` passes, because a real root on Windows has a drive and the leniency keeps prompts portable. |
| `RepoKey` | The value is a lowercase slug (`is_project_key`). |
| `Phase` | The value is `N`, `N-tests`, or `none`, where `N` is digits. |
| `Enum` | The value is one of a fixed list, for `Mode`, `Target type`, and `Source check`. |
| `Path`, `Text` | Any non-empty value. |

An empty value is always an error. The error messages are exact. Examples: `missing required parameter \`Task:\``, `` `Phase:` must be `N`, `N-tests`, or `none` ``, and `give exactly one of \`Phase file:\` or \`No plan:\`, not both`. A mode that is not an initializer mode gives `` `Mode: x` is not an initializer mode ``.

The doc comment says `parse_block` validates a block for harness executors. In this code base, only the tests of `ostra-agents` call it. The tests check that every struct renders a block that its own contract accepts.

### What happens when

- If a planner input is absent, `build` returns an error such as `missing task`, `missing spec file`, or `missing report file`. No agent starts.
- If an agent has the `Consult` purpose, the factory uses `ConsultParams` with the lines `Asked by`, `Question`, and the common four.
- If the workspace has no `Phase file` for a phase-bound agent, the factory writes `No plan` with a reason.
- If a phase must create a project, the implementer gets a `New project` line that tells it to call `ProjectCreate` first (Rule O2).

## The repo brief added to every first message

The repo brief gives an agent the project facts that the agent otherwise must find with its first tool calls. [`crates/ostra-agents/src/brief.rs`](crates/ostra-agents/src/brief.rs) builds it. `augment(first_message, input)` returns the first message, then a line `---`, then the brief.

The selection is a containment test against the text of `INVENTORY.md`, not a fixed list of fields. The reason is that one profile field repeats the inventory in one repo and is the only statement of a rule in another repo. The brief must not state a fact twice and must not withhold a fact. Routing settings never go in the brief, because they mean nothing to an agent and leak tier names into its context.

The brief does not state the parallel execution slot or the session budget. [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) owns both.

### The parts of the brief, in order

1. `## Repo brief for <agent>`: facts from the project profile and the inventory.
2. `## Project instructions`: the project files `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `AGENT.md`.
3. `## Projects created in this session`: projects that an agent created, with the facts of the `ProjectCreate` call (Rule O3). A new project has no inventory until its init runs.
4. `## Workspace artifacts`: the visible artifacts of the workspace (Rule W1). At most `MAX_BRIEF_ARTIFACTS` entries appear, and a last line counts the rest. See [Workspace artifacts and uploads](artifacts-and-uploads.md).
5. `## Workspace documentation`: the documentation books (Rule B5). The text tells an agent with the docs search tool to search the books before it reads code (Rule B8).
6. `## Workspace instructions`: the text that the user set for the workspace.

### The sections of the profile brief for each agent

The function `sections` picks the sections of part 1 for each agent. The output order is always Stack, Commands, Testing, Skills, Conventions, Review, Modules.

| Agent | Sections |
| --- | --- |
| `implementer` | Commands, Skills, Conventions, Modules |
| `write-test` | Commands, Testing, Skills, Conventions, Modules |
| `code-reviewer` | Commands, Review, Conventions, Skills |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | Commands, Testing, Modules |
| `explore` | Stack, Skills, Modules |
| `plan`, `quick-answer`, `advisor` | Stack, Commands, Skills, Modules |
| `generate-spec`, `system-architecture`, `fact-check` | Stack, Modules |
| `documentation` | Stack, Commands, Modules |
| `prompt-generation` | Skills |
| `initializer` | none |

The `initializer` gets no profile brief, because it creates the profile.

The sections have these rules:

- **Stack:** the lines `stack`, `build tool`, and `test framework`.
- **Commands:** each command as `- **name**: \`value\``, under the heading "use these exact strings". The agent must substitute `{MODULE}`, `{TEST}`, and `{PATH}` and must not invent a different invocation.
- **Testing:** each test type with its level command. If the command for one test differs, the line also shows `one test: ...`. The lines `applies to`, the note, and `reports at` appear only if the inventory does not state them.
- **Skills:** a row for each skill that has a path. A skill of kind `convention` always appears. For `write-test`, a skill appears only if its name or kind contains `test` or `spec`. For `code-reviewer`, only conventions appear.
- **Conventions:** naming, the immutability keyword, and notes, each only if the inventory does not state it.
- **Review:** the complete review rule catalog, each rule with its ID, severity, and `auto-fixable` mark. This section is exempt from the containment test. The reason is that the catalog is the whole basis for the judgment of the reviewer, and a partial catalog silently narrows what the review covers.
- **Modules:** the module map rows that cover paths named in the task. See the next part.

### Module rows and scope hints

The full module map of a large repo is bigger than the rest of the brief together. Thus the brief includes it only when the task names a path. `scope_hints` scans the spawn block with the pattern `[\w.-]+/[\w./-]+`. It keeps a match if it has more than 3 characters and does not contain `ostra-`. It keeps at most 40 hints. `relevant_modules` then keeps a row if its glob, without `*` and a trailing `/`, has at least 3 characters and the glob and one hint contain each other. If no hint exists, the section is empty.

### Size caps of the brief

| Constant | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS` | 3600 characters | The profile brief (part 1). Longer text is cut, and the line `(brief truncated; see the inventory for the rest)` follows. |
| `MAX_PROJECT_DOC_CHARS` | 12000 characters | Each project instruction file. A longer file is cut, and the line `(truncated; read the file for the rest)` follows. |
| `MAX_SKILL_ROWS` | 16 | Skill rows in the Skills section. |
| `MAX_MODULE_ROWS` | 10 | Module rows in the Modules section. |
| `MAX_BRIEF_BOOKS` | 20 | Books that part 5 names. A last line counts the rest and tells the agent to use Glob. |

The other parts have their own caps. `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS` cuts only part 1. The headings are constants: `BRIEF_HEADING`, `PROJECT_DOCS_HEADING`, `NEW_PROJECTS_HEADING`, `ARTIFACTS_HEADING`, `BOOKS_HEADING`, and `INSTRUCTIONS_HEADING`. Text in the brief is also cut by field, for example 190 characters for a naming rule and 170 characters for a review rule.

### The containment test

The function `stated_in` compares two texts with all runs of white space reduced to one space. A value shorter than 3 characters counts as stated, because it is too short to be distinctive. The brief leaves out a value that the inventory already states.

```rust
pub fn stated_in(haystack: &str, value: &str) -> bool {
    let text = value.trim();
    if text.chars().count() < 3 {
        return true;
    }
    squash(haystack).contains(&squash(text))
}
```

### What happens when

- If the message already holds one of the five headings (`BRIEF_HEADING`, `PROJECT_DOCS_HEADING`, `ARTIFACTS_HEADING`, `BOOKS_HEADING`, or `INSTRUCTIONS_HEADING`), `augment` returns it unchanged. A second render never stacks two briefs.
- If there is no profile, or the agent is the `initializer`, part 1 is absent. The other parts can still appear.
- If nothing in any part applies, `build_brief` returns `None` and the first message is the spawn block alone.
- If `AGENTS.md` is a link to `CLAUDE.md`, or a copy of it, `project_docs` reads it once. It also skips an empty file.
- If the user instructions tag files or artifacts, the factory adds their absolute paths (Rule W3). A tag for a hidden or missing artifact resolves to nothing.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `instructions.all` | None | Workspace settings | At the next spawn | The `## Workspace instructions` part of the first message | Clear the text. |
| `instructions.agents` | None | Workspace settings | At the next spawn | The same part, after the `instructions.all` text | Clear the entry of the agent. |
| `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `AGENT.md` | None | The repo root of the project | At the next spawn | The `## Project instructions` part | Delete the file or empty it. |

The match of the file names ignores case. The order is `claude.md`, then `agents.md`, then `agent.md`. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) for the instruction settings.

## The submit tool of each agent

Each agent ends its run by calling its own submit tool, `submit_<agent>`. The engine then reads structured data and does not scrape a final message (Hard rule 4). [`crates/ostra-core/src/submit.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/submit.rs) defines the payloads.

Three functions serve the tool:

- `submit_schema(agent)` returns the JSON schema of the payload. The schema comes from `schemars`.
- `submit_description(agent)` returns the text that the model sees: call the tool exactly once, as the last action, after every file that the task asked for exists.
- `validate_submit(agent, input)` checks a payload and returns an error text for the model.

The native loop and the harness bridge both call these functions. The native tool definition and the harness tool list use the schema and the description. See [Native executor loop](native-executor.md) and [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).

### Payload of each agent

| Agent | Payload type | Main fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | `ExploreSubmit` | `research_path`, `scope_covered`, `findings_summary`, `sources_retrieved`, `open_questions`, `not_covered` |
| `generate-spec` | `GenerateSpecSubmit` | `spec_path`, `open_questions`, `external_evidence_rows`, `deliverables`, `requirements`, `summary` |
| `fact-check` | `FactCheckSubmit` | `verdict`, `target`, `findings` |
| `plan` | `PlanSubmit` | `spec_path`, `master_plan_path`, `phases`, `stakes`, `step_count`, `requirement_coverage`, `new_projects` |
| `implementer` | `ImplementerSubmit` | `status`, `report_path`, `changed_files`, `summary`, `stuck`, `handoff` |
| `code-reviewer` | `CodeReviewerSubmit` | `findings`, `security_block`, `ledger_path`, `summary` |
| `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test`, `prompt-generation` | `ReportSubmit` | `status`, `report_path`, `changed_files`, `summary`, `stuck` |
| `documentation` | `DocumentationSubmit` | See [Documentation books and search](documentation-books.md). |
| `system-architecture` | `ArchitectureSubmit` | See [Documentation books and search](documentation-books.md). |
| `initializer` | `InitializerSubmit` | `status`, `summary`, `files`, `result`, `stuck` |
| `quick-answer` | `QuickAnswerSubmit` | `answer`, `sources` |
| `advisor` | `AdvisorSubmit` | `action`, `guidance`, `reason` |

### Shared types

- `SubmitStatus` has 3 values: `ok` (the default), `stuck`, and `handoff`. `stuck` means the agent hit the retry ceiling on the same failure. It carries `StuckInfo` with a `diagnostic` (the exact error) and a `need` (the fact or decision that the agent needs). `handoff` means the agent needs a specialist. It carries `HandoffInfo`, where `specialist` is always `prompt-generation` today.
- `Verdict` has the values `PASS`, `FAIL`, and `ERROR`. `Severity` has `BLOCKER`, `HIGH`, `MEDIUM`, and `LOW`.
- `FactCheckFinding` has a `severity`, a `location`, an optional `element` (an ID such as `R3` or `phase 2` on which Ostra shows the finding), a `claim`, and an `issue`. `FactCheckSubmit::findings_text` renders the findings as the `Prior findings:` line of the next pass, or `none` (Rule D3a).
- `ReviewFinding` has a `severity`, a `file`, a `rule`, a `description`, a `fix`, and a `guidance` for a BLOCKER. `ReviewFinding::line` gives the one-line form that the review ledger and the fix prompts use. Only a BLOCKER adds its guidance to the line.
- `AdviceAction` has 2 values: `retry` (run the step again with `guidance`) and `escalate` (ask the user).

### Validation rules

`validate_submit` parses the payload into the type of the agent. A payload with a wrong shape returns the parse error to the model. Four agents have extra rules:

- `code-reviewer`: `security_block` must be true exactly when a BLOCKER finding exists.
- `documentation`: `check_documentation` returns the issues of the book part.
- `system-architecture`: `check_architecture` returns the issues of the architecture.
- `advisor`: an action `retry` needs a `guidance` that is not empty. It tells the next run what to do differently.

```rust
AgentName::CodeReviewer => {
    let r: CodeReviewerSubmit = serde_json::from_value(input.clone()).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
    let has_blocker = r.findings.iter().any(|f| f.severity == Severity::Blocker);
    if has_blocker != r.security_block {
        return Err("security_block must be true exactly when a BLOCKER finding is present".into());
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

The field comment of `FactCheckSubmit.verdict` says `PASS` only when no finding is HIGH or MEDIUM. `validate_submit` does not check this rule. It checks only the shape of the payload.

### What happens when

- If the payload is invalid, the executor returns the error text to the model as a tool error, and the model can correct the call.
- If the run ends through a coordination call, the run records `end_payload`, a JSON object with `coordination` and `message`, in place of a submit payload.
- If a harness agent calls the submit tool, it then replies with only `Done!`. See [The tool vocabulary of a harness](#the-tool-vocabulary-of-a-harness).

## Subagent coordination between runs

Subagent coordination lets an agent ask a question and continue from its own conversation when the answer arrives. Without it, an agent reads a report from another agent with no context, or guesses. The code is split over four crates:

| Crate | File | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra-core` | [`crates/ostra-core/src/coord.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/coord.rs) | Tool names, limits, input parsing, and message texts. |
| `ostra-engine` | [`crates/ostra-engine/src/coord.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/coord.rs) | The checks, the routing, and the delivery. All are pure functions of the session log. |
| `ostra-server` | [`crates/ostra-server/src/coord.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/coord.rs) | Finds the workspace and the session of a run, then calls the engine. |
| `ostra-tools` | [`crates/ostra-tools/src/coord.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/coord.rs) | The `Coordinate` trait and the tool entry point. |

### The three tools

`COORD_TOOLS` in `crates/ostra-core/src/coord.rs` holds three tools. Each entry pairs the MCP name with the native tool name:

| Constant | Native tool name | MCP name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SUBAGENT_LIST` | `SubagentList` | `subagent_list` |
| `SUBAGENT_ASK` | `SubagentAsk` | `subagent_ask` |
| `SUBAGENT_REPLY` | `SubagentReply` | `subagent_reply` |

The Claude Code harness adds the prefix `mcp__ostra__` to the MCP name. The function `is_coord_tool` tests a native name against this list.

A wake is not a tool. A wake is the message that Ostra delivers to a waiting run. It is a question or an answer (`DeliveryKind::Question` or `DeliveryKind::Answer`). The route `WakeInPlace` and the function `next_delivery` use this meaning.

- `SubagentList` returns the subagent ID of the caller and every subagent of the session, oldest first. Each line shows the agent, the purpose, the project, the status, and the report path. It marks the partners of the caller, such as "your fact checker" or "the reviewer of your phase".
- `SubagentAsk` takes a `message` and exactly one of `agent` or `subagent_id`. The optional `project` applies to a helper. After the call, the run waits.
- `SubagentReply` takes a `message`. A run calls it to answer a question that another subagent asked it.

A subagent ID is the ID of the first execution of a conversation (Rule H1). A run that continues the conversation of an earlier run has the same subagent ID.

Only agents with the `coordinate` capability get the tools and the guide `assets/coordination.md`: `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `implementer`, `code-reviewer`, and `write-test`. The guide tells an agent to ask only when the answer saves real work, to write a question that stands alone, to make every other call first, and to end the turn after the ask. It also says that the answer is evidence to check against the code.

### Limits

| Constant | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_HELPERS_PER_RUN` | 3 | Helpers that one run can start (Rule H4). |
| `MAX_SESSION_ASKS` | 24 | Questions that one session can hold (Rule H4). The check counts all asks of the session. |
| `MAX_CONVERSATION_RUNS` | 6 | Runs of one conversation before a pair loop starts a fresh run (Rule H6). |
| `MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS` | 8000 | The length of a `message`. The text must not be empty. A longer text goes in a file, and the message names the path. |
| `HELPER_AGENTS` | `explore` | The only agent that `SubagentAsk` can start as a helper. |

### The checks of an ask

`SessionState::ask_event` checks a `SubagentAsk` in this order and returns the first error as a tool error:

1. The input must parse. It needs a `message` and exactly one target.
2. The run must still run in its session.
3. A consult run cannot ask. It must answer with `SubagentReply`.
4. A run that owes an answer must reply first, because its asker waits for it.
5. The session must have fewer than `MAX_SESSION_ASKS` asks.
6. For a helper: the agent must be in `HELPER_AGENTS`, the caller must not be a helper, the caller must have started fewer than `MAX_HELPERS_PER_RUN` helpers, and the `project` (default: the project of the caller) must be in the scope of the session.
7. For a subagent: the ID must exist in the session, and it must not be the subagent ID of the caller.

The reason that a helper cannot start a helper: a helper does the research itself. The engine records an `AgentAsked` event, and the caller gets the text from `waiting_text` with `RunEnd::Wait`.

### Where a question goes

A question to a helper starts an `explore` research task, and only the asker waits for it. A question to a subagent goes through `SessionState::route`, which returns one of four routes (Rule H3):

- `WakeInPlace`: the subagent waits for the asker. Ostra delivers the question into its waiting run.
- `Consult`: the subagent ended its run with `ok`, `stuck`, or `handoff`. A consult run continues the conversation of the subagent and answers.
- `Pending`: the subagent is busy. The question waits.
- `Failed`: the subagent does not exist, or its run ended with `error`, `denied`, or `cancelled`. The asker gets the reason as the answer.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Ask to a subagent"] --> B{"Does the subagent have a run?"}
  B -->|no| F1["Failed: no subagent exists"]
  B -->|yes| C{"Is the latest run still live?"}
  C -->|yes| D{"Does it wait on the asker?"}
  D -->|yes| W["WakeInPlace"]
  D -->|no| P1["Pending"]
  C -->|no| E{"Another run of the subagent is live?"}
  E -->|yes| P2["Pending"]
  E -->|no| G{"Final status of the run"}
  G -->|"ok, stuck, handoff"| K["Consult"]
  G -->|"error, denied, cancelled"| F2["Failed: cannot answer"]
  G -->|"other"| P3["Pending"]
```

A latest run that ended with status `waiting` follows the same rule as a live run. It gets `WakeInPlace` if it waits on the asker, and `Pending` if not.

### The flow of one question

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Asker
  participant Tools as ostra-tools coord run
  participant Server as Coordination in ostra-server
  participant Engine
  participant Log as Session log
  participant Answerer
  Asker->>Tools: SubagentAsk with subagent_id
  Tools->>Server: Coordinate call
  Server->>Engine: Engine coordinate
  Engine->>Log: AgentAsked
  Engine-->>Asker: waiting text and RunEnd Wait
  Engine->>Answerer: question by WakeInPlace or consult run
  Answerer->>Engine: SubagentReply
  Engine->>Log: AgentReplied
  Engine-->>Answerer: RunEnd Wait or RunEnd Finish
  Engine->>Asker: MessageDelivered with the answer
```

The tool entry point `ostra_tools::coord::run` finds the `Coordinate` handle of the run. `Coordination::open` in the server returns a handle only if the agent has the `coordinate` capability and the run belongs to a session. Then `ExecCoord::call` finds the workspace with the folded root path and calls `Engine::coordinate`. This function handles the three tools, appends the event, and returns a `CoordReply` with a `RunEnd`:

- `Continue`: the run goes on. `SubagentList` returns this.
- `Wait`: the run waits for a message (Rule H2). `SubagentAsk` returns this. `SubagentReply` also returns it when the replying run asked its own question and waits for that answer.
- `Finish`: a consult run answered and ends.

### Waiting and delivery

A run that waits for a message holds its stage, and the message wakes it in place (Rule H2). The behavior differs by executor:

- **Native run:** the run ends with the status `waiting`. The fold stores it in `waiting_keys`. The planner holds the spawn of the stage. When `next_delivery` has a message, the planner spawns the run with `resumes` set to the waiting run, and the conversation continues.
- **Harness run:** the process stays alive. The planner emits a `Step::Deliver`, and the runner hands the message to the run through `deliver_mail`. The tool result tells the harness to end its turn and reply with only `Waiting`. Ostra then types the answer into the session. After a server restart, a harness run that waited with a live process is still `waiting`, and its answer resumes the harness session.

A harness run that waits gives its execution slot back and takes a slot again before it gets the message. Without this rule, a limit of one slot lets the waiting run hold the only slot, and the run that it waits for cannot start. See [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) for the slot.

`next_delivery` picks the message for a waiting run. An answer to its own question comes first. If there is no answer, the next message is a question from the subagent that it waits on. An answer text starts with "The answer from ... to your question arrived." It adds any user addition made while the run waited. After the question reaches a run, that run must call `SubagentReply`. If it tries to end without a reply, `reply_instruction` tells it to call the reply tool now, because the asker reads only that call.

A consult run starts with `consult_note`. The note tells the run to answer from its conversation, to call the reply tool, and to change no file. The run names any change in its answer.

### Pair loops

A pair loop is a repeat of one pair of runs, such as a spec author and its fact-check, or an implementer and its reviewer. `SessionState::continuation` lets the next spawn continue the conversation of the run before it (Rule H5). The reason is that the agent already knows the work. The spawn starts with `continuation_note`. A fresh run starts instead in these cases (Rule H6):

- The previous run did not end with `ok`, `stuck`, or `handoff`, or it has no submit.
- The head run of the conversation belongs to another agent.
- The routing now forces a different executor.
- The run is on a harness and has no native session ID.
- The user added to the request after the previous run started.
- The conversation already has `MAX_CONVERSATION_RUNS` runs.

Only one run of a conversation is live at a time (Rule H7). The planner holds a spawn while the conversation is busy.

### What happens when

- If an `explore` helper ends with `ok`, the answer is its findings summary, the research document path, and the items not covered.
- If an `explore` helper errors, Ostra retries it once. Only then does the ask get a failure text.
- If a run ends without answering the question that it owes, the fold writes an answer: "... ended its run with status ... without answering. Continue without the answer, or ask again." An interrupted run keeps the question, except a consult run.
- If the agent of a run does not have the `coordinate` capability, the tool returns "... is not available to this run, because its agent does not coordinate with other subagents."
- If the server shuts down during a call, the tool returns "The Ostra server is shutting down." If the workspace is not open, it returns "This run's workspace is not open in Ostra."
- If a run calls `SubagentReply` with no question owed, the engine returns an error that tells it to use `SubagentAsk` or to go on.
- If the tool name is unknown, `Engine::coordinate` returns "Unknown tool".
- If a question is open or a subagent waits, the session does not complete (Rule H9). `coordination_open` holds the finish.

### For the user

No setting turns coordination on or off, and no setting changes the limits. The limits are constants in `ostra-core`, and the `coordinate` capability comes from the embedded `agent.toml` of each agent. The session screens show the waiting status of a run. See [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md) for the stages that hold a spawn.
