sections.title: Project init and skills
sections.summary: How Ostra prepares a project: the init flow, the skill approval gate, the files project.toml and INVENTORY.md, project commands, stack references, project skills, and skill archetypes.
sections.body:
An agent that starts in an unknown project has no commands to run, no rules to follow, and no list of recurring code patterns. Without these facts, each agent must search the code again and can guess a wrong build command or a wrong pattern. The init flow solves this problem once for each project. It reads the code, proposes skills, asks the user to approve them, and writes two files that every later execution reads: `.ostra/INVENTORY.md` and `.ostra/project.toml`.

This page covers the init flow, the files that it writes, the commands in `project.toml`, the stack references, the project skills and their directories, and the skill archetypes. It stops before the agent prompts. [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md) explains how the repo brief carries these facts into a prompt.

## The init flow stage by stage

An init session runs the `initializer` agent in five modes, in a fixed order. The planner function `plan_init` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/init.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/init.rs) decides the next step from the session state. The user starts an init session with `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/init`. The route calls `create_init_session`, which fails when the workspace has no project with that key. The session takes its YOLO setting from `yolo.default` of the workspace settings.

### Flow of one init session

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  D["detect"] --> Q{"slices or existing skills?"}
  Q -- "none" --> F1["session init fails, created project records a problem"]
  Q -- "slices" --> S["scout for each slice, in parallel, max 6"]
  Q -- "existing skills only" --> P["propose"]
  S --> P
  P --> R{"skills proposed?"}
  R -- "none" --> F2["session init fails, created project records a problem"]
  R -- "yes" --> G["skill approval gate"]
  G --> GS["generate-skill for each approved skill, in parallel"]
  GS --> GI["generate-inventory"]
  GI --> C["check INVENTORY.md and project.toml"]
  C --> E["session complete: project initialized"]
```

### What each stage does

1. **Detect** runs once. It reads the existing skills in `.agents/skills/` and `.ostra/skills/`, the instruction files, and any older `.ostra/project.toml`. It names the stack, picks the stack reference, plans the slices, and detects the commands and the test types. It writes `ostra-scout-plan.md` in the session directory. Its result holds `scout_plan_path`, `stack`, `reference_name`, `slices`, `existing_skills`, and `ultracode_bootstrap`.
2. **Scout** runs once for each slice, in parallel, and only reads files. Each scout counts the component types in its slice and captures one exemplar and the invariants for each type. It writes `ostra-findings-<slice-slug>.md` and returns `findings_path`.
3. **Propose** runs once. It merges the findings, ranks the component types by ubiquity, and reconciles them with the existing skills. It writes `ostra-proposal.md` and `ostra-proposal.json`.
4. The **skill approval gate** opens with the skills that propose returned. [Approve skills at the skill approval gate](#approve-skills-at-the-skill-approval-gate) explains it.
5. **Generate-skill** runs once for each skill with the disposition `generate` or `regenerate`, in parallel. Each execution writes only its own directory `.agents/skills/<name>/`.
6. **Generate-inventory** runs once, after every generate-skill execution ends. It writes `.ostra/INVENTORY.md` and `.ostra/project.toml`.

The planner starts every execution that has no result yet and that no execution already runs. Thus all scouts start together, and all generate-skill executions start together. The slot limit of the workspace decides how many run at the same time. See [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md).

### Rules that shape the flow

- **Existing skills reduce the scouting.** Rule I1: when detect returns no slices and at least one existing skill, the setup is complete. Propose then reconciles the existing skills and no scout runs. The detect prompt plans zero slices only when every candidate component type has an existing skill and a `convention` skill exists.
- **Scouts cost a full execution each.** The engine runs only the first 6 slices (`MAX_SCOUTS`). The detect prompt tells the agent about a limit of 12 slices, but the engine cuts the list to 6.
- **The reference name has a fallback.** If detect returns an empty `reference_name`, the engine passes `_generic` to each scout.
- **A slice with an empty slug is dropped.** The slug names the scout and its findings file.
- **A prior failure sends advice.** Each spawn adds an `Advisor guidance` line when the advisor already looked at the same step. The key of the step is `<mode>:<item>`.
- **Adopt mode has no step in this planner.** The initializer prompt defines the mode `adopt` to migrate an Ultracode bootstrap, and the factory can build its spawn. But `plan_track` never starts it. The project view only reports the `ultracode_bootstrap` flag.

### Init of a project that an agent created

Rule O4: when an agent creates a project with the `ProjectCreate` tool, the engine seeds an init track for it. The focus text names the project key, the agent, the stack, the purpose, and the base requirements. The folder is empty, so detect plans one slice that covers the repo root, and propose recommends skills from the stack reference. This track differs from a session init in two ways. When all stages end, it records `FinishInit` instead of completing the session, and the pipeline goes on. When a step fails, the advisor looks at it before the user does. [Failed init steps and the advisor](#failed-init-steps-and-the-advisor) gives the cases. [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md) explains the stage kinds that these steps map to.

### What happens when

- **Detect finds no slices and no existing skills.** The planner calls `Ending::fail` with the message `Detect found no slices to scout and no existing skills, so there is nothing to build skills from.` A session init fails with this message. A created-project init records it as a failed step.
- **Propose returns no skills.** The planner calls `Ending::fail` with the message `Scouting found no recurring components, so there are no skills to propose.` The two kinds of init react in the same way as for detect.
- **An execution of the init ends without a usable result.** The engine runs it again once on an `Error` status. After that, a session init opens a gate. [Failed init steps and the advisor](#failed-init-steps-and-the-advisor) explains both paths.
- **The user stops an execution.** The gate has the title `You stopped the initializer`. The engine leaves a stopped execution to the user, also under YOLO.
- **YOLO is on.** The skill approval gate gets the default dispositions of the proposal. See [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md).

### For the user

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Start | The `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/init` route, from the project overview |
| Default | An init session starts only when the user starts it, or when an agent creates a project |
| Stored in | The session event log of the workspace |
| Takes effect | At once, as a new session |
| State shown by | The project `init_status`: `initialized`, `not_initialized`, `initializing`, or `missing`. The session board shows each stage |
| Stop or change | Stop the session on the session board. Run init again to rebuild the files |

## Limits and names of the init flow

The init flow has five named constants in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/init.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/init.rs). Each limit has a reason in the source.

| Constant | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_SCOUTS` | `6` | The most slices that the engine scouts. Scouts run in parallel, and each one costs a full execution. |
| `MAX_DEFAULT_GENERATE` | `8` | The most skills that the proposal defaults to `generate`. The rest default to `drop`, and the user can still choose them. |
| `MAX_ADVICE` | `2` | Rule O5: advisor rounds for each failing step of a created project before the engine asks the user. |
| `STACK_REFERENCE_NAME` | `stack_reference_name` | The key in the init inputs that holds the reference name. The spawn factory turns it into the path on the `Stack reference:` line. |
| `MAX_STEP_RESULT_CHARS` | `8000` | The longest step result that the advisor receives. The engine cuts the rest and adds the note `(cut at 8000 characters)`. The start of a result names its shape, and a long tail rarely changes the diagnosis. |

The init flow also uses the shared retry limit `ERROR_RETRIES` (value `1`): the engine runs an init execution again once after an `Error` status. [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md) owns this limit and the other retry, review, and sufficiency caps. [Failed init steps and the advisor](#failed-init-steps-and-the-advisor) shows how the init flow applies it.

## Approve skills at the skill approval gate

The gate opens after propose and before any file is generated. Its title is `Approve the skills`. Each skill is grounded in a real exemplar that the scouts captured, so the user decides which skills Ostra writes. The gate payload `GatePayload::SkillApproval` holds the project key and one `SkillProposal` for each skill: `name`, `kind`, `description`, `disposition`, and `exemplars`.

### The four dispositions

| Disposition | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `generate` | A generate-skill execution writes a new `SKILL.md` and registers it with `source = "generated"`. |
| `regenerate` | The same execution overwrites an existing skill with a new one. The old content is not read or merged. |
| `reuse` | The existing file stays unchanged. Generate-inventory only registers it with `source = "reused"`. |
| `drop` | The skill is left out. The engine starts no execution for it. |

### How the engine sets the defaults

The function `proposals` turns the propose result into the gate rows. It sets the default disposition for each skill:

- A skill with the status `existing` defaults to `reuse`.
- A new skill with `recommend` set to true defaults to `generate`.
- A new skill without `recommend` defaults to `drop`.

The row description joins the `description` and the `rationale` of the skill. The `exemplars` list holds the `existing_path` of an existing skill. The proposal lists skills in ranked order, so the most common component types come first.

The function `cap_generate` then keeps the first 8 `generate` defaults in proposal order. It changes later ones to `drop` and adds a note to their description. The reason is cost: each generated skill is one full execution.

```rust
fn cap_generate(mut skills: Vec<SkillProposal>) -> Vec<SkillProposal> {
    let mut kept = 0;
    for s in skills.iter_mut().filter(|s| s.disposition == "generate") {
        kept += 1;
        if kept > MAX_DEFAULT_GENERATE {
            s.disposition = "drop".into();
            s.description = format!(
                "{} (Dropped by default to limit cost; choose generate to include it.)",
                s.description
            );
        }
    }
    skills
}
```

### What the engine does with the answer

The answer is `GateAnswer::Skills` with one `SkillDecision` (`name`, `disposition`) for each skill. The engine reads the decisions in order. For `generate` and `regenerate` it starts one generate-skill execution with these inputs: `Skill name`, `Skill kind`, `Component type`, `Disposition`, `Proposal`, and `Scout findings`. For `reuse` it adds the skill to the `Reused skills` list with its `existing_path`. Other values add nothing. When every generate-skill execution has a result, the engine starts generate-inventory with the `Generated skills` list and the `Reused skills` list.

When the existing skill is under `.ostra/skills/<name>/`, a `regenerate` writes the new skill to `.agents/skills/<name>/` and leaves the old file unchanged. Ostra loads `.agents/skills/` first, and the decision to delete a file of the user belongs to the user.

### For the user

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Choice | One disposition for each skill, in the gate card |
| Default | `reuse` for existing skills, `generate` for the first 8 recommended new skills, `drop` for all others |
| Stored in | The event log, as the gate answer. The result is in `.ostra/project.toml` and `.agents/skills/` |
| Takes effect | When the user answers the gate. Generate-skill executions start at once |
| State shown by | The gate card, then the stage `Generate skills` on the session board |
| Stop or change | Choose `drop` to skip a skill. Choose `regenerate` to rebuild an existing skill from the current code. A plain init run again reuses existing skills |

## Failed init steps and the advisor

An init step fails in two ways: an execution ends without a usable result, or the planner finds nothing to build on. The two ways lead to different results for a session init and for a created-project init.

### An execution ends without a usable result

A result is usable when the execution status is `Ok` and the submit status is `ok`. The function `init_finished` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs) handles every other end:

- **Status `Error`.** The engine runs the execution again once for each key `<mode>:<item>`. The limit is the shared constant `ERROR_RETRIES`, which [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md) explains. This retry does not call the advisor.
- **Status `Interrupted`.** The engine resets the item and runs it again. This reset does not use up the retry.
- **Any other end, or an `Error` after the retry, or a submit with status `stuck`.** The function records a failed step with a message. The planner then reads the failed step.

For a failed step, the next step depends on the kind of init:

- **Session init.** The planner opens a gate with the title `The initializer failed` and the text `The execution ended without a usable result. Retry it, or abandon the init.` The payload is `GatePayload::ExecutionFailed`.
- **Created project, first failures.** Rule O5: the planner starts the advisor agent for the failed step. The advisor receives the failed step label (for example `initializer scout api`), the problem, the step inputs, the step result, the step context, and the earlier guidance. The failed step then runs again with the newest guidance on an `Advisor guidance` line.
- **Created project, after 2 advisor rounds.** The planner opens the same failure gate for the user. `MAX_ADVICE` is the limit.
- **A step that the user stopped.** Rule P4: it goes to the user and not to the advisor, because the advisor retries it. The gate has the title `You stopped the initializer`.

### The planner finds nothing to build on

The function `plan_track` reads a missing `scout_plan_path` or `proposal_path` as an empty string and goes on. It stops in only two cases, and both call `Ending::fail`:

- Detect returns no slices and no existing skills.
- Propose returns no skills.

The result of `Ending::fail` depends on the kind of init:

- **Session init.** The call becomes `Step::Fail`. The runner appends `SessionFailed` and the session fails with the message. No gate opens and no advisor runs.
- **Created project.** The call becomes `Step::RecordInitProblem` for the detect or propose execution. The engine records it as a failed step, so the advisor rounds of the previous list apply.

The label of a failed step is `initializer <mode> <item>` for a mode with an item, such as a scout slice or a skill name, and `initializer <mode>` for the others.

## Files that the init writes: inventory and profile

Generate-inventory writes two files in `.ostra/` of the project. Both files are committable, and every executor that Ostra runs reads them. The contract for both files is [`assets/refs/inventory-and-profile.md`](assets/refs/inventory-and-profile.md). The design principle is to route work by the inventory and not by skill descriptions, because models do not reliably route from front matter. Every skill row carries a name and a path, because a path is the one mechanism that works on every harness.

### INVENTORY.md

The path is `.ostra/INVENTORY.md`. It is a plain Markdown file with five sections in a fixed order:

1. `Commands`: a table with the purposes build, test, test-one, format, lint, typecheck, and run.
2. `Skills Inventory`: one row for each skill with `Skill`, `Kind`, `Path`, and `Load when`.
3. `Skill Application Mapping`: which skills to load for which file type.
4. `Module / Area Map`: path globs with an area name.
5. `Review Rule Set`: rules with a stable ID, a severity, and an auto-fixable flag.

The `Path` column is mandatory, and it must equal the `path` of the same skill in `project.toml`. Every skill of the project appears in `Skills Inventory`, whether generated, reused, or written by hand. A creation or test skill also appears in at least one mapping row.

### project.toml

The path is `.ostra/project.toml`. It is the machine-readable twin of the inventory, and Ostra parses it into `ProjectProfile` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs). The keys use snake_case. Ostra ignores an unknown key, so a misspelled key is lost without an error.

| Key | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | number | The value `1`. It is a number and never a string. |
| `generated_at` | string | The date of the generation, `YYYY-MM-DD`. |
| `stack` | string | The stack name, for example `java-spring`. |
| `build_tool`, `test_framework` | string | Top-level strings next to `stack`. |
| `[commands]` | table | The keys `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `format`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `run`. |
| `[test_types.<name>]` | table | The keys `command`, `command_one`, `matches`, `note`, and `reports`. The test stage assigns each check one of these levels. |
| `[[module_map]]` | array | Rows with `glob` and `area`. |
| `[[skills]]` | array | Rows with `name`, `kind`, `path`, `component_type`, and `source`. |
| `[conventions]` | table | The keys `immutability_keyword`, `naming`, and `notes`. It is one table. |
| `[[review_rules]]` | array | Rows with `id`, `rule`, `severity` (`H`, `M`, or `L`), and `auto_fixable`. |

The `source` of a skill entry is `generated`, `reused`, `adopted`, or `user`. The `kind` is `convention`, `creation`, `test`, or `other`. The profile has no model or executor routing, because routing is a workspace setting. Ostra ignores a routing table in the profile, and the table misleads a reader. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md).

### Rules for writing the profile

- TOML has no null. Omit a key with no value. A `null` makes the file unreadable and the init fails.
- Write `stack` as one string. A `[stack]` table is wrong for a new profile. Ostra still reads that table in a profile that was written before stacks became free text.
- Write `[conventions]` as one table and never as `[[conventions]]`.
- Omit a command that the repo does not have, because an empty string reads as a command that runs nothing.

### Checks at submit and at the end

The submit of generate-inventory runs `check_inventory_submit`. It refuses the submit when `inventory_path` does not name an existing file. It also refuses when `check_profile` cannot parse the profile. The refusal names the line and the fix, for example that TOML has no null and the key must be omitted. The agent can fix the file and submit again, because the execution still runs.

After the last stage, the runner calls `init_problem`. The init fails when `.ostra/INVENTORY.md` is missing or `.ostra/project.toml` does not parse. A session init fails with `Init did not finish: <problem>. Run init again.` A created-project init records `The init did not finish: <problem>.` on the inventory execution. The reason is stated in the source: later executions route by these two files, so a broken file fails the init now. Otherwise every agent silently gets an empty profile. When the check passes, the project gets the status `initialized`.

The completion report of a session init is `# Project initialized`. It names the two files and counts the generated skills and the reused skills.

## Project commands in project.toml

The `[commands]` table gives agents the exact strings to build, test, format, and run the project. Without it, each agent infers a command and can pick a wrong one. The struct `Commands` has seven optional keys: `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `format`, `lint`, `typecheck`, and `run`. The engine and the policy read the profile fresh for each execution, so a saved command applies to the next run. The repo brief puts the commands in each prompt and tells the agent to substitute `{MODULE}`, `{TEST}`, and `{PATH}`. See [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md).

The user edits the commands in the commands panel of the project screen. The panel calls `PUT /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/commands`. The function `save` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/commands.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/commands.rs) handles the call. The body replaces the whole `commands` table. Thus a key that the body omits is removed. Other keys of the profile stay unchanged.

```rust
fn clean(v: Option<String>) -> Result<Option<String>, &'static str> {
    let Some(v) = v else { return Ok(None) };
    let v = v.trim();
    if v.is_empty() || v == "—" {
        return Ok(None);
    }
    if v.contains(['\n', '\r']) {
        return Err("Write the command on one line; chain steps with `&&`.");
    }
    if v.chars().any(char::is_control) {
        return Err("Remove the control characters from the command.");
    }
    if v.len() > MAX_COMMAND_LEN { /* error: shorten to 2000 characters */ }
    Ok(Some(v.to_string()))
}
```

### Rules for one command

- Ostra trims the command.
- A blank command, or the single character `—`, is stored as no command.
- A command with a line break is refused. The message tells the user to write the command on one line and to chain steps with `&&`.
- A command with a control character is refused.
- A command longer than `MAX_COMMAND_LEN` is refused. The value is `2000`. The check counts bytes with `len`, and the message says characters. The message advises a script: move the steps into a script and call that.

The reason for the single line is that the engine runs the string as one shell command. The source does not state more.

### What happens when

- **The file `.ostra/project.toml` does not exist.** The route answers status 409. The message tells the user to initialize the project first, because its commands live in `.ostra/project.toml`, which init writes.
- **The file does not parse.** The route answers status 409. The message tells the user to fix `.ostra/project.toml` first and shows the parse error.
- **A command is invalid.** The route saves nothing. It returns one validation issue for each bad field, with the path `commands.<field>`, and the message `Fix the commands and save again.`
- **The format command changes.** The function `saved_format` keeps the approval of the old format command current for the new one. A format command that arrives from a repository, a `git pull`, or an agent edit does not run until the user approves it. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) for the approval and [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) for the format step.
- **The save succeeds.** The server announces a workspace update, because the project view carries the profile. Open browsers fetch it again.

### For the user

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Keys | `commands.build`, `commands.test`, `commands.test_one`, `commands.format`, `commands.lint`, `commands.typecheck`, `commands.run` |
| Default | The values that the initializer detected. A key is empty when the repo has no such command |
| Stored in | `.ostra/project.toml`, table `[commands]` |
| Takes effect | At the next execution, because the profile is read fresh each time |
| State shown by | The commands panel of the project screen. See [Project, Files, and dependency screens](web-project-screens.md) |
| Stop or change | Clear the field and save to remove the command. Edit the file by hand to change it outside the UI |

## Stack references and the stack name

The initializer needs a catalog of the component types that a stack usually has, and the grep patterns to find them. Without it, each scout invents a catalog on each run. A stack reference is a Markdown file `assets/refs/<name>.md` that holds this catalog. Ostra embeds the files in the binary and writes them to the assets directory at start, with `{{assets_dir}}` filled in, in the function `materialize_assets` in [`crates/ostra-agents/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-agents/src/lib.rs). The function `reference_path(name)` gives the absolute path for the `Stack reference:` line of a scout.

### The reference files

| File | Stack | Picked when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `java-spring.md` | `java-spring` | `pom.xml` or `build.gradle` with `@SpringBootApplication` or a `spring-boot` dependency |
| `typescript-node.md` | `typescript-node` | `package.json` with `tsconfig.json`, for Express, Nest, Fastify, or Next |
| `python.md` | `python` | `pyproject.toml`, `requirements.txt`, or `manage.py`, for Django, FastAPI, or Flask |
| `go.md` | `go` | `go.mod` |
| `_generic.md` | fallback | No other reference matches |

The folder `assets/refs/` holds two more files that are not stack references: `inventory-and-profile.md` (the output contract) and `skill-archetypes.md` (the templates). The meta-author skill is in a different folder, `assets/skills/`.

Each stack reference has these sections: `Detection signals`, `Slicing`, `Conventional commands`, `Test framework`, `Test component catalog`, `Component catalog`, `Conventions to look for`, and `Review rule seeds`. The review rule seeds carry stable IDs, such as `C1`, `S1`, and `T1`, which generate-inventory copies into the review rule set. The file `_generic.md` has no fixed catalog. It has a section `Empirical component discovery`: the scout groups file names by suffix, groups directory names, and counts imports to infer the component types.

### The stack name and the reference name are two values

The **stack** is free text that names what the project is built with, for example `rust`, `elixir-phoenix`, or `Kotlin Ktor`. The set of real stacks has no end, so the stack is not a pick from the list. The **reference name** is the file stem of the reference that the initializer chooses. The detect prompt forbids the stack name `generic`, because later agents read the stack as the real stack of the repo. If no reference matches, the initializer keeps its own stack name and uses `_generic` as the reference. It also notes in the scout plan that the stack needs a reference later.

The function `stack_names()` lists the stacks that have a seed reference. It returns every reference whose first line starts with `# Stack Reference:`, except names that start with `_`. The result is sorted: `go`, `java-spring`, `python`, `typescript-node`. The server sends this list to the setup screens and the workspace screens as `stacks`.

### Rules for the stack value

The functions in [`crates/ostra-core/src/slug.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/slug.rs) validate a stack value. A stack is valid when it is not empty, has no space at the start or end, has at most `MAX_STACK_LEN` (`64`) characters, and has no control character. The function `stack_issue` returns the message for a refused value:

- With a control character: the message tells the user to remove the control character, because the stack is one line of plain text.
- Longer than 64 characters: the message tells the user to shorten the stack to 64 characters or fewer, for example `rust` or `python-django`.
- Otherwise: a message to name the stack in plain text, or to leave it empty so the initializer detects it from the code.

The settings validation reports a bad value at the path `projects[<index>].stack`. The `ProjectCreate` tool uses the same check.

### What happens when

- **The project stack setting is empty.** The initializer detects the stack from the code. When the folder has no source files, the stack setting or the user focus must name the stack, so that detect can choose a reference.
- **The project stack setting is set.** The planner shows it to agents before the stack in `project.toml`.
- **No reference file exists for a detected stack.** The initializer uses `_generic.md`.
- **The reference name is empty in the detect result.** The engine passes `_generic` to the scouts.

### For the user

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Setting | `projects[].stack` of the workspace settings |
| Default | Empty, so the initializer detects the stack |
| Stored in | The workspace settings file |
| Takes effect | At the next init. A saved profile keeps its own `stack` until init runs again |
| State shown by | The project overview and the repo brief |
| Stop or change | Clear the field to return to detection. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) |

To add a stack reference, add a file `assets/refs/<name>.md` that starts with `# Stack Reference: <name>`, and rebuild. The file then appears in `stack_names()`.

## Project keys and slugs

The same file `slug.rs` also holds the key rules for projects and artifacts. A project key is a lowercase slug with the pattern `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*`. The function `is_project_key` checks it, so `backend` and `web-2` are valid, and `-web`, `Web`, and the empty string are not. The function `suggest_project_key` builds a key from a folder name. It lowercases letters, replaces each run of other characters with one `-`, removes trailing dashes, and returns `project` when nothing is left. For example, `Shop Backend_v2` gives `shop-backend-v2`. The function `topic_slug(text, max)` builds the same slug for an artifact name and cuts it to `max` characters without a trailing dash.

## Project skills and where they live

A project skill is a directory with a `SKILL.md` file. The file teaches an agent one recurring task or one set of rules for this project. Skills live in the project folder, so the team can commit and review them. The constants `SKILLS_DIR` and `LEGACY_SKILLS_DIR` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs) name the two directories that Ostra loads. The constant `HARNESS_DIRS` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/skills.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/skills.rs) names the harness directories.

### Skill directories

| Directory | Constant | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.agents/skills/` | `SKILLS_DIR` (`paths.rs`) | The cross-harness standard. Ostra writes every new skill here. |
| `.ostra/skills/` | `LEGACY_SKILLS_DIR` (`paths.rs`) | The place of older Ostra projects. Ostra reads it. The initializer never writes there. |
| `.claude/skills`, `.codex/skills`, `.grok/skills`, `.gemini/skills`, `.ultracode/skills` | `HARNESS_DIRS` (`skills.rs`) | The own directories of the harnesses. Ostra lists these skills and does not load them until the user adopts them. |

The function `find_project_skill` returns the first `SKILL.md` that it finds, so a skill in `.agents/skills/` hides a skill with the same name in `.ostra/skills/`. The lookup order (`SKILL_DIRS`) and the instruction file names (`INSTRUCTION_FILES`) have entries in [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md), which also owns the data paths and the environment variables. The initializer reads the instruction files as facts about the repo, and it never edits them.

### How an agent loads a skill

The repo brief lists the registered skills of the project by name and path. The skill tool then resolves a name in this order:

1. The project skill directories, `.agents/skills/` first.
2. A workspace artifact named `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
3. The skills that ship with Ostra, for example `meta-author`.

The tool also accepts a `path` and reads that file. It removes the prefix `ostra:` from a name, and it refuses a name with `/` or `..`. A harness executor loads a skill by reading its path, because a path works on every harness. The brief rules (which skills each agent sees and `MAX_SKILL_ROWS`) belong to [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md). The tool itself belongs to [Native tools](tools.md).

### The scan of a project

The function `scan` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/skills.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/skills.rs) builds the list that the Skills screen shows. It merges three sources in this order:

1. The `[[skills]]` entries of `project.toml`. Each entry has `exists = false` when its `SKILL.md` is not on disk or its path leaves the project.
2. The skill directories in `.agents/skills/` and `.ostra/skills/` that `project.toml` does not list. A directory is skipped when an earlier skill has the same path or the same name.
3. The skills in the harness directories, with the origin `Harness`.

Only a registered skill (one with an `entry`) reaches the repo brief. The description of a skill comes from the `description` field in the YAML front matter, including a folded (`>`) or literal (`|`) block.

The function `in_project` resolves symlinks and refuses a path that leaves the project. The reason is stated in the source: skill paths come from `project.toml`, and the repository itself can supply that file.

### Change a skill from the Skills screen

The server routes call these functions. Save, delete, and adopt call `check_name` first. A valid name has 1 to 64 characters of letters, digits, `-`, and `_`, and starts with a letter or digit, because the name becomes a directory name. The read of a harness skill takes a path and does not call `check_name`.

| Action | Route | Rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Save | `PUT .../projects/{key}/skills/{name}` | The kind must be `convention`, `creation`, `test`, or `other`. The content must not be empty. It must not exceed `MAX_SKILL_BYTES` (`512 * 1024`), because agents read the file whole. The write goes to the path in `project.toml`, or to the directory that already holds the skill, or else to `.agents/skills/`. A new entry gets `source = "user"`. |
| Delete | `DELETE .../skills/{name}` | Removes the entry and the skill directory in both skill directories. Answers 404 when neither exists. |
| Adopt | `POST .../skills/{name}/adopt` | Copies the harness skill directory to `.agents/skills/<name>/` and registers it with `source = "adopted"`. The copy skips symlinks. It refuses a name that is taken. |
| Read a harness skill | `GET .../harness-skill?path=` | Reads one unadopted harness skill by its path. |

### What happens when

- **The project folder is missing.** The list shows the project with a `blocked` reason and no skills. Reads fail.
- **An init session runs for the project.** The screen reads the skills but refuses every change. The message tells the user to wait for the init session to finish, because the initializer writes the skills.
- **A save resolves outside `.agents/skills/` and `.ostra/`.** The server answers status 409 and tells the user to edit the file in the Files tab. The resolved path stops a symlinked `.agents` or `.ostra` from carrying the write out of the project.
- **`project.toml` does not parse.** Save, delete, and adopt answer status 409. The message tells the user to fix `.ostra/project.toml` first.
- **The content is larger than 512 KB.** The save answers status 400.

### For the user

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where | The Skills screen of the workspace. See [Workspace, settings, and setup screens](web-workspace-and-setup.md) |
| Default | The skills that init generated or reused, registered in `[[skills]]` |
| Stored in | `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and the `[[skills]]` table of `.ostra/project.toml` |
| Takes effect | At the next execution, because the skill tool and the brief read the files each time |
| State shown by | The Skills screen: origin, `exists`, and the description |
| Stop or change | Delete the skill, or choose `drop` at the next init. Edit by hand any file that Ostra refuses to write |

## Skill archetypes and the meta-author skill

A generated skill needs a fixed shape, so that a model that reads it can follow it on the first pass. [`assets/refs/skill-archetypes.md`](assets/refs/skill-archetypes.md) defines three templates. Each generate-skill execution fills the template that matches its skill kind and no other.

| Archetype | Skill kind | Use | Template parts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | `creation` | A recurring component type, such as an entity or a route. The skill name is the component type. | Front matter, `Location`, `Base / interface`, steps with a template from the exemplar, a checklist. |
| B | `convention` | Exactly one for each repo, named `convention`. It holds rules that the repo follows consistently. | Rules with a PASS and a FAIL example, and the directory structure. |
| C | `test` | A recurring test type. The name is `unit-test-<component-type>`. | Location, framework, fixture, steps for set-up, one test for each path, and assertions, then a checklist. |

The rules for the archetypes:

- Ground every template line in a real exemplar. Mark an invariant that the agent cannot confirm with `{TODO: confirm}`. Never invent an annotation, a base class, or a registration.
- Include a convention rule only when the repo follows it consistently. Do not repeat a rule that an instruction file already states, because every agent already receives that file.
- When the repo has no tests, ground a test skill in the test convention of the stack reference and mark it `convention-seeded`.
- When the repo has no source, fill archetype B from the conventions of the stack reference and say so in the skill.

### The meta-author skill

Every generated skill must also follow the skill `meta-author`, which ships with Ostra in [`assets/skills/meta-author/SKILL.md`](assets/skills/meta-author/SKILL.md). The initializer reads it in generate-skill mode. The prompt-generation agent loads it with the skill tool by the name `meta-author`, and it works from any repo. The skill defines 16 writing laws, a structure for reading top to bottom, and a self-review checklist that the agent runs against its own output. These laws are the main ones:

- Define a term before its first use, and use one word for one concept.
- Write one instruction in each sentence, and write ALL or ANY, never an implied quantity.
- Show a PASS and a FAIL example for every rule.
- State both branches of every decision, and give a fallback for every rule.
- Prefer instructions grounded in real files over invented ones.
- Write a plain statement and not a metaphor (law 16).

The initializer prompt applies law 16 to every word that it writes: the scout plan, the findings, the proposal, each generated skill, and the summary.

### What the initializer writes

- Detect, scout, and propose are read-only for the project. They write only in the session directory.
- Generate-skill writes only under `.agents/skills/<name>/`.
- Generate-inventory writes only under `.ostra/`.
- No mode writes under `.ostra/skills/`, edits an instruction file, or changes source code. No mode writes the memory store under `.ostra/memory/`, because Ostra owns it.

These limits keep a generate mode from damaging a file that it does not own. Sibling generate-skill executions run at the same time, and each one owns one directory, so they cannot conflict.

sections.title: Native executor loop
sections.summary: How one agent runs on an API key: the turn loop, token continues, context compaction, policy-checked tool dispatch, the submit call, usage records, cancellation, and the limits of the loop.
sections.body:
A model on an API key does not run an agent by itself. It returns one response at a time. Something must send the conversation again, run the tools that the model asks for, stop a run that never ends, and collect the result. The native executor in `crates/ostra-exec-native` does this work for one execution of one agent. Every tool call passes the policy engine before it runs. The `submit_<agent>` call of the agent ends the run with structured data.

This page covers the setup of a run, the turn loop, token continues, compaction, tool dispatch, the end of a run, usage and cost records, cancellation, and the limits. It stops before the model providers and the tool code. [Model providers and pricing](providers-and-pricing.md) explains the providers. [Native tools](tools.md) explains each tool.

## Where the native executor fits

`NativeExecutor` implements the `Executor` trait of `crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs`. The trait has one method: `run(spec, host, cancel)`. It returns an `ExecutionResult`. The engine builds the `ExecutionSpec` and an `ExecutionHost`. [Architecture and crate map](architecture.md) explains the executor contract in full. The harness executors implement the same trait for Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, and Antigravity. See [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).

The loop uses these parts of the contract:

- `ExecutionSpec`: the agent, the route (model), the effort, the system prompt, the first message, the capabilities, the submit schema, `timeout_secs`, the `ExecContext`, and an optional `ResumeInfo`.
- `ExecutionHost.emit`: sends an `ExecutionDelta` to the Activity view and the event store.
- `ExecutionHost.ask_permission`: waits for the answer of the user to a permission ask.
- `ExecutionHost.record_message` and `transcript`: save and read the transcript, so that a resume can continue from it.
- `ExecutionHost.yolo`: tells whether the session is in YOLO mode now.
- `CancellationToken`: tells the run to stop.

The `NativeExecutor` constructor takes the providers, a skill resolver, and an optional code navigation handle. The methods `with_mcp`, `with_manage`, and `with_coord` add the connectors for external MCP servers, the management tools, and subagent coordination. If a connector is missing, the run has no such tools. See [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md) and [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md).

## Set up a run

`Run::execute` prepares everything before the first model call. It does these steps in order:

1. Find the provider and the model with `Providers::for_model(route.model)`. If the provider has no API key, the run fails with: ``The `<provider>` provider has no API key. Set its key in the environment or the OS keychain.`` Any other lookup error fails with ``Cannot run model `<model>`: <error>``.
2. Open the MCP tools with `McpConnector::open`. Each note that the connector returns becomes a `Status` delta.
3. Build the `PolicyInputs` from the `[commands]` table of `project.toml`. The build commands are `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `lint`, and `typecheck`. The test commands are `test` and `test_one`. The loop drops empty values and the placeholder `—`. The read-only MCP tools of the opened servers go into the same inputs.
4. Create the `ExecutionPolicy` and the `ToolEnv`. The `ToolEnv` holds the roots, the report file, the memory database, and the connectors. It also holds the hosts that `WebFetch` can reach and the names of the environment variables that agent commands must not inherit. Those names are the MCP `oauth.client_secret_env` variables of the workspace.
5. Choose the sandbox with `sandbox_for`. See the next part.
6. Build the tool list.
7. Build the first messages.

### Sandbox choice

`sandbox_for` reads the `[sandbox]` table of the global config at the start of each execution. A change therefore applies to the next execution. The sandbox mode of the workspace, when it sets one, replaces the global mode. If the decision is to sandbox, the loop creates a scratch directory, the egress proxy, and the decoy file watch. All Bash calls of the execution share them. If the decision is not to sandbox and it has a warning, the loop emits the `Status` delta `Bash runs without a sandbox. <warning>`. It also writes one `tracing` warning for each process. If the sandbox cannot start, the run fails with the error text, for example `Cannot start the sandbox's egress proxy: ...`. The `Scratch` value removes the scratch directory when the execution future ends or is dropped. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md) for the rules of each layer.

### The tool list

The tool list for the model has these items, in this order:

1. The tools that `ostra_tools::definitions(capabilities)` returns. The loop removes `WebFetch` when the provider offers a server-side fetch and the agent has the `WebFetch` capability, because the provider then runs the fetch.
2. The `Document` tool of the agent, when the agent has the `Document` capability.
3. The tools of the MCP servers.
4. The `submit_<agent>` tool, last. This tool is the only one that has `cache: true`. The loop uses `spec.submit_schema` as its input schema when the schema is not null. Otherwise it uses the default schema of the tool.

The server tools `web_search` and `web_fetch` go into the request only when the provider offers them and the capabilities of the agent ask for them.

### Start messages and resume

A new run starts with one user message: `spec.first_message`. The loop records it with `record_message`. A resume (`spec.resume`) rebuilds the messages from the stored transcript of the earlier execution. `stored_messages` does this:

- It skips records that have an unknown role and records that have no content.
- It merges adjacent messages of one role, because a resume that stopped after a user turn stores its note as a message of its own.
- It lets a `compaction` record replace every message before it, because that record holds the window that compaction produced.

`resume_turn` then adds one user turn. For each tool call that the interruption left open, the turn holds an error result: `Interrupted: this call did not finish.` The turn ends with the note of the resume. If the resume has no note, the text is `The previous run was interrupted. Continue from where it stopped.` If the stored transcript is empty, the loop starts from `first_message`.

Rule P2 decides what the loop records. When a run resumes in place (`resume.from` equals the execution ID and the transcript is not empty), the stored transcript already belongs to this run. The loop records only the new turn. Then the replayed prefix is the same as before and the prompt cache hits. Otherwise the loop records every message of the rebuilt list, because the new execution has no transcript yet. The tests `resumes_from_transcript` and `resuming_in_place_records_only_the_new_turn` check both cases.

## The turn loop

The loop runs at most `MAX_TURNS` (400) iterations. Each iteration sends the conversation to the model and handles the response. The loop exists because the model asks for tools in one response and needs their results in the next.

### Flow of one turn

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Start of turn"] --> B{"Cancelled?"}
  B -- yes --> Z1["Return Cancelled"]
  B -- no --> C{"Context at 95 percent and last message is a user turn?"}
  C -- yes --> D["Compact"]
  C -- no --> E["Send chat request"]
  D --> E
  E --> F{"Stop reason and tool calls"}
  F -- "PauseTurn" --> A
  F -- "Refusal" --> Z2["Return Error"]
  F -- "MaxTokens, no tool calls" --> G["Add continue message, at most 3 times"]
  G --> A
  F -- "No tool calls" --> H{"Reminded before?"}
  H -- no --> I["Add reminder"]
  I --> A
  H -- yes --> Z3["Return Ok without submit"]
  F -- "Tool calls" --> J["Run tools"]
  J -- "Results" --> A
  J -- "Submit or coordination end" --> Z4["Return status and submit"]
```

### Steps of one turn

Each iteration does these steps:

1. If the cancel token is set, return `Cancelled` with the usage so far.
2. Build the `ChatRequest`: the system prompt as one cached block, the tool list, the server tools, the effort of the spec, and `ToolChoice::Auto`. `max_tokens` is the whole output limit of the model. The user chose the effort and knows what it spends, so the request does not cut any effort level short. The test `asks_for_the_whole_output_limit_of_the_model` checks the value for a listed model (64,000 for `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`) and an unlisted model (`DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT`).
3. Compact the conversation when the rules in the next part say so.
4. Send the request with `Run::chat`. This call streams text and thinking deltas to the host. See [Output flush](#output-flush-to-the-activity-view).
5. Add the usage of the response to the totals, and emit the `Turn` and `Usage` deltas.
6. Keep the text of the response as `final_text` when it is not blank. Record the assistant message and add it to the conversation.
7. Handle the stop reason and the tool calls, as the next parts show.

If the model call fails with an error other than `Cancelled`, the run ends with `Error` and the message `The model call failed: <error>`. The loop does not retry. Retries for a failed request live in the provider. See [Model providers and pricing](providers-and-pricing.md).

### What happens when a response ends in each way

- **`PauseTurn`:** the loop starts the next iteration at once and adds no message. The assistant message that the loop already added stays in the conversation. The pause counts as one turn.
- **`Refusal`:** the run ends with `Error`. The message is `The model refused to continue (category <c>): <text>`. The category part is absent when the provider gives none.
- **`MaxTokens` with no tool call:** this is a token continue. See the next part.
- **No tool call, other stop reason:** the loop reminds the model one time, then ends the run. See [The end of a run](#the-end-of-a-run).
- **Tool calls:** the loop runs them. A `MaxTokens` stop that has tool calls also goes to tool dispatch.
- **400 turns pass:** the loop returns `Error` with `The run passed 400 model turns without calling <submit tool>.` The limit guards against a run that never submits.

## Token continues

A model can hit its output limit in the middle of a text answer. The loop then asks it to go on. When the stop reason is `MaxTokens` and the response has no tool call, the loop adds this user message: `You reached the output limit. Continue from exactly where you stopped.` It records the message and starts the next turn.

`MAX_TOKEN_CONTINUES` (3) limits these continues. The counter is for the whole run, and it does not reset between turns. On the fourth hit, the run ends with `Error` and the message `The model kept hitting its output limit without finishing.` Without this limit, a model that always fills its output could use turns and money until `MAX_TURNS` ends the run. A response that hits the limit and has tool calls is not a continue, because the tool results give the model the next turn.

## Compaction of the conversation

Each request sends the whole conversation again. When the conversation fills the context window of the model, the next request fails. Compaction replaces the whole conversation with a summary before that happens.

### When the loop compacts

The loop compacts at the start of a turn when all of these are true:

- The estimated size of the next request is at least `COMPACT_AT` (0.95) of the context window.
- The last message of the conversation has the user role. Compaction needs this, because a tool call that is still open has no result yet, and the summary loses it. The loop adds tool results as a user message, so the condition is true after each tool turn.
- The run has no earlier failed try, or the estimate has grown by `COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH` (0.02) of the window since the size of the failed try. See the retry rule below.

The estimate is the context size of the last response plus a guess for the messages added after it. The context size of a response is `context_of`: input tokens, cache read tokens, cache write tokens, and output tokens. The guess is `estimate_tokens`: one token for each 4 characters of the new messages. The loop does not guess the whole conversation, because the last response gives an exact count for everything before it.

The context window comes from the models.dev price catalog (`ostra_core::pricing::context_window`). If the catalog does not list the model, the loop uses `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` (200,000 tokens). The default threshold is then 190,000 tokens.

```rust
let next = measured + estimate_tokens(&messages[measured_len.min(messages.len())..]);
let retry_ok = failed_compaction_at.is_none_or(|at| {
    next as f64 >= at as f64 + COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH * window as f64
});
// A user turn last means no tool call is open, as compaction requires.
if next as f64 >= COMPACT_AT * window as f64
    && retry_ok
    && messages.last().is_some_and(|m| m.role == Role::User)
{
    // ... ask the provider to compact
}
```

### What compaction does

1. The loop emits the `Status` delta `Compacting the conversation: about <tokens> of <window> context tokens used.`
2. It calls `Provider::compact` with the whole conversation and `COMPACT_INSTRUCTIONS`. The instructions tell the model to keep the task and its requirements, the files it read, the files it changed, the decisions and their reasons, the failed commands, what is left to do, and the exact next step. They also tell it to keep paths, identifiers, and error messages word for word, and to call no tool. A provider that has a server-side compaction can ignore the instructions. Other providers send them as a last user turn. See [Model providers and pricing](providers-and-pricing.md).
3. The loop adds the usage of the compaction call to the totals, with no tool call IDs. The compaction cost is part of the cost of the execution.
4. If a summary came back, the loop adds the user message `AFTER_COMPACTION` to the new window. The message says that the conversation was compacted, tells the model to continue from the next step in the summary, and warns that earlier tool results are gone, so the model must read a file again when it needs the content.
5. The loop stores the new window as one record with the role `compaction` (`COMPACTION_RECORD`), and uses it as the conversation. A resume reads this record and starts from the window. The test `a_stored_compaction_replaces_the_messages_before_it` checks this.

### What happens when compaction does not work

- **The provider returns no summary:** the loop emits `Compaction returned no summary, so the run continues without it.` It remembers the size at which it failed.
- **The provider returns an error:** the loop emits `Compaction failed, so the run continues without it: <error>` and remembers the size. The run does not end.
- **The run is cancelled during compaction:** the run returns `Cancelled`.
- **The next try:** the loop waits until the estimate grows by `COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH` (0.02) of the window above the size of the failed try. For a window of 200,000 tokens, this is 4,000 tokens. Each try sends the whole conversation, so a try on each turn costs the full price again and again. The test `a_compaction_without_summary_is_not_retried_every_turn` checks this.

### For the user

No setting changes the compaction constants. They are compiled into `crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`. The route of the agent changes the window, because the window depends on the model.

| Control | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Compaction threshold `COMPACT_AT` | 0.95 of the window | Source code | After a new build | `Status` deltas in the Activity view, and the `context_tokens` field of the usage | Choose a model with a different window. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) |
| Window of an unlisted model `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` | 200,000 tokens | Source code | After a new build | The `Compacting the conversation` status | Choose a model that the catalog lists |

## Dispatch of tool calls

`Run::run_tools` handles the tool calls of one response. It keeps the results in the order of the calls, because the provider needs one result for each call ID.

### Order and concurrency

The loop walks the calls from first to last. It treats them in three classes:

- **Concurrent:** `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `WebFetch`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, `Skill`, and each code tool (`is_code_tool`). A run of consecutive concurrent calls starts together and the loop waits for all of them (`join_all`). These tools only read, so their order does not change the result.
- **Coordination:** the tools that `is_coord_tool` names (list, ask, and reply). They are `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, and `SubagentReply`, and they run alone. If one of them ends the run, the loop gives each later call the result `Not run: the run stopped to wait for another subagent.` `RunEnd` decides the end. `Continue` keeps the loop going, `Wait` ends the run with `Waiting`, and `Finish` ends it with `Ok`. This is Rule H2. The run submits the payload of `coord::end_payload`. See [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md).
- **Serial:** every other tool, such as `Write`, `Edit`, and `Bash`. Each runs alone, in order, because a write or a command can change what the next call sees.

A call to the submit tool is handled when the walk reaches it. See [The end of a run](#the-end-of-a-run).

### The path of one tool call

`Run::tool_end` handles one call. The policy engine decides before the tool runs. [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) owns the rules, the reasons, and the permission modes. The loop only asks it and acts on the answer.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["canonical_call and ToolCall delta"] --> B{"Input is valid JSON?"}
  B -- no --> E1["Error result, call not run"]
  B -- yes --> C["policy.check with host.yolo"]
  C --> D{"Decision"}
  D -- Deny --> E2["Error result: Denied by layer and rule"]
  D -- Ask --> F["host.ask_permission"]
  D -- Allow --> G["ostra_tools::execute"]
  F -- "AllowOnce or AlwaysInWorkspace" --> G
  F -- Deny --> E3["Error result: user denied"]
  G --> H["Git repair, build time, observations"]
  H --> I["ToolResult delta, truncated to 8 KB"]
```

The steps are:

1. `env.canonical_call` makes the call canonical. The policy check, the question to the user, and the tool then see the same target for each relative path and each Bash working directory. The loop replaces a `cwd` that the model supplies for Bash with the working directory of the shell. The test `relative_paths_are_checked_against_the_shell_cwd` checks this.
2. The loop emits the `ToolCall` delta and adds 1 to `tool_calls` in the usage.
3. If the input has the marker `__invalid_json`, the call does not run. The result is an error: `The tool input was not valid JSON, so the call did not run: <input, cut at 500 bytes>`.
4. The loop sets the YOLO flag of the policy from `host.yolo()` for each call, because the user can switch YOLO while the execution runs. Then `policy.check` returns `Allow`, `Ask`, or `Deny`, and the loop emits a `Policy` delta with the decision.
5. On `Deny`, the result is an error: `Denied by <layer> `<rule>`: <reason>`. The model sees the reason and can change its plan.
6. On `Ask`, the loop waits for `host.ask_permission`. `AllowOnce` lets the call run. `AlwaysInWorkspace` lets it run and adds a session allow rule when the policy can suggest one for the call. `Deny` returns the error `The user denied this call (<reason>). Continue without it, or explain in your report why it is needed.`
7. The tool runs with `ostra_tools::execute`. It gets a live output callback that emits `ToolOutput` deltas and the cancel token.

### After the tool runs

These steps run after the tool returns:

- **Git repair (Bash only):** `ostra_sandbox::repair_git_dirs` checks the protected repositories. When it undoes a change to git metadata, the loop appends a note to the result and emits a `Policy` delta that denies with the guard `GIT_METADATA`. The delta counts as a containment signal, like a refusal of the guard. The test `a_planted_commondir_is_undone_and_reported` checks this. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) for the pause after three signals.
- **Build time (Bash only):** when the command is a build or test command, `is_build_command` adds the duration to `build_ms` in the usage. The configured commands of `project.toml` count as build commands.
- **Observations:** `policy.observe` can ask for more output. `AppendNote` adds a note to the result text. `RecallLessons` reads up to 5 lessons from the memory database of the project and appends them as a numbered list, with area and source. This helps the agent after a streak of failed builds. The test `build_streak_recalls_lessons` checks this. See [Storage](storage.md) for the recall ranking.
- **The result:** the loop emits a `ToolResult` delta with the output cut to `EMIT_LIMIT` (8 KB). The model gets the full text. A diff of an edit goes only to the delta, not to the model.

A tool that returns an error always gives `RunEnd::Continue`, so a failed coordination call does not end the run.

## The end of a run

A run ends in one of six ways. The `ExecutionStatus` of the result tells which.

| Cause | Status | `submit` | Message or note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `submit_<agent>` accepted with `status` `ok` or no `status` | `Ok` | The input of the call | |
| `submit_<agent>` with `status` `stuck` | `Stuck` | The input of the call | |
| `submit_<agent>` with `status` `handoff` | `Handoff` | The input of the call | |
| A coordination tool returns `Wait` | `Waiting` | The `end_payload` | The run waits for another subagent |
| A coordination tool returns `Finish` | `Ok` | The `end_payload` | A consult run that answered |
| The model sends a second response with no tool call in the run | `Ok` | None | `final_text` holds the last text. The first such response gets a reminder |
| Cancel | `Cancelled` | None | `Cancelled.` |
| Timeout, model error, refusal, 400 turns, 4 token continues, setup error | `Error` | None | `error` holds the reason |

The loop never returns `Denied` or `Interrupted`. The enum has them for other parts of the engine.

### The submit call

`AgentName::submit_tool_name` gives the name of the submit tool. Before the checks, the loop coerces JSON strings in the input to the types of the submit schema with `coerce_json_strings`. [Native tools](tools.md) owns the tool definitions and this coercion.

`Run::submit` then runs these checks in order. Each failure returns an error result to the model, and the run goes on, so the model can call the tool again. The test `invalid_submit_is_retried` checks this.

1. The input has the marker `__invalid_json`. The error says to call the tool again with a valid object.
2. The policy check returns `Deny`. The error is `Denied by <layer> `<rule>`: <reason>`. An agent that owes a reply to another subagent gets a denial here, because it must reply first. The test `a_run_that_owes_an_answer_is_reminded_to_reply_and_cannot_submit` checks this.
3. `validate_submit` rejects the input against the schema of the agent. The error is `The <tool> input is invalid: <reason>. Fix it and call <tool> again.` [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md) owns the submit tool of each agent and its schema.
4. `doc::check_submit` rejects the input, for example when a document is missing. The error ends with `Nothing was recorded.` The test `explore_submits_only_after_its_document` checks this. [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md) owns the typed stage documents.
5. The status is `ok` and the agent has a report file that does not exist. The agent `CodeReviewer` is exempt. The error is `Write your report to <path> before you call <tool>, because the engine reads the report at that path.` The test `submit_needs_the_report_file` checks this.

When all checks pass, the result is `Result received.` Each other call in the same response gets the result `Not run: the run ended with the submit call.` The submit call does not add to `tool_calls`.

### A run with no submit call

If the model answers with no tool call, the loop cannot know whether the work is done. It adds a user reminder one time for each run (`reminded`): `Call <submit tool> now with your result. The engine reads only that call, so a result given in text is lost.` If the run owes a reply to another subagent (`owes_reply`), the reminder is the reply instruction of `coord::reply_instruction` instead. The loop sets `reminded` on the first such response and never resets it. If the model sends a second response with no tool call in the run, the run returns `Ok` with `submit` empty and the last text as `final_text`. Tool-call turns between the two responses do not reset the flag. The engine then decides what an `Ok` result without a submit payload means. The test `missing_submit_gets_one_reminder` checks this.

## Usage and cost records

The loop keeps one `Usage` total for the execution in a shared value, and it reports usage in two forms. After each model response the loop emits a `Turn` delta and then a `Usage` delta. The `Turn` delta holds the usage and cost of that response alone and the IDs of the tool calls that the response made. The `Usage` delta holds the running total. Both deltas come after the thinking and text of the response and before its `ToolCall` deltas. The test `each_response_reports_its_own_cost_before_its_tool_calls` checks the order. The `Turn` delta lets a screen show the cost of each tool call, which the total does not give.

The provider fills `cost_usd` for a response, with the price formula of the catalog. [Model providers and pricing](providers-and-pricing.md) owns the formula. The loop only adds the numbers. A compaction call adds its usage in the same way, with an empty call ID list.

The fields of `Usage` are:

| Field | Meaning | How the total changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `input_tokens` | Prompt tokens, without cache reads and writes | Sum |
| `output_tokens` | Output tokens | Sum |
| `cache_read_tokens` | Tokens read from the prompt cache | Sum |
| `cache_write_tokens` | Every cache write, 5-minute and 1-hour TTL together | Sum |
| `cache_write_1h_tokens` | The part of the cache writes that used the 1-hour TTL, which costs more | Sum |
| `cost_usd` | Cost in US dollars | Sum |
| `tool_calls` | Calls that went through tool dispatch | The loop adds 1 for each call |
| `build_ms` | Wall time of build and test commands | The loop adds the duration of each such Bash call |
| `context_tokens` | Size of the latest request: its prompt and its output | The latest nonzero value, not a sum |

The result of every end, also an error, a cancel, and a timeout, carries the usage total. The run does not lose the cost of the turns that finished. The engine stores the result in the `executions` table. See [Storage](storage.md).

## Cancellation and timeout

A run must stop when the user stops it, and it must stop when it takes too long. `NativeExecutor::run` wraps the loop for both cases. It starts the loop as a future and waits in a `select` for the first of three events:

```rust
let outcome = tokio::select! {
    r = &mut fut => return r,
    _ = cancel.cancelled() => ExecutionStatus::Cancelled,
    _ = tokio::time::sleep(budget) => ExecutionStatus::Error,
};
inner.cancel();
let _ = tokio::time::timeout(CLEANUP_GRACE, &mut fut).await;
```

The loop receives a child token (`inner`) of the token of the caller. After a cancel or a timeout, the wrapper cancels the child token. Providers and tools watch this token. A running Bash command is killed, and a streaming request stops. The wrapper then gives the loop `CLEANUP_GRACE` (3 seconds) to end, so the tools can kill their processes. After that, it returns without more waiting. The test `cancel_is_immediate` checks that a run with a `sleep 30` command ends in less than 5 seconds.

### What happens when

- **The user cancels:** the result has the status `Cancelled`, the usage so far, and the `Status` delta `Cancelled.`
- **The time budget ends:** the result has the status `Error`, the usage so far, the error `timed out after <n> s`, and the `Status` delta `Timed out after <n> s.` The test `timeout_is_an_error` checks this.
- **The cancel comes between two turns:** the loop checks the token at the start of each turn and returns `Cancelled`.
- **The cancel comes during a model call or a compaction call:** the provider returns `ProviderError::Cancelled` and the loop returns `Cancelled`.
- **The run waits for a permission answer:** the time budget keeps running, because the wait is inside the loop future.
- **The future is dropped:** the scratch directory of the sandbox is removed.

The budget is `ExecutionSpec.timeout_secs`, with a minimum of 1 second. The engine copies it from the agent definition. See [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md). The user stops a session or an execution in the console. [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) explains how the stop reaches the cancel token.

### For the user

| Control | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time budget `timeout_secs` | Set by each agent definition | The agent registry in the source | After a new build | Status `error` and the message `timed out after <n> s` on the execution screen | No user setting. Stop the run earlier in the console |
| Cancel | Not applicable | The cancel token of the execution | At once, and the run ends within 3 seconds of cleanup | Status `cancelled` and the `Cancelled.` message | Use the stop control of the session or execution |

## Output flush to the Activity view

A model streams its answer in very small pieces. If the loop emitted one delta for each piece, the Activity view shows one row for each token. The `Coalescer` collects the pieces and emits readable chunks.

The `Coalescer` holds one buffer and a flag for thinking or text. It emits the buffer in these cases:

- The buffer reaches `FLUSH_AT` (160 bytes), or the buffer ends with a newline.
- The stream switches between thinking and text. The loop first emits the old kind, then starts the new one.
- A server tool is used (`ServerToolUsed`). The loop flushes, then emits the `Status` delta `<name>: <summary>`.
- The model call ends. `Run::chat` flushes the rest, also when the call failed.

The test `coalescer_chunks` checks that ten pushes of three bytes give one text chunk of 30 bytes, and one thinking chunk after the switch.

Tool output has its own limit. A `ToolResult` delta carries at most `EMIT_LIMIT` (8 KB, 8 \* 1024 bytes). The `truncate` function cuts at a character boundary and appends `... (<n> more bytes)`. This cut only affects what the Activity view and the event store keep. The model gets the full output of the tool, up to the cap of the tool itself. See [Native tools](tools.md) for the caps of each tool.

## Limits and defaults of the loop

| Constant | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_TURNS` | 400 | Model turns in one execution. At 400, the run ends with `Error` |
| `MAX_TOKEN_CONTINUES` | 3 | Continue messages after a `MaxTokens` stop without a tool call, for the whole run |
| `COMPACT_AT` | 0.95 | Share of the context window at which compaction starts |
| `COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH` | 0.02 | Share of the window by which the context must grow before a retry of a compaction that gave no summary or failed |
| `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` | 200,000 tokens | Window for a model that the catalog does not list |
| `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT` | 32,000 tokens | `max_tokens` for a model that the catalog does not list |
| `EMIT_LIMIT` | 8 KB | Size of an emitted `ToolResult` output |
| `CLEANUP_GRACE` | 3 seconds | Time that a cancelled or timed-out run has to kill its tools |
| `Coalescer::FLUSH_AT` | 160 bytes | Size of a buffered text or thinking chunk |
| `COMPACT_INSTRUCTIONS` | Text | The instruction that tells the model what the summary keeps |
| `AFTER_COMPACTION` | Text | The user message that follows a summary |
| `COMPACTION_RECORD` | `compaction` | The role of the transcript record that stores a window |

## What the loop does not do

- It does not retry a failed model request. The provider retries, and then the run ends with `Error`.
- It does not guarantee a summary. A provider can return none, and then the conversation keeps its size. A conversation that grows past the window then fails at the provider.
- It counts tokens in new messages with an estimate of 4 characters for each token. The estimate can be wrong, and the next response gives the exact count.
- It does not keep tool results across a compaction. The model must read a file again if it needs the content.
- It does not make the policy engine a sandbox. The policy engine judges each call, and the sandbox limits what a Bash command can reach. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) and [Sandbox](sandbox.md).
- It does not decide what an `Ok` result without a submit payload means. The engine decides.
- It does not wait more than `CLEANUP_GRACE` for a tool to stop after a cancel or a timeout.
