sections.title: Harness executors
sections.summary: How Ostra runs one agent inside Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, or Antigravity under a PTY: launch, adapters, hook bridge, MCP shim, nudges, prompt detection, terminal log, usage watch, and scratch homes.
sections.body:
## What a harness executor does

A harness is an installed coding agent program: Claude Code (`claude`), Codex (`codex`), Grok Build (`grok`), or Antigravity (`agy`). Each harness has its own tools, its own permission system, and its own loop. Ostra must still check every tool call, collect one result for each agent, and show the terminal to the user. The crate `ostra-exec-harness` solves this problem. It starts the harness in a PTY (a pseudo-terminal) and routes every tool call through the policy engine of Ostra.

The harness executor `HarnessExecutor` implements the `Executor` trait. See [Architecture and crate map](architecture.md) for the trait and for `ExecutionSpec`. The native executor is the other implementation. See [Native executor loop](native-executor.md).

These parts work together in one harness execution:

- **Launch plan.** `launch::plan` builds the command line, the environment, and the config files for one harness.
- **PTY session.** `PtySession` runs the harness in a terminal and mirrors the screen.
- **Hook bridge.** The harness runs `ostra hook` for each hook event. The command asks the server for a decision.
- **MCP stdio shim.** The harness runs `ostra mcp-stdio` as an MCP server. The command forwards each message to the server and serves the `submit_<agent>` tool and the other Ostra tools.
- **Live execution.** `LiveExecution` records what arrives through the hooks and the shim. The executor waits on it.
- **Supervisor.** `HarnessExecutor::supervise` watches the run and decides how it ends.

The agent ends its run with one call: its `submit_<agent>` tool, which the MCP shim serves. Ostra reads only that call. A run that ends without it fails. [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md) explains the submit tools.

### Where each part lives

| File | Content |
| --- | --- |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/executor.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/executor.rs) | `HarnessExecutor`, the launch steps, the supervision loop, and the prompt markers |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/launch.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/launch.rs) | The launch plan of each harness and `materialize` |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/command.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/command.rs) | How a command name becomes a program on Windows |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/live.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/live.rs) | `LiveExecution`, `LiveRegistry`, and the Stop verdict |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/outcome.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/outcome.rs) | The `End` values and the conversion to `ExecutionResult` |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/adapters`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/adapters) | One adapter for each harness |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/bridge.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/bridge.rs) | `HarnessBridge`, `run_hook_cli`, and `run_mcp_stdio` |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/protocol.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/protocol.rs) | The wire shapes, the environment names, and the paths |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/services.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/services.rs) | The `BridgeServices` trait that the server implements |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/pty.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/pty.rs) | `PtySession` and `PtyRegistry` |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/term_log.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/term_log.rs) | The terminal log on disk |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/usage_watch.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/usage_watch.rs), [`transcript.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/transcript.rs) | Live usage from the session file of the harness |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/sandbox.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/sandbox.rs) | The wrap of the CLI in the sandbox and the cleanup |
| [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/setup.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/setup.rs) | Install and login checks and the Antigravity integration |
| [`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs) | The server side: the routes, the policy for each execution, and the tools |

This page stops at the border of two other subsystems. [Sandbox](sandbox.md) explains the profile, the backends, and the egress proxy. [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) explains the guards and the permission rules.

## Launch of one harness execution

The method `HarnessExecutor::launch` prepares and starts the CLI. If a step fails, the executor returns `ExecutionResult::error` and the run never starts. Every launch error starts with the prefix `harness-launch:` (the constant `LAUNCH_PREFIX`). The engine reads the prefix `harness-` and opens a `HarnessFailure` gate instead of a normal retry. See [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md) for the gate.

These steps run in order:

1. Copy the executor config and compute the sandbox settings for the workspace.
2. Read the command with `GlobalConfig::harness_command`. Check it with `which::which`. If it is missing, return the error ``"`<command>` (<display name>) is not installed"``.
3. For Antigravity, call `ensure_agy_integration`. See [Machine setup and the Antigravity integration](#machine-setup-and-the-antigravity-integration).
4. Create the execution folder `.state/harness/<execution id>/` in the session folder. The helper `harness_execution_dir` gives the path.
5. Build `LaunchInput`: the extra args from `harness.<name>.args`, the bridge URL and socket, a new token, the session ID to resume, and the names of credential variables.
6. Call `launch::plan` to make the `LaunchPlan`.
7. Call `launch::materialize` to write the files and make the symlinks of the plan.
8. Call `sandbox::wrap`. If the config allows it and no sandbox exists, the plan stays unchanged and Ostra sends a status message that the harness runs without a sandbox.
9. Create the terminal log. The log appends to the old file only when the run resumes under the same execution ID.
10. Call `PtySession::spawn`, hand the sandbox members to the session with `hold`, and send the status message that the harness runs in the terminal.

After the launch, `run` puts the PTY in the `PtyRegistry`, starts the usage follower as a task, and calls `supervise`. After `supervise` returns, `run` does these steps:

1. Repair planted `commondir` files in the repositories one last time.
2. Cancel the usage follower and wait for it, so that no live usage arrives after the final result.
3. If the run was cancelled, type Esc and wait 400 ms. Esc ends the turn of the CLI, so the CLI saves its session whole and a later run can resume it.
4. Read the screen text, then call `terminate` with a grace time of 3 seconds.
5. Remove the PTY from the registry, call `sandbox::cleanup`, and for Codex delete the profile file.
6. Convert the end to an `ExecutionResult` with `outcome::result`, then remove the live execution. The token stops working at that point.

### What happens when

- **The command is not on `PATH`.** The launch fails with `harness-launch:` and the not-installed message. The run never starts.
- **A fresh launch has a first message longer than `MAX_ARG_PROMPT`.** `MAX_ARG_PROMPT` is 96 KiB (98,304 bytes). `prompt_arg` calls `first_prompt` only when the run has no session ID to resume. `first_prompt` then writes the first message to `first-message.md` in the execution folder. The prompt argument tells the agent to read that file before its first other tool call. A long text cannot go on the command line.
- **The run resumes.** If the engine gives a native session ID, the plan uses the resume form of the harness. `prompt_arg` does not call `first_prompt`, so Ostra writes no `first-message.md`. The prompt is the resume note, or a default text: "Ostra resumed this session after an interruption." The text names the submit tool.
- **The run is an inspection.** The harness opens a finished session read-only. The CLI gets no prompt, and the bridge refuses every tool call. See [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) for inspect.
- **The sandbox is not available.** If the config requires a sandbox, `wrap` returns an error and the launch fails. If the config allows no sandbox, the run starts and the Status delta says so. Ostra writes the warning to the log only once for each server run.

### How the command name becomes a program

On Unix, `command::resolve` starts the name as given. On Windows, it searches `PATH` with the extensions in `PATHEXT`, in `PATH` order. npm installs a CLI as three files: an extensionless script for Git Bash, a `.cmd` file, and a `.ps1` file. Windows cannot start the first file. `cmd.exe` cannot pass the multi-line arguments that a harness receives.

Therefore, for an npm `.cmd` file, Ostra reads the script path from the shim and starts `node` with that script. Ostra uses `node.exe` next to the shim if it exists. Otherwise it uses `node` from `PATH`. The tests use the constant `SHIM`, a sample npm shim file.

Three Windows errors can occur:

1. The command is not on `PATH`: "Install `<command>` or name its full path, because it is not on this machine's PATH."
2. The command is a batch file that is not an npm shim: "Set the harness command to an .exe, because <path> is a batch file and cmd.exe cannot pass the multi-line arguments a harness receives."
3. The command is an npm `.cmd` shim, but `node.exe` is neither beside the shim nor on `PATH`: "Install Node.js, because <path> is an npm command that runs with node." The function `from_file` in `command.rs` returns this error.

### For the user

`<name>` is one of `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`.

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `harness.<name>.command` | The harness name: `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy` | The table `[harness.<name>]` in the global settings file (`$OSTRA_CONFIG`, else `<config dir>/ostra/config.toml`) | At the next execution. The server calls `set_global` when settings change, and each launch reads them again | The setup check shows `command`, `installed`, `version`, and `logged_in` for each harness | Set a program name or a full path. An empty value falls back to the harness name |
| `harness.<name>.args` | An empty list | The same table | At the next execution | The Terminal tab of the execution shows the CLI and its errors | Remove entries from the list |

The extra args go before the flags that Ostra adds. For Codex, the words `resume <session>` go first when the run resumes. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) for the settings files.

Caution: do not add `-p` or `--profile` to `harness.codex.args`. Ostra then does not write its restricted profile, Codex asks to trust the folder, and Ostra refuses that prompt. The run fails.

## Launch plan of each harness

The function `launch::plan` returns a `LaunchPlan` for one execution. The plan holds the program, the arguments, the environment, the working folder, files to write, symlinks to make, the session ID that Ostra chose, the variables to remove, and an optional `tty_param` for Seatbelt. The working folder is the repository root of the project. Each flag in the plans was checked against an installed CLI. The source comment names these versions: claude 2.1.280, codex 0.153.4, grok 1.0.30, and agy 1.2.6.

Three plans pass the `ostra` MCP server to the harness, each in its own way:

- `plan_claude` writes the MCP server object to `claude-mcp.json`.
- `plan_codex` passes the `ostra` MCP server in `-c` arguments.
- `plan_grok` writes the `ostra` MCP server table to the private `config.toml`.

The plan `plan_agy` writes the agent file `ostra-<agent>.md` into `LaunchPlan.files`. It writes `first-message.md` there only on a fresh launch, and only when the first message is longer than `MAX_ARG_PROMPT`. The reason is that `prompt_arg` calls `first_prompt` only when `inp.resume_session` is empty. On a resumed run, `prompt_arg` sends `resume_prompt`, or no prompt for an inspection. The plan `plan_agy` never writes an MCP entry, and `LaunchPlan.links` is empty. Setup registers the `ostra` server once for the whole machine through `agy mcp add`. See [Machine setup and the Antigravity integration](#machine-setup-and-the-antigravity-integration) for the exact test. [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md) explains the workspace MCP servers that the `ostra` server adds.

### Environment that every plan sets

Every plan sets four variables. The hook and the shim read them.

| Variable | Constant | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_URL` | `ENV_URL` | The base URL of the server, for example `http://127.0.0.1:4100` |
| `OSTRA_EXECUTION` | `ENV_EXECUTION` | The execution ID |
| `OSTRA_TOKEN` | `ENV_TOKEN` | The token of this execution |
| `OSTRA_HARNESS` | `ENV_HARNESS` | The harness name |

The plan also adds the git variables from `ostra_core::git::agent_env()`. The plan removes every credential variable of the Ostra environment, except the variables that the CLI reads to sign in. These variables stay:

| Harness | Variables that the harness keeps |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` |
| Codex | `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_BASE_URL` |
| Antigravity | `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY` |
| Grok Build | none |

The agent shell inside the CLI can read the variables that stay. Antigravity keeps its login in the OS keychain. The macOS sandbox denies the keychain, so Antigravity needs one of the two variables there.

The PTY launcher also removes the variables in `PARENT_SESSION_ENV`. See [PTY sessions](#pty-sessions).

### Flags of each harness

Ostra caps the effort at the highest value that the CLI accepts: `max` for Claude Code, `xhigh` for Codex, and `high` for Grok Build and Antigravity.

| Harness | Main flags | Hooks and MCP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `--session-id <uuid>` or `--resume <id>`, `--setting-sources user`, `--settings <file>`, `--strict-mcp-config`, `--mcp-config <file>`, `--append-system-prompt-file`, `--add-dir <session dir>`, `--disallowed-tools Agent,Task,AskUserQuestion,EnterPlanMode,ExitPlanMode`, `--tools <list>`, `--permission-mode default`, `--model`, `--effort` | `claude-settings.json` in the execution folder holds the hooks. `claude-mcp.json` holds the MCP server |
| Codex | `-c` overrides, `-p <profile>`, `--disable multi_agent`, `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`, `-C <repo>`, `-m <model>` | Hooks and the `ostra` MCP server go in `-c` overrides. No file holds them |
| Grok Build | `--session-id <uuid>` or `--resume <id>`, `--leader-socket`, `--cwd`, `--no-subagents`, `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`, `--rules <system prompt>`, `-m`, `--reasoning-effort` | A per-execution `config.toml` in a private `GROK_HOME` holds the hooks and the MCP server |
| Antigravity | `--conversation <id>` when it resumes, `--agent ostra-<agent>`, `--add-dir`, `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--model`, `--effort`, `-i <prompt>` | One global plugin holds the hooks. `agy mcp add` registers the MCP server, through the setup code and not through the plan |

The prompt goes last as a positional argument. For Antigravity, it follows `-i`. When the run is an inspection, the prompt is absent.

Only Claude Code and Antigravity get `--add-dir` for the workspace artifacts folder and the books folder. The function `artifacts_dir_args` runs only in `plan_claude` and `plan_agy`. It adds one `--add-dir` for each of the two folders that exists, so the CLI can read them outside its working folder. Codex and Grok Build get no `--add-dir` for these folders.

### Claude Code

Claude Code loads only the user settings (`--setting-sources user`) and only the MCP config of Ostra (`--strict-mcp-config`). The project and local settings are files of the repository. Their hooks, env, and permissions can run outside the guards of Ostra. Flag settings win over user settings, so a user settings file cannot switch off the hooks of Ostra. The settings file sets `disableAllHooks` to `false`. If the CLI runs in the sandbox of Ostra, the file sets `sandbox.enabled` to `false`, because macOS cannot nest Seatbelt sandboxes.

The settings file registers five hooks: `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, and `PostToolUseFailure` with the matcher `*`, and `Stop` and `SessionStart`. The tool list comes from the capabilities of the agent: `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `WebSearch`, and `WebFetch`. A `Skill` capability adds `Read`. Ostra always adds `ToolSearch`. Interactive Claude Code connects MCP servers after it starts and shows their tools only as deferred tools. Without `ToolSearch`, the `mcp__ostra__*` tools never reach the model.

An inspection uses the constant `INSPECT_TOOLS` (`Read,Bash,Grep,Glob`) and no MCP config. The CLI keeps plain tools for the bridge to refuse. A model that has no tool replies with nothing when the user asks it to run a command.

### Codex

Codex reads the trust of a folder only from config files, not from `-c`. Ostra therefore writes a profile file `ostra-restricted-<id>.config.toml` in `$CODEX_HOME` (default `~/.codex`) and passes `-p ostra-restricted-<id>`. The profile marks the repository, and each parent folder up to its git root, as `trust_level = "untrusted"`. The walk covers at most 32 folders. Codex then opens the folder restricted. Its `.codex/` config, hooks, and exec policies stay off, and the saved trust of the user does not change. Each execution has its own profile name, so deleting it at the end never affects another run.

Codex also receives `-c check_for_update_on_startup=false`. Codex updates itself at startup and then exits, which ends the run before it starts. The system prompt goes in `-c developer_instructions`. The hook timeout and the tool timeout are `HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS`. The flag `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` is needed because the hooks of Ostra change with each execution and so can never hold saved hook trust. Project hooks stay off anyway, because the folder opens restricted.

### Grok Build

Grok Build reads its hooks and MCP servers from its home folder. Ostra builds a private home `grok-home` in the execution folder and sets `GROK_HOME` to it. The home holds symlinks to every entry of the real `GROK_HOME` (default `~/.grok`) except the entries in `GROK_PRIVATE`: `config.toml`, `trusted_folders.toml`, and `leader.sock`. Entries that start with `leader-` or end with `.lock` are also skipped. The session therefore runs its own leader and reads the hooks of this execution.

The private `config.toml` is the user config, without any older `ostra` MCP table, plus the hooks, the `ostra` MCP server, and an `env` table with the four `OSTRA_*` variables. The private `trusted_folders.toml` is the user list plus the session folder. Ostra trusts the session folder because it is the folder of Ostra. Ostra never trusts the repository for the user. See [Prompt detection](#prompt-detection-login-trust-model-offers-and-fatal-errors). Ostra also sets `GROK_SUBAGENTS=0`.

### Antigravity

Antigravity reads hooks and MCP servers only from global config. Ostra installs one integration that does nothing unless `$OSTRA_EXECUTION` is set. Each execution writes one agent file, `~/.gemini/config/plugins/ostra/agents/ostra-<agent>.md`. The agent file holds the system prompt, the model, the effort, the tool list, the timeout, and the flags `subagent: false`, `hidden: true`, and `inheritMcp: true`. The effort values `xhigh` and `max` become `high` in that file. See [Machine setup and the Antigravity integration](#machine-setup-and-the-antigravity-integration).

The execution also writes `first-message.md` in the execution folder, but only on a fresh launch with a first message longer than `MAX_ARG_PROMPT`. On a resumed run, the prompt after `-i` is the resume note or the default resume text. An inspection sends no `-i` prompt.

### Files and quoting

The function `materialize` writes each file of the plan with owner-only permission and creates the symlinks. It skips a link that already exists. The owner-only mode matters because the Grok config holds the bridge token.

Hook commands run through a shell. On Unix, `shell_quote` uses POSIX single quotes. On Windows, the word must mean the same in Git Bash and in `cmd`. These rules apply to a word on Windows:

- Separators become `/`.
- A word made only of ASCII letters, digits, and the characters `-_./:=@+,` stays bare.
- Any other word gets double quotes, unless it holds one of the characters `"`, `%`, `$`, `` ` ``, `!`, or `'`. A space is one such case, but not the only one.
- A word with one of those characters falls back to POSIX quoting, because either shell expands them inside double quotes.

`posix_quote` is for text that the bash parser of Ostra reads.

## The supervision loop and how a run ends

The method `supervise` runs a loop until the run reaches one of the `End` values. The budget is `timeout_secs` of the `ExecutionSpec`, with a minimum of 30 seconds. The loop wakes at least every 500 ms. It also wakes when the live execution changes, when the PTY exits, or when the run is cancelled.

### Flow of one loop turn

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Wait for cancel, change, or PTY exit"] --> B{"Cancelled or PTY exited?"}
  B -->|"cancelled"| C["End Cancelled"]
  B -->|"exited"| D["End Submitted or Exited"]
  B -->|"change"| E{"Submit recorded?"}
  E -->|"yes"| F["Wait for Stop, quiet Antigravity, or 20 seconds"]
  F --> G["End Submitted"]
  E -->|"no"| H{"Run waits for a wake message?"}
  H -->|"yes"| I["Type the wake message"]
  I --> A
  H -->|"no"| J{"Gave up or budget used?"}
  J -->|"yes"| K["End GaveUp or Timeout"]
  J -->|"no"| L["Answer prompts, nudge if quiet"]
  L --> A
```

### The end values

The enum `End` in `outcome.rs` has eight values. The function `outcome::result` turns each value into an `ExecutionResult`.

| End | Cause | Status | Error text |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Submitted` | The agent called its submit tool, and the turn ended | From the `status` field of the submit: `stuck` is `Stuck`, `handoff` is `Handoff`, else `Ok` | none |
| `Cancelled` | The cancellation token fired | `Cancelled` | none |
| `Auth` | A login prompt is on the screen | `Error` | `harness-auth: <name> is not logged in. Log in from its terminal, then retry.` |
| `Exited` early | The CLI exited in less than `LAUNCH_WINDOW` (20 s) with no tool call | `Error` | `harness-auth:` if the screen has an auth marker, else `harness-launch:`, then the last 12 non-empty screen lines |
| `Exited` late | The CLI exited before the agent submitted | `Error` | `<name> exited (code <n>) before the agent called <submit tool>.` |
| `GaveUp` | Three Stop events came without a submit | `Error` | `The agent ended its turn three times without calling <submit tool>.` |
| `Idle` | The session stayed quiet after two reminders | `Error` | `The session went quiet without calling <submit tool>, and two reminders did not help.` |
| `Fatal` | A fatal marker or a refused trust prompt | `Error` | `harness-launch: <name> could not start the session: <why>.` and the last 12 screen lines |
| `Timeout` | The budget passed | `Error` | `The execution passed its <n> s budget and was stopped.` |

The prefixes are `AUTH_PREFIX` (`harness-auth:`) and `LAUNCH_PREFIX` (`harness-launch:`). If the error starts with `harness-`, the engine does not retry the execution by itself. It opens a `HarnessFailure` gate. The gate tells the user to log in from the terminal and retry, or to run the execution on the native executor.

If Antigravity needs a login and the sandbox is Seatbelt, the `Auth` error has another text. It asks the user to set `GEMINI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY` in the Ostra environment. On macOS, Antigravity keeps its login in the keychain, which the sandbox closes to agents.

Every result also carries the usage and the final text. The usage comes from the session file of the harness. The count `tool_calls` is the larger of the file count and the count of the bridge. The final text is the last message from the Stop hook, else the last message in the session file. See [Usage watch and transcript facts](#usage-watch-and-transcript-facts).

### What happens when

- **The agent submits.** The loop records the time of the first submit. The run ends in one of three cases: a Stop event arrives after the submit (`stopped_after_submit`), Antigravity has been quiet for `AGY_QUIET_AFTER_SUBMIT` (4 s), or `AFTER_SUBMIT_GRACE` (20 s) passes. Antigravity has no Stop hook, so it uses the quiet time. The grace time closes a harness that does not end its turn.
- **The PTY exits.** If a submit exists, the end is `Submitted`. If not, the end is `Exited`.
- **The run waits for a wake message.** After a coordination call, the process stays up and the wait does not count against the budget (Rule H2). The loop adds the waiting time to the deadline. Wake is a message and not a tool. When Ostra has a message, it types the message in the terminal with `type_line`. If Ostra has no message, the end is `Fatal` with the text "Ostra has no message to wake this run with." See [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md) for ask, reply, and wake.
- **The user cancels.** The end is `Cancelled`. Esc and `terminate` run in the same way as in the steps after the launch.
- **The run is an inspection.** The loop does not look for a submit, a wait, a give-up, or an idle time. If the CLI exits or the budget passes, `run` returns `Ok` with the text "The read-only session ended."
- **The git check.** Every `GIT_CHECK_EVERY` (2 s), the loop calls `ostra_sandbox::repair_git_dirs` for the repositories of the repo root and the workspace root. A repair removes a planted `commondir`. Each repair becomes a deny from the `git-metadata` guard, which is a containment signal. Ostra cannot check some commands of the CLI with a hook, so it checks the repositories on a clock. This keeps short the time that a planted `commondir` can reach the git of the user. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) for containment signals.
- **A session ID appears.** The loop sends a `NativeSessionId` delta each time the session ID changes. The engine saves the ID to resume the run later.

## Idle nudges and Stop nudges

A harness can stop without its submit call, or go quiet. Ostra reminds it in two ways. Both ways use the same text: "Call the `<tool>` tool now, with your result, before you stop. Ostra reads only that call, so a run that ends without it is recorded as failed. If a required file is not written yet, write it first." If the run owes an answer to another agent, the text asks the run to call `subagent_reply` first. That rule is Rule H3. The reply tool name depends on the harness.

### Stop nudges

The Stop hook calls `LiveExecution::on_stop`. The method decides one verdict for each Stop event, in this order:

```rust
let verdict = if self.inspect.load(Ordering::SeqCst) || s.waiting {
    StopVerdict::Allow
} else if s.submit.is_some() {
    s.stopped_after_submit = true;
    StopVerdict::Allow
} else if s.stops_without_submit < MAX_STOP_NUDGES {
    s.stops_without_submit += 1;
    let nudge = if self.owes_reply.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
        ostra_core::coord::reply_instruction(ostra_core::coord::reply_tool(
            ostra_core::ExecutorKind::Harness(self.harness),
        ))
    } else {
        missing_submit_instruction(self.agent)
    };
    StopVerdict::Block(nudge)
} else {
    s.gave_up = true;
    StopVerdict::Allow
};
```

In the Block branch, `nudge` is the reply instruction when `owes_reply` is set. Otherwise it is `missing_submit_instruction`. The constant `MAX_STOP_NUDGES` is 2. The first two Stop events without a submit get `Block`, so the adapter answers with a block and the harness continues its turn. The third Stop event gets `Allow` and sets `gave_up`. The loop then ends with `GaveUp`. This is why the error text says three times.

An inspection and a waiting run always get `Allow`. An inspection expects no submit. A waiting run ends its turn on purpose, and the answer arrives later.

### Idle nudges

A harness that prints nothing and sends no hook cannot send a Stop event. The loop therefore checks the time. If both the last hook activity and the last terminal output are older than `idle_nudge`, the loop types the reminder into the terminal with `type_line`. The default is `DEFAULT_IDLE_NUDGE`, 240 seconds. The constant `MAX_IDLE_NUDGES` is 2. After two reminders, the next quiet period ends the run with `Idle`.

```rust
if !inspect && s.last_activity.elapsed().min(pty.idle_for()) >= idle_nudge {
    if nudges >= MAX_IDLE_NUDGES {
        return End::Idle;
    }
    nudges += 1;
    live.touch();
    let _ = pty.type_line(&live.nudge()).await;
    ...
}
```

A tool call, a hook event, or terminal output resets the quiet time. The nudge itself also resets it.

### For the user

No setting controls the nudges. `idle_nudge` is a field of `HarnessExecutorConfig`, and the code sets it to 240 seconds. Each idle nudge sends a Status delta that says the session went quiet and that Ostra reminded it to submit. The execution view shows this Status line. A Stop nudge shows in the terminal as the reminder text. To stop a nudge loop, stop the execution from the console.

## Prompt detection: login, trust, model offers, and fatal errors

A harness can show a screen that waits for the user: a login, a folder-trust question, or a new-model offer. Nobody watches the terminal of a run, so a screen that waits for the user uses the whole budget. The supervisor reads the screen text and reacts. It does this only when `tool_calls` is 0 and the run is younger than 120 seconds. After the first tool call, the checks stop, because a normal screen can then contain words such as "login" in a file name.

### Markers

The markers are lowercase strings. The supervisor lowercases the screen before it compares.

| Constant | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTH_MARKERS` | The harness needs a login | `please log in`, `not logged in`, `run /login`, `invalid api key`, `oauth token has expired`, `finish signing in`, `select login method`, `sign in with chatgpt`, `waiting for auth`, `login with google` |
| `FATAL_MARKERS` | The harness cannot start the session | `failed to construct executor`, `unknown component:`, `unknown model`, `model not found` |
| `TRUST_MARKERS` | A folder-trust prompt | `do you trust the files in this folder`, `trust this folder`, `trust this project`, `open restricted` |
| `MODEL_OFFER_MARKERS` | A new-model offer | `use existing model` |

The full lists are in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/executor.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/executor.rs). The `AUTH_MARKERS` also include the browser sign-in text of Grok Build (`make sure your browser shows this code`), which it shows when its saved token has expired.

### Answers to a trust prompt

The supervisor answers a trust prompt at most 6 times (`trust_steps < 6`). After each key press it waits 400 ms. The function `trust_answer` returns one of three answers: `Confirm` (Enter), `Down` (the Down key), or `Refuse` (end the run with a reason). The function reads the highlighted option, because the default option differs between versions. For example, Claude Code 2.1.280 shows "No, exit" first.

| Harness | Answer | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | Move to "Yes" and press Enter | Claude Code loads only user settings and the MCP config of Ostra, so trust adds nothing from the repository |
| Codex | Move to "Open restricted" and press Enter. For any other trust prompt, end the run with `Fatal` | "Trust and continue" saves trust. Then Codex loads the `.codex/` config and hooks of the repository, outside the guards of Ostra |
| Grok Build | Always end the run with `Fatal` | Trust makes Grok run the own hooks and MCP servers of the folder, so only the user can decide it |
| Antigravity | Move to "Yes" and press Enter | The same function as for Claude Code |

The `Fatal` text for Codex asks the user to remove `-p` or `--profile` from `[harness.codex].args`. The `Fatal` text for Grok Build asks the user to trust the folder in Grok first: run `grok` in that folder and answer yes. Then run the execution again.

### Model offers

Codex can show a new-model offer at startup (the source names "Meet GPT-6 Luna" in Codex 0.157). Ostra keeps the routed model, because accepting the offer switches the run and the default model of the user. The function `keep_model_key` presses Enter if "Use existing model" is highlighted. If "Try new model" is highlighted, it presses Down. The Status line says the run keeps its routed model.

### Login and fatal markers

If an auth marker is on the screen, the end is `Auth`. If a fatal marker is on the screen, the end is `Fatal` with the text `the harness reported "<marker>"`. Antigravity prints a resume line `agy --conversation=<id>`. If the live execution has no session ID yet, the loop reads the ID from the screen. The ID must have 32 or more characters of hex digits and hyphens.

### For the user

No setting controls the markers. To fix a login failure, log in from the terminal of the harness. The setup screens give a Terminal for this. See [Workspace, settings, and setup screens](web-workspace-and-setup.md). For Grok Build, trust the folder in Grok yourself. For Codex, remove `-p` and `--profile` from `harness.codex.args`.

## Harness adapters

Each harness sends hook payloads in its own shape and accepts decisions in its own shape. The policy engine reads one shape: Claude Code tool names and input shapes. An adapter converts between the two. The trait `Adapter` in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/adapters/mod.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/adapters/mod.rs) has seven methods: `kind`, `meta`, `parse_pre`, `parse_post`, `pre_response`, `post_response`, and `stop_response`. The function `for_harness` returns the adapter for a `HarnessKind`.

The method `parse_pre` returns `PreParse`. A `PreParse::Call` holds a canonical `ToolCall` for the policy engine. A `PreParse::Refuse` holds a reason, and the bridge denies the call without a policy check. The method `meta` reads the session ID, the transcript path, the working folder, and the last assistant message.

### Differences between the adapters

| Harness | Payload keys | Tool names that map to canonical tools | Answer to an allowed PreToolUse | Answer to a Stop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code (`Claude`) | `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `session_id`. CamelCase names also work | Own names are canonical. `MultiEdit` and `NotebookEdit` become `Edit`. `LS` becomes `Glob`. `PowerShell` stays opaque | `hookSpecificOutput` with `permissionDecision: allow` and an optional `additionalContext` | `{"decision":"block","reason":...}` or `{}` |
| Codex (`Codex`) | `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `session_id` | `Bash`, `exec_command`, `shell`, and `local_shell` become `Bash`. `apply_patch` becomes `ApplyPatch` | `{}`, or only `additionalContext` | Same as Claude Code |
| Grok Build (`Grok`) | `toolName`, `toolInput`, `sessionId`. Snake case names also work | `read_file`, `hashline_read` become `Read`. `write`, `write_file` become `Write`. `search_replace`, `hashline_edit`, `edit_file` become `Edit`. `run_terminal_command`, `monitor` become `Bash`. `grep` becomes `Grep`. `list_dir`, `glob` become `Glob`. `web_fetch` and `web_search` become `WebFetch` and `WebSearch` | Claude-shaped, with a reason clipped to 256 characters | A block, with the reason clipped to 256 characters |
| Antigravity (`Agy`) | `toolCall.name`, `toolCall.args` with PascalCase arguments. The session key is `conversationId` | `view_file`, `view_file_outline`, `view_code_item` become `Read`. `write_to_file` becomes `Write`. `replace_file_content` becomes `Edit`. `run_command`, `send_command_input` become `Bash`. `grep_search` becomes `Grep`. `find_by_name`, `list_dir` become `Glob`. `read_url_content` becomes `WebFetch`. `search_web` becomes `WebSearch` | `{"decision":"allow"}` | `{}` |

Any other tool becomes `Other:<name>`. The policy engine decides what to do with it. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).

### Why the answers differ

- **Claude Code.** Decisions go only in `hookSpecificOutput`, because a top-level `overwrite` field fails the hook schema.
- **Codex.** The PreToolUse schema rejects `permissionDecision: "allow"` without an `updatedInput`, and it rejects `ask`. An allowed call therefore answers `{}`.
- **Grok Build.** Grok clips every reason to its own `MAX_REASON_CHARS`, which is `GROK_REASON_MAX` (256) characters. The function `fit_reason` flattens white space. If the text is longer, it keeps the head and the last sentence, joined by " … ". It does so only if the head is at least `MIN_HEAD` (120) characters. Otherwise it keeps the first 256 characters. The reasons of Ostra lead with the correction and end with the instruction. Grok also caps the hook payload at 128 KiB, and a larger `toolInput` becomes a truncated string. Ostra cannot judge a truncated input, so it refuses the call with `TRUNCATED_REFUSAL`: split the call into smaller ones. The `PATH_KEYS` for a file path are `file_path`, `filePath`, `path`, `target_file`, and `targetFile`.
- **Antigravity.** The hook output is proto-validated, and an unknown field discards the whole response. PreToolUse therefore answers only `decision` and `reason`, and PostToolUse answers `{}`. The PostToolUse payload has no tool result, only `stepIdx` and, on failure, `error`. The outcome has `result_known: false`.

### Refused tools

Every adapter refuses two groups of tools before the policy check:

- **Spawn tools.** `Task`, `Agent`, `task`, `spawn_agent`, `spawn_subagent`, `invoke_subagent`, `define_subagent`, and any name that ends with `spawn_agent`. The reason is `LEAF_REFUSAL`: every Ostra agent is a leaf. A delegated task runs outside the guards of Ostra, and its result never reaches the engine.
- **Ask tools.** `AskUserQuestion`, `ask_user_question`, `request_user_input`, and `ask_question`. The reason is `ASK_REFUSAL`: Ostra asks the user from the gate of the pipeline, because nobody watches the terminal for questions.

### Ostra tool names and outcomes

The function `ostra_mcp_tool` recognizes a tool of the `ostra` MCP server by its name prefix, and `canonical_ostra_tool` maps the bare name to a canonical tool. [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md) owns the tool names.

The function `outcome_from` builds the `ToolOutcome` of a finished call. The output is clipped to `MAX_OUTCOME_CHARS` (64 KiB), and the text `[output truncated]` marks the cut. The exit code comes from the `PATTERNS` list in `exit_code_from`: four regular expressions for `Exit code N`, `exited with code N`, `exit status N`, and `exit code N`. If a Bash call has no code, Ostra assumes 1 for a flagged error and 0 for success, unless the call was interrupted. Codex gives no exit status, so its code stays unknown, and the policy reads the output text.

## Hook bridge

The hook bridge lets the policy engine of the server decide each tool call of a CLI that runs in another process. `HarnessBridge::handle_policy` is the server side. The command `ostra hook` is the CLI side.

### Hook events

The enum `HookEvent` has seven values: `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `Stop`, `SessionStart`, `PreInvocation`, and `PostInvocation`. The hook command line passes the event as `--event` in snake case, for example `pre_tool_use`. The parser also accepts the Pascal case names.

| Harness | Events that the launch plan registers |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `Stop`, `SessionStart` |
| Codex | `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, `SessionStart` |
| Grok Build | `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, `SessionStart` |
| Antigravity | `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PreInvocation`, `PostInvocation` |

The hook timeout is `HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS`, 86,400 seconds (24 hours). A permission ask waits for the user, so the hook must not time out first.

### One tool call through the bridge

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant CLI as Harness CLI
  participant Hook as ostra hook
  participant Route as POST /internal/policy
  participant Bridge as HarnessBridge
  participant Srv as ServerBridge
  participant Pol as ExecutionPolicy
  CLI->>Hook: PreToolUse payload on stdin
  Hook->>Route: PolicyRequest with Bearer token
  Route->>Bridge: handle_policy
  Bridge->>Bridge: authorize and parse_pre
  Bridge->>Srv: policy_check
  Srv->>Pol: check
  Pol-->>Srv: PolicyDecision
  Srv-->>Bridge: Allow, Deny, or Ask
  Bridge-->>Route: PolicyResponse
  Route-->>Hook: JSON body
  Hook-->>CLI: adapter answer on stdout
```

If the policy answer is `Ask`, the bridge calls `resolve_ask` and waits for the user, or for YOLO mode to answer. A yes gives `Allow`. A no gives a deny with the text "The user denied this call. Continue without it, or choose another way." See [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md) for YOLO.

### What `handle_policy` does for each event

1. **Authorize.** The execution must be in the `LiveRegistry` with the same token, and the server must also know it (`BridgeServices::authorize`). If not, a PreToolUse gets a deny with the text "This execution is not running under Ostra any more, so no tool call may run. Stop now." Other events get `{}`.
2. **Check the harness.** If the harness in the request differs from the harness of the execution, a PreToolUse gets a deny.
3. **Record the session.** The bridge stores the session ID and the transcript path from the payload.
4. **PreToolUse.** `PreParse::Refuse` becomes a deny. For a `Call`, the bridge counts the tool call and calls `decide`. The function `decide` denies a `submit_*` tool of another agent with the text that names the right submit tool. Otherwise it asks the server for a decision. A deny text has the form `<reason> (Ostra <layer>: <rule>)`, so the model reads the correction first and then the rule that fired.
5. **PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure.** The bridge marks activity and calls `policy_observe`. The notes that come back go to the model in `additionalContext`. These notes carry the build-streak warnings and the lessons of failures.
6. **Stop.** The bridge calls `stop_event` and then `on_stop`. See [Idle nudges and Stop nudges](#idle-nudges-and-stop-nudges).
7. **Other events.** `SessionStart`, `PreInvocation`, and `PostInvocation` only mark activity.

### What happens when

- **A PreToolUse payload cannot be read.** The hook never fails open. The bridge denies the call.
- **The server is not reachable.** `ostra hook` prints a deny for a PreToolUse: "Stop and end your turn: Ostra could not check this call (<why>)." The exit code is 0. Other events print nothing. The same deny happens if `OSTRA_URL` or `OSTRA_TOKEN` is missing, if the client cannot be built, if the server answers with an error status, or if the answer is unreadable.
- **`$OSTRA_EXECUTION` is not set.** The command reads the payload and exits with 0 without output. Antigravity registers its hooks globally, so the hook also runs in the sessions that a user starts alone. The hook is then inert.
- **The command line is wrong.** The command prints `ostra hook: <error>` on stderr and exits with 1. The arguments are `--execution`, `--harness`, and `--event`. The execution falls back to `$OSTRA_EXECUTION`, and the harness falls back to `$OSTRA_HARNESS`.
- **The request takes a long time.** A PreToolUse request has no timeout, because an ask waits for the user. Requests for the other events time out after 60 seconds.

### Authorization

`LiveRegistry::register` makes the token from two random UUIDs without hyphens, so the token has 64 hex characters. `authorize` compares the tokens in constant time. The token ends when `LiveRegistry::remove` runs at the end of the run. The `Bearer` header carries the token. A request without it gets status 401.

## MCP stdio shim

The command `ostra mcp-stdio` is an MCP server on stdio. The harness starts it as the MCP server named `ostra` (`MCP_SERVER_NAME`). It reads one JSON-RPC message for each line. It forwards each message in its own task to `POST /internal/mcp` with the same token. Messages in a batch are also forwarded one by one. The shim answers a line that is not JSON with the error `-32700` (parse error). If the server fails, the shim answers with `-32603` and the text "Ostra server error: <why>".

The execution comes from `--execution` or from `$OSTRA_EXECUTION`. If the execution, the URL, or the token is missing, the shim runs offline. It answers `initialize`, `server/discover`, and `ping`, lists no tools, and answers every `tools/call` with the text "Ostra tools work only inside an Ostra execution." A global registration of the shim is therefore inert outside Ostra.

### Methods that the bridge answers

`HarnessBridge::handle_mcp` handles these methods:

| Method | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| `initialize` | The version that the client asks for if the list `MCP_VERSIONS` has it, else `MCP_INITIALIZE_DEFAULT` (`2025-11-25`). The capabilities hold `tools` with `listChanged: false` |
| `server/discover` | The `supportedVersions` and the capabilities |
| `ping` | `{}` |
| `tools/list` | The submit tool of the agent first, then the other Ostra tools of the execution |
| `tools/call` | See below |
| `resources/list`, `prompts/list` | An empty list |
| Any other method | The error `-32601` (method not found) |

A message without an `id` is a notification and gets no answer. An unknown execution gets the error `-32001` ("execution is not running under Ostra").

The constant `MCP_VERSIONS` is `2024-11-05`, `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. The version `2026-07-28` is left out on purpose. Its results need `resultType`, `ttlMs`, and `cacheScope`. Claude Code rejects a `tools/list` without them, so the run gets no Ostra tools. Without that version in `server/discover`, clients fall back to the `initialize` handshake.

### The submit call

The call to the submit tool of the agent is the end of the run. The schema and the checks of each submit tool belong to [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md). The function `call_tool` in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/bridge.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/bridge.rs) runs these steps in order:

1. If the run owes a reply to another agent, the call fails with the reply instruction (Rule H3).
2. `coerce_json_strings` repairs string-encoded JSON arguments against the submit schema. For example, a model can send an array as a JSON string. The repair runs before the schema check on this path.
3. `validate_submit` checks the repaired arguments against the submit schema of the agent. If they fail, the text is: "Fix the arguments and call `<name>` again: <message>. Nothing was recorded."
4. The bridge runs `check_submit` for the typed stage documents. A failure also records nothing.
5. `record_submit` stores the payload. The first call wins. A later call gets "A result was already recorded for this run. End your turn now."

A success returns "Recorded. Your run is complete: end your turn now, without further tool calls." A call to the submit tool of another agent returns the error that names the right tool. See [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md) for the typed documents. See [Native tools](tools.md) for the coercion rules.

### Other Ostra tools

For each other tool, the bridge converts the name to the canonical tool, counts the call, and calls `decide`. A deny returns a tool error. An allowed call goes to `BridgeServices::mcp_call`. [Native tools](tools.md) owns the definitions of these tools. The result has a `RunEnd` value:

- `Continue`: the run goes on.
- `Wait`: the run asked another subagent. The bridge clears `owes_reply` and sets `waiting`, so a Stop is allowed. The process stays up (Rule H2).
- `Finish`: the bridge records a submit payload from the message of the call and the run ends.

### For the user

No setting controls the shim. A user can see the calls of a run in the execution view, with the policy decision of each call.

## Server side of the bridge

The file [`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs) connects the bridge to the policy engine and the tools. The trait `BridgeServices` in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/services.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/services.rs) lists what the bridge needs: `authorize`, `policy_check`, `resolve_ask`, `policy_observe`, `mcp_call`, `mcp_tools`, and `stop_event`. The struct `ServerBridge` implements it. `McpOut` holds the text of a tool result and its `RunEnd`.

### The wrapper around the executor

The struct `Wrapped` wraps `HarnessExecutor` for the engine. Before the harness starts, it does these steps:

1. Open the workspace MCP tools with the connector. This happens first because the harness lists the Ostra tools once, at startup. [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md) explains the connector.
2. Build an `ExecutionPolicy` and a `ToolEnv` for the execution. The policy inputs come from the build and test commands in `project.toml`.
3. Put the result in the `running` map under the execution ID.

After the run, `Wrapped` removes the entry. After that, the bridge denies each late call, because `authorize` finds no execution.

### Routes

The function `internal_routes` serves two routes: `POST /internal/policy` (`POLICY_PATH`) and `POST /internal/mcp` (`MCP_PATH`). Each route needs a `Bearer` token. On Unix, `serve_bridge_socket` serves the same two routes on a Unix socket in the egress folder. A sandbox that has its own network namespace reaches the bridge through this socket. Nothing else of the server answers there, so the sandbox cannot reach `/api`. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

### Policy decisions and logging

The method `check` sets YOLO from the host and then asks the policy. If the execution is an inspection, it denies every call with the guard `read-only-session` and the text `INSPECT_DENIAL`: "Answer from what you already did, without tools: this is a read-only look back at a run that has ended, so Ostra refuses every tool call." The text leads with the correction, because Grok clips reasons. The method sends a `ToolCall` delta and a `Policy` delta to the host, so the execution view shows each call and its decision.

Two groups of tools pass the hook without a check, because the MCP handler checks and logs them when it runs them:

- **Workspace MCP tools** (Rule M2). [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md) explains them.
- **Management tools** (Rule O1). The user then sees an ask only once.

The list `MCP_TOOLS` holds the Ostra tools that the MCP handler serves: `report`, `document`, `memory`, `memory_recall`, `docs_search`, the `code_<op>` tools, the project tools, and the coordination tools. The hook path does not log these tools again. See [Native tools](tools.md) for the tools.

The method `mcp_tools` lists no tools for an inspection. It lists management tools only if the execution has a management handle, and coordination tools only if it has a coordination handle.

### Observation

After a call, `policy_observe` does two things. If the call wrote files and did not fail, it sends the paths to the write sink, so the Files view updates live. Then it runs `ExecutionPolicy::observe`. An observation is either a note for the model or a recall of lessons. A recall reads at most 5 lessons for the query from the lesson memory. See [Storage: databases and lesson memory](storage.md).

## PTY sessions

A `PtySession` runs the CLI in a pseudo-terminal. The CLI is a terminal program, so it needs a terminal. The session also mirrors the screen with a `vt100` parser, so a browser that connects during the run gets the current screen and the scrollback.

### Size limits

| Constant | Value | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_COLS`, `DEFAULT_ROWS` | 120, 40 | The starting size of the terminal |
| `MAX_COLS`, `MAX_ROWS` | 1000, 500 | The largest size |
| `MIN_COLS`, `MIN_ROWS` | 20, 5 | The smallest size |
| `SCROLLBACK` | 2000 lines | The history of the screen model |
| `WRITE_QUEUE` | 256 writes | The queue of pending input |
| `STREAM_BUFFER` | 256 chunks | How far a viewer can fall behind |

The function `clamp_size` applies the limits to every start and resize. The minimum exists because `vt100` 0.16 underflows, and panics the reader thread, on a one-row screen that wraps a line and on a one-column screen that draws a wide character. No harness TUI draws usefully below these sizes.

### Start of the process

The spawn code sets the environment in this order:

1. The environment of Ostra.
2. The removal of `PARENT_SESSION_ENV`.
3. The removal of `plan.env_remove`.
4. `TERM=xterm-256color` and `COLORTERM=truecolor`.
5. `plan.env`.

The list `PARENT_SESSION_ENV` holds 16 variables, such as `CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, `GROK_SESSION_ID`, and `ANTIGRAVITY_AGENT`. They tie a process to the harness session that started Ostra. A child that inherits them runs as a nested child of that session. Claude Code does not save such a session, so Ostra cannot resume it.

The session starts three threads: one that writes the input queue to the PTY, one that reads the output, and one that waits for the exit. On Unix, the child leads its own session, so its process group holds the CLI and its descendants. Ostra adopts that group as a process tree. If the plan has a `tty_param`, the launcher passes the device path of the PTY as `-D <param>=<path>` to `sandbox-exec`.

### Terminal queries

TUIs send queries to their terminal: the cursor position, device attributes, and the colors. Ostra alone answers them. Browsers mute their own replies, so any number of viewers, or none, gives the harness exactly one answer. The function `answer_queries` finds the queries in the output and returns the replies. It keeps at most 64 trailing bytes, because they can start a sequence that the next read completes.

The reply set is small on purpose. Mode queries (`?<digits>$`) are echoed back only if they hold 1 to 5 digits, so program output cannot type into the input of the program. The tests check this. The answers are fixed: the cursor position, a status report, primary and secondary device attributes, the foreground color `d0d0d0`, the background color `1c1c1c`, the kitty keyboard flags, and the XT version `ostra`.

### Input, snapshot, and stop

- **`write`.** The method queues bytes for the program. If the queue holds 256 writes, the call fails with `WouldBlock`, so a harness that stops reading cannot block a caller. If the terminal is closed, it fails with `BrokenPipe`.
- **`type_line`.** The method types text like a person. It sends the text in bracketed paste, waits 150 ms, and then sends Enter. Bracketed paste keeps TUIs from treating a newline in the text as a submit. The supervisor uses it for nudges and wake messages.
- **`snapshot` and `stream`.** A snapshot resets the terminal, then replays the scrollback as plain lines, and then draws the formatted screen with its input modes. Scrollback rows are plain text because formatted rows position the cursor absolutely. `stream` returns the snapshot and a broadcast receiver under one lock, so a viewer neither misses nor repeats output. A viewer that falls more than 256 chunks behind is resynced from a new snapshot.
- **`terminate`.** The method asks the CLI to exit. If the CLI lives after the grace time, the method kills the process tree. Then it waits at most 2 more seconds. On Unix the request is SIGTERM to the process group. On Windows it closes the pseudoconsole, which sends `CTRL_CLOSE_EVENT`, and then it kills the job. At the end, it drops the sandbox members, which kills what the CLI left running, also when the CLI had already exited.

The struct `PtyRegistry` keeps the live PTYs by execution ID. The server uses it to forward browser input, resizes, and streams. The `inserted` watch changes on each insert, so a viewer that waits for a run to start can wake. See [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) for the `term:<id>` channel and its limits. See [Session, execution, and gate screens](web-session-screens.md) for the Terminal tab.

## Terminal log

The terminal log keeps the raw bytes of a harness terminal on disk, so the Terminal tab can replay a run that has ended. The `TermLog` writes `terminal.log` in the execution folder. The helper `terminal_transcript` gives the path.

- **The cap.** `TRANSCRIPT_CAP` is 2 MiB (2,097,152 bytes). The file grows to at most twice the cap. If it passes that, `TermLog` rewrites it with the last `TRANSCRIPT_CAP` bytes through a temporary file and a rename. Writes stay appends and memory stays flat.
- **The permissions.** The file is readable by its owner only (mode 0600 and 0700 for the folder), because harness output can carry secrets. A rewritten file keeps the mode.
- **A new run or a resume.** `TermLog::create` replaces an earlier log. If the run resumes under the same execution ID, `keep` is true and the log gets new bytes after the old ones.
- **A failed write.** The log stops, and the run goes on.
- **A read.** `read_transcript` returns the last `TRANSCRIPT_CAP` bytes, or `None` if the file is missing or empty.

### For the user

No setting controls the log. The Terminal tab of an ended execution replays it. The log stays with the session folder after the run. Delete the execution folder to remove it.

## Usage watch and transcript facts

Without a live reader, the spend of a harness run shows only after the run ends. The function `usage_watch::follow` reads the session file during the run, so the spend shows live, like native spend. Antigravity records no token counts, so `follow` returns at once for it.

### How `follow` works

1. Look for the session file every `LOCATE_EVERY` (2 seconds), until it exists. The path depends on a session ID that the harness can report late.
2. Watch the folder of the file with the platform watcher, not the file, so a replaced file is still seen. If the watcher cannot be created, poll every `POLL_EVERY` (5 seconds) and write a warning to the log.
3. After each change, wait `SETTLE` (500 ms), because a turn writes many lines in a burst and one read covers them.
4. Read the new bytes with `TranscriptReader::poll`. Send an `ExecutionDelta::Usage` only if the usage differs from the last one sent.

The executor cancels the follower and waits for it before it builds the final result, so no usage arrives after the result.

### Where the session files are

| Harness | Session file | Location variable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/projects/<dir>/<session>.jsonl` | `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*-<session>.jsonl` | `CODEX_HOME` |
| Grok Build | `~/.grok/sessions/<cwd>/<session>/updates.jsonl` | `GROK_HOME` |
| Antigravity | `brain/<conversation>/.system_generated/logs/transcript_full.jsonl`, for the last message only | none |

The path from the hook payload (`transcript_path`) comes first. If it is missing, `locate` searches by session ID.

### How each harness counts usage

The reader is incremental. It reads only the bytes that the file gained. A partial last line waits for the next read. A last line without a newline counts as complete when it parses. If the file becomes shorter than the offset, the reader starts again.

- **Claude Code.** The file has one line for each content block, and each line repeats the usage of the message. Usage therefore counts once for each message ID. Each message is priced with its own model, because a session can switch models.
- **Codex.** The `token_count` events carry running totals. `input_tokens` includes cached input, and `output_tokens` includes reasoning. Ostra converts each increase to a delta and prices it with the model of the current turn.
- **Grok Build.** Each `turn_completed` update carries the usage of that turn. `inputTokens` includes cached input. The cost comes from `costUsdTicks`, where 10^10 ticks make one dollar. Grok computes this cost itself.
- **Antigravity.** There is no usage. The last `PLANNER_RESPONSE` is the final message.

The cost of Claude Code and Codex comes from `pricing::cost`. See [Model providers and pricing](providers-and-pricing.md).

### For the user

No setting controls the watch. The execution view and the Cost screen show the live usage. Antigravity shows no token count or cost.

## Per-execution scratch homes

A harness CLI writes state in its own home folders. Ostra must let it write there. But Ostra must not let an agent leave a hook or an instruction that a later session of the user runs. The file [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/sandbox.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/sandbox.rs) solves this. The function `wrap` runs the CLI under the sandbox profile of the execution. The CLI, its Bash tool, and everything it starts inherit the sandbox. [Sandbox](sandbox.md) explains the profile, the backends, and the egress proxy. This section describes only what the harness crate adds.

### The execution folder and its contents

Each execution has the folder `.state/harness/<execution id>/` in the session folder. The folder can hold these entries:

| Entry | Constant or file | Content | Removed at the end |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `claude.json` | `CLAUDE_JSON_COPY` | A private copy of `~/.claude.json` | Yes |
| `tmp` | `SCRATCH` | The folder that the sandbox mounts as `/tmp` | Yes |
| `grok-home/config.toml` | `GROK_CONFIG` | The Grok config, which holds the bridge token | Yes |
| `claude-settings.json`, `claude-mcp.json`, `system-prompt.md`, `first-message.md` | files of the launch plan | The plan files. `first-message.md` exists only for a fresh launch with a long first message | No |
| `terminal.log` | `terminal_transcript` | The terminal log | No |

The function `cleanup` removes the first three entries. The executor also deletes the Codex profile file. The home overlay and the writable list use the execution folder as a writable path.

### What the sandbox changes for a harness

Under bubblewrap, the home folder is overlaid. The CLI can write its state folders, but it cannot leave files that the later shells or CLI sessions of the user run. Seatbelt has no overlay. There the rest of the home stays read-only, and a write at the top of the home (the `~/.claude.json` of Claude Code) fails. The CLIs survive that.

The function `harness_dirs` gives, for each harness, the writable state folders and the entries that stay read-only. The entries are settings, instructions, and hooks. A hook or instruction written there runs in the later sessions of the user for that CLI.

| Harness | Writable | Read-only entries (a trailing `/` marks a folder) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or `~/.claude`, and `~/.local/state/claude` | `settings.json`, `settings.local.json`, `CLAUDE.md`, `commands/`, `agents/`, `skills/`, `plugins/`, `hooks/`, `output-styles/` |
| Codex | `$CODEX_HOME` or `~/.codex` | `config.toml`, `AGENTS.md`, `hooks.json`, `rules/` |
| Grok Build | `$GROK_HOME` or `~/.grok` | `config.toml`, `trusted_folders.toml`, `hooks/` |
| Antigravity | `~/.gemini` | `settings.json`, `GEMINI.md`, `config/plugins/` |

### The Claude config copy

Claude Code rewrites `~/.claude.json` through a temporary file and a rename. A read-only home refuses that. With a mount namespace and an existing `~/.claude.json`, Ostra copies the file to the private `claude.json` in the execution folder and links the original path to the copy inside the sandbox. The copy has owner-only permissions.

### The bridge address inside the sandbox

The hook bridge must stay reachable from the CLI. The function `bridge_addr` needs the callback URL in the form `http://<ip>:<port>`. A host name such as `localhost` is an error, with the text "The hook bridge URL `<url>` is not http://<ip>:<port>." The sandbox forwards the bridge to loopback. Inside a network namespace, the port stays the same. Under Seatbelt, the port is a new one. If the URL inside differs from the callback URL, `replace_url` rewrites the plan files and `OSTRA_URL`, and `materialize` writes the files again. The replacement skips a port that continues with another digit, so `41000` does not match `4100`.

The egress proxy allows the model hosts of the harness, and the hosts in `*_BASE_URL` variables, in Claude Code settings `env`, and in the Codex `model_providers`. Those hosts can be a gateway on this machine or on the LAN. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md) for the host rules.

### Seatbelt variables

Seatbelt denies `/tmp` and the keychain. The function `seatbelt_env` therefore sets `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR` to the `TMPDIR` of the sandbox, because Claude Code makes its own folder in `/tmp` otherwise. It sets `SSL_CERT_FILE` to `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` (`MACOS_CERTS`) if `SSL_CERT_FILE` is not set and the file exists. CLIs built on `rustls-native-certs` (Codex) read the trusted roots from the keychain unless they get a bundle.

### What happens when

- **No sandbox backend exists and the config allows it.** The plan runs unchanged, and the Status delta warns the user.
- **No backend exists and the config requires one.** `wrap` returns the error and the launch fails.
- **The egress proxy, the decoy files, or the forward fail to start.** `wrap` returns an error such as "starting the sandbox's egress proxy: <error>".
- **The run ends.** `cleanup` deletes the three private entries. Ostra drops the sandbox members, which kills the processes that the CLI left.

### For the user

The sandbox settings belong to [Sandbox](sandbox.md). The harness crate reads three environment variables to find the state folders: `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `CODEX_HOME`, and `GROK_HOME`. Set them before you start Ostra. A change takes effect at the next execution, because each launch reads them. If a variable is not set, the default is `~/.claude`, `~/.codex`, or `~/.grok`.

## Machine setup and the Antigravity integration

The file [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/setup.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/setup.rs) has the machine-level helpers. They work before any execution runs.

### Install and login state

`harness_status` returns a `HarnessStatus` with the command, `installed`, `version`, and `logged_in`. It uses `which` for the install check. It runs `<command> --version` with a timeout of 15 seconds and takes the first non-empty line. The login check differs for each harness:

| Harness | Login check |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `<command> auth status` prints JSON with `loggedIn` |
| Codex | `<command> login status` exits with 0 and prints "Logged in" |
| Grok Build | The file `auth.json` exists in the Grok home |
| Antigravity | `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/antigravity-oauth-token` or `~/.gemini/oauth_creds.json` exists |

`all_harness_status` runs the check for the four harnesses. `login_command` gives the command for the Terminal view: `auth login` for Claude Code, `login` for Codex and Grok Build, and no argument for Antigravity. `install_script` gives the official installer pipeline, for example `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash`. On Windows, Claude Code uses `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex` and Codex uses `npm install -g @openai/codex`. Grok Build and Antigravity have no Windows installer command, so their terminal says where to look. `installer_tool` names the download tool that the setup terminal checks first: `curl`, or `npm` for Codex on Windows. `install_dirs` lists `~/.local/bin` and `~/.grok/bin`, and on Windows also `AppData\Roaming\npm`. These folders join the `PATH` of the server at start, because a server that started before an install does not see a change of the shell profile. See [Workspace, settings, and setup screens](web-workspace-and-setup.md) for the setup terminals.

### The Antigravity integration

Antigravity reads hooks and MCP servers only from global config. The function `ensure_agy_integration` installs one integration. The launch runs it before each Antigravity execution. It is idempotent. It does these steps:

1. Write `plugin.json` and `hooks.json` in `~/.gemini/config/plugins/ostra/`. The hooks file registers `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` with the matcher `.*`, and `PreInvocation` and `PostInvocation`. Each command is `<ostra> hook --harness agy --event <event>` and has no `--execution`.
2. Set `plugins.ostra.enabled` to `true` in `~/.gemini/config/config.json`. Other keys stay.
3. Run `<command> mcp list` and test each output line. If no line passes the test, run `<command> mcp add ostra <binary> mcp-stdio`. This is the one registration that Antigravity honors.

The test in step 3 is strict. Ostra treats the server as registered only when a line of the `agy mcp list` output starts with the name `ostra` (`MCP_SERVER_NAME`) and also holds the path of the current Ostra binary:

```rust
let registered = listed
    .lines()
    .any(|l| l.split_whitespace().next() == Some(MCP_SERVER_NAME) && l.contains(&bin));
if !registered {
    // run `agy mcp add ostra <bin> mcp-stdio`
}
```

An `ostra` entry that points to another binary does not pass the test, so Ostra runs `agy mcp add` again. This happens, for example, after a move or a rebuild of the Ostra binary to a new path.

The helper `run` in `setup.rs` runs the `agy mcp list` command and gives these results:

- **The command is missing, times out after 15 seconds, or fails to start.** The output is empty.
- **The command exits with a non-zero code.** Ostra uses its text as it is.

In both cases, the text normally has no line that starts with `ostra` and holds the binary path, so Ostra runs `agy mcp add`.

If `agy mcp add` exits with a code other than 0, the launch fails with "`agy mcp add` exited <code>: <text>". If it does not finish, the launch fails with "`agy mcp add` did not finish".

Every hook command is inert unless `$OSTRA_EXECUTION` is set, so the plugin does nothing in a session that the user starts alone. Each execution writes its own agent file `ostra-<agent>.md` in the `agents` folder. The `tools:` list of that file names only native tools from a verified mapping: `view_file`, `write_to_file`, `replace_file_content`, `run_command`, `grep_search`, `find_by_name`, `search_web`, and `read_url_content`. An agent file with no `tools:` list gets no native tools. One unknown tool name makes the whole session fail to start. The source records this for agy 1.2.8, where `command_status` is unknown.

### For the user

No setting controls the integration. It writes in the `~/.gemini` folder. To remove it, delete the folder `~/.gemini/config/plugins/ostra`, remove `plugins.ostra` from `~/.gemini/config/config.json`, and run `agy mcp remove ostra` if your Antigravity version has that command. The next Antigravity execution installs the integration again.

## Constants of the harness crate

| Constant | Value | File | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GIT_CHECK_EVERY` | 2 s | `executor.rs` | The interval of the repository repair check |
| `DEFAULT_IDLE_NUDGE` | 240 s | `executor.rs` | The quiet time before an idle nudge |
| `MAX_IDLE_NUDGES` | 2 | `executor.rs` | Idle nudges before the end `Idle` |
| `AFTER_SUBMIT_GRACE` | 20 s | `executor.rs` | The wait for the turn to end after a submit |
| `AGY_QUIET_AFTER_SUBMIT` | 4 s | `executor.rs` | The terminal quiet time that ends an Antigravity turn after a submit |
| `AUTH_MARKERS`, `FATAL_MARKERS`, `TRUST_MARKERS`, `MODEL_OFFER_MARKERS` | lists of strings | `executor.rs` | The screen texts that the supervisor recognizes |
| `MAX_STOP_NUDGES` | 2 | `live.rs` | Stop events that the bridge turns back |
| `LAUNCH_WINDOW` | 20 s | `outcome.rs` | The time in which an early exit is a launch failure |
| `AUTH_PREFIX`, `LAUNCH_PREFIX` | `harness-auth:`, `harness-launch:` | `outcome.rs` | The prefixes of the error text |
| `HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS` | 86,400 s | `launch.rs` | The timeout of hooks and MCP tool calls |
| `MAX_ARG_PROMPT` | 96 KiB | `launch.rs` | The largest first message on the command line of a fresh launch |
| `INSPECT_TOOLS` | `Read,Bash,Grep,Glob` | `launch.rs` | The Claude Code tools of an inspection |
| `GROK_PRIVATE` | `config.toml`, `trusted_folders.toml`, `leader.sock` | `launch.rs` | The Grok home entries that Ostra does not link |
| `ENV_URL`, `ENV_EXECUTION`, `ENV_TOKEN`, `ENV_HARNESS` | `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_HARNESS` | `protocol.rs` | The variables of the hook and the shim |
| `POLICY_PATH`, `MCP_PATH` | `/internal/policy`, `/internal/mcp` | `protocol.rs` | The routes of the bridge |
| `MCP_SERVER_NAME` | `ostra` | `protocol.rs` | The name of the MCP server in every harness |
| `MCP_VERSIONS`, `MCP_INITIALIZE_DEFAULT` | four versions, `2025-11-25` | `bridge.rs` | The MCP versions of the shim |
| `MAX_OUTCOME_CHARS` | 64 KiB | `adapters/mod.rs` | The largest tool output that goes to the policy observer |
| `LEAF_REFUSAL`, `ASK_REFUSAL` | texts | `adapters/mod.rs` | The reasons for the refusal of spawn and ask tools |
| `PATTERNS` | four regular expressions | `adapters/mod.rs` | The exit code patterns |
| `GROK_REASON_MAX`, `MIN_HEAD` | 256, 120 | `adapters/grok.rs` | The reason limit of Grok and the least head length |
| `TRUNCATED_REFUSAL`, `PATH_KEYS` | text, list | `adapters/grok.rs` | The refusal of a truncated input and the path keys |
| `DEFAULT_COLS`, `DEFAULT_ROWS`, `MAX_COLS`, `MAX_ROWS`, `MIN_COLS`, `MIN_ROWS` | 120, 40, 1000, 500, 20, 5 | `pty.rs` | The terminal size |
| `SCROLLBACK`, `WRITE_QUEUE`, `STREAM_BUFFER` | 2000, 256, 256 | `pty.rs` | The history, the input queue, and the viewer buffer |
| `PARENT_SESSION_ENV` | 16 names | `pty.rs` | The variables that the PTY child does not inherit |
| `TRANSCRIPT_CAP` | 2 MiB | `term_log.rs` | The size of the terminal log |
| `LOCATE_EVERY`, `SETTLE`, `POLL_EVERY` | 2 s, 500 ms, 5 s | `usage_watch.rs` | The timing of the usage watch |
| `CLAUDE_JSON_COPY`, `SCRATCH`, `GROK_CONFIG` | `claude.json`, `tmp`, `grok-home/config.toml` | `sandbox.rs` | The private entries of the execution folder |
| `MACOS_CERTS` | `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` | `sandbox.rs` | The certificate bundle for Seatbelt |
| `INSPECT_DENIAL`, `MCP_TOOLS` | text, list | `ostra-server/src/bridge.rs` | The inspection refusal and the Ostra MCP tool list |

The example `harness_probe` in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/examples/harness_probe.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/examples/harness_probe.rs) runs one execution in a real harness against an allow-all bridge. Its constant `CODE_FILES` holds the small Rust project that the probe writes when `PROBE_CODE` is set.
