sections.title: Native tools
sections.summary: How the `ostra-tools` crate defines and runs each tool: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob, Skill, WebFetch, Report, Document, Memory, code, and management tools, with every cap, timeout, and shell rule.
sections.body:
An agent must read files, change files, run commands, and record results. Two sets of code for these actions give different results between executors. The `ostra-tools` crate holds one implementation. Its tool names and input shapes follow the tools of Claude Code, because the agent prompts are tuned to those names.

This page covers the tool definitions, the way a call runs, argument coercion, each tool, shell discovery, and process trees. The page stops before the policy checks. Ostra runs the policy first, and nothing in `ostra-tools` checks permissions or guards. For the checks, see [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).

## Where the tools run

Two callers use the same `execute` function in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/lib.rs). The native executor calls it for every tool of the agent. The server calls it for the harness executors through the MCP shim. For the native loop, see [Native executor loop](native-executor.md). For the shim and the hook bridge, see [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).

### The native loop

The native loop gets its tool list from `definitions(capabilities)`. It serves each tool in that list, including Read, Write, Edit, and Bash, with one exception. When the provider offers server-side web fetch and the agent has the `WebFetch` capability, the loop removes the local `WebFetch` definition from the list (`crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`, lines 451-459). The provider then runs the fetch, and the loop serves no local `WebFetch` call.

### The MCP shim

A harness CLI has its own Read, Write, Edit, and shell tools. Ostra does not replace them. The MCP shim (`ostra mcp`, served by `ServerBridge` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs)) adds only the Ostra tools in this table.

| MCP name | Native name | Capability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `report` | `Report` | `Report` |
| `document` | `Document` | `Document` |
| `memory` | `Memory` | `Memory` |
| `memory_recall` | `MemoryRecall` | `MemoryRecall` |
| `docs_search` | `DocsSearch` | `DocsSearch` |
| `code_outline`, `code_find`, `code_callers`, `code_callees`, `code_implementations`, `code_neighbors`, `code_impact`, `code_map` | `CodeOutline`, `CodeFind`, `CodeCallers`, `CodeCallees`, `CodeImplementations`, `CodeNeighbors`, `CodeImpact`, `CodeMap` | `Code` |
| `project_list`, `project_create` | `ProjectList`, `ProjectCreate` | `ManageProjects` |
| `subagent_list`, `subagent_ask`, `subagent_reply` | `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, `SubagentReply` | `Coordinate` |

The shim also lists the tools of the workspace MCP servers. For those, see [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md).

### What the shim lists for a run

- A read-only inspect run gets no tools.
- A run gets the management tools only when its `ToolEnvConfig.manage` handle exists.
- A run gets the coordination tools only when its `ToolEnvConfig.coord` handle exists.
- The `Document` tool appears only for an agent that writes a typed document: explore, generate-spec, and plan.

### What happens when a harness calls a tool

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Harness CLI
    participant S as MCP stdio shim
    participant B as ServerBridge
    participant P as Policy
    participant T as ostra_tools execute
    H->>S: tools/call memory
    S->>B: "POST MCP_PATH, mcp_call"
    B->>B: canonical_call
    B->>P: "check(call)"
    P-->>B: Allow, Ask, or Deny
    B->>B: resolve_ask when the decision is Ask
    B->>T: "execute(env, id, call)"
    T-->>B: ToolOutput
    B->>B: "policy_observe, emit ToolResult"
    B-->>S: McpOut with text and end
    S-->>H: tool result
```

If the policy denies the call, `mcp_call` returns an error that names the layer and the rule. If the user denies an ask, it returns "The user denied this call" with the reason. If the tool output has `is_error`, the shim returns the text as an error and adds the notes of `policy_observe`.

## Tool definitions and capabilities

An agent definition lists capabilities. The function `definitions(capabilities)` in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/defs.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/defs.rs) maps each capability to its tool definitions, in declaration order. It lists a capability once, even if the agent repeats it. A `ToolDefinition` has a `name`, a `description`, and a JSON `input_schema`.

| Capability | Tools |
| --- | --- |
| `Read` | `Read` |
| `Write` | `Write` |
| `Edit` | `Edit` |
| `Shell` | `Bash`. On Windows also `PowerShell` and `Cmd`. |
| `SearchText` | `Grep` |
| `Glob` | `Glob` |
| `Skill` | `Skill` |
| `WebFetch` | `WebFetch` |
| `WebSearch` | None. The model provider runs it. |
| `Report` | `Report` |
| `Document` | None here. `document_tool_definition(agent)` builds it. |
| `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch` | `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch` |
| `Code` | The 8 code tools |
| `ManageProjects` | `ProjectList`, `ProjectCreate` |
| `Coordinate` | `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, `SubagentReply` |

### Web search

`wants_web_search(capabilities)` returns true when the list holds `WebSearch`. The loop then turns on the search tool of the provider. If a model calls `WebSearch` as a local tool, `execute` returns an error, because the tool has no local code.

### The Document definition

`document_tool_definition(agent)` returns `None` for an agent that writes no typed document. For explore, generate-spec, and plan, it builds the schema of the matching document kind and moves its `$defs` to the top of the input schema. A test checks that every `$ref` points at a definition that the schema carries.

### Submit tools

`submit_tool_definition(agent)` builds the `submit_<agent>` tool from the agent description and schema in `ostra_core::submit`. For the end of a run with this tool, see [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md).

### Why descriptions are plain text

Each description is a constant string in `defs.rs`, for example `READ` and `BASH`. A test fails if a description has an em dash. The descriptions carry the numbers that the model needs, such as the 2000-line read default and the 600000 ms timeout limit.

## Constants that hold descriptions, names, and the shell script

The constants in `defs.rs` are not tool names. Each one holds the description text of one tool, which `definitions` puts in the `description` field. The tool name is a separate string in the `def` call. Three other constants are in the table because a reader can look them up: `SCRIPT`, `EVERY`, and the project tool names in `ostra-core`.

| Constant | File | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `READ` | `defs.rs` | "Reads a file from the local filesystem." and the rules for `offset` and `limit` | The `description` of `Read`. |
| `WRITE` | `defs.rs` | "Writes a file to the local filesystem, replacing it if it exists." | The `description` of `Write`. |
| `EDIT` | `defs.rs` | "Performs an exact string replacement in a file." | The `description` of `Edit`. |
| `BASH` | `defs.rs` | "Executes a bash command and returns its combined stdout and stderr." | The `description` of `Bash`. |
| `GREP` | `defs.rs` | "Searches file contents with a regular expression (ripgrep syntax)." | The `description` of `Grep`. |
| `GLOB` | `defs.rs` | "Finds files by name pattern." | The `description` of `Glob`. |
| `SKILL` | `defs.rs` | "Loads a skill: a SKILL.md file of instructions for a kind of task." | The `description` of `Skill`. |
| `WEB_FETCH` | `defs.rs` | "Fetches a URL and returns its content as markdown." | The `description` of `WebFetch`. |
| `REPORT` | `defs.rs` | "Writes your report to the exact `Report file:` path your prompt declared." | The `description` of `Report`. |
| `DOCUMENT` | `defs.rs` | "Writes your document: the research document, the spec, or the plan, as typed JSON." | The `description` of `Document`. `document_tool_definition` uses it with the schema of the document kind. |
| `MEMORY` | `defs.rs` | "Records a durable lesson in this project's memory, for future runs to recall." | The `description` of `Memory`. |
| `MEMORY_RECALL` | `defs.rs` | "Recalls lessons earlier runs recorded for this project." | The `description` of `MemoryRecall`. |
| `DOCS_SEARCH` | `defs.rs` | "Searches the documentation books Ostra's docs stage wrote about this workspace's projects, and returns the best-matching sections with only the passages that matched." | The `description` of `DocsSearch`. |
| `CODE_OUTLINE` | `defs.rs` | "Lists a source file's imports (with the project file each resolves to) and its definitions with line ranges, without reading the file." | The `description` of `CodeOutline`. |
| `CODE_FIND` | `defs.rs` | "Finds definitions by name across the project: functions, types, methods, constants, fields." | The `description` of `CodeFind`. |
| `CODE_CALLERS` | `defs.rs` | "Lists every place that uses a symbol, grouped by the enclosing function or type, with line numbers." | The `description` of `CodeCallers`. |
| `CODE_CALLEES` | `defs.rs` | "Lists the project definitions that one function or type body uses: what it calls, the types it names, the fields it touches." | The `description` of `CodeCallees`. |
| `CODE_IMPLEMENTATIONS` | `defs.rs` | "Lists implementations: what a class, interface, trait, or struct implements or extends, and what implements or extends it." | The `description` of `CodeImplementations`. |
| `CODE_NEIGHBORS` | `defs.rs` | "Shows how one file connects to the rest of the project: the files it uses and the files that use it." | The `description` of `CodeNeighbors`. |
| `CODE_IMPACT` | `defs.rs` | "Shows what a change can break." | The `description` of `CodeImpact`. |
| `CODE_MAP` | `defs.rs` | "Summarizes the project's structure: its packages with their dependencies on each other, the most depended-on files, and import cycles." | The `description` of `CodeMap`. |
| `POWERSHELL` | `defs.rs` | "Executes a Windows PowerShell command and returns its combined output. Windows only, alongside Bash." | The `description` of `PowerShell`. |
| `EVERY` | `defs.rs` | An array of the 17 `Capability` values | The list that `input_schema` passes to `definitions` to find the schema of a local tool. |
| `PROJECT_LIST` | `defs.rs` | "Lists the projects in this workspace: each key, folder, stack, whether it is initialized, and whether it is in this session's scope." | The `description` of `ProjectList`. |
| `PROJECT_LIST` | `crates/ostra-core/src/manage.rs` | `"ProjectList"` | The native name of the list tool. `is_manage_tool` and `changes_ostra` compare a tool name with it. |
| `PROJECT_CREATE` | `crates/ostra-core/src/manage.rs` | `"ProjectCreate"` | The native name of the create tool. Only this name makes `changes_ostra` return true. |
| `PROJECT_TOOLS` | `crates/ostra-core/src/manage.rs` | `[("project_list", "ProjectList"), ("project_create", "ProjectCreate")]` | The pairs of MCP name and native name. The shim, the harness adapters, and the agent mapping read it. |
| `SCRIPT` | `crates/ostra-tools/src/bash.rs` | The `bash -c` script of the Bash tool. A Unix version and a Windows version exist. | What every Bash call runs. See [Run a Bash command](#run-a-bash-command). |

## Per-execution tool state

One `ToolEnv` serves one execution. It is built from a `ToolEnvConfig` and holds the state in this list.

- `cwd`: the working directory of the shell. It starts at `repo_root`.
- `read_files`: the set of paths that the run has read. Ostra stores each path in its folded form, so a verbatim Windows path and a resolved path match despite case, prefix, and separator differences.
- `http`: the HTTP client of WebFetch.
- `private_hosts`: the hosts that WebFetch can reach even when they resolve to private addresses.
- `scrub_env`: the variables that Ostra removes from every child process.
- `sandbox`: the backend and profile that Bash runs under. If this is `None`, Bash runs without a sandbox.

### The config

`ToolEnvConfig` carries `agent`, `repo_root`, `workspace_root`, `session_dir`, `report_file`, `memory_db`, `memory_source`, `skill_resolver`, and four optional handles: `code`, `mcp`, `manage`, and `coord`. The `workspace_root` is empty outside a workspace. A missing handle makes the matching tools return an error. For example, a missing `CodeNav` gives "Code navigation is not available in this run. Use Grep, Glob, and Read instead."

### Resolve a path

`ToolEnv::resolve` turns a path from the model into a host path. It expands a leading `~/` to the home directory. It resolves a relative path against the current shell directory. Under bubblewrap, the sandbox shows the scratch directory as `/tmp`. Then `sandbox_to_host` maps the path back, so the in-process tools and the sandboxed shell see the same file.

### Make the call canonical

`canonical_call` rewrites a call before the policy sees it. Ostra checks the policy on this rewritten call and then runs the same call. Thus the policy and the tool see the same target.

- `Read`, `Write`, and `Edit`: `file_path` becomes absolute.
- `Grep`, `Glob`, `Skill`, and `Document`: `path` becomes absolute, if the call has one.
- `Bash`, `PowerShell`, and `Cmd`: `cwd` is set to the current shell directory.
- `WebFetch`: `url` becomes its parsed form. A test shows that `https://evil.example\@docs.rs/x` becomes a URL with the host `evil.example`, which is the host that the client will contact.

Any other tool passes through unchanged.

## Run a call with execute

The function `execute(env, call_id, call, live, cancel)` runs one call and returns a `ToolOutput`.

1. Find the input schema of the tool. `input_schema` searches the definitions of all 17 capabilities, and for `Document` it uses the schema of the agent.
2. Coerce string arguments to JSON values. See the next part.
3. Dispatch on the tool name: the fixed names first, then the code, management, coordination, and gateway tool families.
4. Wait for the result, or for the cancel token.
5. Record `duration_ms`.

The `ToolOutput` has these fields: `text`, `is_error`, `exit_code`, `duration_ms`, `diff`, and `end`. The `diff` field holds the unified diff of a Write or Edit for the Activity view. The `end` field is a `RunEnd` for coordination calls: `Continue`, `Wait`, or `Finish`.

### What happens when

- **The tool name is unknown.** `execute` returns the error "Unknown tool `<name>`."
- **A required argument is missing.** The tool returns "Missing required parameter `<key>`."
- **The cancel token fires.** For most tools, `execute` returns the error "Cancelled." and drops the work.
- **The tool is Bash, PowerShell, or Cmd.** These tools are not wrapped in the cancel select, because they drain their own output and stop their own process tree when the token fires. See [Run a Bash command](#run-a-bash-command).

## Argument coercion

Weaker models often send an object or an array as a string that holds its JSON text. Without a repair, the argument fails the schema check. The function `coerce_json_strings` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/args.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/args.rs) parses such a string back before the tool reads it.

The rules:

- Only top-level arguments change.
- The argument must be a string in the call, and its schema must not allow a string. A schema allows a string when it has `type` string (alone or in a list), an `enum`, a string `const`, or an `anyOf` or `oneOf` entry that allows a string.
- The trimmed text must start with `{` or `[`.
- The text must parse as a JSON object or array. If the parse fails, the string stays as it is.
- The function returns `true` when it changed anything.

The reason for the string rule: a `path` argument whose text looks like JSON is still a path. The test in `args.rs` keeps `{"looks": "like json"}` as a string for a `path` property, and keeps `[1]` for a property that allows a string or a null.

```rust
for (key, prop) in props {
    let Some(Value::String(text)) = args.get(key) else { continue };
    if allows_string(prop) { continue; }
    let t = text.trim();
    if !(t.starts_with('{') || t.starts_with('[')) { continue; }
    if let Ok(v @ (Value::Object(_) | Value::Array(_))) = serde_json::from_str::<Value>(t) {
        args.insert(key.clone(), v);
        changed = true;
    }
}
```

## Run a Bash command

The Bash tool in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/bash.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/bash.rs) runs one command in a new `bash` process and returns the combined output of stdout and stderr. The working directory persists between calls. A model that runs `cd sub` in one call is in `sub` in the next call.

### The script

Every call starts `bash -c` with the fixed script `SCRIPT`. The command text does not go on the command line. It goes in the variable `OSTRA_CMD`, and the script runs it with `eval`. This keeps quoting intact. A test shows that `printf '%s|' "a b" 'c"d' $'e\nf'` returns the exact text.

```bash
exec 2>&1
__ostra_cmd=$OSTRA_CMD
__ostra_pwd=$OSTRA_PWD_FILE
cd -- "$OSTRA_CWD" || exit 1
unset OSTRA_CMD OSTRA_PWD_FILE OSTRA_CWD
trap 'pwd -P > "$__ostra_pwd" 2>/dev/null' EXIT
eval "$__ostra_cmd"
```

The `EXIT` trap writes the final directory to a temporary file named `ostra-pwd-<uuid>`. The tool reads this file after the shell ends and sets the new `cwd`. Because `eval` runs in the same shell, a `cd` reaches the trap. The directory is saved even when the command exits with a non-zero code. On Windows, the trap runs `cd -P . && pwd -W`, because Git Bash prints an MSYS path (`/c/Users/me`) with `pwd -P`, and the other tools need the Windows path.

### Steps of one call

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Clamp the timeout"] --> B["Use cwd, or the repo root if cwd is gone"]
    B --> C["Start bash with the script in a new process tree"]
    C --> D["Read stdout and stderr chunks"]
    D --> E{"What ends first?"}
    E -->|exit| F["Exit status"]
    E -->|deadline| G["Timed out"]
    E -->|cancel token| H["Cancelled"]
    G --> I["Kill the tree, wait 5 seconds"]
    H --> I
    F --> J["Drain output until 300 ms of silence"]
    I --> J
    J --> K["Kill the tree if a process still holds the pipe"]
    K --> L["Read the pwd file and set cwd"]
    L --> M["Build the result text"]
```

### The environment of the child

Before the start, Ostra changes the environment of the child.

- It removes the credential variables that the settings name, and `BRIDGE_ENV`. For these settings, see [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md). The executor adds the secrets of the workspace MCP servers with `with_scrub_env`.
- It removes every inherited variable that starts with `OSTRA_`.
- It removes `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF`.
- It sets `GIT_PAGER=cat` and `PAGER=cat`, so no pager waits for input.
- It adds the git settings of `ostra_core::git::agent_env`: `core.fsmonitor=false`, `safe.bareRepository=explicit`, and `protocol.ext.allow=never`. Ostra adds them after any `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` entries of its own environment, so both sets apply.
- It closes stdin (`Stdio::null()`).

The reason for the removal: a command that the model writes can print its environment. The credentials must not be in it. `configured_secret_vars` reads `config.toml` when Ostra builds the `ToolEnv`, so a change applies to the next execution.

### Sandbox

If the `ToolEnv` has a sandbox, the tool does not run `bash` directly. It builds the command with the profile and backend, and it makes the pwd file writable inside the sandbox. The file must exist before the start, because `/tmp` can be private or denied in the sandbox. If this setup fails, the tool returns "Cannot prepare the sandbox: ...". For the sandbox, see [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

### Output capture

The tool keeps the output in memory in a bounded form. The `Capture` type keeps the first 128 KiB (`CAPTURE_HALF`) and the last 128 KiB of the bytes. If more bytes arrive, it inserts the line `... [N bytes dropped] ...` between them. Then the text is cut in the middle to `MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS`, which is 30000. The cut keeps the first and last 15000 and inserts `... [N characters truncated] ...`. This cut compares UTF-8 byte counts, not characters. If the output is empty, the result is `(no output)`.

If the call has a `live` callback, the tool sends each chunk to it during the run. A `Utf8Stream` holds back an incomplete trailing byte sequence, so the callback always gets valid text. The live stream is not truncated, but the final result is.

### Timeouts and kills

The `timeout` argument is in milliseconds. The default `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS` is 120000. The tool clamps the value to the range from 1 to `MAX_TIMEOUT_MS`, which is 600000. If the deadline passes or the cancel token fires, the tool kills the whole process tree and waits at most `KILL_WAIT` (5 seconds) for the child to end. The wait has a limit because, on Windows, a process killed during its own creation never exits.

After the child ends, the tool reads the remaining output until the pipe is silent for `DRAIN_GRACE` (300 ms). If a background process still holds the pipe after that time, the tool kills the tree. Thus a command such as `sleep 30 & echo started` returns in less than 5 seconds. The group kill runs on a timeout, on a cancel, and when a process holds the pipe. On Windows, closing the job also kills every process that remains.

### The result

| Case | `is_error` | `exit_code` | Text |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exit code 0 | false | 0 | The output |
| Exit code `c` other than 0 | true | `c` | The output, then `Exit code: c` |
| Killed by a signal | true | none | The output, then "The command was terminated by a signal." |
| Timeout | true | none | "The command timed out after N ms and was stopped. Output so far:" and the output |
| Cancel | true | none | "The command was cancelled. Output so far:" and the output |
| Wait failure | true | none | "Waiting for the command failed: ..." |

### What happens when

- **The `command` is missing or has only spaces.** The tool returns "Missing required parameter `command`." or "The command is empty."
- **The saved directory does not exist.** The tool uses `repo_root` and saves it as the new `cwd`.
- **`bash` does not start.** The tool returns "Cannot start bash: ..."
- **On Windows, Git Bash is missing.** The tool returns the text of `NO_GIT_BASH`. See [Shell discovery](#shell-discovery-and-process-trees).
- **The command changes directory and then fails.** The new directory still persists, because the trap runs on every exit.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `timeout` (tool argument, set by the model) | 120000 ms, maximum 600000 ms | The tool call | For that call | The tool result in the Activity view | The user cannot set it. Cancel the execution to stop a command. |
| Credential variable names | The default credential variables and `BRIDGE_ENV` | `config.toml` | At the next execution | `printenv` in a Bash call shows none of them | Edit the settings that name them. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md). |
| Permission mode and rules (`permissions.mode`, `permissions.allow`, `permissions.ask`, `permissions.deny`) | See the policy page | The settings files | See the policy page | The policy decision on the tool call | See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md). |

## Windows shell tools

On Windows, the `Shell` capability grants three tools: `Bash`, `PowerShell`, and `Cmd`. They do not exist on Linux or macOS. The code is in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/winshell.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/winshell.rs), which compiles only on Windows.

### Why Bash is still the first choice

The command parser of Ostra is tree-sitter-bash. The write-scope and secret-read guards read a parsed command, so a PowerShell or Cmd command is opaque to them. The policy treats these two tools like an unparsed shell command. It never auto-allows them. The permission mode always decides. It refuses the call when the raw text names a state file of Ostra or a credential path. The tool descriptions tell the model to use Bash for anything that a POSIX shell can do. For the guards, see [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).

### What the tools do the same as Bash

The code reuses `Capture`, `Utf8Stream`, `spawn_reader`, `scrubbed_vars`, `configured_secret_vars`, `KILL_WAIT`, and the timeout limits of the Bash tool. Thus the limits are the same: a 120000 ms default, a 600000 ms maximum, a 30000 character output cap, and a kill of the whole process tree at the end of the call. The scrub list is the same: credentials and every `OSTRA_*` variable. The git environment of `agent_env` also applies.

### What differs

- **PowerShell** starts `powershell.exe` with `-NoProfile -NonInteractive -Command`. The script runs `Set-Location -LiteralPath '<cwd>'`, then the command inside `try`, and a `finally` block that writes `(Get-Location).Path` to the pwd file. The code doubles each `'` in the path (`ps_single_quote`).
- **Cmd** starts `cmd.exe` with one raw argument: `/d /s /c "cd /d "{cwd}" && {command} & cd > "{pwd_file}""`. The tool passes it raw, because the standard library quotes an inner `"` as `\"`, which `cmd` does not understand. The `/s` option removes the outer quotes. The trailing `cd` records the directory and keeps `ERRORLEVEL`. The command is not in parentheses, because a `)` in the command ends the group.
- The tools do not use the sandbox. The code starts the program directly.
- A timeout returns the same message as Bash. A cancel returns "The command was cancelled." A process without an exit code returns "The command was terminated."

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The `Shell` capability of an agent | Grants `Bash`, `PowerShell`, and `Cmd` on Windows | The agent definitions | At the next execution | The tool list of the execution | Use the permission rules to deny a tool. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md). |

## Shell discovery and process trees

Both topics live in `ostra-core`, because the tools, the harness executors, and the sandbox use them. For the crate map, see [Architecture and crate map](architecture.md).

### Find the shell

The function `ostra_core::shells::bash()` returns the program that the Bash tool runs.

- **Unix:** the plain name `bash`, which the system finds in `PATH`.
- **Windows:** the absolute path of `bin\bash.exe` in the Git for Windows install. The result is cached in a `OnceLock` (`FOUND`).

The reason for the absolute path on Windows: the first `bash` in `PATH` is often `C:\Windows\System32\bash.exe`, the WSL launcher. That program runs the command in a Linux VM with a different view of the files.

`git_root()` finds the install in this order:

1. Run `git --exec-path`. Walk up from the result (`<root>/mingw64/libexec/git-core`) to the first directory that has `bin\bash.exe`.
2. Check `%ProgramFiles%\Git`.
3. Check `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Git`.

If none exists, `bash()` returns "Git Bash was not found." followed by `NO_GIT_BASH`. That text tells the user to install Git for Windows on the machine that runs Ostra and then to restart Ostra, because Ostra does not use the WSL `bash.exe`. The restart is necessary because the cached result stays.

`powershell()` returns `System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe` under the system directory. `cmd()` returns `System32\cmd.exe`. Both use the `SystemRoot` variable and fall back to `C:\Windows`. They use fixed paths, so the first match in `PATH` cannot replace them.

### Stop a process and all its children

A killed shell must not leave its children. The `Tree` type in [`crates/ostra-core/src/proctree.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/proctree.rs) stops a child and everything it starts as one unit.

| Platform | Mechanism | `terminate` | `kill` | `end` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unix | The child leads its own process group (`process_group(0)`). | Sends SIGTERM to the group and to the child. | Sends SIGKILL to the group and to the child. | Does nothing. |
| Windows | The child runs in a Job Object with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` and no breakaway. | Does nothing, because console programs have no such request. | Calls `TerminateJobObject`. | Closes the job handle, which kills what remains. |

On Windows, a child must be in its job before it starts anything. Otherwise its first children escape the job. The flow has three steps:

1. `prepare_tokio` or `prepare_std` sets `CREATION_FLAGS`: `CREATE_SUSPENDED | CREATE_NO_WINDOW`. The child starts suspended. The no-window flag stops a server without a console from opening a window for each command.
2. `Tree::of_tokio` or `Tree::of_std` assigns the child to a new job.
3. The function `resume` calls `NtResumeProcess`, which resumes all threads that the kernel holds for the process. A thread snapshot cannot be used, because a snapshot taken right after creation can miss the new thread.

If the assignment or the resume fails, the code terminates the process and returns the error. The Bash tool then returns "Cannot start bash: ...".

`Tree::adopt_running(pid)` takes over a child that Ostra did not create with these flags, such as a PTY child. On Windows, the processes that the child started before this call are not in the job.

## Read, Write, and Edit

The file tools are in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/fs.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/fs.rs). The rule for all three: a run must read an existing file before it writes or edits it. The reason, from the tool descriptions: the run then never overwrites content it has not seen.

### Which paths count as read

The `ToolEnv` marks a path as read in these cases:

- `Read` shows the file. A binary file is also marked.
- `Write` creates or replaces the file.
- `Edit` creates the file with an empty `old_string`.
- `Skill` loads a skill file.
- `Report` writes the declared report file. A later `Edit` of the report then works without a `Read`.
- `Document` writes the markdown file and its `.json` file.

### Read

`Read` takes `file_path`, and optionally `offset` (1-based) and `limit`. Each result line is `{line number right-aligned to 6 characters}<TAB>{line}`. The tool removes a trailing `\r`.

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_LINES` | 2000 | Lines returned when `limit` is missing. |
| `MAX_LINE_CHARS` | 2000 | A longer line is cut and ends with `... [line truncated]`. |
| `MAX_READ_BYTES` | 50 MiB | A larger file returns an error that points to `head`, `tail`, or `sed -n`. |

The tool adds a note `(Showing lines A to B of N. Use offset and limit to read other lines.)` when it shows only part of the file. It returns these other results:

- **The file does not exist.** An error: "File does not exist: <path>".
- **The path is a directory.** An error that points to Glob or `ls`.
- **The file looks binary.** The first 8192 bytes hold a zero byte or invalid UTF-8. The result is not an error. It says that the file is binary and gives its size.
- **The file is empty.** A result that says the file exists and is empty.
- **The offset is past the end.** A result that gives the line count.

### Write

`Write` takes `file_path` and `content`. It creates the parent directories and writes the complete content. Nothing is appended.

- If the path is a directory, it returns an error.
- If the file exists and the run has not read it, it returns an error that says to read it first.
- A new file returns "File created successfully at: <path>". A replaced file returns "The file <path> has been updated."
- The `diff` field of the output holds a unified diff with 3 lines of context. `unified_diff` cuts it at 50000 bytes.

### Edit

`Edit` takes `file_path`, `old_string`, `new_string`, and optionally `replace_all`. The checks run in this order:

1. `old_string` and `new_string` are equal: an error.
2. The file does not exist and `old_string` is empty: the tool creates the file with `new_string`.
3. The file does not exist and `old_string` has text: an error.
4. The run has not read the file: an error.
5. `old_string` is empty and the file exists: an error.
6. `old_string` matches 0 places: an error. It tells the model to read the file again.
7. `old_string` matches more than 1 place and `replace_all` is not set: an error with the count.

If all checks pass, the tool replaces the first match, or every match with `replace_all`. A single replacement returns the lines around the change, from 4 lines before to 4 lines after. A `replace_all` with more than 1 match returns "All N matches were replaced."

## Grep and Glob

Both tools are in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/search.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/search.rs). They run in `spawn_blocking`, because the walk reads many files. Both use the same directory walker.

### The walker

The walker includes hidden files, so it searches `.ostra/`. It follows `.gitignore`, `.git/info/exclude`, the global git ignore, and the ignore files of parent directories, even outside a git repository. It never enters a `.git` directory.

The walker also hides credential stores and the data directory of Ostra, except its `assets` directory (`SecretFilter`). The reason from the code: a search from a parent directory must not walk into them.

### Grep

`Grep` takes `pattern` (a Rust regex) and optional `path`, `glob`, `type`, `output_mode`, `-i`, `-n`, `-A`, `-B`, `-C`, `head_limit`, and `multiline`.

| `output_mode` | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `files_with_matches` (default) | `Found N files`, then the paths, newest first. |
| `content` | Lines as `path:line:text`. Context lines use `-` as the separator. Groups that are not adjacent have a `--` line between them. |
| `count` | One `path:count` row for each file, then `Found N matches across M files`. |

- With `-C`, the tool sets both context sizes. `-A` and `-B` override it.
- `-n` defaults to true and affects only `content` mode.
- A matching line longer than 500 bytes is cut and ends with `...`.
- `head_limit` limits the lines in `content` mode, and the files or rows in the other modes. Content mode adds "(Output limited to N lines by head_limit.)" when it cuts.
- `multiline` lets `.` match a newline.
- The result is cut to `MAX_GREP_OUTPUT`, which is 30000 bytes, and gets a note of the number of characters that it dropped.
- A binary file stops its search at the first zero byte.
- If `path` names a file, Grep searches only that file and ignores `glob` and `type`.
- If nothing matches, the result is `No files found` or `No matches found`.

The `glob` argument can hold several patterns. Commas and spaces outside braces separate them, so `*.{ts,tsx}` stays one pattern. The `type` argument accepts aliases: `rs` is `rust`, `python` is `py`, `typescript` and `tsx` are `ts`, `javascript`, `jsx`, and `mjs` are `js`, `md` is `markdown`, `yml` is `yaml`, `sh` and `bash` are `sh`, and a few more.

The errors:

- A bad regex returns "Invalid regex `<pattern>`: ...".
- An unknown `output_mode` returns an error that names the three valid modes.
- A missing path returns "Path does not exist: <path>".

### Glob

`Glob` takes `pattern` and an optional `path`, which must be a directory. The `*` does not cross a directory separator, but `**` does. The tool matches the pattern against the path relative to the root and uses forward slashes, so `**/*.rs` works on Windows. It returns file paths newest first (by modification time) and stops at `MAX_GLOB_RESULTS`, which is 100. If there are more, the result ends with "(Results are truncated: showing 100 of N. Use a more specific path or pattern.)" If the path is not a directory, the tool returns "Not a directory: <path>".

## Load a skill

The `Skill` tool in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/misc.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/misc.rs) returns the text of a `SKILL.md` file with the line "Skill loaded from <path>. Follow its instructions for this task." For the skills themselves, see [Project init and skills](init-and-skills.md).

The tool resolves the skill in this order:

1. **`path` argument.** The tool reads the file at that path. If it does not exist, the error is "No skill file at <path>."
2. **`name` argument.** The tool also accepts `skill` as the key. It removes a leading `ostra:`. A name that holds `/` or `..` is refused, because a name is not a path.
3. **Project skill.** `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` first, then the older `.ostra/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
4. **Workspace artifact.** A custom skill at `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` among the visible artifacts of the workspace. See [Workspace artifacts and uploads](artifacts-and-uploads.md).
5. **Embedded skill.** The `skill_resolver` of the config returns skills that Ostra ships.

The project skill wins over an artifact, and the artifact wins over an embedded skill. A test confirms that a skill in `.agents/skills` wins over one in `.ostra/skills`. If nothing matches, the error names the paths that the tool tried and says not to guess a path.

## Fetch a web page

`WebFetch` in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/web.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/web.rs) fetches an `http` or `https` URL and returns its content as markdown. The `prompt` argument is optional. The tool only prints it above the content, to remind the model what it looks for. The tool does not filter with it. When the provider offers server-side web fetch, the native loop does not offer this local tool. See [The native loop](#the-native-loop).

### Protection against private addresses

A model that can fetch any URL can reach the machine of the user or its local network. The client has three protections.

- **A DNS resolver that drops private addresses.** `PublicResolver` removes private and loopback addresses from each answer. It uses `ostra_sandbox::egress::is_private`. If no public address remains, the request fails. Because the check runs in the resolver, a DNS answer that changes between the check and the connection cannot bypass it.
- **A check of IP literals.** A URL whose host is a private IP address never reaches the resolver. `private_literal` refuses it first.
- **No proxy.** A proxy resolves the name itself and skips the address check.

The refusal says: "Add the allow rule `WebFetch(domain:<host>)` to fetch <url>, because it points at a private or loopback address, which WebFetch refuses by default."

### Redirects

The policy checked only the first URL. Thus the client follows a redirect only when the new URL has the same host and port as the previous one, and uses `http` or `https`. After more than `MAX_REDIRECTS` (10) redirects, it returns an error. A redirect to another host is not followed. The tool returns a normal result that tells the model to fetch the new URL with a new `WebFetch` call, so the policy checks that URL too.

```rust
let redirect = reqwest::redirect::Policy::custom(|attempt| {
    let same_host = attempt.previous().last().is_some_and(|prev| {
        prev.host_str() == attempt.url().host_str()
            && prev.port_or_known_default() == attempt.url().port_or_known_default()
    });
    if attempt.previous().len() > MAX_REDIRECTS { attempt.error("too many redirects") }
    else if same_host && matches!(attempt.url().scheme(), "http" | "https") { attempt.follow() }
    else { attempt.stop() }
});
```

### Content handling

| Constant or rule | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request timeout | 20 seconds | The client stops a slow request. |
| `MAX_BODY_BYTES` | 5 MiB | The tool reads at most this many bytes and cuts the rest without an error. |
| `MAX_TEXT_CHARS` | 100000 | The text is cut with `truncate_end` and gets a note of the dropped characters. |
| User agent | `ostra/<version>` | Sent with each request. |

The tool converts HTML to markdown with `htmd`. It treats a response as HTML when the content type has `html`, or when the content type is empty and the first 512 characters have `<html` or `<!doctype html`. It returns other text types as they are: `text/*`, JSON, XML, JavaScript, YAML, and markdown. It refuses a body with a zero byte in the first 8192 bytes, and any other type, with "The response is `<type>`, which is not text, so it cannot be shown."

The result starts with `Prompt: ...` if the model gave one, then `Redirected to: <url>` if the final URL differs, then `Content of <url> (HTTP <status>):`. A status outside 200 to 299 returns the same text as an error.

### What happens when

- **The URL does not parse.** An error: "Invalid URL `<url>`: ...".
- **The scheme is not http or https.** An error that names the scheme.
- **The fetch fails.** An error: "Fetching <url> failed: ...".
- **The cancel token fires.** `execute` returns "Cancelled."

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `WebFetch(domain:<host>)` entry in `permissions.allow` | No host is allowed | The settings files. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md). | At the next execution, because the executor reads `permissions.allow` when it builds the `ToolEnv` | The refusal text of the tool call | Add or remove the entry. The match is exact and not case-sensitive. |

The entry has a double effect. It lets the policy allow the host, and it lets `PublicResolver` resolve that exact host to a private address. A wildcard does not apply to the resolver. For the permission rules, see [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).

## Write the report and the typed document

The agents of the pipeline return their work with `Report`, `Document`, and a `submit_<agent>` tool. The code is in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/misc.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/misc.rs) and [`crates/ostra-tools/src/doc.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/doc.rs).

### Report

`Report` takes `content` (the complete report, in markdown) and an optional `reason`. It writes the content to the `report_file` path of the config. The model cannot choose the path, because later stages find the report there. The call replaces the file and returns "Report written to <path> (N bytes)." If the run has no declared report file, it returns an error.

The `reason` argument belongs to the lesson gate. If the gate refuses the report because the run did not record a lesson after a failure, the model records the lesson with `Memory`, or sends a `reason` that says why no lesson applies. The gate is a policy rule, not part of this crate. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).

### Document

Only explore, generate-spec, and plan write a typed document. `Document` takes `path`, and either `document` or `update` (with `remove`).

- `document` replaces the whole stored document.
- `update` replaces each top-level field it names. A list whose items have an `id` is merged by id. `remove` drops list items by id. A number in `remove` is accepted as an id.
- A call with `document` and `update` (or `document` with `remove`) returns an error.
- A `remove` call with no stored document returns an error.

Two checks run on the path, in this order:

1. **The file name.** The name must start with the prefix of the document kind and end with `.md`. A plan file must not contain `-phase-`. The code uses `starts_with`, `ends_with`, and `contains`, and does not call `fold`. If the check fails, the error says the expected name shape: `<prefix>{run-stamp}-{topic-slug}.md`.
2. **The directory.** The parent directory of the file must be the session directory. This check compares both paths through `ostra_core::paths::fold`, so a Windows path matches despite case and prefix differences. If the check fails, the error has its own text: "Write the <kind> directly inside <session dir>, the session dir your prompt names, because the next stage reads it there."

The tool validates the document against its schema. If the schema check fails, nothing is written. If it passes, Ostra writes the markdown and a `.json` file beside it. A plan also gets one `-phase-{N}.md` file for each phase. The result lists the counts of the document and the findings of the Ostra checks. If any error remains, the result says that the submit call is refused until the model fixes it with an `update`. Warnings do not block the submit.

The reason for the tool: Ostra renders the markdown from the typed document and shows each part in the browser. Writes to these files with Write, Edit, or the shell are refused. For the document types, see [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md).

## Record and recall lessons

`Memory` and `MemoryRecall` read and write the lesson store of the project at `memory_db`. For the store and its ranking, see [Storage: databases and lesson memory](storage.md).

- **`Memory`** takes `area`, `lesson`, and an optional `source`. It trims the values. An empty `area` or `lesson` returns an error. If `source` is missing, the tool uses `memory_source` of the config, for example `implementer x_123`. It records the lesson and returns the new total. Recording the same area and lesson again updates the lesson in place.
- **`MemoryRecall`** takes `query`, and optionally `area` and `limit`. The default limit is `DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT` (8) from the store. The tool clamps it to the range from 1 to `MAX_RECALL_LIMIT` (50). The result lists `N. [area] lesson (source: ..., date)`, most relevant first. If nothing matches, it returns "No lessons recorded for this query."

Both tools run the database work in `spawn_blocking`.

## Search the documentation books

`DocsSearch` searches the books that the docs stage wrote for the workspace. It takes `query`, and optionally `project` and `limit`. The `limit` has a default of 5 and a maximum of 15. The tool builds the index from the books of `workspace_root` on each call. The ranking and the passage rules belong to [Documentation books and search](documentation-books.md). The code tools have their own limits, which [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) lists.

- **No workspace.** A run with an empty `workspace_root` gets "This run has no workspace, so there are no documentation books. Read the code instead."
- **No books.** The result says that the workspace has no books yet.
- **No match.** The result says that no section matches, and suggests other names or the code.
- **A match.** The result lists `N sections matched, most relevant first`, each with its title, project, matching passages, and the Markdown file name.

A book describes the code at the time the docs stage wrote it. Thus the description of the tool tells the model to check a passage against the code before it relies on it.

## Code tools

The 8 code tools (`CodeOutline`, `CodeFind`, `CodeCallers`, `CodeCallees`, `CodeImplementations`, `CodeNeighbors`, `CodeImpact`, and `CodeMap`) have their schemas in `defs.rs`. Each tool takes paths relative to the project root, and an absolute path inside the project also works (`PATH_NOTE`). The schemas set the `limit`, `depth`, and default values of each tool. For these values, the index, and the output of each tool, see [Code navigation](code-navigation.md).

The tool code in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/code.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/code.rs) holds no index. It passes the call, with the `repo_root`, to the `CodeNav` handle of the config. The server owns the index and the graph. If the handle is `None`, the tool returns an error that tells the model to use Grep, Glob, and Read.

## Project management tools

A management tool is a call that an agent makes to Ostra itself, not to the files it works on. There are two: `ProjectList` and `ProjectCreate`. The tools of the `ManageProjects` capability use the `Manage` trait in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/manage.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/manage.rs). The server binds that trait to the workspace and the engine in [`crates/ostra-server/src/manage.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/manage.rs). If the run has no `Manage` handle, the tool returns "<tool> is not available to this run, because its agent does not manage projects." The policy has already checked the call, and for `ProjectCreate` the user has already approved it, when it reaches this code.

### ProjectList

`ProjectList` takes no arguments. It returns the workspace root, then one line for each project: the key, the path, the stack (or `not set`), the init status (`initialized`, `not initialized`, `initializing`, or `folder missing`), and `, in this session's scope` for a project of the session. Without projects, it returns "No projects yet." The model calls it before `ProjectCreate`, so the key and the folder are not taken.

### ProjectCreate

`ProjectCreate` creates an empty project, adds it to the workspace, and puts it in the scope of the session. `ProjectCreateInput::parse` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/manage.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/manage.rs) trims every field and drops empty requirements. It then checks the input, before the user is asked. The reason: a malformed call is refused before it costs the user an approval.

| Field | Rule | Limit constant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | Lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. It starts with a letter or a digit. | None |
| `stack` | A valid stack name (`is_stack_name`) | None |
| `purpose` | Not empty, at most 800 Unicode characters | `MAX_PURPOSE_CHARS` |
| `requirements` | 1 to 20 entries | `MAX_REQUIREMENTS` |
| each requirement | At most 400 Unicode characters | `MAX_REQUIREMENT_CHARS` |
| `folder` | Relative to the workspace root. It has no `..` and is not absolute. It defaults to the key. | None |
| `git_init` | Runs `git init` in the new folder. It defaults to true. | None |

Rule O1 says that `ProjectCreate` changes Ostra, so the user approves each call unless YOLO is on. The card shows `ask_reason()`: "Create project `<key>` (<stack>) in `<folder>/` of the workspace: <purpose>". The text is cut to 250 characters, because some harnesses clip the reason of an ask.

The server then runs these steps in `ExecManage::create`:

1. Ask the engine state (`project_creation_refusal`). It refuses the call in these cases: the session is not a pipeline session, the session has ended, the run that asked has ended, the project is already in the session, the approved plan does not name the key as new, or the run is not in a phase that the plan puts in that project.
2. Find the target folder with `create_target`. The folder must be inside the workspace root, must not be the root itself, and must be new or empty and outside every other project. The check resolves symbolic links of the parents.
3. Claim the folder, so no other git operation uses it. If another operation holds it, the call returns "Another git operation holds this folder. Try again."
4. Create the directory and, if `git_init` is true, run `git init --quiet` with the quick git timeout.
5. Import the project into the workspace with the key and the stack.
6. Record a `CreatedProject` event in the session, with the key, path, stack, purpose, requirements, execution, and agent. The event carries every fact, because the fold of the log cannot read workspace settings.

If step 4 or step 5 fails, the server removes the folder that it created, and the call returns the error. If step 6 fails, the project exists but is not in the session, and the error says so. On success, the result tells the model to tag the deliverables of the new project with its key, and to write a first deliverable that creates the skeleton. Ostra initializes the project from the stack and requirements before any phase runs in it.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Approval of each `ProjectCreate` call | The user approves each call | The permission card of the session | At the call | The card, and the new project in the workspace | Deny the card. The agent then puts the work in a project that is already in scope. YOLO mode approves it without a card. See [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md). |

## Coordination tools

`SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, and `SubagentReply` use the `Coordinate` trait of [`crates/ostra-tools/src/coord.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/coord.rs). Their `ToolOutput.end` value (`Continue`, `Wait`, or `Finish`) tells the loop to continue, wait for a message, or end a consult run. The rules and limits of coordination are on [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md).

## Limits at a glance

The constants `MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS`, `MAX_LINE_CHARS`, and `MAX_TEXT_CHARS` of `ostra-tools` compare sizes in UTF-8 bytes, even though the names say characters. The `ProjectCreate` rows count Unicode characters (`MAX_PURPOSE_CHARS` and `MAX_REQUIREMENT_CHARS`, in `crates/ostra-core/src/manage.rs`). The `ask_reason` text also cuts at 250 Unicode characters.

| Constant | Value | Tool | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS` | 120000 | Bash, PowerShell, Cmd | The timeout when `timeout` is missing. |
| `MAX_TIMEOUT_MS` | 600000 | Bash, PowerShell, Cmd | The largest timeout. A smaller value than 1 becomes 1. |
| `MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS` | 30000 | Bash, PowerShell, Cmd | The size of the result text, in bytes. |
| `CAPTURE_HALF` | 128 KiB | Bash, PowerShell, Cmd | The head and the tail that the capture keeps in memory. |
| `DRAIN_GRACE` | 300 ms | Bash, PowerShell, Cmd | The silence that ends the output drain. |
| `KILL_WAIT` | 5 seconds | Bash, PowerShell, Cmd | The wait for a killed child. |
| `DEFAULT_LINES` | 2000 | Read | Lines for each read. |
| `MAX_LINE_CHARS` | 2000 | Read | The length of one line, in bytes. |
| `MAX_READ_BYTES` | 50 MiB | Read | The largest file. |
| `MAX_GLOB_RESULTS` | 100 | Glob | Paths in the result. |
| `MAX_GREP_OUTPUT` | 30000 | Grep | The size of the result text, in bytes. |
| `MAX_BODY_BYTES` | 5 MiB | WebFetch | The bytes that the tool reads. |
| `MAX_TEXT_CHARS` | 100000 | WebFetch | The size of the content, in bytes. |
| `MAX_REDIRECTS` | 10 | WebFetch | Redirects to the same host. |
| `MAX_RECALL_LIMIT` | 50 | MemoryRecall | The largest `limit`. |
| Diff cap | 50000 bytes | Write, Edit | The size of the `diff` field. |
| `MAX_PURPOSE_CHARS` | 800 | ProjectCreate | The `purpose` length, in Unicode characters. |
| `MAX_REQUIREMENTS` | 20 | ProjectCreate | The requirement count. |
| `MAX_REQUIREMENT_CHARS` | 400 | ProjectCreate | The length of one requirement, in Unicode characters. |
