sections.title: Code navigation
sections.summary: How the built-in tokenizer, the per-project index, the dependency graph, LSP servers, and the code_provider program answer code questions for the Files view and for agents, with every limit.
sections.body:
## Why Ostra has its own code index

Without a code index, the Files view shows plain text, and an agent must read whole files to find where a name is defined. One language server for each language fixes this, but each server needs an install, a start time, and a project load. The `ostra-code` crate gives every project a built-in answer for 16 languages with no install. A project can add its own program or Language Server Protocol (LSP) servers for better answers.

This page covers these parts:

- The tokenizer and the language tables.
- The per-project index and the file watcher that keeps it current.
- Import resolution, the outline, and usage search.
- The dependency graph and the impact walk.
- LSP servers and the project `code_provider` program.
- Completion, signature help, and jump hints.
- The agent code tools.
- The routes and socket messages that carry the answers, and every limit.

The page stops before the Files view screens. See [Project, Files, and dependency screens](web-project-screens.md) for the screens. See [Project files, Git dock, and cloning](project-files-and-git.md) for the file list and the write touches that this page uses.

### Terms on this page

- **Provider**: a source of answers that implements the `CodeProvider` trait. The three kinds are the `code_provider` program (`CommandProvider`), an LSP server (`LspProvider`), and the built-in provider (`NativeProvider`).
- **Built-in provider**: the tokenizer and the index. It reports the provider name `native` (`NATIVE_PROVIDER`).
- **File list**: the project-relative paths that the Files view holds (`FileIndex`). The index reads only paths on this list, so ignored files stay out.
- **Package**: a folder that holds a manifest file such as `Cargo.toml`. The code calls a package a unit.
- **Touch**: a note that one project file changed on disk.

## How a request reaches an answer

`Code::ask` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs) builds a chain of providers for each request and returns the first answer. The order is fixed: the `code_provider` program, then each language server in the order of the settings, then the built-in provider. The built-in provider is last and answers every request. Thus a failed external program never leaves the Files view empty.

### Flow of one request

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Request: file, usages, deps, symbols"] --> B["Code::ask checks path, symbol, and limit"]
    B --> C{"Project has an approved code_provider?"}
    C -- yes --> D["CommandProvider runs the program"]
    C -- no --> E
    D -- "answer" --> Z["Answer stamped with provider name"]
    D -- "null or failure" --> E["Each LspProvider in settings order"]
    E -- "answer" --> Z
    E -- "None or failure" --> F["NativeProvider: tokenizer and index"]
    F --> Z
```

### Which source answers which request

Only some requests go through the whole chain. The other requests use one or two sources.

| Request | `code_provider` program | LSP servers | Built-in provider |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| File display (`code/file`) | Yes | Yes, laid over the built-in answer | Yes |
| Usages (`code/usages`) | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Symbols (`code/symbols`) | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Dependencies (`code/deps`) | Yes | No, a server returns nothing | Yes |
| Dependency graph (`code/graph`) | No | No | Yes |
| Completion (`code_complete`) | No | Yes | Fallback |
| Signature help (`code_signature`) | No | Yes | No |
| Supertype and implementation jump (`code_navigate`) | No | Fallback | First |
| Outside file (`code/external`) | No | Yes | No |
| Agent code tools | No | No | Yes |

### Checks before the chain

`Code::ask` checks each request before it builds the chain:

- The path must stay inside the project root. `files::contain` refuses a path that leaves it.
- The path must name a file. Otherwise the route returns `400` with `Name a file with path.`
- A symbol must have 1 to 256 bytes (`MAX_SYMBOL_LEN`) and no whitespace or control character. Otherwise the route returns `400` with `` Name one symbol with symbol, such as `parse_config`. ``
- The limit is clamped. Usages use 1 to 2,000 and default to 500. Symbols use 1 to 200 and default to 50.

The server reads the provider settings again for each request. Thus a saved change applies to the next request.

### What happens when

- **A provider returns `null` or has no answer for the request.** The chain asks the next provider. The answer has no warning.
- **A provider fails or breaks the protocol.** The chain asks the next provider. The final answer carries the warning `` The code provider `<name>` failed, so the built-in index answered: <reason> ``. Several warnings join with one space and come before the warning of the answer itself.
- **The built-in provider fails**, for example because it cannot read the file. The route returns `400` with the reasons.
- **The answer type does not match the route.** The route returns `500` with `The code provider answered a different request.`
- **The settings file waits for approval.** The server removes `code_provider` and every language server from the settings, so only the built-in provider answers. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) for the approval rules.

```rust
pub async fn ask(providers: &[Arc<dyn CodeProvider>], req: &ProviderRequest) -> Result<Answer, String> {
    let mut problems = vec![];
    for p in providers {
        match p.answer(req).await {
            Ok(Some(mut a)) => {
                let warning = (!problems.is_empty()).then(|| problems.join(" "));
                a.stamp(&p.name(), warning);
                return Ok(a);
            }
            Ok(None) => {}
            Err(e) => { /* log, then push the reason to problems */ }
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

## Tokenizer and language tables

The tokenizer in [`crates/ostra-code/src/lex.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/lex.rs) turns source text into tokens for every language with one table-driven loop. It never fails. Text that it does not understand is skipped. The language tables in [`crates/ostra-code/src/lang.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/lang.rs) hold the rules of each language, so one entry serves display, outline, usages, and imports.

### The lexer steps

The loop `Lexer::run` reads the bytes in order. At each position it tries these rules and takes the first that matches:

1. Skip whitespace.
2. Read a block comment. Rust block comments nest, because `nested_comments` is `true` for Rust.
3. Read a line comment. A shell `#` starts a comment only at the start of a word. A PHP `#[` starts an attribute, not a comment.
4. Read a family form. Rust has attributes (`#[...]`) and lifetimes (`'a`).
5. Read a string. Python also reads the prefixes `r`, `b`, `f`, and `u`. Triple quotes work in the languages that set `triple_quotes`.
6. Read a number.
7. Read an identifier and class it as a keyword, a constant, a builtin type, or a plain identifier. A Rust name that ends in `!` becomes one macro token.
8. Read punctuation. Skip a control byte with its UTF-8 sequence.

### Token positions

A token holds its byte range for the analysis. It also holds a 1-based line, a 0-based column, and a length for the browser. The column and the length count UTF-16 units, because a browser string index counts UTF-16 units. A 4-byte UTF-8 character counts as 2 units. A comment or string that spans lines becomes one token for each line, and the later tokens set `cont`. The display answer never has a token that spans lines.

### The display answer

`render` in [`crates/ostra-code/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/lib.rs) lexes a file and runs the outline analysis. It returns a `CodeFile` with the language id, the symbols, the imports, and a flat token list. Each token takes four numbers: line, column, length, and an index into `classes`. The 11 classes (`CLASSES`) have this order: keyword, type, function, name, constant, macro, attribute, string, number, comment, operator. A token with no class is left out.

### The language families

The table `ALL` has 22 languages. Each `Lang` entry sets the comment syntax, the string delimiters, the keywords, the builtin types and constants, the extra identifier characters, and the definition keywords. A `Family` groups the languages that share definition and import rules.

| Family | Languages |
| --- | --- |
| `Rust` | `rust` |
| `Js` | `typescript`, `javascript` |
| `Python` | `python` |
| `Go` | `go` |
| `Jvm` | `java`, `kotlin`, `scala`, `csharp`, `swift`, `php` |
| `C` | `c`, `cpp` |
| `Ruby` | `ruby` |
| `Lua` | `lua` |
| `Shell` | `shell` |
| `Data` | `sql`, `toml`, `yaml`, `json`, `css`, `html` |

The `Data` family gets colors only. It has no definitions and no imports, and its files stay out of the index. The other 16 languages form `NAV_LANGUAGES` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/code.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/code.rs). A language server entry can name only those 16 ids.

### The language tables in lang.rs

Each language is one `static Lang` in `lang.rs`. A language that looks like another one copies its entry with `..` and changes only some fields. The table below lists each constant of the file and what it holds.

| Constant | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `C_COMMENT` | The block comment pair `Some(("/*", "*/"))`. `RUST`, `TYPESCRIPT`, `GO`, `JAVA`, and `C` use it. |
| `RUST` | Family `Rust`. Line comment `//`, nested block comments, `"` strings that can span lines. 37 keywords, 18 builtin types, the constants `true`, `false`, `None`, `Some`, `Ok`, `Err`. 10 definition keywords: `fn`, `struct`, `union`, `enum`, `trait`, `type`, `mod`, `const`, `static`, `impl`. |
| `JS_KEYWORDS` | The 51 keywords that `TYPESCRIPT` and `JAVASCRIPT` share, from `abstract` to `yield`. |
| `JS_DEFS` | The 9 definition keywords of the `Js` family: `function`, `class`, `interface`, `type`, `enum`, `namespace`, `const`, `let`, `var`. |
| `TYPESCRIPT` | Family `Js`. Line comment `//`, `C_COMMENT`, strings with `"`, `'`, and a backtick. `JS_KEYWORDS`, 9 builtin types, the constants `true`, `false`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`, `Infinity`. `$` can appear in a name. Decorators with `@` are attributes. |
| `JAVASCRIPT` | A copy of `TYPESCRIPT` with the id `javascript` and no builtin types. |
| `PYTHON` | Family `Python`. Line comment `#`, no block comment, strings with `"` and `'`, triple quotes. 34 keywords, 10 builtin types, the constants `True`, `False`, `None`. Decorators with `@` are attributes. Definition keywords: `def`, `class`. |
| `GO` | Family `Go`. Line comment `//`, `C_COMMENT`, strings with `"`, `'`, and a backtick. Definition keywords: `func`, `type`, `const`, `var`. |
| `JVM_MODIFIERS` | The 16 modifier words: `abstract`, `final`, `private`, `protected`, `public`, `static`, `override`, `open`, `internal`, `sealed`, `virtual`, `readonly`, `async`, `partial`, `data`, `inline`. The function `is_modifier` tests a word against the list. No code calls `is_modifier` now. |
| `JAVA` | Family `Jvm`. Line comment `//`, `C_COMMENT`, strings with `"` and `'`, triple quotes for text blocks. 8 builtin types, the constants `true`, `false`, `null`. `$` can appear in a name. Annotations with `@` are attributes. Definition keywords: `class`, `interface`, `enum`, `record`. The other `Jvm` languages copy this entry with `..JAVA`. |
| `KOTLIN` | Own keywords and builtin types. Definition keywords: `fun`, `class`, `interface`, `object`, `typealias`, `val`, `var`. |
| `SCALA` | Own keywords. Definition keywords: `def`, `class`, `object`, `trait`, `enum`, `type`, `val`, `var`. |
| `CSHARP` | Own keywords, and `triple_quotes` is `false`. Definition keywords: `class`, `struct`, `interface`, `enum`, `record`, `namespace`. |
| `SWIFT` | Own keywords. Definition keywords: `func`, `class`, `struct`, `enum`, `protocol`, `extension` (an `Impl`), `typealias`, `let` (a constant), `var`. |
| `PHP` | Line comments `//` and `#`, and `triple_quotes` is `false`. Definition keywords: `function`, `class`, `interface`, `trait`, `enum`, `namespace`, `const`. |
| `C` | Family `C`. Line comment `//`, `C_COMMENT`, strings with `"` and `'`. Definition keywords: `struct`, `union`, `enum`. |
| `CPP` | A copy of `C` with the id `cpp`, more keywords, and the definition keywords `struct`, `class`, `union`, `enum`, `namespace`. |
| `RUBY` | Family `Ruby`. Line comment `#`, strings with `"`, `'`, and a backtick that can span lines. `?` and `!` can end a name. Definition keywords: `def`, `class`, `module`. |
| `LUA` | Family `Lua`. Line comment `--`, strings with `"` and `'`. Definition keyword: `function`. |
| `SHELL` | Family `Shell`. Line comment `#`, strings with `"`, `'`, and a backtick that can span lines. Definition keyword: `function`. |
| `SQL`, `TOML`, `YAML`, `JSON`, `CSS`, `HTML` | Family `Data`: colors only, with no definitions. `SQL` uses the line comment `--` and ignores keyword case. `TOML` allows `-` in a name. `YAML` and `JSON` copy `TOML`. `CSS` has block comments only. `HTML` copies `CSS` with the comment pair `<!--` and `-->` and no keywords. |
| `ALL` | The list of the 22 `Lang` entries. `by_id` and `for_path` search it. |

`for_path` picks the language from the file name. These rules apply:

- `Makefile` and `Dockerfile` have no language.
- `Gemfile` and `Rakefile` are Ruby. `.bashrc`, `.zshrc`, and `.profile` are shell.
- All other files use the lowercase extension from this table.

| Language id | Extensions |
| --- | --- |
| `rust` | `rs` |
| `typescript` | `ts`, `tsx`, `mts`, `cts` |
| `javascript` | `js`, `jsx`, `mjs`, `cjs` |
| `python` | `py`, `pyi` |
| `go`, `java`, `swift`, `php`, `lua`, `sql`, `toml` | `go`, `java`, `swift`, `php`, `lua`, `sql`, `toml` |
| `kotlin` | `kt`, `kts` |
| `scala` | `scala`, `sc` |
| `csharp` | `cs` |
| `c` | `c`, `h` |
| `cpp` | `cc`, `cpp`, `cxx`, `hpp`, `hh`, `hxx`, `ipp`, `m`, `mm` |
| `ruby` | `rb`, `rake`, `gemspec` |
| `shell` | `sh`, `bash`, `zsh` |
| `yaml` | `yaml`, `yml` |
| `json` | `json`, `jsonc` |
| `css` | `css`, `scss`, `less` |
| `html` | `html`, `htm`, `xml`, `svg`, `vue`, `svelte` |

### What happens when

- **The extension is unknown.** `render` returns an empty answer with `language` set to `null`.
- **The file is larger than 1 MiB (`MAX_FILE_BYTES`).** The built-in provider skips the tokenizer and returns the warning `The file is larger than the size Ostra tokenizes, so it shows without color.`
- **The file contains bytes that are not UTF-8.** The reader replaces them, so the tokenizer still runs.

## Per-project index

The index answers usages, dependencies, and symbol search without a compiler. Its problem is cost: a query that reads every file is slow on a large project. The index in [`crates/ostra-code/src/index.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/index.rs) keeps, for each file, the set of names that the file mentions, its definitions, and its imports. It never keeps the text. A usages query then re-reads only the files that mention the name.

### What the index holds

`Indexes<K>` holds one slot for each project, keyed by workspace and project key. A slot builds its `ProjectIndex` on the first query. The index has no copy on disk, so a server restart drops it and the first query builds it again.

For each file, an `Entry` holds these items:

- The sorted, distinct names that the file mentions, as interned numbers.
- The mentions: each name with its use, which is bare, qualified, or a member.
- The definitions with kind, position, container, the implemented trait (`via`), and a one-line signature.
- The raw imports, the resolved targets, and the supertype links (`class A extends B`).

A posting list maps each name to the files that mention it. A second map links each name to the files that define it.

### How the index stays current

`sync` compares the size and the modification time of each listed file with the stored stamp. It re-analyzes only the files that changed, on at most 8 worker threads. It removes the files that left the file list.

A call to `Indexes::with` decides how much to check:

- If the file list is a new object, or the last full check is older than 30 seconds (`FULL_SYNC`), `sync` checks every listed file.
- Otherwise `sync` checks only the paths that a touch marked.

```rust
let list_changed = st.list.as_ref().is_none_or(|l| !Arc::ptr_eq(l, list));
let stale = st.last_full.is_none_or(|t| t.elapsed() > FULL_SYNC);
if list_changed || stale {
    st.index.sync(&list.paths, None);
    ...
} else if !dirty.is_empty() {
    st.index.sync(&list.paths, Some(&dirty));
}
f(&mut st.index)
```

The paths that a write marked live in a separate set, `dirty`. Thus a write never waits for an index build. The full check every 30 seconds catches edits that no touch reported. See [Index watcher and write touches](#index-watcher-and-write-touches) for the sources of touches.

### Which files the index skips

- Files that are not on the file list, such as ignored files.
- Files of the `Data` family.
- Files larger than 1 MiB (`MAX_FILE_BYTES`).
- Binary files: a NUL byte in the first 8,000 bytes.
- Minified files: more than 50,000 bytes with an average line longer than 1,000 bytes.
- Files that push the total above 256 MiB (`MAX_INDEX_BYTES`). The index sets `truncated`, and each usages or symbols answer then carries the warning in `TRUNCATED`: `The project is larger than the size Ostra indexes, so some files are not searched.`

### Queries on the index

- `usages` matches by name alone. It lists the definitions, then the mentions outside the definitions. It reads files in this order: the file that asked, the other files of its folder, then the rest by path.
- `deps` lists what a file imports and which files import it. It stops at 2,000 importers (`MAX_IMPORTERS`) and sets `truncated`.
- `symbols` finds definitions by name. The score decides the order.

| Match | Score |
| --- | --- |
| Exact, same case | 110 |
| Equal ignoring case | 100 |
| Prefix | 80 |
| Substring | 60 |
| Initials, 2 or more letters (`pn` finds `parse_name` and `ParseName`) | 40 |

A higher score comes first. Among equal scores, the shorter name comes first, then the alphabetical order.

### What happens when

- **A user saves a file in Ostra, or an agent writes it.** A touch marks the path. The next query re-reads that file only.
- **A file changes outside Ostra.** The watcher reports it within about 2 seconds, or the 30-second check catches it.
- **The project root changes.** `Indexes::with` creates a new index.
- **A file grows over 1 MiB, is deleted, or becomes ignored.** `sync` removes it from the index.
- **The first query on a project runs.** The index reads every source file. The server runs this work on a blocking thread, so other requests continue.

### For the user

The index has no setting. A user can rebuild it.

| Control | Default | Stored | Takes effect | Shows state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rebuild index (`POST .../code/reindex`) | Not running | In memory on the server | When the call ends | The `CodeReindex` answer: `indexed_files`, `millis`, `truncated` | Wait for the call to end. The call drops the file list and the index, then builds both again. |

## Import resolution and outline

The index needs to know which file an import names, and which names a file defines. The `Resolver` in [`crates/ostra-code/src/resolve.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/resolve.rs) answers the first question. The analysis in [`crates/ostra-code/src/outline.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/outline.rs) answers the second.

### Resolving imports

The resolver works from the file list and from the text of the manifests. It reads only manifests, so it is cheap next to a full index. `Indexes` caches one resolver for each file list.

The manifest names are in `MANIFESTS`: `Cargo.toml`, `package.json`, `go.mod`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts`, `composer.json`, `Gemfile`, `Package.swift`, and `mix.exs`. A file name that ends in `.csproj`, `.gemspec`, or `.rockspec` also counts. The nearest ancestor folder with a manifest is the package of a file. The project top is the package when no folder has a manifest.

Each family has its own rules:

- **Rust.** The resolver reads the crate name from `[package]` in `Cargo.toml` and replaces `-` with `_`. It follows `crate::`, `self::`, and `super::`. A `mod name;` line resolves to `name.rs` or `name/mod.rs` in the module folder.
- **JavaScript and TypeScript.** A relative spec resolves from the folder of the file. The aliases `@/` and `~/` resolve near the closest `package.json` or `tsconfig.json`. A workspace package resolves through the `exports`, `module`, or `main` fields of its `package.json`. The resolver tries the extensions in `JS_EXTS` and an `index` file, and it maps `.js` to `.ts` and `.tsx`.
- **Python.** A relative import counts the leading dots. An absolute import tries each ancestor folder and `src`. It tries `.py`, `.pyi`, and `__init__.py`, and then a folder.
- **Go.** The resolver maps a module path from `go.mod` to its folder. A Go import always resolves to a folder.
- **Java, Kotlin, Scala, C#, Swift, PHP.** The resolver matches dotted names to paths. PHP `require` resolves a path.
- **C and C++.** A quoted include tries the file folder, the project root, `include`, and `src`. Other includes match the end of a path.
- **Ruby, Lua, and shell.** The resolver tries the usual load folders (`lib` for Ruby), then matches the end of a path.

A spec that no rule resolves is an external package. Its `target` is `null` in the answer.

### The outline analysis

`outline::analyze` makes one pass over the tokens of a file. It returns the display class of each token, the definitions, the raw imports, and the supertype links. Definitions come from keyword rules (`fn`, `class`, `def`), member rules inside class bodies, and a few family forms: C function bodies, Go receivers, and Python indentation. The analysis matches names by text and has no type information.

The list `NOT_BEFORE_MEMBER` has 16 keywords: `new`, `return`, `await`, `throw`, `typeof`, `case`, `yield`, `else`, `in`, `of`, `is`, `as`, `extends`, `implements`, `delete`, and `void`. A name after one of them is a call or an expression, not a member definition. `void` is the exception: in the `Js` family it is an operator, and in other languages it is a return type.

`signature` builds the one-line signature of a definition. It starts at the line start and stops before the body. It cuts the text at 300 bytes (the local constant `MAX` of `signature`). `preview` cuts a source line at 240 bytes (the local constant `MAX` of `preview`). Both functions are in `lib.rs`.

## Usage search

A search by name alone mixes definitions that share a name. For example, `a.name` and `b.name` of two unrelated classes both match `name`. The code in [`crates/ostra-code/src/usage.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/usage.rs) fixes this when the request names a position. The route `code/usages` then calls `usages_at` in place of `usages`.

### The two modes

- **By name.** The request has a symbol but no line. The index lists every definition and every mention of the name. It reads at most 4,000 files (`MAX_SCAN_FILES`) and stops at the limit.
- **By position.** The request has a symbol, a path, and a line. The index finds the token at that position. A token on a definition means that definition. A token on a use resolves through the declared type of its receiver.

In the second mode, a mention elsewhere counts only when it can mean the same definition. If the index cannot tell which definition a position means, it falls back to the search by name.

### How a member resolves

A member after `.`, `->`, or `::` resolves through the type of its receiver. The index reads the type from the declaration tokens in the file: `Repo repo`, `repo: Repo`, or `repo = new Repo()`. Then it looks in that type and in its supertypes, up to 8 hops (`MAX_SUPER_DEPTH`). The index also treats a call through an interface method as a use of the implementing method.

These tables widen what the index can see:

- `WRAPPERS` are types whose members are the members of their first type argument: `Box`, `Rc`, `Arc`, `Option`, `Result`, `Optional`, `Readonly`, and `Promise`.
- `PASSTHROUGH` are library calls that return the wrapped value: `unwrap`, `expect`, `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_default`, `unwrap_or_else`, `get`, `orElse`, `orElseThrow`, `orElseGet`, `clone`, `as_ref`, `as_mut`, `borrow`, and `borrow_mut`.
- `FIRST_ARG` are calls that return their first argument: `verify`, `spy`, and `requireNonNull`.
- The index follows a receiver chain such as `a.b().c().d()` for at most 6 calls (`MAX_CHAIN`).

### What the search does not guarantee

The index has no compiler. A receiver whose type the tokens do not show falls back to a guess from the dependency graph. Thus an answer can include a definition that only shares the name, or miss a use through a value of unknown type. Confirm an answer with a text search before you change code because of it. An LSP server gives exact answers for its languages. See [Language servers over LSP](#language-servers-over-lsp).

## Dependency graph and impact walk

A flat list of imports misses most links between files, because many languages use a name without an import line. The graph in [`crates/ostra-code/src/graph.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/graph.rs) adds links from the names that a file mentions. It builds from the index and reads no file. It builds on the first graph query after a link, and the next link drops it.

### How the graph builds

1. Each file gets a package, a test flag, and a hub flag. A path is a test when it sits in a folder such as `test`, `tests`, `__tests__`, `spec`, `specs`, `testdata`, or `fixtures`, or when its name matches a test pattern such as `_test.go`, `.spec.`, `test_`, or `Test.java`. A hub is an index module that re-exports a folder: stem `lib`, `main`, `mod`, `index`, or `__init__`, or a file with `export * from`.
2. Import edges come from the resolver. A Rust `mod` line is a containment edge and counts as no real import.
3. Reference edges come from the mentions. For each mention, `resolve` looks at the definitions of that name and keeps the nearest tier that the file can see.
4. Each edge records the import lines and the names that the file uses from the other file.

The tiers run from near to far. The nearest tier wins.

| Tier | Where the definition sits |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | A file that the mentioning file imports, or a folder that it imports |
| 1 | The same folder |
| 2 | The same package |
| 3 | A package that the mentioning package imports |

These rules narrow a mention:

- A name of one letter makes no edge.
- A name that the file defines itself means that definition.
- `Thing::go` and `module.fn` use the qualifier. A qualifier names a type first, then a defining module. `self.x`, `this.x`, and `Self::x` mean definitions of the same file.
- A definition counts only when it has the same language family. A non-test file never links to a test file.
- A name defined in more than 3 files (`MAX_DEF_FILES`) links none of them, unless the mentioning file imports a defining file directly.
- JavaScript, TypeScript, and Python see another file only through an import or a re-export (tier 0). A Go package also sees its own folder (tier 1). The other families see up to tier 3. The reason: modules that import explicitly see names from other files only through an import.

### Which edges a walk follows

`Edge::follow` decides. A walk follows an edge that carries at least one name. It also follows an import-only edge, unless the edge enters a hub. The reason: a `mod` line is containment, not use. An import-only edge into an index module is a re-export path, and the names on that path already link to the files that define them.

### Queries

| Query | What it returns | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `neighbors` | What a file uses and what uses it, strongest link first | The tool limit |
| `reach` | A breadth-first walk from seed files, up to a depth, in either direction | 5,000 files (`MAX_REACH`) |
| `path_between` | The shortest chain by which one file depends on another | None |
| `related` | Files to read next to a file | A bridge file with more than 200 links is skipped (`MAX_BRIDGE_DEGREE`) |
| `hubs` | The files that the most other files depend on | The tool limit |
| `units` | Packages, what each depends on, and the loops between packages | None |
| `cycles` | Files that import each other in a loop. Only real imports count. | The tool limit |
| `callers` | The definitions that mention a symbol, grouped with their lines | 5,000 references (`MAX_CALLER_REFS`) |
| `symbol_impact` | The definitions that use a symbol, then those that use them, hop by hop | The tool limit |
| `callees` | The definitions that the body of a symbol names | The tool limit |
| `implementations` | What a type or method implements and what implements it | 8 definitions per answer for the tools (`MAX_IMPL_GROUPS`) |

The weight of an edge is 2 for each name, up to 8 names (`MAX_LINK_NAMES`), plus 1 when the edge has an import. `related` starts from the direct links. It adds a quarter of the smaller weight for each file that sits one step further through a shared neighbor.

### The graph views

The route `code/graph` returns one of four views. The Files view draws them. The browser does the layout. See [Project, Files, and dependency screens](web-project-screens.md).

| View | Query parameters | What it shows | Cap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `packages` | None | Every package and the links between packages | None |
| `package` | `package` (`.` names the project top) | The files of one package and the packages they use | 150 files (`MAX_VIEW_FILES`). The view keeps the files with the most dependents. |
| `file` | `path`, `depth` | One file and the files within `depth` hops | 80 nodes (`MAX_VIEW_NEIGHBORS`) |
| `symbol` | `path`, `symbol`, `line`, `depth` | One definition, its users on the left, what it uses on the right | 300 edges (`MAX_VIEW_EDGES`). Implementation links stay first, then the heaviest references. |

Other caps in the views: a type node lists 40 members (`MAX_MEMBERS`), a node lists 30 top-level definitions of its file (`MAX_FILE_DEFS`), and a symbol view reads 200 callees for each definition (`MAX_VIEW_CALLEES`). The depth is clamped to 1 to 3 (`MAX_GRAPH_DEPTH`), and the default is 1. The answer sets `truncated` when it leaves nodes out.

The graph gives each node a column. A node sits left of what it uses, and nodes that use each other in a loop share a column. The code finds the loops with an iterative Tarjan search for strongly connected components. A sink has column 0, and a user has a negative column.

### What happens when

- **The path, package, or symbol is not in the index.** The route returns `404` with `That package, file, or symbol is not in the code index. The index leaves out ignored files, files over 1 MB, and languages it does not parse.`
- **The request has both `package` and `path`.** The route returns `400` with `Give either package or path, not both.`
- **The request has no parameter.** The route returns the `packages` view.
- **A language server is set.** The graph still uses the index only.

## Language servers over LSP

The index does not know types. A language server does, so it gives exact definitions, references, and completions. The code in [`crates/ostra-code/src/lsp`](crates/ostra-code/src/lsp) runs one server process for each project and server command, and talks JSON-RPC with the `Content-Length` framing of the Language Server Protocol.

Caution: approve a language server command only after you read it. The server runs the build scripts and macros of the project, so Ostra starts it under the workspace sandbox. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md) for the sandbox rules.

### The life of a server

`LspPool::get` starts a server when the first request needs it. A pool entry is keyed by the project and the command. These steps run:

1. `spawn_process` starts the command in the project folder through `ostra_sandbox::host_command`.
2. The client sends `initialize` with `processId`, the project root, the workspace folder, the `initializationOptions` of the entry, and the capabilities that Ostra uses. The wait is 60 seconds (`INIT_TIMEOUT`), because some servers read the project first.
3. The client sends `initialized` and checks the answer. A server that does not count columns in UTF-16 gets refused with `<name> counts columns in <encoding>. Ostra needs a server that counts them in utf-16.`
4. The server stays in the pool and serves requests.

The caller waits for the server only up to its wait time. A request waits for the `timeout_secs` of the entry. A hint waits 3 seconds (`HINT_WAIT`). If the caller stops waiting, the start continues in the background, and the next caller finds the running server. The error then reads `<name> is still starting. Ask again in a moment.`

### Pool rules

| Rule | Value | Constant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Idle time before a server stops | 10 minutes | `IDLE` |
| Check interval for idle and dead servers | 60 seconds | `SWEEP` |
| Running servers across all projects | 8. A new server stops the least recently used one. | `MAX_SERVERS` |
| Open documents for each server | 32. A new document closes the least recently used one. | `MAX_OPEN` |
| Wait before a failed or dead server starts again | 30 seconds | `RETRY` |
| Outside URIs that the pool remembers | 20,000. A new one forgets the oldest. | `MAX_EXTERNALS` |
| Definitions from one `workspace/symbol` lookup | 50 | `MAX_DEFINITIONS` |
| Largest message from a server | 256 MiB. A larger message ends the connection. | `MAX_MESSAGE` |
| Completion items kept from one answer | 1,000. A longer list becomes incomplete. | `MAX_COMPLETIONS` |
| Last stderr lines kept for an error | 20 lines of at most 300 characters | `STDERR_LINES` |

A server that started under other sandbox settings is replaced on the next request. The pool also replaces a dead server after the 30-second retry wait.

### What Ostra asks the server

- **File display.** The provider starts from the built-in answer. It asks `textDocument/semanticTokens/full` and `textDocument/documentSymbol`. The server tokens go over the built-in tokens: a built-in token that overlaps a server token is dropped, and the rest stay. The outline from the server replaces the built-in outline when it is not empty. Imports always come from the tokenizer. If the built-in answer already has a warning, for example for a large file, the server is not asked.
- **Usages.** With a position, the provider asks `textDocument/definition` there. Without a position, it asks `workspace/symbol` and keeps the items with the exact name. Then it asks `textDocument/references` with `includeDeclaration` set to `false`. The provider drops references outside the project, because the own uses of a library crowd out the project uses. The answer lists the file that asked first, removes duplicates, and sets `truncated` when definitions and references exceed the limit.
- **Symbols.** The provider asks `workspace/symbol`. It answers only when the server has `workspaceSymbolProvider` and returns items.
- **Dependencies.** A server returns nothing. The built-in provider answers.
- **Document sync.** The provider sends `didOpen` for a new document and `didChange` with the full text when the text hash changes. It sends `didClose` when it drops the least recently used document.
- **File changes.** A touch sends `workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles` to each running server of the project, with type 2 for a changed file and type 3 for a deleted file.

The client answers the few requests that a server sends back: `workspace/configuration` with `null` values, `workspace/workspaceFolders` with the project folder, the registration and refresh requests with `null`, and `workspace/applyEdit` with `applied: false`. Any other server request gets the error `-32601`.

### Outside files

A server can point at a file outside the project, such as a library source or a class in a jar. The location then has a `uri`. `external::describe` accepts two schemes: `file://` and `jdt://` (the jdtls scheme). For a Java server, `with_extensions` adds `extendedClientCapabilities.classFileContentsSupport: true` to the `initializationOptions` unless the user sets it. Then jdtls answers jar definitions with `jdt://` URIs, and Ostra reads the class text with `java/classFileContents`.

The route `code/external` reads an outside file. It reads only a URI that a server of this process returned, so the browser cannot name an arbitrary file. A path under the home folder shows as `~/...`. The text must be UTF-8 and at most 1 MiB. `code/usages` with a `uri` runs a usages search from the outside file.

### When the server is not ready

The client tracks `$/progress` tokens and the rust-analyzer `experimental/serverStatus` message. When either shows work, an answer carries the warning `<name> is still loading the project, so this answer may be incomplete.` A server can drop a request when it loads the project. The error codes `-32801` (`CONTENT_MODIFIED`) and `-32802` (`SERVER_CANCELLED`) then become `<name> is still loading the project and dropped the request.`

### What happens when

- **The server fails to start.** The request returns an error, the chain falls to the built-in provider, and the answer carries a warning. The pool does not start that server again for 30 seconds.
- **The server exits.** Each pending request fails with `The language server exited with <status>.` and the last stderr line.
- **A request takes longer than `timeout_secs`.** The client sends `$/cancelRequest` and fails with `<name> did not answer <method> within <n> seconds.`
- **A user changes the command.** The pool keys a server by project and command. The new command starts a new server. The old server stops after 10 idle minutes or when the pool needs room.
- **A user changes `initialization_options` only.** The running server keeps the old options. The new options apply when the server restarts.
- **A server stops.** The client sends `shutdown` and waits 3 seconds, sends `exit`, waits 2 seconds for the process, and then kills it. It also kills what the server left running in its sandbox.

### For the user

A project can list any number of servers. Each file asks one server, so each language id belongs to one entry.

```toml
[[projects.language_servers]]
command = ["rust-analyzer"]
languages = ["rust"]
timeout_secs = 20
```

| Setting | Default | Stored | Takes effect | Shows state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `projects.language_servers` (array of tables) | Empty | `[[projects.language_servers]]` under a project in `workspace.toml` of the workspace | At the next request | The provider name beside each answer, and the warning text of the answer | Remove the entry and save |
| `projects.language_servers.command` | None. Required, and the first item must name a program. | Same table | At the next request. A new command starts a new server. | Same | Change or remove the entry |
| `projects.language_servers.languages` | None. Required. Use ids from `NAV_LANGUAGES`. | Same table | At the next request | Same | Remove an id. Do not list one id in two entries. |
| `projects.language_servers.timeout_secs` | `10` seconds. Valid values: 1 to 120 seconds. | Same table | At the next request | The timeout error text | Set another value |
| `projects.language_servers.initialization_options` | None | Same table | When the server starts again | Not shown | Remove the entry, or wait for the idle stop, then save |

Save-time validation and the approval of a `workspace.toml` that arrives with a repository belong to [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md). Until the user approves the file, the server ignores every entry.

## Project code_provider program

A project that has its own index, such as a generated code database, can answer code questions itself. The `code_provider` setting names a program. Ostra starts it once for each request in the project folder, writes one JSON request to its stdin, and reads one JSON value from its stdout. The code is in [`crates/ostra-code/src/provider.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/provider.rs), and the request type is in [`crates/ostra-core/src/code.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/code.rs).

### The protocol

The program gets one line of JSON. The field `op` names the request, and `version` is `1` (`PROTOCOL_VERSION`). The environment variable `OSTRA_CODE_PROTOCOL` holds the same version.

```json
{"op":"usages","version":1,"root":"/work/app","symbol":"parse_config","path":"src/main.rs","line":12,"col":8,"limit":500}
```

| `op` | Fields besides `op`, `version`, and `root` | The program answers with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `file` | `path` | A `CodeFile`: `language`, `classes`, `tokens`, `symbols`, `imports` |
| `usages` | `symbol`, `path`, `line`, `col`, `limit` | A `CodeUsages`: `definitions`, `references`, `truncated` |
| `deps` | `path` | A `CodeDeps`: `imports`, `importers` |
| `symbols` | `query`, `limit` | A `CodeSymbols`: `items` |

The program can answer `null` or print nothing. Ostra then asks the next provider. The program never gets graph, completion, signature, or jump requests, and the agent code tools never use it.

### How Ostra checks the answer

`parse_answer` rejects an answer that breaks one of these rules. The rejection becomes a warning on the answer of the next provider.

- The output must be UTF-8 and at most 64 MiB (`MAX_OUTPUT`).
- The JSON must match the shape of the `op`.
- `tokens` must hold groups of four numbers: line, column, length, class. It can hold at most 16,777,216 numbers (`MAX_TOKENS`). Each line must be 1 or more, and each class index must be inside `classes`.
- A list of symbols, imports, importers, or locations can hold at most 20,000 items (`MAX_ITEMS`).
- Every path must be project-relative. A path that is empty, starts with `/`, holds `\` or a NUL byte, or has a `.` or `..` segment is refused. Every location needs a line of 1 or more.
- Ostra clears `uri` on each location, because it reads outside files only for language servers.
- Ostra fills in `path`, `symbol`, and the empty `name` fields from the request.

The reason for the path and line rules is in the error text: the browser needs `1-based` lines and project-relative paths to open the right place.

### Process rules

The program starts through `ostra_sandbox::host_command` with the workspace sandbox settings. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md). The process stops when its future is dropped (`kill_on_drop`). A program can answer without it reads its input, because Ostra ignores a closed pipe. The stderr limit is 1 MiB (`MAX_STDERR`). When the program exits with an error, Ostra puts the last stderr line in the message `It exited with <status>: <line>`.

### What happens when

- **The program is missing.** The error is `` Cannot start `<program>`: <reason>. `` and the built-in provider answers.
- **The program takes longer than `timeout_secs`.** The error is `It took longer than <n> seconds.`
- **The program exits with a non-zero status.** The error holds the status and the last stderr line.
- **The answer is larger than 64 MiB.** The error is `Its answer is larger than 64 MB.`
- **A user changes the setting.** The next request uses the new setting, because the server reads it for each request.

### For the user

```toml
[projects.code_provider]
command = ["ctags-nav", "--json"]
timeout_secs = 10
```

| Setting | Default | Stored | Takes effect | Shows state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `projects.code_provider.command` | None. Without it, the project has no provider program. The first item must name a program. | `[projects.code_provider]` under a project in `workspace.toml` of the workspace | At the next request | The provider name beside each answer. It is the file name of the program. A failure shows as a warning. | Remove the table and save |
| `projects.code_provider.timeout_secs` | `10` seconds. Valid values: 1 to 120 seconds. | Same table | At the next request | The error `It took longer than <n> seconds.` | Set another value |

An unapproved `workspace.toml` removes the program from the settings. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) for the approval of commands.

## Completion, signature help, and jump hints

The file editor asks for hints at the cursor of the unsaved text. A request for the saved file cannot answer these questions, because the user has typed since the last save. The browser sends the full text over the socket. The server code is in [`crates/ostra-code/src/hint.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/hint.rs) and in `Code` of [`crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs).

### Socket messages

| Browser sends | Server answers | Answered by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code_complete` | `code_completion` | The first language server that answers, else the index |
| `code_signature` | `code_signature_help` | The first language server that answers. The index has none. |
| `code_navigate` | `code_navigation` | The index first, then the language servers |

Each message has an `id`, the workspace, the project key, the path, the text, the 1-based line, and the 0-based UTF-16 column. The answer repeats the `id`, with a `result` or an `error`. A newer request of the same kind from the same socket stops the older one, and the older one never answers. Each socket queues at most 8 hint answers (`HINT_QUEUE`). The channel rules are in [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md).

### Checks on a hint request

The server refuses a request with an error text in these cases:

- The text is larger than 1 MiB. The message is `The file is larger than 1 MB, the size Ostra sends to a language server.`
- The line is 0 or beyond the last line of the text. The message is `The cursor line is outside the text.`
- `trigger` is not one character. The message is `Send one typed character as trigger.`

### Completion

The server asks each configured language server in order, with a wait of 3 seconds (`HINT_WAIT`). The first server that returns a list wins. A server answers only for the languages in its entry and only when it has `completionProvider`. A trigger character that the server does not list gives an empty list, because the browser opens the list on characters of every language. A failed server adds the warning `<name> did not complete, so the code index did: <reason>`.

If no server answers, the index completes names. `from_index` takes the word that ends at the cursor and calls `symbols` for names that start with it. It returns at most 50 items (`MAX_INDEX_COMPLETIONS`) and marks the list as incomplete, so the editor asks again when the word grows. After a trigger character, the index returns an empty list, because it does not know members.

The `LSP` completion kinds map to the 25 `CompletionKind` values. The index maps its symbol kinds the same way.

### Signature help

Only a language server answers. `LspProvider::signature` in `crates/ostra-code/src/lsp/mod.rs` (lines 1127-1139) sets the trigger kind of the request. The rules run in this order:

1. Trigger kind 2: the user typed a character, and the server lists it in `triggerCharacters`. A retrigger also counts when the server lists the character in `retriggerCharacters`.
2. Trigger kind 3: the editor already shows hints (a retrigger) and rule 1 did not match.
3. No answer: the user typed a character, the server does not list it, and the request is not a retrigger. The provider returns `Ok(None)` and no hint shows.
4. Trigger kind 1: the user typed no trigger character. Kind 1 applies only in this case.

If no server answers, the result is `null`. If a server fails and none answers, the server returns `502` with the reasons.

```rust
let kind = match at.trigger {
    Some(c) if listed(&caps["triggerCharacters"], c)
        || (at.retrigger && listed(&caps["retriggerCharacters"], c)) => 2,
    _ if at.retrigger => 3,
    Some(_) => return Ok(None),
    None => 1,
};
```

### Supertype and implementation jumps

The target is `supertypes` or `implementations`. The index answers first, because it is fast and holds every language that it parses. `navigate_index` takes the identifier at the cursor. It uses the definition in the same file when the file defines the name. Otherwise it asks across the project for up to 8 definitions (`NAVIGATION_GROUPS`). It returns at most 50 locations (`MAX_NAVIGATION`) without duplicates. If the index has no file or no definition for the name, the language servers answer through the type hierarchy and `textDocument/implementation`. If nothing answers, the result is `null`.

## Agent code tools

An agent that has only Grep and Read needs many calls to learn a project. The eight code tools answer the same questions in one call. They run over the index of the project and return compact text. The code is in [`crates/ostra-code/src/tools.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/tools.rs). See [Native tools](tools.md) for how the native loop dispatches tools.

### The tools

| Native name | MCP name | Input | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CodeOutline` | `code_outline` | `path`, `limit` | Imports with their targets, then the symbols with line ranges |
| `CodeFind` | `code_find` | `query`, `limit` | Definitions whose name matches, best match first |
| `CodeCallers` | `code_callers` | `symbol`, `path`, `limit` | The definitions that use the symbol, with their lines |
| `CodeCallees` | `code_callees` | `path`, `symbol`, `line`, `limit` | The definitions that the body of the symbol names |
| `CodeImplementations` | `code_implementations` | `symbol`, `path`, `line`, `limit` | What the type or method implements, and what implements it |
| `CodeNeighbors` | `code_neighbors` | `path`, `limit` | The files that the file uses and the files that use it, plus related files |
| `CodeImpact` | `code_impact` | `symbol` with `path`, or `paths`, plus `direction`, `depth`, `limit` | What a change can break |
| `CodeMap` | `code_map` | `prefix` | Packages, the most depended-on files, and loops |

The list is `CODE_TOOLS` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs). Every input rejects unknown fields. A path can be project-relative or absolute inside the project. An agent that works from the workspace root can start a path with the project folder name. The tool removes that name when the file exists only without it.

### Limits and defaults

- `limit` defaults to 40 (`DEFAULT_LIMIT`) and is clamped to 1 to 300 (`MAX_LIMIT`). `CodeOutline` defaults to 300. `CodeImpact` defaults to 100.
- `CodeImpact` has `depth` from 1 to 10, and the default is 3.
- A name list in an answer shows at most 12 names (`MAX_NAMES`) and then `+N more`.
- `CodeImplementations` shows at most 8 definitions (`MAX_IMPL_GROUPS`) when a name has several.
- `CodeNeighbors` adds up to 5 files that sit two steps away through a shared neighbor.
- `CodeMap` lists up to 15 hubs and 10 import loops, and it limits the list to `prefix` when you give one.

### CodeImpact modes

`CodeImpact` has two modes. The answers differ, so pick the mode for the question.

- **With `symbol`.** The walk follows the names. It lists the definitions that use the symbol (hop 1), then the definitions that use something in hop 1, up to `depth`. It ends with the files to change or recheck. A file that uses something else from the same file stays out. If the name has several defining files, the call fails and lists them. Pass `path` to pick one. This mode follows users only, so `direction` set to `dependencies` is an error.
- **With `paths`.** The walk follows the file graph. `direction` is `dependents` by default. It lists the files that depend on the seeds, hop by hop. The value `dependencies` lists the files that the seeds use. A seed that the index does not hold gets a line that says so.

The call fails with `` Give either `symbol` or `paths`, not both. `` when you pass both. It fails with `` Give `symbol` (one function or type) or `paths` (whole files). `` when you pass neither.

### How an agent reaches the tools

- A native run calls the tool by its native name. `ToolEnv` holds a `CodeNav` object. `CodeTools` in the server implements it.
- A harness run calls the MCP tool `code_<op>` through the MCP stdio shim. Claude Code names it `mcp__ostra__code_<op>`. See [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).
- `CodeTools::call` finds the innermost project whose folder holds the repo root of the run. Then it makes sure the watcher runs, and it queries the index on a blocking thread. If no project holds the folder, the tool returns `<dir> is not inside a project of an open workspace, so it has no code index.`
- A run without a `CodeNav` object gets `Code navigation is not available in this run. Use Grep, Glob, and Read instead.`

The permission policy treats each code tool as a known tool of Ostra. The tools only read the index. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).

### Which agents get the tools

The capability `code` is in the `agent.toml` of 13 agents: `code-reviewer`, `documentation`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `explore`, `fact-check`, `generate-spec`, `implementer`, `initializer`, `plan`, `prompt-generation`, `quick-answer`, `system-architecture`, and `write-test`. `render_prompt` puts the guide `assets/code-tools.md` before the prompt of each such agent. The guide lists the eight tools with the tool names of the executor. It tells the agent to use the tools before text search. It also warns that the index matches names, not types. Thus an answer can include a definition that only shares the name, or miss a use through a value of unknown type. The agent must confirm an answer with a text search before it changes code because of it. See [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md).

### What happens when

- **The path is not in the index.** The tool returns the error `<path> is not in the code index. Give a project-relative path of a source file; the index leaves out ignored files, files over 1 MB, and languages it does not parse.`
- **A symbol has no definition.** `CodeCallers` says so and lists no callers. `CodeCallees` and `CodeImplementations` return an error that points to `CodeOutline` or `CodeFind`.
- **A list is cut.** The answer ends with a line such as `(more callers; raise limit)`.
- **The language has no end line for bodies.** `CodeCallees` says that it read only the first line.

## Index watcher and write touches

The index must see an edit that a shell command, an editor, or a checkout makes, not only the edits of Ostra tools. Two mechanisms feed it. A touch reports a write. The watcher in [`crates/ostra-server/src/code_watch.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/code_watch.rs) reports the writes that Ostra does not know about. The 30-second check of `Indexes::with` is the last safety net.

### Touches

`Code::touch` marks a path in the index and tells the running language servers. It has three callers:

- The write handler `absorb` in `crates/ostra-server/src/files/mod.rs`. It reports a file that an agent write tool changed.
- `announce_save` in `crates/ostra-server/src/files/mod.rs`. It reports a file that the user saved in the editor.
- `on_outside_change` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs). It is the callback of the watcher, and it reports a file that changed outside Ostra.

The first two callers report writes that Ostra knows about. See [Project files, Git dock, and cloning](project-files-and-git.md) for the write path.

### The watcher

`code_watch::start` watches the root folder and each folder that holds a listed file, with `RecursiveMode::NonRecursive`. It does not watch the whole tree, so ignored build output adds no watches. The server starts a watch when a project gets its first code request, hint, graph request, or tool call. A watch for an old root is replaced when the root changes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Disk as Project folder
    participant Watch as ostra-code-watch thread
    participant Code as Code in the server
    participant Index as Indexes and LspPool
    participant Browser
    Disk->>Watch: notify event
    Watch->>Watch: collect events, wait for a quiet gap
    Watch->>Code: on_outside_change(Batch)
    Code->>Index: touch(path) for each changed path
    Code->>Browser: ProjectFsChanged on workspace:id
    Browser->>Code: next code request
    Code->>Index: with() syncs the touched paths
```

The thread collects events into a `Batch`. A batch ends after 250 ms without an event (`QUIET`), or after 2 seconds from the first event (`MAX_WAIT`). Then the callback `on_outside_change` runs. The batch is `structural` when a file or folder was created, removed, or renamed. A structural batch drops the cached file list. Each changed path goes to `Code::touch`. A new folder gets its own watch at once.

The message `ProjectFsChanged` goes to the channel `workspace:<id>`. It lists the changed paths. If a batch has more than 200 paths (`MAX_PUSHED_PATHS` of `code.rs`), the list is empty, and the browser reloads the whole listing. The write path of the Files view has its own cap, which [Project files, Git dock, and cloning](project-files-and-git.md) explains.

The watcher skips a path in these cases:

- The path is inside `.git`.
- `.gitignore` of the root or `.git/info/exclude` ignores it.
- The event is not a create, remove, rename, or data change.

### What happens when

- **The platform refuses a watch for some folders.** The server logs `watching <root>: <n> folders refused (the OS watch limit?); the periodic check covers them`. The 30-second check covers those folders.
- **The platform refuses the root.** `ensure_watch` logs `cannot watch <root>; outside edits reach the code index within 30 s`.
- **The server drops the project.** The thread ends when the watcher is dropped, because the event channel closes.

### For the user

The watcher has no setting.

| Control | Default | Stored | Takes effect | Shows state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The watch of one project | On, from the first code request | In memory on the server | At once | The warning lines in the server log when the OS refuses folders | Raise the OS limit on watches, or wait for the 30-second check |

## Code routes and socket messages

The routes sit under `/api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/code`. The handlers are in [`crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs), and the logic is in `Code`. The socket messages are in `crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs`.

| Route | Method | Query | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `/code/file` | `GET` | `path` | `CodeFile`: tokens, symbols, imports, provider, warning |
| `/code/usages` | `GET` | `symbol`, `path`, `line`, `col`, `limit`, or `uri` with `line` | `CodeUsages` |
| `/code/deps` | `GET` | `path` | `CodeDeps` |
| `/code/symbols` | `GET` | `q`, `limit` | `CodeSymbols` |
| `/code/graph` | `GET` | `package`, `path`, `symbol`, `line`, `depth` | `CodeGraph` |
| `/code/external` | `GET` | `uri` | `CodeExternalFile` |
| `/code/reindex` | `POST` | None | `CodeReindex` |

### Route limits

- `DEFAULT_USAGES` is 500 and `MAX_USAGES` is 2,000.
- `DEFAULT_SYMBOLS` is 50 and `MAX_SYMBOLS` is 200. The query text is cut at 256 characters.
- `MAX_URI_LEN` is 4,096. A longer or empty `uri` returns `400` with `Name the dependency file with uri.`
- `MAX_GRAPH_DEPTH` is 3.

### Error cases of the outside-file routes

- A `uri` that no server of this process returned gives `404` with `Ostra does not know this dependency file, because no language server of this project has pointed at it since the Ostra server started. Open it again from the code that uses it.`
- A server that left the settings gives `404` with `The language server that found this dependency file is no longer in the project's settings.`
- A usages request with a `uri` and no `line` of 1 or more gives `400` with `Name the 1-based line of the symbol in the dependency file.`
- A server failure gives `502` with the reason.

## Limits and constants

This table lists every limit of the code navigation code. The part of this page that owns each limit explains it. `MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT` is a setting limit. [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) owns the save-time validation that uses it.

| Constant | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_FILE_BYTES` | 1 MiB | The largest file that the tokenizer, the index, and a server read |
| `CLASSES` | 11 classes | The order of the token classes in each native answer |
| `MAX` (in `signature` and `preview` of `lib.rs`) | 300 bytes, 240 bytes | The cut of a one-line signature, and the cut of a source line preview |
| `MAX_INDEX_BYTES` | 256 MiB | Source bytes that one index reads before it stops adding files |
| `TRUNCATED` | The text `The project is larger than the size Ostra indexes, so some files are not searched.` | The warning that a usages or symbols answer carries when the index set `truncated` |
| `MAX_SCAN_FILES` | 4,000 files | Files that a usages query reads |
| `MAX_IMPORTERS` | 2,000 | Importers that a deps answer lists |
| `FULL_SYNC` | 30 seconds | The time after which the index checks every file again |
| `MAX_DEF_FILES` | 3 files | A name defined in more files links none of them without a direct import |
| `MAX_LINK_NAMES` | 8 names | Names listed for one edge, and names that add weight |
| `MAX_REACH` | 5,000 files | Files that one walk visits |
| `MAX_CALLER_REFS` | 5,000 | References that a callers query reads |
| `MAX_BRIDGE_DEGREE` | 200 links | The largest bridge file that `related` uses |
| `MAX_VIEW_FILES` | 150 | Files in a package view |
| `MAX_VIEW_NEIGHBORS` | 80 | Nodes in a file view |
| `MAX_VIEW_CALLEES` | 200 | Callees that a symbol view reads for one definition |
| `MAX_MEMBERS` | 40 | Members that a type node lists |
| `MAX_FILE_DEFS` | 30 | Top-level definitions that a node lists |
| `MAX_VIEW_EDGES` | 300 | Links in a symbol view |
| `TOP` and `NONE` | `u32::MAX` | Internal markers: the top level of a file in a symbol view, and an unvisited node in the loop search |
| `MAX_SUPER_DEPTH` | 8 hops | Supertype hops of a member lookup |
| `MAX_CHAIN` | 6 calls | Calls that a receiver chain follows |
| `WRAPPERS`, `PASSTHROUGH`, `FIRST_ARG` | Name lists | Types and calls that the member lookup sees through |
| `MANIFESTS`, `JS_EXTS` | Name lists | Manifest file names and JavaScript extensions of the resolver |
| `NOT_BEFORE_MEMBER` | 16 keywords | Keywords that stop a name from counting as a member definition |
| `C_COMMENT`, `RUST`, `JS_KEYWORDS`, `JS_DEFS`, `TYPESCRIPT`, `JAVASCRIPT`, `PYTHON`, `JVM_MODIFIERS`, `JAVA`, `KOTLIN`, `SCALA`, `CSHARP`, `SWIFT`, `CPP`, `RUBY`, `LUA`, `SHELL`, `ALL` | Language tables | The rules of each language. The part `The language tables in lang.rs` lists each one. |
| `MAX_INDEX_COMPLETIONS` | 50 | Index completions for each request |
| `MAX_NAVIGATION` | 50 | Locations for each jump |
| `NAVIGATION_GROUPS` | 8 | Definitions asked across the project for a jump |
| `DEFAULT_LIMIT`, `MAX_LIMIT` | 40, 300 | The default and the largest `limit` of an agent code tool |
| `MAX_NAMES` | 12 | Names listed in one line of a tool answer |
| `MAX_IMPL_GROUPS` | 8 | Definitions that `CodeImplementations` shows |
| `PROTOCOL_VERSION` | 1 | The version of the `code_provider` protocol |
| `NATIVE_PROVIDER` | `native` | The provider name of the built-in provider |
| `NAV_LANGUAGES` | 16 ids | The language ids that a language server entry can name |
| `MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT` | 120 seconds | The largest `timeout_secs` |

| `DEFAULT_USAGES`, `MAX_USAGES` | 500, 2,000 | The default and the largest `limit` of a usages route |

| `MAX_PUSHED_PATHS` | 200 | Paths in one `ProjectFsChanged` from the watcher |

sections.title: External MCP servers
sections.summary: How Ostra connects to external MCP servers: tool names, server settings, the stdio and HTTP client, the gateway, OAuth sign-in, tool refresh, and how native runs and harnesses call the tools.
sections.body:
## Why Ostra has one MCP client

An agent can need a tool that Ostra does not ship, such as an issue tracker or a search over private documents. A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server offers such tools. Without a shared layer, each executor needs its own MCP setup, its own sign-in, and its own permission check. Then the native loop and the four harnesses see different tools under different rules.

Ostra solves this with one MCP client. The crate `ostra-mcp` holds the client. The type `McpGateway` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/mcp.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/mcp.rs) keeps one connection for each MCP server of a workspace, signs in, and discovers tools. It serves the tools to native runs directly and to harnesses through Ostra's own MCP server. Thus one policy and one allowlist cover every executor.

This page covers these topics:

- How a tool is named inside Ostra.
- The settings of an MCP server and their save-time checks.
- The client: the handshake, the stdio transport, the streamable HTTP transport, and tool results.
- The gateway: connections, status, and the refresh of the tool list.
- OAuth sign-in for remote servers.
- How native runs and harnesses reach the tools.

The page stops before the policy rules for MCP tools. See [Policy engine](policy-engine.md) for those rules.

### The parts and the path of a tool call

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S["MCP server settings of the workspace"] --> G["McpGateway"]
  G --> C1["Client with stdio transport"]
  G --> C2["Client with HTTP transport"]
  C1 --> E1["Local MCP server process"]
  C2 --> E2["Remote MCP server"]
  G --> N["Native run: ExecMcp"]
  G --> H["Harness: Ostra MCP server at /internal/mcp"]
  N --> P1["Provider tool list"]
  H --> P2["Harness through the MCP shim"]
```

## Tool names inside Ostra

Four spellings name the same tool. Each spelling exists because a different part of the system reads it. The module [`crates/ostra-core/src/mcp.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/mcp.rs) converts between them.

| Spelling | Example | Where it appears |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server name | `create_issue` | The MCP server itself, the `disabled_tools` list, and `McpToolInfo.name` |
| Bare name | `github__create_issue` | Ostra's own MCP server, which serves tools to harnesses |
| Harness name | `mcp__ostra__github__create_issue` | What a harness shows. The harness adds `mcp__` and the server name `ostra` |
| Canonical name | `mcp__github__create_issue` | The native loop, the policy, permission rules, the Activity view, and `McpToolInfo.canonical` |

The canonical name uses the spelling of Claude Code. The constant `PREFIX` is `mcp__`. The constant `SEPARATOR` is `__`.

### How `bare_name` builds a bare name

The function `bare_name(server, tool)` follows these rules:

1. If the tool name has only ASCII letters, digits, `_`, and `-`, and `server__tool` has at most 52 characters, the bare name is `server__tool`.
2. Otherwise, the function replaces each other character with `_` and cuts the tool part to fit.
3. Then it adds `_` and an 8-digit hexadecimal hash of the original tool name. The hash is the low 32 bits of an FNV-1a hash.

The limit `MAX_BARE_NAME` is 52 because a harness adds the 12 characters of `mcp__ostra__` and providers cap tool names at 64 characters. The hash makes sure that two tools never share a name. For example, `docs` and `search.pages/v2` give `docs__search_pages_v2_` and 8 hexadecimal digits. A tool of 80 `x` characters and a tool of 81 `x` characters on one server give two different names of 52 characters.

```rust
pub fn bare_name(server: &str, tool: &str) -> String {
    let plain = format!("{server}{SEPARATOR}{tool}");
    let clean = tool
        .chars()
        .all(|c| c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || c == '_' || c == '-');
    if clean && plain.len() <= MAX_BARE_NAME {
        return plain;
    }
    let hash = format!("{:08x}", fnv1a(tool.as_bytes()) as u32);
    // ... replace other characters with `_` ...
    let room = MAX_BARE_NAME - server.len() - SEPARATOR.len() - 1 - hash.len();
    sanitized.truncate(room);
    format!("{server}{SEPARATOR}{sanitized}_{hash}")
}
```

### Functions that recognize a name

- `is_gateway_tool(tool)` is true when the name starts with `mcp__` and the rest contains `__`. A harness-native MCP call arrives as `Other:mcp__...` and does not count.
- `is_gateway_bare(bare)` is true when the name contains `__`. Ostra's own tools never contain `__`.
- `canonical(bare)` adds the prefix. `bare(canonical)` removes it. `server_of(name)` returns the server of a canonical or bare name.

### Rules for server names

A server name has lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. It starts with a letter and has at most `MAX_SERVER_NAME` (24) characters. The name has no underscore, because the first `__` must always split the server from the tool. The name `ostra` is not allowed, because it names Ostra's own MCP server.

### What happens when two tools get the same canonical name

If two tools of one execution have the same canonical name, the gateway keeps the first and drops the others. The order is the server order in the file, then the tool order that the server lists.

## Configure an MCP server

A workspace lists its external MCP servers in the `mcp_servers` setting. Each entry is a `[[mcp_servers]]` table in `.ostra/workspace.toml`. An entry sets `command` for a local server that Ostra starts over stdio, or `url` for a remote server that Ostra reaches over streamable HTTP. A new workspace has no entry.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | The server name. It forms the canonical tool names |
| `enabled` | When `false`, the gateway does not connect and agents get no tool of the server |
| `command` | The program and its arguments for a local server. Ostra runs it in the workspace root |
| `env` | More environment variables for a local server |
| `url` | The `http` or `https` address of a remote server |
| `headers` | Headers that Ostra sends with each request to a remote server |
| `oauth` | Client settings for OAuth sign-in. See the part on OAuth sign-in |
| `disabled_tools` | Names of server tools that Ostra does not offer to agents |
| `agents` | The agents that get the tools. An empty list means every agent |
| `timeout_secs` | The seconds that one tool call can take |

### Values of `env` and `headers`

A value of `env` or `headers` has one of three forms:

- **`${VAR}`.** Ostra reads the variable `VAR` from the environment of the Ostra process when the connection starts. If the variable is not set, the status shows a message that names it. Ostra reads its own environment, so the user must restart Ostra after the user sets a new variable.
- **A name that Ostra keeps from MCP servers.** Ostra refuses a provider key, a bridge token, and the variable of an `oauth.client_secret_env`. The status message tells the user to name a variable of the server's own. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) for the list that `credential_env_names` builds.
- **A literal text.** Ostra moves the text into its encrypted registry and writes the marker `${ostra_secret}` (the constant `SAVED_SECRET`) into the file. Thus the value never reaches the browser or a folder file. If Ostra cannot read a saved value, the status message tells the user to enter the field again.

The function `is_literal_value` decides which form a value has. A value is literal when it is not blank, is not the marker, and does not contain `${`.

### How Ostra binds and cleans up a saved value

A saved value belongs to the server name and to the place where the server connects. The function `mcp_secret_key` in [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/trust.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/trust.rs) builds the registry key from these parts, in this order:

- The text `mcp_secret:`, the length of the path of the workspace root, a colon, the path, and `|`.
- The server name and `|`.
- The first 16 hexadecimal characters of the SHA-256 hash of the JSON array of `url` and `command`, and `|`.
- The field: `headers.<key>` or `env.<key>`.

Because the key holds the hash, a server that points at another URL or command never receives the old value. The length of the root path makes sure that the path of one workspace is never the prefix of the keys of another workspace.

On each save, the function `seal_mcp_values` does these steps:

1. It stores each literal value in the registry.
2. It writes `${ostra_secret}` in place of the literal value.
3. It deletes every saved value of the workspace root that no field names.

The function `stash_file_literals` runs before the save. It keeps the literal values that the file on disk holds, because the browser saw only the marker and sends the marker back.

If the registry cannot store a value, Ostra writes a warning to the log and leaves the literal in the file for that save.

### Save-time checks

The function `validate` in `crates/ostra-core/src/mcp.rs` runs when the user saves settings. Each issue has the path `mcp_servers[<index>].<field>`. The checks are:

- The name must pass the rules for server names, and it must not be `ostra`.
- Two entries must not have the same name.
- Exactly one of `command` and `url` must be set.
- The first item of `command` must not be empty.
- The `url` must start with `http://` or `https://`.
- `headers` and `oauth` apply to remote servers only. A local server gets secrets in `env`.
- Each name in `agents` must be an agent name.
- `timeout_secs` must be from 1 to `MAX_TIMEOUT_SECS` (600).

### Approval of a changed file

Rule A1 protects against a program that arrives in a folder file. The gateway starts no server from a `workspace.toml` that waits for approval. It also starts a server from the approved copy of the file, not from a second read. The hash of the approval covers `name`, `enabled`, `command`, `env`, `url`, `headers`, and `oauth`. A change of `disabled_tools`, `agents`, or `timeout_secs` needs no approval. If the file waits for approval, the status shows the message `PENDING_MESSAGE`. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) for the approval flow.
