sections.title: Workspace artifacts and uploads
sections.summary: How Ostra stores workspace artifacts as visible or hidden files, names them with tags, lists them in the agent brief, and how it stages and claims user uploads. Includes the caps and the REST routes.
sections.body:
Some files help every task of a workspace: style guides, sample data, and custom skills. Without a shared place, the user must attach the same file to each request. Some of these files must also stay out of the reach of agents. A second problem exists for uploads. A new task uploads files before its session exists, so no session folder can hold them yet. Ostra solves the first problem with workspace artifacts. It solves the second problem with uploads that it stages and then claims.

This page covers these topics:

- The two kinds of workspace artifact (visible and hidden) and the folders that hold them.
- Artifact paths, tags, and the way a tag reaches an agent.
- The size and count caps.
- The rules to add, hide, move, and delete an artifact.
- The artifact list in the agent brief and the search index of session artifacts.
- User uploads: staging, the safe file name, and the claim by a session.
- The REST routes of both.

The Artifact screen is outside this page. The [Session, execution, and gate screens](web-session-screens.md) page owns it.

## Terms and the folders that hold the files

The code uses the word artifact for two different things. This page uses one term for each.

| Term | Meaning | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace artifact | A file that the user keeps for every session of one workspace. | The folders in the second table below. |
| Session artifact | A file that an agent writes in a session folder, such as a spec, a plan, or a report. | `<workspace>/.ostra/sessions/<session id>/` |
| Upload | A file that the user attaches to one request as context. | The staging area, then the session folder. |

The data folder (`<data dir>`) and the runtime folder name `.ostra` (`RUNTIME_DIR`) are in [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md). These folders hold the files:

| Kind of file | Path | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visible artifact | `<workspace>/.ostra/artifacts/` | `artifacts::dir` |
| Hidden artifact | `<data dir>/hidden-artifacts/<workspace id>/` | `artifacts::hidden_dir` |
| List of hidden units | `<data dir>/hidden-artifacts/<workspace id>.units.json` | `artifacts::hidden_units_file` |
| Staged upload | `<workspace>/.ostra/uploads/<upload id>/<name>` | `paths::upload_staging` |
| Claimed upload | `<session root>/uploads/<name>` | `paths::session_uploads` |

A workspace artifact has no ID. Its normalized path inside the artifacts folder names it, for example `guides/style.md`. A staged upload has an upload ID. The ID has 32 hexadecimal characters from a version 4 UUID. The workspace ID names the hidden folder and the units file.

## Visible and hidden artifacts (Rule W2)

A visible artifact sits in `<workspace>/.ostra/artifacts/`, and every agent can read it. A hidden artifact sits in the data folder of Ostra. The module comment of `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` states the goal: no agent, harness, or sandboxed command can read a hidden artifact. The user can still list, edit, download, and move hidden artifacts.

The user hides one folder or one file as a hidden unit. The units file stores the units as a JSON array of paths, for example `["data/x.csv","notes"]`. A path is hidden when it is a unit or lies under a unit. Thus a hidden folder hides every file that the user adds to it later.

Rule W2 sets one invariant for every change: a file is stored in the hidden folder exactly when its path is within a hidden unit. The functions `is_within`, `is_hidden`, and `tidy_units` in `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` implement the test:

```rust
pub fn is_within(path: &str, unit: &str) -> bool {
    path == unit || path.starts_with(&format!("{unit}/"))
}

pub fn is_hidden(units: &[String], path: &str) -> bool {
    units.iter().any(|u| is_within(path, u))
}
```

The match needs the `/` after the unit. Thus the unit `notes` hides `notes/later/b.md` but not `notesheet.md`. `tidy_units` sorts the units and removes duplicates. It also removes each unit that lies inside another unit.

### Hide or show a unit

`set_hidden` in `ostra-server/src/artifacts.rs` changes the state of one unit. This diagram shows its decisions:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["normalize the path"] --> B{"artifact exists?"}
  B -- "no" --> N["404 not found"]
  B -- "yes" --> C{"hidden is true?"}
  C -- "yes" --> D{"already inside a unit?"}
  D -- "yes" --> Z["no change"]
  D -- "no" --> E["add the path as a unit"]
  C -- "no" --> F{"path is a unit?"}
  F -- "yes" --> E2["remove the unit"]
  F -- "no" --> G{"inside a hidden folder?"}
  G -- "yes" --> H["409: show the folder instead"]
  G -- "no" --> Z
  E --> R["relocate files"]
  E2 --> R
```

Before it adds or removes a unit, `set_hidden` drops each saved unit that lies inside the path. The new unit covers them. Then `relocate` moves the files and saves the units. A request to show a file inside a hidden folder fails with status 409, because the folder hides all that it holds. The message names the folder to show instead.

### What happens when

- **The units file is missing.** A workspace that hid files before Ostra recorded units has no units file. `hidden_units` then treats each file in the hidden folder as a unit.
- **The units file holds invalid JSON.** `hidden_units` returns an empty list. The files stay in the hidden folder, but `list` reports them as visible.
- **The user adds a file inside a hidden folder.** `root_for` selects the hidden folder, so the new file is hidden at once.
- **The user moves a hidden file.** It stays hidden. A file that lands inside a hidden folder becomes hidden.
- **The user deletes a file.** `delete` removes the file and the empty folders above it. It removes a unit only when the unit is the deleted file. A hidden folder stays a unit after its last file is gone.
- **A path names a link.** `list`, `visible_file`, and `subtree` do not follow links. The comment gives the reason: a link could name any file on the machine.

### For the user

No setting changes these rules. The user controls them with the Artifacts page, which calls the routes in the route table below.

| Control | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | State shows in | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hide a file or folder: `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts/hidden` with `hidden: true` | Visible | The units file and the hidden folder in the data folder | At once | The `hidden` field of each entry from `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts` | Send `hidden: false` for the unit itself |
| Add a file: `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts?path=` | Visible, unless a hidden unit holds the path | The visible folder or the hidden folder | At once | The same list | Delete the file, or hide it |

## Artifact paths and normalization

Every route that takes an artifact path calls `artifacts::normalize` first. The function returns one canonical path or an error text for the user. This prevents a path from leaving the artifacts folder. It also keeps one name for one file.

`normalize` applies these rules:

- It trims spaces and changes each `\` to `/`.
- It removes a leading `./` and a trailing `/`.
- It refuses an empty path, an absolute path, and a path that starts with `/`.
- It refuses a `..` segment and a Windows drive prefix.
- It refuses a segment that starts with a dot, such as `.env` or `.git`.
- It refuses a segment with a control character.

The error text is: Name the artifact with a relative path such as `guides/style.md`. The route returns it with status 400. The server also checks containment. The function `contained` calls `tree::contain` on the canonical folder and returns status 403 when a path escapes it. The source states no reason for the dot rule, so this page states the rule alone.

`visible_file` returns a path only for a regular file that lies inside the canonical artifacts folder. A link is not a regular file for this function, so it returns nothing for a link.

## Artifact tags in requests and instructions (Rule W3)

A tag names a file in text that the user writes. The form is `@<key>/<path>`. The key `_artifacts` (the constant `TAG_ROOT`) names a workspace artifact, for example `@_artifacts/guides/style.md`. No project key can equal `_artifacts`, because project keys start with a letter or a digit. Any other key names a project of the workspace.

The function `tags` finds tags with the pattern `(?:^|\s)@([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)/(\S+)`. A tag must start the text or follow white space. Thus `me@host/x` is not a tag. `tags` removes the characters in the constant `TRAILING` from the end of a path. These characters are the period, comma, semicolon, colon, exclamation mark, question mark, closing parenthesis, closing bracket, closing brace, double quote, single quote, and backtick. `tags` returns each tag once, in order of first use.

A tag reaches an agent in three places:

1. **Instruction text.** `with_tagged_files` in `ostra-engine/src/factory.rs` calls `tagged_files`. It appends the list "Files these instructions name" with the absolute path of each resolved tag. A tag for `_artifacts` resolves only to a visible file. A tag for a project resolves only when the file or folder exists inside the canonical project root. A tag that does not resolve stays plain text.
2. **Save-time check of instructions.** `tag_issues` runs when the user saves workspace settings. It checks each `_artifacts` tag in `instructions.all` and in `instructions.agents.<agent>`. A tag for a missing artifact and a tag for a hidden artifact each give one issue on that field. The save returns status 422. The [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) page owns the save-time validation.
3. **Request context files.** The user attaches files to a new request or to an addition. `validate_files` in `ostra-engine/src/runner.rs` accepts at most `MAX_CONTEXT_FILES` files, and [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) owns the runner. A file with the project `_artifacts` must be an existing visible file. The error text is: Tag a workspace artifact that exists and is not hidden. The route returns it with status 409. The engine then writes the absolute path beside the tag in the task text for every agent.

The two messages of `tag_issues` give the reason for the rule. For a hidden artifact: "Unhide the artifact or remove its tag, because agents never see a hidden artifact." For a missing artifact: "Add the artifact on the Artifacts page or remove its tag, because the workspace has no such artifact."

## Size and count caps

These constants limit artifacts and uploads. No setting changes them.

| Constant | Value | File | What it limits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` | 25 MB (`25 * 1024 * 1024`) | `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` | One artifact that the user uploads or saves. The reason in the message: agents read artifacts whole. |
| `MAX_ARTIFACTS` | 2000 | `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` | Artifacts in one workspace, visible and hidden together. The reason in the message: every agent brief lists them. |
| `MAX_BRIEF_ARTIFACTS` | 40 | `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` | Artifacts that the repo brief names. |
| `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | 25 MB | `ostra-engine/src/uploads.rs` | One upload. The reason in the message: every agent reads uploads. |
| `MAX_UPLOADS` | 20 | `ostra-engine/src/uploads.rs` | Uploads that one request or one addition claims. |
| `MAX_CONTEXT_FILES` | 50 | `ostra-engine/src/runner.rs` | Files tagged on one request. [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) owns this limit. |
| `ARTIFACT_INDEX_CAP` | 4 MB (`4 * 1024 * 1024`) | `ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs` | The size of a session artifact that the search index reads for headings. |
| `ARTIFACT_LIMIT` | 4 MB | `ostra-server/src/api.rs` | The size of a session file that `GET /api/artifacts` returns as text. |

The upload routes add a body limit of the cap plus 1,024 bytes (`DefaultBodyLimit`). The server rejects a larger body before the handler runs. `check_room` counts the files of both artifact folders. It refuses a new file when the count is `MAX_ARTIFACTS` or more. `artifacts::list` stops reading a folder when its count reaches `MAX_ARTIFACTS`.

The constant `ARTIFACT_PREFIX` (`"ostra-"`) in `ostra-core/src/paths.rs` has a comment. The comment says that it replaces the `ultracode-` prefix of an earlier tool. No other source file in the crates uses it.

## Add, move, and delete rules (Rule W4)

An agent can read an artifact at any time. If the user deletes or moves the file during a run, the agent can read a path that no longer exists. Rule W4 prevents this. `blocked` in `ostra-server/src/artifacts.rs` returns a message when work is live. It checks in this order:

1. A session with the status `Running`, `Waiting`, `Stalled`, or `Paused`. The message says: Stop session {id} or wait for it to end, then {verb}, because its agents may be reading the artifact.
2. A running execution. The message says: Wait for execution {id} to finish, then {verb}, because it may be reading the artifact.

Sessions with another status do not block. `delete` and `move_to` call `blocked` and return status 409 with the message. `list` puts the delete message in the field `delete_blocked` of `WorkspaceArtifacts`, so a client can disable the delete control.

The route handlers add a second guard. `artifact_move` and `artifact_delete` call `w.work.try_write()`. The route that creates a session calls `start_work`, and `start_work` holds `w.work.read()` until the session starts. If a session starts at that moment, the write lock fails. The handler then returns status 409 with the text: Try again in a moment, because work is starting in this workspace. Thus no session starts between the busy check and the file change.

`upload` and `set_hidden` do not call `blocked`.

### Add an artifact

`upload` in `ostra-server/src/artifacts.rs` adds one file. It runs these checks in order:

1. Normalize the path (400 on failure).
2. Refuse a body over `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` (400).
3. Refuse a path that exists in the visible or the hidden folder (409). The message says to delete it first or choose another name.
4. Call `check_room` (409 when the workspace holds `MAX_ARTIFACTS` files).
5. Select the folder with `root_for`, check containment, and write the file.

The result is a `WorkspaceArtifact` with the `hidden` flag. The route then announces the save to the Files view.

### Move an artifact

`move_to` moves a file or a folder. It refuses a target inside the source (400), a source that does not exist (404), and a target that exists (409). It rewrites each unit that lies inside the source to the new path. If a hidden folder hid the source, the target becomes a unit.

`relocate` does the move. It builds a plan for both folders and checks every target file before it moves anything. A target file that exists gives status 409. Then it creates the folders and moves each file with a rename. If the rename fails, it copies the file and removes the source, because the data folder can be on another file system than the workspace. It removes the empty folders and then saves the units.

### Delete an artifact

`delete` removes one file, visible or hidden. It does not remove a folder. After the file is gone, `prune` removes each empty folder up to the artifact root, so no empty folder stays behind.

### Download an artifact

`download` finds the file in the visible folder first and then in the hidden folder. The user can download a hidden artifact. The reply has the type `application/octet-stream`. It also has the header `Content-Disposition` with the type `attachment` and the parameter `filename*=UTF-8''<encoded name>`. The function `attachment` percent-encodes each byte of the name except letters, digits, and `-._~`.

## The artifact list in the brief and the search index

Every agent execution gets a repo brief. [Agents, prompts, and coordination](agents-and-prompts.md) owns the brief. This part states what the brief holds about artifacts (Rule W1).

`ArtifactsBrief::read` in `ostra-agents/src/brief.rs` lists the visible folder only. A hidden artifact never appears in the brief. If the folder holds no file, the function returns nothing and the brief has no artifact part. Otherwise the part has the heading `## Workspace artifacts` and these lines:

- One line for each of the first `MAX_BRIEF_ARTIFACTS` (40) paths, sorted by path: the absolute path and the size in bytes.
- A last line "and N more, find them with Glob" when the folder holds more files.
- A text that tells the agent to read the relevant files with Read and not to write in the folder, because the folder belongs to the user.
- A text that tells the agent that an artifact named `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` is a skill. The agent loads it with the Skill tool by its path.

`skill_path` in `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` finds such a skill. The Skill tool looks in the project skill folders first, then in the workspace artifacts, then in the skill resolver. The [Native tools](tools.md) page owns the Skill tool.

Three layers keep agents from changing the visible folder. The guard `WORKSPACE_ARTIFACTS` (`workspace-artifacts`) in `ostra-policy/src/guards.rs` denies a write inside it. The sandbox profile mounts the folder as read-only. The harness launch adds the folder with `--add-dir`, so a harness can read it. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md), [Sandbox](sandbox.md), and [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).

### Search index of session artifacts

The nav search indexes session artifacts, not workspace artifacts. `index_artifacts` in `ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs` runs when the tree node of a session is rebuilt. For each session artifact with an absolute path, it takes these steps:

1. Read the file metadata. Skip the artifact when the file is missing.
2. Skip the artifact when the stored label and modification time match the index.
3. Build the index text: the file name, then each heading of the file when the size is at most `ARTIFACT_INDEX_CAP` (4 MB) and the file is valid UTF-8 text.
4. Store the text. If the store fails, log a warning and go on.

Agents write session artifacts through their tools, so the index catches up at each rebuild.

## User uploads: stage, then claim (Rule C3)

An upload is a file that the user attaches to one request. A new task uploads before its session exists, so the engine first stages the file in the workspace. A session then claims it into its own `uploads/` folder. The functions `stage`, `check`, and `claim` in `ostra-engine/src/uploads.rs` implement the flow.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Browser
  participant Server as upload route
  participant Engine
  participant Staging as staging area
  participant Session as session uploads folder
  Browser->>Server: POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/uploads?name=
  Server->>Engine: stage_upload(name, bytes)
  Engine->>Staging: write .ostra/uploads/id/name
  Engine-->>Browser: UploadRef (id, name, size)
  Browser->>Server: POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/sessions with upload IDs
  Server->>Engine: create_session
  Engine->>Staging: check(ids)
  Engine->>Session: claim(ids)
  Staging-->>Session: move each file
```

### Stage a file

`stage` writes the bytes and returns an `UploadRef` with the fields `id`, `name`, and `size`. It follows these steps:

1. Refuse an empty file. The error text is: The file is empty.
2. Refuse a file over `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`. The error text says to upload files of at most 25 MB, because every agent reads them.
3. Make the upload ID with `Uuid::new_v4().simple()`. The ID has 32 hexadecimal characters.
4. Make the file name safe with `safe_name`.
5. Create `<workspace>/.ostra/uploads/<id>/` and write the file in it.
6. Write a `.gitignore` with the line `*` in the staging root when it does not exist, so git ignores staged uploads.

`safe_name` keeps the last segment of the name after `/` or `\`. It removes control characters and changes each of these characters to `_`: colon, asterisk, question mark, double quote, less-than sign, greater-than sign, and vertical bar. It trims white space and removes leading dots, so the name is never hidden. It keeps at most 120 characters. If the result is empty, the name is `upload`. Thus `../../etc/passwd` becomes `passwd`, and `.env` becomes `env`.

### Claim the staged files

The session creation and the amend route pass a list of upload IDs. Both call `claim`. The creation code first calls `check` before it makes the session folder, so a bad ID fails before Ostra creates anything.

`check` refuses more than `MAX_UPLOADS` (20) IDs. It also resolves each ID with `staged_file`. The function `valid_id` accepts only 32 hexadecimal characters, so an ID such as `../x` cannot leave the staging folder. A missing upload gives the error: An upload is missing. Upload the file again, then send.

`claim` moves each file to `<session root>/uploads/`. It never overwrites a file. If the name exists, it adds a number before the extension, starting at 2. Then it moves the file. If the rename fails, it copies the file. After the move, it removes the staged folder of that ID.

```rust
let mut n = 2;
while target.exists() {
    target = dest.join(format!("{stem} ({n}){ext}"));
    n += 1;
}
if std::fs::rename(&src, &target).is_err() {
    std::fs::copy(&src, &target).map_err(io)?;
}
```

The unit test `staged_uploads_move_into_the_session_without_overwriting` stages `spec.pdf` twice. The claim gives `spec.pdf` and `spec (2).pdf`. A second claim of the same ID fails, because the first claim removed the staged folder.

The result is a list of `UploadedFile` values with `name`, `path`, and `size`. The engine stores them in the session state and in the `RequestAmended` event. `upload_list` in `ostra-engine/src/state.rs` writes the absolute path of each file in the task text. The heading is "Files the user uploaded with the request", or "Files uploaded with this addition" for an amendment. Each agent must read each file before it starts.

### What happens when

- **The user uploads and never sends the request.** The staged folder stays. No code in the crates removes an unclaimed staged upload, because only `claim` removes a staged folder.
- **The request names more than 20 uploads.** The route returns status 409 with the text: Upload at most 20 files at a time.
- **The session has ended and the user adds context.** `amend` returns an error before it claims, so the uploads stay staged. The text is: This session has ended. Start a new task instead.
- **An addition has no text, no files, and no uploads.** `amend` returns the error: Say what to add or change, tag a file with @, or upload one.
- **A disk write fails.** `stage` returns: Saving the upload failed. `claim` returns: Keeping the upload failed. Both include the system error text.
- **Two uploads have the same name.** Each gets its own upload ID. The claim renames the second file with a number.

### For the user

No setting changes the upload rules.

| Control | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | State shows in | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Upload a file in the composer: `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/uploads?name=` | No upload | `<workspace>/.ostra/uploads/<id>/` | At once for staging. At the next session creation or amendment for the claim | The `UploadRef` in the reply, then the `uploads` of the session | Leave the upload ID out of the request. No route deletes a staged upload |

## REST routes for artifacts and uploads

`ostra-server/src/api.rs` registers these routes. The logic of the workspace routes is in `ostra-server/src/artifacts.rs`. See [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) for the route groups and the security middleware.

| Method and route | Handler | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts` | `artifacts_list` | Lists all artifacts, visible and hidden, sorted by path. Returns `WorkspaceArtifacts` with `dir`, `artifacts`, and `delete_blocked`. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts?path=` | `artifact_upload` | Adds the raw body as a new artifact. Returns a `WorkspaceArtifact`. |
| `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts?path=` | `artifact_delete` | Deletes one file when Rule W4 allows it. Returns the new list. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts/download?path=` | `workspace_artifact_download` | Returns the file bytes as an attachment. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts/hidden` | `artifact_hidden` | Takes `{path, hidden}`. Hides or shows one unit. Returns the new list. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts/move` | `artifact_move` | Takes `{from, to}`. Moves a file or a folder. Returns the new list. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/uploads?name=` | `upload` | Stages the raw body. Returns an `UploadRef`. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/sessions` | `create_session` | Takes upload IDs and tagged files in the body. Claims the uploads. |
| `POST /api/sessions/{id}/amend` | `amend` | Takes text, files, and upload IDs. Claims the uploads. |
| `GET /api/artifacts?path=` | `artifact` | Returns one session artifact as text, with headings and the typed document view. |
| `GET /api/artifacts/download?path=` | `artifact_download` | Returns one session file as an attachment. |

The `artifacts` route has one body limit for all its methods: `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` plus 1,024 bytes. The `uploads` route uses `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` plus 1,024 bytes.

The two session routes use `session_file`. It canonicalizes the path and accepts it only when it lies inside the `sessions` folder of one workspace. Other paths give status 403 with the text: Only files inside a session directory can be opened here. A missing file gives 404, and a folder gives 400. `GET /api/artifacts` returns the text only when the file is at most `ARTIFACT_LIMIT` (4 MB) and valid UTF-8. Otherwise it returns `binary: true`, an empty `content`, and the size, so the client offers a download.

The Files view also serves workspace artifacts. It treats the key `_artifacts` as a project key and reads both folders. It has no diff and no change list for it. See [Project files, Git dock, and cloning](project-files-and-git.md).

### Error status codes of the artifact routes

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| 400 | The path is not a relative path, the file is over 25 MB, or a move target lies inside the source. |
| 403 | The path escapes the artifact folder. |
| 404 | The workspace has no artifact at the path, or the workspace does not exist. |
| 409 | The path exists, the workspace holds 2000 artifacts, a move target exists, Rule W4 blocks the change, or the write lock is busy. |
| 500 | A file system call failed. The text starts with: The artifact could not be changed. |

An engine error of kind `Invalid` also returns status 409. This includes every upload error on this page.

## What the design does not guarantee

- A hidden artifact is a plain file in the data folder. Ostra does not encrypt it. A person or a process outside Ostra with access to the data folder can read it.
- The claim that no agent can read a hidden artifact depends on the policy and the sandbox. This page does not describe them. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) and [Sandbox](sandbox.md).
- Rule W4 does not cover hide, show, or add. A change of the hidden state when a session runs moves files that an agent can read.
- An upload is not hidden from agents. Every agent of the session reads it.
- Ostra removes no staged upload that nobody claims.
- The count cap is approximate. `artifacts::list` stops reading a folder at the cap, and it does not stop the other folders of the walk.

sections.title: Storage: databases and lesson memory
sections.summary: How the `ostra-store` crate keeps state in three SQLite files: the workspace database with the event log, the machine registry with onboarding flags, and the per-project lesson memory with its recall ranking.
sections.body:
Ostra must keep state across restarts: the log of each session, the list of workspaces on the machine, and the lessons that agents learn about a project. Without a durable store, a restart loses running sessions and every lesson. The `ostra-store` crate keeps this state in three kinds of SQLite file. This page explains each file, its tables, how it opens and migrates, and the rules that keep concurrent writers safe. Secret sealing in the registry belongs to [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md).

## The three SQLite stores

The crate has three stores. Each store has its own type, its own file, and its own scope.

| Store | Type | File | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace database | `WorkspaceDb` | `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db` | One for each workspace |
| Machine registry | `RegistryDb` | `registry.db` in the Ostra data folder (`~/.local/share/ostra` on Linux) | One for each machine |
| Lesson memory | `MemoryStore` | `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3` | One for each project |

The functions `workspace_db`, `registry_db_path`, and `project_memory_db` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs) build these paths. The [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) lists the data folder, the runtime folder name, and the variable that moves the data folder.

The crate re-exports the public types from [`crates/ostra-store/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-store/src/lib.rs). The module `secrets` seals credentials and has its own page. The module `util` holds the shared helpers for timestamps and enum columns.

## Open a database file

The workspace database and the registry share one open function, `open_connection`. It runs these steps in this order:

1. Create the parent folder. On Unix, set its mode to `0700`.
2. Open the SQLite file and set the busy timeout to 5000 ms.
3. Set `journal_mode` to `WAL` and `foreign_keys` to `ON`.
4. Run the migrations that the file has not run yet.
5. On Unix, set the mode of the database file, the `-wal` file, and the `-shm` file to `0600`.

The owner-only modes have a reason. The event log holds tool output, the registry holds credentials, and SQLite creates its side files with the process umask. A side file that does not exist yet is skipped without an error. On other platforms the mode step does nothing.

Each handle holds one connection in an `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`. A clone of the handle shares that connection. If a thread panics while it holds the lock, the next call takes the connection anyway, because `lock` recovers a poisoned mutex.

`WorkspaceDb::open_in_memory` runs the migrations on a memory connection. It sets no pragma and no file mode.

### What happens when

- **Another process holds the file lock:** the call waits up to 5000 ms. After that, SQLite returns an error and the call fails with `StoreError::Sqlite`.
- **The parent folder is missing:** `open_connection` creates it.
- **The file mode cannot change:** the open call fails with `StoreError::Io`, except when the file does not exist.

## Run schema migrations

Each database keeps its schema version in the SQLite `user_version` pragma. The list `MIGRATIONS` in each module holds one SQL text for each version. The function `migrate` skips the entries below the stored version. It runs each other entry in its own transaction and sets `user_version` to the entry number in the same transaction.

```rust
fn migrate(conn: &Connection, migrations: &[&str]) -> Result<(), StoreError> {
    let current: i64 = conn.pragma_query_value(None, "user_version", |r| r.get(0))?;
    for (i, sql) in migrations.iter().enumerate().skip(current.max(0) as usize) {
        let tx = conn.unchecked_transaction()?;
        tx.execute_batch(sql)?;
        tx.pragma_update(None, "user_version", (i + 1) as i64)?;
        tx.commit()?;
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

The workspace database has three migrations. The registry has one.

| Version | Database | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Workspace | Creates the tables `meta`, `projects`, `sessions`, `events`, `executions`, `messages`, `activity`, `gates`, `decisions`, and `tool_calls` with their indexes |
| 2 | Workspace | Adds the column `sessions.title` and the column `executions.summary` |
| 3 | Workspace | Creates the search tables `search_docs` and `search_fts`, the triggers that feed them, and a backfill of the existing sessions |
| 1 | Registry | Creates the tables `workspaces`, `push_subscriptions`, and `kv` |

Append a new entry to `MIGRATIONS` to change a schema. Do not edit an old entry, because `migrate` never runs an entry again after the file passed its version. The function does not check for a `user_version` that is higher than the list, so an older build opens a newer file without an error.

The tests in [`crates/ostra-store/tests/workspace_db.rs`](crates/ostra-store/tests/workspace_db.rs) cover two upgrade paths. A version 1 database gains the new columns and keeps its sessions. A database reset to version 2 without the search tables gets the search tables again and its sessions are searchable. A transaction that fails rolls back, so a half-applied migration does not leave the version changed.

## Workspace database tables

The workspace database holds the session event log, which is the source of truth, and the tables that the engine materializes beside it for the console. The fold that turns events into session state is on [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md). This page covers only the rows.

| Table | Key | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `meta` | `key` | Text values. The key `workspace_id` holds the workspace ID. The key `ui_state` holds the console layout state of the workspace. |
| `projects` | `key` | The project path, its `init_status`, and its `stack` |
| `sessions` | `id` | One summary row for each session |
| `events` | `(session_id, seq)` | The event log: the event type, its JSON payload, and its time |
| `executions` | `id` | One row for each agent execution, with its usage, cost, and result |
| `messages` | `(execution_id, seq)` | The role and the JSON content of each message of an execution |
| `activity` | `(execution_id, seq)` | The stream deltas of an execution |
| `gates` | `id` | The gates of a session, with their answers |
| `decisions` | `id` | The judge decisions of a session |
| `tool_calls` | `id` (auto number) | One row for each tool call, with its policy decision and output |
| `search_docs`, `search_fts` | `id` | The text index of sessions and artifacts |

The indexes are `executions_session`, `executions_status`, `gates_session`, `decisions_session`, and `tool_calls_execution`.

### How values are stored

- A unit enum is stored as its serde name in a text column. The helpers `enum_str` and `enum_from` in [`crates/ostra-store/src/util.rs`](crates/ostra-store/src/util.rs) convert it. `enum_str` fails with `StoreError::Invalid` when the enum does not serialize to a string.
- The columns `sessions.kind`, `sessions.projects`, `executions.purpose`, and `executions.params` hold JSON text.
- A time is an RFC 3339 text in UTC with milliseconds, for example `2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`. `parse_time` fails with `StoreError::Invalid` when a stored value does not parse. Because every time has the same format, a text comparison orders times correctly.
- A boolean is an integer.

### Column lists

Four constants name the columns that a read query selects. The `raw_*` reader functions read the columns by position, so the order of a constant and the order of its reader must stay the same.

| Constant | Columns | Reader |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SESSION_COLS` | 13: `id` to `updated_at`, then `title` | `raw_session` |
| `EXECUTION_COLS` | 17: `id` to `summary` | `raw_execution` |
| `GATE_COLS` | 10: `id` to `answered_at` | `raw_gate` |
| `DECISION_COLS` | 9: `id` to `at`, without `session_id` | `raw_decision` |

`create_session` also uses `SESSION_COLS` as its insert column list.

## Create the workspace database file

`WorkspaceDb::open` runs `open_connection` and then writes `.ostra/.gitignore` when that file does not exist. The file holds the patterns `workspace.db*`, `sessions/`, and `uploads/`. The reason is that the event log keeps every tool output, so a `git add -A` in the workspace root must not publish it. If the file exists, the store does not change it.

The method `set_workspace_id` writes the workspace ID to `meta`. `get_session` and `list_sessions` read it and put it in each `SessionSummary`. If the key is missing, the ID is an empty string.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | When a change takes effect | What shows the state | How to change it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `.ostra/.gitignore` | Created with 3 patterns when absent | The `.ostra` folder of the workspace | At once, because the store reads it only to test that it exists | `git status` in the workspace | Edit the file. Delete it to get the default file back at the next open. |

The tool output limit and the column lists are constants. A user cannot change them.

## Append an event to the log

The event log is append-only. `append_event` gives each event of a session the next sequence number, so the fold can replay the events in order. It runs these steps in one transaction:

1. Start an `IMMEDIATE` transaction, which takes the write lock before the first read.
2. Read `MAX(seq) + 1` for the session. The first event gets `1`.
3. Insert the row with the event type, the JSON payload, and the time.
4. Set `sessions.updated_at` to the same time.
5. Commit and return a `StoredEvent`.

```rust
let tx = conn.transaction_with_behavior(TransactionBehavior::Immediate)?;
let seq: i64 = tx.query_row(
    "SELECT COALESCE(MAX(seq), 0) + 1 FROM events WHERE session_id = ?1",
    params![session.as_str()],
    |r| r.get(0),
)?;
...
tx.execute(
    "INSERT INTO events (session_id, seq, type, payload, at) VALUES (?1, ?2, ?3, ?4, ?5)",
    params![session.as_str(), seq, kind, payload.to_string(), at_text],
)?;
```

The `type` column holds the `type` field of the serialized event, or `unknown` when the field is missing. The primary key `(session_id, seq)` makes a duplicate sequence number an error. The test `concurrent_appends_get_distinct_seqs` starts 8 threads that append 10 events each to one session. The result is the sequence `1` to `80` with no gap and no duplicate. Two sessions count separately, so each session starts at `1`.

`events(session)` returns all events in order. `events_after(session, after)` returns the events with `seq` greater than `after`, so a reader can resume from the last sequence number that it saw.

If the session row does not exist, the `UPDATE` of `updated_at` changes no row and raises no error.

`append_message` and `append_activity` use the same method for their own tables. They start an `IMMEDIATE` transaction and number the rows for one execution. `activity_after(execution, after)` reads the deltas after a sequence number.

## Session, execution, gate, and decision rows

The engine writes the materialized rows with these methods. The methods keep the rules below.

### Sessions

- `create_session` inserts a row with the status `Running`, the lane `Research`, the stage label `Intake`, a cost of `0`, and no title.
- `update_session` changes only the fields of `SessionUpdate` that are `Some`. A field that is `None` stays as it is. The fields `category` and `title` are `Option<Option<_>>`, so `Some(None)` clears them. All changes and the new `updated_at` commit in one transaction.
- If the session does not exist, `update_session` fails with `StoreError::NotFound`.
- `list_sessions` returns the newest session first. `SessionSummary.open_gates` is the count of gates of the session with no answer.

### Executions

- `insert_execution` inserts a row with the status `Running`, an empty usage, and a cost of `0`.
- `update_execution_usage` stores the live usage and cost while the execution runs.
- `finish_execution` stores the status, usage, cost, error, `submit` payload, final text, and end time. It keeps the old `native_session_id` when the result has none. If no row matches, it fails with `StoreError::NotFound`.
- `set_execution_status` runs `UPDATE executions SET status = ?1, ended_at = COALESCE(?2, ended_at)`. For a terminal status, `?2` is the current time, so the call overwrites an end time that exists. For a non-terminal status, `?2` is `NULL`, so the old end time stays. A second call with a terminal status therefore replaces the first end time.
- `reopen_execution` sets the status to `Running` and clears the error and the end time (Rule P2). The usage, the transcript, and the Activity rows stay, so a resumed run adds to them. [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) explains pause and resume.
- `mark_running_interrupted` changes every `running` execution to `interrupted` and returns them. The runner calls it in its restart recovery, because no process still runs those executions.
- `list_executions` returns the executions of a session, oldest first. `list_sessionless_executions` returns the side-panel executions that have no session, newest first, up to a limit.

The view that the store builds sets `can_resume` to true only for a harness executor that has a `native_session_id`. The store sets `has_transcript` and `has_terminal` to `false`, and `pending_gate` and `repo_root` to `None`. The layers above the store fill those fields.

### Gates and decisions

- `upsert_gate` inserts a gate or, if the ID exists, refreshes its title, explanation, and payload. It keeps the open time and the answer.
- `answer_gate` stores the answer, its source, an optional reason, and the answer time. If the gate does not exist, it fails with `StoreError::NotFound`. `open_gates` returns the gates with no answer, for one session or for the whole workspace.
- `insert_decision` stores a judge decision. A new decision has `overridden` set to `0` and `can_override` set to `1`. `mark_overridden` replaces the output and the reason and sets `overridden` to `1`. `set_can_override` changes the second flag. The rules for a decision are on [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md).

## Tool call output limit

`record_tool_call` stores one row for each tool call. It cuts the `output` text to `TOOL_OUTPUT_LIMIT`, which is `8 * 1024` bytes (8 KiB). The cut moves back to a character boundary, so a multibyte character is never split. The function then appends a line `[truncated: N bytes]`, where `N` is the original length in bytes. The input, the policy decision, the rule name, and the duration are stored whole. `tool_calls(execution)` returns the rows in insert order.

The limit keeps the event log small, because tool output can be large. The test `tool_calls_truncate_output` stores 20,000 characters and checks that the stored text is shorter than 9,000 bytes. The policy rules that produce the decision are on [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).

## Search sessions and artifacts

The search index lets the console find a session or an artifact by words. It has a content table `search_docs` and an FTS5 index `search_fts` on the columns `label` and `body`. The index uses the tokenizer `unicode61 remove_diacritics 2` and the prefix sizes `2 3`.

Two kinds of row go in the index:

- **A session row:** triggers on the `sessions` table keep it. The label is the title, or an empty text. The body is the request. An update of the title or the request updates the row.
- **An artifact row:** `index_artifact(session, path, label, body, mtime)` writes it. The key is `(kind, ref)`, so a second call for the same path replaces the old label and text. `mtime` is the file modification time in milliseconds. `indexed_artifacts(session)` returns a map from path to label and `mtime`, so the caller can skip a file that did not change.

`search_text(text, limit)` builds its query with `fts_prefix_query`. That function splits the text on every character that is not a letter or a digit. It quotes each word, appends `*`, and joins the words with a space. Every word must match as a word prefix. For example, `ord canc` becomes `"ord"* "canc"*`. A double quote inside a word is doubled, so query syntax in the text cannot change the query. An empty query returns no hit.

The results sort by `bm25(search_fts, 4.0, 1.0)`. A match in the label counts four times as much as a match in the body. A lower rank is better. Each `TextHit` carries the kind, the reference (a session ID or an artifact path), the session, the label, the body, and the rank.

The server search code reads up to `TEXT_ROWS` (200) rows from this index. [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) describes the search route.

### What happens when

- **A reindex changes the artifact text:** the old words stop matching, because the update replaces the row. The test searches for a removed word and gets no hit.
- **The user types search syntax such as `"zz*) OR (`:** the query quotes it, and the result is empty.
- **A workspace has sessions from before version 3:** the migration copies them into `search_docs`, so they are searchable.

## Spend and cost queries

Two methods total the spend of executions. Both filter on `started_at`. They count an execution by its start time, not by its end time.

- `spend_since(since)` returns the sum of `cost_usd` of executions that started at or after `since`. The activity route uses it for the spend of today and of the week.
- `cost_report(since)` reads `usage` of each execution in the window and groups it four ways: by session, by stage, by agent, and by executor. When `since` is `None`, the window holds all executions.

A group row, `CostRow`, holds the key, the execution count, the summed `Usage`, and `cache_reads_per_tool_call`. That value is the cache read tokens divided by the tool calls. It is `0` when the group has no tool call. The rows of each group sort by cost, highest first, then by key. The report also has a `total` row with the key `total`.

Two keys stand for a missing value. An execution with no session counts under the key `side-panel`. An execution with no stage counts under the key `none`. The cost formula and the price catalog are on [Model providers and pricing](providers-and-pricing.md). The session budget is on [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md).

## Machine registry database

The registry holds the data that belongs to the machine and not to one workspace. `RegistryDb::open` opens `registry.db` with `open_connection` and then sets `secure_delete` to `ON`. This pragma zeroes freed pages, so a replaced plaintext credential does not stay in the file. The server opens it through `open_registry` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs), which sets the owner-only modes again.

The single migration in `MIGRATIONS` creates three tables:

| Table | Columns | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspaces` | `id`, `name`, `root` (unique), `created_at` | The workspaces of the machine |
| `push_subscriptions` | `endpoint` (key), `p256dh`, `auth`, `workspace_id` (may be empty), `created_at` | The Web Push subscriptions |
| `kv` | `key` (key), `value` (bytes) | Flags, approvals, and sealed secrets |

`RegistryDb::open` returns a handle without an encryption key. A secret method on that handle fails with `StoreError::Locked` until `with_sealer` gives it a key. `open_in_memory` gives the handle a key that lives as long as the process. How the key is made, stored, and used to seal values is on [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md).

### Workspace records

- `add_workspace` fails with `StoreError::Invalid` when the root path already belongs to a workspace. The message names the other workspace ID.
- `list_workspaces` sorts by creation time, then by ID. `get_workspace` and `workspace_by_root` return an `Option`.
- `rename_workspace` returns `false` when the ID does not exist.
- `remove_workspace` deletes the push subscriptions of that workspace and then the workspace row, in one transaction. The method itself deletes no file on disk. A subscription that has no workspace stays. The test `registry_workspaces_push_kv` checks both rules.
- The server removes a workspace with `delete_workspace` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs). That function calls `unregister` in [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/runtime.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/runtime.rs). `unregister` calls `remove_workspace`, then `trust::forget`, then deletes the workspace files. See the removal caution below.

### Push subscription records

`add_push_subscription` is an upsert on the endpoint. A second call for the same endpoint refreshes the keys and the workspace, and it keeps the first `created_at`. A call with no workspace makes the subscription global. `list_push_subscriptions` sorts by creation time, then by endpoint. `remove_push_subscription` returns `false` when the endpoint is unknown.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | When a change takes effect | What shows the state | How to change it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace records | Empty on a new machine | Registry table `workspaces` in `registry.db` | At once | The workspace list of the console | Create, rename, or remove a workspace in the console. Removal deletes only `workspace.toml`, `workspace.db`, and its `-wal` and `-shm` files. The project folders, the session artifact folders (`sessions_root` under the workspace), and the per-project `.ostra/` files stay on disk. Removal does not delete the artifacts of past sessions. |

Caution: copy `workspace.db` before you remove a workspace if you need its history. `unregister` deletes `workspace.toml` and `workspace.db` with its `-wal` and `-shm` files. The workspace settings and the whole workspace database are lost, with its sessions, events, and cost history. `unregister` also calls `trust::forget` for the workspace root. `trust::forget` deletes the registry keys with the prefixes `trust:workspace:`, `trust:migrated:`, `trust:migrated-paths:`, and `workspace_access:` for that root. It also deletes every saved MCP value (prefix `mcp_secret:`) and every MCP OAuth entry (prefix `mcp_oauth:`) of that root. It does not delete the `trust:format:` approvals, because the registry keys them for each project.

The workspace list changes only through the workspace routes of the console. See [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md). The [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) lists the data folder that holds `registry.db`.

## Registry key-value entries

The `kv` table is a general store of byte values under text keys. Other crates keep their own entries here, and each uses its own key names. These callers use it:

- The trust code in `ostra-workspace`.
- The sign-in code in `crates/ostra-server/src/auth.rs`, for keys such as `auth:token:<name>`.
- The MCP gateway, for OAuth entries.
- The credential and git code in `ostra-server`.
- The master key code.

This list names the main callers and is not complete. Some callers do not call `kv_get`. The files `credentials.rs`, `git.rs`, and `mcp.rs` in `crates/ostra-server/src` reach the table through `secret_scan`, `secret_get`, `secret_set`, and `kv_delete`. Search the code for `kv_` and `secret_` to find every caller.

| Method | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `kv_get(key)` | Returns the bytes or `None`. |
| `kv_set(key, value)` | Inserts the key or replaces its value. |
| `kv_replace(key, expected, new)` | Sets `new` only while the key still holds `expected`. Returns `false` when it did not. |
| `kv_delete(key)` | Returns `false` when the key is absent. |
| `kv_scan(prefix)` | Returns every entry whose key starts with `prefix`, in key order. |

`kv_replace` is a compare-and-set. It lets two callers race for one value, and only one wins. The test `kv_replace_lets_only_one_caller_claim_a_value` stores `100` under the key `auth:token:t`, replaces it with `used:1`, and checks that a second replace that expects `100` returns `false`. A missing key also returns `false`.

## Onboarding flags

The registry keeps two flags in `kv`. Both are one-time marks.

| Key constant | Key text | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ONBOARDED_AT` | `onboarded_at` | The time that the first-run setup finished, as RFC 3339 text |
| `SECRETS_VACUUMED` | `secrets_vacuumed` | The rewrite of the registry file after credential sealing finished |

`onboarded_at()` returns `None` before the setup is done. `mark_onboarded()` runs an `INSERT OR IGNORE` and then reads the value back, so a second call keeps the first time and returns it. The test `registry_onboarding_keeps_the_first_time` closes the registry, opens it again, and gets the same time.

The server sets the flag in two places. The route `POST /api/onboarding/complete` calls `mark_onboarded`. The function `create` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/setup.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/setup.rs) calls it after it creates and attaches a workspace. The route `GET /api/onboarding` returns `onboarded_at` and the number of workspaces. `RegistryDb` has no method that resets the flag.

The flag `SECRETS_VACUUMED` is internal. `seal_plaintext_secrets` sets it after the file rewrite, so plaintext that an interrupted rewrite left in the file is removed at the next start. The sealing steps are on [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md).

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | When a change takes effect | What shows the state | How to change it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `onboarded_at` flag | Not set on a new machine | Registry table `kv`, key `onboarded_at` | At once | The field `onboarded_at` of `GET /api/onboarding` | Finish the setup, or call `POST /api/onboarding/complete`. No route clears the flag. |

## Project lesson memory

Agents repeat mistakes when they forget what an earlier run learned. The lesson memory keeps short lessons for each project, and later agents recall them. A lesson has an `area`, a `lesson` text, a `source`, and a creation time. The `area` names a module, for example `orders::Service`. The text after `::` is a sub-scope.

`MemoryStore` keeps its data in `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3`. The schema comes from Ultracode's `mcp/lib/memory.js`. The constant `SCHEMA` creates the `lessons` table, the FTS5 table `lessons_fts` on `area` and `lesson`, and three triggers that keep the index in step with insert, update, and delete.

The store has these rules:

- **No cap and no expiry.** The store never removes a lesson by itself.
- **Dedupe on `(area, lesson)`.** The table has `UNIQUE(area, lesson)`.
- **One connection for each call.** Each method opens a new connection, so parallel executions wait on the SQLite file lock and do not share a handle. The busy timeout is 5000 ms.
- **Schema on every open.** `open` creates the folder and runs `SCHEMA` with `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS`. The memory file has no `user_version` and no migration list, and it does not use WAL.
- **A missing file recalls nothing.** `recall`, `list`, `forget`, and `delete` return an empty result or `false` when the file does not exist, and they do not create it.

### Record, forget, and delete

- `record(area, lesson, source)` inserts the lesson. If the pair exists, the newest call wins: it replaces `source` and `created_at`. It returns the total number of lessons. The test `dedupes_on_area_and_lesson` records one pair twice and gets one lesson with the second source.
- `forget(area, lesson)` deletes one exact pair and returns `false` when the pair is absent. It is for one lesson that is confirmed stale.
- `delete(id)` deletes a lesson by its row ID.

## Recall ranking

`recall(area, query, limit)` returns at most `limit` lessons, most relevant first. It builds up to two lists, which the code calls buckets, and then merges them. A caller sets the limit. The constant `DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT` is `8`.

First, `recall` trims `area` and treats an empty area as no area. Then it turns `query` into an FTS query with `fts_query_from_text`. That function splits the text on every character that is not a letter or a digit, quotes each token, and joins the tokens with `OR`. A lesson that holds any token matches. A query with no token counts as no query.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["recall(area, query, limit)"] --> B{"File exists?"}
  B -- no --> Z["Return an empty list"]
  B -- yes --> D{"Which inputs?"}
  D -- "area and query" --> E["List 1: area and area::* matches, by bm25"]
  D -- "area only" --> F["List 1: area and area::* lessons, newest first"]
  D -- "no area" --> G{"Query?"}
  E --> H["List 2: all matches of the query, by bm25"]
  G -- yes --> H
  G -- no --> I["List 2: all lessons, newest first"]
  F --> J["Merge, drop repeated pairs, stop at limit"]
  H --> J
  I --> J
```

The four input cases give these lists:

| Inputs | List 1 | List 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Area and query | Lessons in the area or in `area::*` that match the query, best `bm25` first | All lessons that match the query, best `bm25` first |
| Area only | Lessons in the area or in `area::*`, newest first | None |
| Query only | None | All lessons that match the query, best `bm25` first |
| Neither | None | All lessons, newest first |

The merge walks list 1 and then list 2. It keeps the first copy of each `(area, lesson)` pair. It stops when the result has `limit` lessons. The test `area_scope_then_global_fill` shows this. A recall for the area `orders` and the query `ownership` returns the lesson of `orders::Service` first and the lesson of `billing` second.

The ranking uses `bm25(lessons_fts)` with equal weights for `area` and `lesson`. SQLite returns a lower value for a better match, and the query sorts in ascending order. The area filter uses `l.area = ?` and `l.area LIKE 'area::%'`. Because `LIKE` has no escape here, the characters `%` and `_` in an area name act as wildcards. The comparison with `LIKE` ignores the case of ASCII letters.

Two other query styles exist in the crate. They differ from this one, so do not mix them.

| Function | Words | Prefix match | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fts_query_from_text` | Any word matches (`OR`) | No | Lesson recall, list, and search |
| `fts_prefix_query` | Every word must match | Yes (`*`) | Session and artifact search |

### Callers and their limits

- The `Memory` tool calls `record`, and the `MemoryRecall` tool calls `recall`. `MemoryRecall` clamps its `limit` argument to the range `1` to `50` (`MAX_RECALL_LIMIT`). See [Native tools](tools.md).
- The native loop calls `recall(None, Some(query), 5)` after a repeated build failure and shows the lessons in the tool result. The rule that triggers it is on [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).
- The workspace search calls `list` for each project. See [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) for its limits.
- The harness bridge in `ostra-server` opens the same file for harness executions.

## Edit lessons from the memory browser

A user can read and change the lessons of a project in the console. The server uses the same `MemoryStore` for this, through one route with three methods: `/api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/memory`.

- `GET` calls `list(q, 500, 0)`. With a query `q`, the list sorts by `bm25`. Without it, the list shows the 500 newest lessons.
- `PATCH` with a lesson `id` calls `update(id, area, lesson)`. It sets `source` to `user` and `created_at` to the current time. Without an `id`, it calls `record` with the source `user`. An empty area or an empty text returns the error `A lesson needs an area and text.`
- `DELETE` with the query `id` calls `delete`.

### What happens when

- **`update` gets an ID that does not exist:** it fails with `StoreError::NotFound`.
- **`update` makes a pair that already exists:** the `UNIQUE(area, lesson)` rule rejects the change, and the call fails with `StoreError::Sqlite`.
- **The project key is unknown:** the route returns a not-found error and does not open a file.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | When a change takes effect | What shows the state | How to change it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lesson store content | Empty until an agent or a user records a lesson | `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3` | At once. The next recall reads the new content. | The Memory screen, or `GET` on the memory route | Edit or delete a lesson in the Memory screen, or call the `PATCH` or `DELETE` method. See [Workspace, settings, and setup screens](web-workspace-and-setup.md). |
| Recall `limit` | `8` (`DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT`), range `1` to `50` | The `limit` argument of a `MemoryRecall` call | At the next call | The count in the tool result | Pass a different `limit`. |

The `.ostra/memory` folder belongs to the project. To remove all lessons of a project, delete the file `knowledge.sqlite3`. The next open creates an empty store.

## Store errors

Every store method returns `StoreError`. The enum has six variants.

| Variant | Message | Raised when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Sqlite` | `sqlite: ...` | SQLite reports an error, for example a busy file or a failed `UNIQUE` rule |
| `Io` | `io: ...` | A folder, a file mode, or a file write fails |
| `Json` | `json: ...` | A stored payload does not serialize or parse |
| `NotFound` | `not found: ...` | An update, finish, answer, or override names a row that does not exist |
| `Invalid` | The text itself | A workspace root is already registered, a time does not parse, or an executor or agent name does not parse |
| `Locked` | `the registry has no encryption key, so credentials cannot be read or saved` | A secret method runs on a registry that has no key |

The message of `Locked` tells the user what is wrong, so the server can show it as it is.
