sections.title: Policy engine and containment
sections.summary: How Ostra checks every tool call in two layers, guards then permissions, how it analyzes shell commands, stops build loops, counts containment signals, and what the policy does not guarantee.
sections.body:
An agent runs any tool call that its model produces. Without a check, a mistaken or prompt-injected agent can write outside its scope, read a credential, forge a record of the pipeline, or loop on a failing build. The policy engine in the `ostra-policy` crate checks every tool call from every executor before the tool runs.

This page covers:

- the two layers and the order of a check
- each guard of layer 1 and the reason for it
- the permission modes and the allow, ask, and deny rules of layer 2
- shell command analysis
- the git write checks
- the build streak and the lesson gate
- containment signals and the pause after 3
- what the policy does not guarantee

The page stops before the sandbox. The [Sandbox](sandbox.md) page explains the operating system layer that bounds what a process can do.

## How one tool call passes the two layers

Every tool call passes two layers in order. Layer 1 holds the guards. Nothing overrides a guard: not a permission rule, not a user answer, and not YOLO. Layer 2 holds the permissions, in the model of Claude Code: one mode plus allow, ask, and deny rules. `ExecutionPolicy::check` in [`crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs`](crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs) runs both layers and returns one `PolicyDecision`. The decision is `Allow`, `Ask`, or `Deny`.

The policy sees a tool call in canonical form (`ToolCall` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/policy.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/policy.rs)). The canonical tool names are the native names, such as `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash`, `Grep`, and `Glob`. A Codex patch is `ApplyPatch`. A harness tool with no canonical equivalent is `Other:<name>`. Harness adapters translate their payloads into these names before the policy runs. The [Native executor loop](native-executor.md) calls the policy for each native tool call. The [Harness executors](harness-executors.md) page explains how a hook call reaches it.

### Flow of one check

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Tool call in canonical form"] --> B["Layer 1: guards"]
    B -->|"denial"| C["Deny, rule layer guard"]
    B -->|"no denial"| D["Layer 2: rules, then mode"]
    D -->|"deny"| E["Deny, rule layer permission"]
    D -->|"allow"| F["Allow"]
    D -->|"ask"| G{"YOLO on?"}
    G -->|"yes"| H["Allow, rule yolo"]
    G -->|"no"| I["Permission card for the user"]
    I -->|"allow-once or always-in-workspace"| F
    I -->|"deny"| J["Deny"]
```

### The decision and its rule

Every denial and every ask names the rule that made it. Some allows name no rule. `PolicyDecision::allow()` sets `rule: None`, and layer 2 returns it for the Read family, for `Skill` from a path, and for known tools. An allow that comes from a session rule, from `session-dir`, or from YOLO names its rule.

`RuleRef` holds a `layer` (`guard` or `permission`) and a `rule`. The rule is a guard ID, the text of a permission rule such as `Bash(git push *)`, or a mode name such as `mode:plan`. The Activity view shows the rule with every denial. A denial reason starts with the correction, because Grok clips a reason to 256 characters.

```rust
pub fn check(&self, call: &ToolCall) -> PolicyDecision {
    let parsed = (call.tool == "Bash")
        .then(|| bash::parse(call.str_field("command").unwrap_or_default()));
    if let Some(d) = self.layer1(call, parsed.as_ref()) {
        return from_denial(d);
    }
    let decision = self.layer2(call, parsed.as_ref());
    if !self.yolo() {
        return decision;
    }
    // Under YOLO every ask becomes an allow; denials stand.
    ...
}
```

### What happens when

- **A guard refuses the call.** The result is `Deny`. Layer 2 never runs. Bypass mode and YOLO do not change it.
- **Layer 2 asks and YOLO is on.** The result is `Allow` with the rule `yolo`. The [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md) page owns YOLO.
- **Layer 2 allows with `mode:bypass` and YOLO is on.** The result is `Allow` with the rule `yolo`.
- **YOLO is on and the mode is `plan`.** The policy treats the mode as `bypass` for the check. Deny rules and guards still refuse.
- **Layer 2 asks and YOLO is off.** The executor shows a permission card. The user answers `allow-once`, `always-in-workspace`, or `deny` (`PermissionAnswer`). The [Session pipeline and planner](session-pipeline.md) page explains gates.
- **The user answers `always-in-workspace`.** The live policy adds the suggested rule as a session allow rule at once (`add_session_allow`). The engine also appends the rule to the workspace allow list and saves it (`add_allow_rule`).
- **A rule in the settings does not parse.** The policy ignores the rule and logs a warning. See [Permission rules](#permission-rules).

One `ExecutionPolicy` serves one execution. It holds the YOLO flag, the session allow rules, and the build streak. A new execution starts with an empty streak and no session rules. After each tool call, `ExecutionPolicy::observe` runs as the post-tool observer. It drives the build streak and the lesson gate. See [Build streak and lesson gate](#build-streak-and-lesson-gate).

## Layer 1 guards and tool enforcement

A guard refuses one kind of mistake or attack and gives the agent a correction. Each guard has an ID. The ID is the `rule` of the denial. Most guards port a hook library of Ultracode, the system that Ostra grew from.

Guards fall into two groups. The first group always applies. The second group applies only when tool enforcement is on. Tool enforcement answers one question: does Ostra check where tool calls read and write? Rule G1 sets the reason. With enforcement off, an agent can reach files by any route, such as one script that edits several files. The sandbox then bounds the script. The permission rules and the workflow gates still apply.

### Guards that always apply

| Guard ID | What it refuses | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `secret-read` | A read of Ostra's data folder (registry, master key, server log), a workspace database, any path under `/proc/self`, `/proc/thread-self`, or `/proc/<digits>`, or the harness state folder of an execution. The data folder assets are readable. | These files hold credentials, session records, or another process's memory. An agent never needs them. |
| `git-metadata` | A write to any path with a `.git` component. | Files under `.git` decide which programs git runs, so only git commands change them. |
| `state-ownership` | A write to engine state: a session `.state` folder, the lesson store `knowledge.sqlite3`, `workspace.db`, `registry.db`, and their `-wal`, `-shm`, and `-journal` files. Also a write to an agent-owned ledger by another agent. | A hand-written value forges a pipeline decision instead of recording one. Later sessions recall the lesson store as fact. |
| `artifact-ownership` | A write to a spec, plan, or research file by an agent that does not own that kind. Each kind has one owner: `ostra-spec-*` belongs to `generate-spec`, `ostra-plan-*` belongs to `plan`, and `ostra-research-*` belongs to `explore`. | The spec is the requirements contract and only `generate-spec` rewrites it. Only the plan agent writes the plan and its phase files. Only explore writes research. |
| `document-tool` | A direct write to a typed document (research, spec, or plan) in the session folder. | Ostra renders the markdown from the typed document. A direct write is overwritten and the browser does not show it. |
| `no-tests-from-implementer` | A write by the `implementer` to a test path in the repo. | The implementer never writes tests. Tests run only after the user asks at the closing gate. |
| `workspace-artifacts` | A write, move, or delete in the workspace artifacts folder. | Artifacts belong to the user. Agents read them and propose changes in a report (Rule W1). |
| `workspace-docs` | A write, move, or delete in the workspace books folder. | The engine writes the books from the submit calls of the docs stage (Rule B5). |
| `manage-tools` | A `ProjectCreate` call from any agent except the implementer of a phase that the approved plan puts in a new project. Also a `ProjectCreate` with a wrong key or a malformed input. Also any write outside the session folder and temp by that implementer before the project exists. | The user must never be asked about a project that cannot run. Before the project exists, no project root holds the work (Rule O2). |
| `lesson-gate` | A report write, a `Report` call without a `reason`, or a `submit_*` call with status `ok`, while a recovered build failure has no recorded lesson. | A recorded lesson stops the next run from deriving the same fix again. |
| `build-streak` | A build or test command after 5 consecutive failures. | Retrying is not the next step, because the agent lacks the information that the fix needs. |
| `answer-only` | A write, a `Report`, a `Document`, a `Memory`, or a management call from a consult run. | A consult run answers another subagent's question and changes nothing (Rule H3). |
| `reply-first` | A `submit_*` call from a run that owes an answer to another subagent. | The other subagent waits for the reply (Rule H3). |
| `windows-path` | On Windows only: an alternate data stream, a reserved device name, a UNC or device path, a drive-relative path, or a `..` after a junction or symlink. | Such a spelling can name a protected file under a name that the guards do not compare. |

The `secret-read` check uses `Roots::is_secret`. It calls `proc_of_process` in [`crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs`](crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs). That function refuses any path whose first folder is `proc` and whose second folder is `self`, `thread-self`, or only digits. A shell word that holds a dynamic `/proc/` path gets a second check on its source text. The `PROC_SECRET` pattern limits that text check to `environ`, `mem`, and `fd`.

### Guards that need tool enforcement

| Guard ID | What it refuses | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `write-scope` | A write outside the repo root and the session folder. For the read-only `quick-answer`, any write. For the session-only agents (`explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `advisor`, `documentation`, `system-architecture`), a write to project source. The `initializer` can write only to the project runtime folder and the project skills folder. A `Document` target outside the session folder. | The next stage reads the session folder. A role that does not change code never writes project source. Session-only agents can write to the OS temp folder. |
| `report-path` | A write to an `ostra-*` file in the session root that is not the declared report path of the execution. | The next stage reads that exact path. Any mechanism can write it, including a shell heredoc or chunked appends. |
| `self-protection` | A write to a protected path (the Ostra binary, its configuration, and its databases). A command that runs the `ostra` binary. Inline interpreter code that writes files or starts a process. A PowerShell or cmd command that names protected files. | These files enforce the pipeline. Running the binary lets a caller grant itself what the guards withhold. Code passed to an interpreter has no path that the guards can read. |

The three containment guards are `secret-read`, `self-protection`, and `git-metadata`. See [Containment signals and the pause after 3](#containment-signals-and-the-pause-after-3).

### Test paths

The `no-tests-from-implementer` guard uses two patterns (`TEST_DIR` and `TEST_FILE`). A path is a test path when a folder is `__tests__`, `__mocks__`, `test`, or `tests`. A path is also a test path when the file name matches one of these forms:

- `*.test.*` or `*.spec.*` with a JavaScript or TypeScript extension
- `test_*.py` or `*_test.py`
- `*_test.go`
- `*_spec.rb` or `spec_*.rb`
- a name that ends in `Test`, `Tests`, `test`, or `tests` with the extension `java`, `kt`, `kts`, or `cs`

The path `src/testing/helpers.ts` and the path `src/contest.ts` are not test paths.

### Which agent owns which ledger

The `state-ownership` guard knows three agent-owned files. Only the listed agents write them:

- **`ostra-review-ledger*.md`:** `code-reviewer`, `implementer`, and `write-test`. The engine counts the iterations of the ledger to cap the review loop.
- **`ostra-security-block.json`:** `code-reviewer`. The file records unwaivable BLOCKER findings.
- **`ostra-implementer-progress*.md`:** `implementer`. A re-run reads it to learn which steps already succeeded.

The lesson store `knowledge.sqlite3` and the databases `workspace.db` and `registry.db` have no agent owner. The `Memory` tool writes the lesson store. The engine writes the databases. Fact-check snapshot copies (a folder that starts with `factcheck-snapshot-`) are not the artifact, so the `artifact-ownership` and `document-tool` guards skip them.

### The order of the guards

`layer1` checks a call in this order. The first guard that refuses ends the check.

1. In a consult run (`answer_only`), refuse every write (`answer-only`).
2. For `Report`, refuse a call without a `reason` while a lesson is pending (`lesson-gate`). Then end layer 1 for this call.
3. For `Document`, run `check_document`. Then end layer 1 for this call.
4. For a management tool, run `check_manage` (`manage-tools`). Then end layer 1 for this call.
5. For `submit_*`, refuse when the run owes a reply (`reply-first`). Refuse status `ok` while a lesson is pending (`lesson-gate`). Then end layer 1 for this call.
6. For PowerShell and cmd, scan the raw text for protected names.
7. For each write path, run `check_write`.
8. For a read path, run `check_windows_path` and `check_read` (`secret-read`).
9. For `Bash`, run `check_shell`, `check_shell_reads`, and `check_write` on every shell write target. Then apply the build streak gate.

`check_write` runs these guards in order: `manage-tools`, `windows-path`, `self-protection`, `workspace-artifacts`, `workspace-docs`, `git-metadata`, `state-ownership`, `artifact-ownership`, `document-tool`, `no-tests-from-implementer`, `write-scope`, and `report-path`.

### What happens when

- **An agent reads engine state with `cat`, `grep`, or `head`.** The guard allows it. A plain reader does not change state. The `secret-read` guard still refuses secret files.
- **An agent writes engine state with any other command.** The `state-ownership` guard refuses it, and the reason names the Memory tool for the lesson store.
- **An agent hides a write in `python3 -c` code.** With enforcement on, the `self-protection` guard refuses code that uses a file-write API (`WRITE_API`, `PY_OPEN_WRITE`) or starts a process (`SPAWN_API`). With enforcement off, the code runs. The sandbox bounds it.
- **A write goes to the session folder.** The `write-scope` guard allows it for every agent. The other guards still apply.
- **A call names a path with `~`.** The guard resolves `~` to the home folder.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change or stop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tool_enforcement` | `disabled` | The global `config.toml` holds the machine value. A workspace override lives in the registry and never in `workspace.toml`. | At the next execution that starts | The Activity view names the guard in each denial. The Workspace page shows the global value. | Set `enabled` or `disabled` in the settings editor or in `config.toml`. Delete the workspace override to follow the global value. |

Turn enforcement on when you want write scope, the report path, and self-protection. Leave it off when you rely on the [Sandbox](sandbox.md) to bound agents. The [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) page explains why a folder file cannot set this value.

## Permission modes

A permission mode sets what layer 2 does when no rule matches. The `PermissionMode` enum has four values. Rules always run before the mode. A deny rule refuses in every mode.

| Mode | Edits | Shell commands | Reads | Other tools |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `default` | Ask, except in the session folder and OS temp | Ask, except read-only commands and commands that an allow rule covers | Allow | Known tools allow. An unknown tool asks. |
| `acceptEdits` | Allow inside the repo root. Ask elsewhere. | Allow `mkdir`, `touch`, `cp`, and `mv` when every target is in the repo, the session folder, or temp. Allow read-only commands. Ask for the rest. | Allow | Same as `default` |
| `plan` | Deny, except in the session folder and OS temp | Deny every command that is not read-only | Allow | An unknown tool is denied. A workspace MCP tool is denied unless its server marks it read-only. |
| `bypass` | Allow | Allow | Allow | Allow |

These facts hold in every mode:

- A file tool read (`Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`) is allowed unless a rule matches. The `secret-read` guard still refuses secret files.
- A write to the session folder or to OS temp is allowed. A project that itself lives under temp is project source, not scratch.
- A command that Ostra fully understands and that only reads is allowed. See [Commands that run without asking](#commands-that-run-without-asking).
- An explicit ask rule still asks in `bypass` mode. A deny rule still refuses.
- A write to a file that runs code later still asks. The next section explains it.

### Files that run code later

In `default` and `acceptEdits`, a write to a file that runs code later always asks. In `plan` it is denied. The reason: such a write outlives the session and runs outside the policy. Bypass and YOLO allow it. Two lists define these files in `runs_code_later`.

The file names are `.mcp.json`, `.envrc`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `.lefthook.yml`, `lefthook.yml`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `.npmrc`, `.yarnrc.yml`, and `.pnpmfile.cjs`.

The path endings are `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/settings.local.json`, `.codex/config.toml`, `.gemini/settings.json`, `.vscode/tasks.json`, `.vscode/settings.json`, `.vscode/launch.json`, `.cargo/config.toml`, and `.cargo/config`.

The folders are `.github/workflows/`, `.github/actions/`, `.devcontainer/`, `.husky/`, `.claude/hooks/`, and `.grok/`.

### How layer 2 decides an edit

For each write path, layer 2 follows these steps. A call with many paths, such as an `ApplyPatch`, is denied when one path is denied. Otherwise it asks when one path asks.

1. A matching deny rule refuses. A matching ask rule asks.
2. A file that runs code later takes the mode default.
3. A path in the session folder or in temp is allowed. The rule name is `session-dir`.
4. A matching allow rule allows.
5. In `acceptEdits`, a path inside the repo root is allowed.
6. Any other path takes the mode default.

### The decision for each tool family

| Family | Tools | Without a matching rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bash | `Bash` | See [Shell command analysis](#shell-command-analysis) |
| Edit | `Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, `ApplyPatch` | The six steps above |
| Read | `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob` | Allow in every mode, with no rule name |
| WebFetch | `WebFetch` | Ask in `default`, `acceptEdits`, and `plan`. Allow in `bypass`. |
| Skill from a path | `Skill` with a path | Follows the `Read` rules for that path |
| Known tools | `WebSearch`, `Skill`, `Report`, `Document`, `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, the code tools, `ProjectList`, the coordination tools, `submit_*`, and harness bookkeeping tools such as `Other:TodoWrite` | Allow in every mode, with no rule name |
| Changes Ostra | `ProjectCreate` | Ask in every mode. See below. |
| Workspace MCP tools | `mcp__<server>__<tool>` | Allow. In `plan`, allow only a tool that its server marks read-only. |
| Any other tool | `Other:<name>` | The mode default: ask in `default` and `acceptEdits`, deny in `plan`, allow in `bypass` |

Rule O1 covers `ProjectCreate`. The user answers every call that changes Ostra, in every mode, and whatever the allow rules say. YOLO answers it. A deny rule still refuses it, and `plan` mode denies it. The policy suggests no allow rule for it. Rule M1 covers workspace MCP tools: they are allowed unless a rule says otherwise. The tools of a harness's own MCP server (`Other:mcp__github__search`) are not workspace tools, so they take the mode default. The [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md) page owns the tool names.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change or stop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `permissions.mode` | `default` | The registry, for each workspace. A folder file never sets it, because a repository could otherwise loosen its own limits (Rule A2). | At the next execution that starts. A running execution keeps the mode it started with. | The Workspace page. Each decision names its mode, for example `mode:plan`. | Choose `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, or `bypass` in the settings editor. |

Choose `plan` to make a session read-only. Choose `bypass` only in a sandboxed workspace, because it removes every ask that a rule does not force.

## Permission rules

A permission rule uses the syntax of Claude Code: `Tool` or `Tool(spec)`. A rule with no spec matches every use of the tool. Layer 2 checks the deny rules first, then the ask rules, then the allow rules. The first list with a match decides. Deny beats ask, and ask beats allow.

### Rule syntax

| Rule form | What it matches |
| --- | --- |
| `Bash(npm run test *)` | A glob over one simple command. `*` matches any text. A trailing ` *` also matches the bare command. |
| `Bash(npm test:*)` | The legacy prefix form. It matches `npm test` and `npm test` followed by a space and more words. |
| `Edit(src/**)`, `Write(...)` | A gitignore-style path. An `Edit` rule covers every file-writing tool (`Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, `ApplyPatch`). |
| `Read(~/.ssh/**)` | The same path syntax. A `Read` rule covers `Read`, `Grep`, and `Glob`. A `Grep(...)` rule covers only `Grep`. |
| `WebFetch(domain:docs.rs)` | The host `docs.rs` and any subdomain of it. |
| `mcp__github` | Every tool of the MCP server `github`. `mcp__github__create_issue` matches one tool. |

Path patterns anchor in this way: `//x` is absolute, `~/x` is under the home folder, `./x` and `/x` are relative to the repo root, a pattern with a slash inside is relative to the repo root, and a bare name matches at any depth. A pattern that ends in `/` matches everything below it. The pattern `dir/**` also matches `dir`.

A rule names a tool from `KNOWN_TOOLS`, or an `mcp__` tool, or `Other:<harness tool>`, or a `submit_` tool. `KNOWN_TOOLS` holds `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Cmd`, `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, `ApplyPatch`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Skill`, `WebSearch`, `WebFetch`, `Report`, `Document`, `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, the seven code tools (`CodeOutline`, `CodeFind`, `CodeCallers`, `CodeCallees`, `CodeImplementations`, `CodeNeighbors`, `CodeImpact`), `CodeMap`, `ProjectList`, and `ProjectCreate`.

### How a rule matches a command

- **Each simple command matches alone.** With the allow rule `Bash(npm test *)`, the command `npm test && curl evil` asks, because `curl evil` has no allow rule.
- **A deny rule on any simple command denies the whole line.** With the deny rule `Bash(git push *)`, the command `npm test && git push` is denied.
- **Three forms of each command are tried:** the full words, the words without leading `VAR=value` assignments, and the words without wrappers such as `sudo` or `env`. A wrapper cannot hide a denied command.
- **A command with a dynamic name never matches an allow rule.** A name such as `$CMD` is known only when the shell runs.
- **A rule matches text.** It does not limit what the allowed program does.

The URL host comes from the same parser that `WebFetch` uses. Thus `https://evil.example\\@docs.rs/` is the host `evil.example`, and the rule `WebFetch(domain:docs.rs)` does not match it.

### Where rules come from

The engine builds the rule lists when an execution starts. It concatenates the global rules first and the workspace rules second. The live policy adds session allow rules when the user answers `always-in-workspace`. While a `workspace.toml` waits for the user's approval, Ostra ignores its allow rules. Its ask and deny rules still apply. The [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) page explains the approval.

The suggested rule for an answer of `always-in-workspace` has these forms:

- A shell command gives `Bash(<command> <subcommand> *)`, for example `Bash(npm run *)`. The policy skips the subcommand when it starts with `-`, holds a `/`, or is a glob.
- A write gives `Edit(/src/**)`, from the first folder under the repo root.
- A read gives `Read(/src/**)` in the same way.
- A fetch gives `WebFetch(domain:<host>)`.
- Any other tool gives its name. `ProjectCreate` gives nothing.

### What happens when

- **The user saves a rule that is invalid.** `validate_rule` returns a message that tells how to fix it, for example "Close the parenthesis". The settings save fails with that message.
- **A rule is invalid at run time.** The policy ignores it and logs `ignoring invalid permission rule`. An invalid deny rule therefore refuses nothing. Fix the rule in the settings editor.
- **A rule names an unknown tool.** `parse_rule` refuses it and lists the known tools.
- **A path pattern is empty or a `WebFetch` rule lacks `domain:`.** Validation refuses the rule.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shown by | How to change or stop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `permissions.allow` | Empty list | `[permissions]` in the global `config.toml` and in `workspace.toml` | At the next execution that starts. The `always-in-workspace` answer also applies at once to the live policy. | The settings editor. The Activity view shows the matching rule. | Delete a rule from the list. |
| `permissions.ask` | Empty list | Same as `permissions.allow` | At the next execution that starts | The settings editor | Delete a rule from the list. |
| `permissions.deny` | Empty list | Same as `permissions.allow` | At the next execution that starts | The settings editor. A denial names the rule that refused it. | Delete a rule from the list. |

Add a deny rule for `Bash(git push *)` when agents must never push. The policy does not treat `git push` as a working tree write. See [Git write checks](#git-write-checks).

## Shell command analysis

The policy cannot judge a shell command from its raw text. A command line holds pipelines, lists, substitutions, nested shells, and redirects, and each part can write a file. The `bash` module in [`crates/ostra-policy/src/bash.rs`](crates/ostra-policy/src/bash.rs) parses the text with tree-sitter-bash. It returns a `Parsed` value. The value holds the simple commands in execution order, a `complete` flag, and a `modelled` flag.

### What the parser returns

A `SimpleCommand` holds these fields: `assignments`, `words`, `redirects`, `heredoc_body`, `text`, `piped_input`, and `pipeline_text`. A `Word` holds its `raw` text, its unquoted `value` when the word is static, and a `glob` flag. A word with a variable or a substitution has no static value. The `glob` flag is also set for a brace expansion such as `{a,b}`.

The parser includes these commands in the list:

- commands inside `$(...)` and backticks
- the string of `bash -c "..."` and the arguments of `eval`, for the shells in `SHELLS` (`sh`, `bash`, `zsh`, `dash`, `ksh`, `fish`, `ash`, `mksh`)
- a heredoc body that a shell reads

Nested parsing stops at `MAX_DEPTH`, which is 4 levels. A deeper level sets `complete` to false.

The effective command is the word that really runs. The parser skips `VAR=value` words and these wrappers: `sudo`, `doas`, `env`, `nohup`, `nice`, `ionice`, `stdbuf`, `time`, `timeout`, `command`, `exec`, `xargs`, `strace`, `watch`, and `builtin`. It also skips their options and the options that take a value.

### The complete and modelled flags

`complete` is false when the parser hits a syntax error or the nesting limit. `modelled` is false when the source holds a statement that the command list does not model. These statements are standalone assignments, `export`, loop headers, functions, and a `[[ ]]` test that holds an expansion or a subscript. A statement kind in `STRUCTURAL` only groups commands, and it keeps `modelled` true. `STRUCTURAL` holds `program`, `list`, `subshell`, `compound_statement`, `if_statement`, `elif_clause`, `else_clause`, `while_statement`, `do_group`, and `negated_command`.

A test over plain words is modelled. This holds for `[ -f x ]` and for `[[ -d src ]]`. In `Walker::visit`, the `test_command` node covers both forms. The test stays modelled when its text has none of `$`, a backtick, `[`, `]`, or `(`. Otherwise `modelled` is false.

The reason for `modelled`: an assignment or `export` can change `PATH` or `GIT_CONFIG_*` for a later command. A loop header or a test with an expansion can run code when the shell evaluates it.

| Parse result | `default` and `acceptEdits` | `plan` | `bypass` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `complete` is false | Ask. Rule name `unparsed`. | Deny. Rule name `mode:plan`. | Allow |
| `modelled` is false | Ask. Rule name `unmodelled`. | Deny. Rule name `mode:plan`. | Allow |

Layer 1 still checks the commands that the parser found. The ask text truncates the command to 200 characters.

### Write targets

`write_targets` lists every path that a command creates, overwrites, moves, or deletes. It reads these sources:

- a redirect with `>`, `>>`, `>|`, `&>`, `&>>`, `<>`, or `>&` to a name that is not a file descriptor
- the non-flag words of `tee`, `rm`, `rmdir`, `shred`, `truncate`, `touch`, `mkdir`, and `unlink`
- the destination of `cp`, `install`, `ln`, and `mv`, in every spelling of the target directory option (`-t D`, `-tD`, `--target-directory D`, `--target-directory=D`, and unique abbreviations). `mv` also removes each source, so each source is a target.
- the files of `sed` and `perl` with an in-place option
- the `of=` value of `dd`
- the working tree of a git write subcommand. See [Git write checks](#git-write-checks).

The parser skips these names: `/dev/null`, `/dev/stdout`, `/dev/stderr`, `/dev/tty`, `-`, `&1`, `&2`, an empty word, and a word of only dots. A dot-only word is prose, not a path. A `~user/...` path is unresolved, because the resolver does not model another account's home.

A write target is unresolved when a variable, a substitution, or a glob stands in a write position. A relative write after a `cd` with a dynamic target is also unresolved. `unresolved_writes` finds these commands. Layer 2 never allows such a command without asking, because the real target was not checked. The functions `command_cwds` and `cwd_unknown` track `cd` and `pushd`. A `popd` makes the directory unknown. The parser does not model subshell scope.

### Heredocs and inline code

The parser keeps four rules from the Ultracode shell-path library:

- A heredoc body that goes to a data sink is content. The guards do not scan it as a command.
- A heredoc body that a shell reads runs. The parser parses it as commands.
- A heredoc body, a `-e` or `-c` string, or piped stdin that goes to an interpreter is inline code. `inline_code` returns the channel and the text. The interpreters are in `INTERPRETERS`: `node`, `nodejs`, `bun`, `deno`, `ts-node`, `tsx`, `python`, `python2`, `python3`, `perl`, `ruby`, `php`, `Rscript`, and `osascript`. Versioned names such as `python3.12` also count.
- A placeholder such as `<ID>` is not a redirect.

`check_shell` uses inline code. It refuses code that names a protected state file (`STATE_NAME`). With enforcement on, it also refuses code that matches a file-write API or a process-spawn API.

### Plain readers

Layer 1 lets a plain reader name engine state and protected files, because a reader changes nothing. The `PLAIN_READERS` list holds `cat`, `bat`, `head`, `tail`, `less`, `more`, `nl`, `grep`, `egrep`, `fgrep`, `rg`, `ag`, `ack`, `ls`, `find`, `fd`, `tree`, `stat`, `wc`, `file`, `du`, `cksum`, `md5sum`, `sha1sum`, `sha256sum`, `diff`, `cmp`, `jq`, `yq`, `cut`, `tr`, `sort`, `uniq`, `strings`, `xxd`, `od`, `readlink`, `realpath`, `dirname`, `basename`, `test`, `true`, `echo`, `printf`, and `sed` without an in-place option. Any other command that names such a path gets a `state-ownership` or `self-protection` denial. The `secret-read` guard has no exception for readers. `check_shell_reads` checks every path-like word and every redirect target of every command, except the words of `echo` and `printf`, which only print the name.

Two patterns find the path-like text. `PATH_CANDIDATE` is `[~\w./@-]*/[~\w./@-]+`. It finds a word with a slash. `WIN_PATH_CANDIDATE` finds a drive path or a backslash path, and the policy applies it only on Windows, in addition to `PATH_CANDIDATE`. The function `path_candidates` runs both patterns on the text of a command. It trims trailing `)`, `,`, `;`, `:`, quotes, backticks, and spaces, and drops empty results.

### PowerShell and cmd

Ostra cannot parse PowerShell and cmd. Layer 1 scans their raw text for pipeline state names and for paths that resolve to secrets, engine state, or protected files. A hit is denied. Layer 2 never allows these tools on its own, so they ask in `default` and `acceptEdits`.

## Commands that run without asking

Layer 2 allows a shell command without asking, in every mode, only when `is_read_only` accepts it and every write target is in the session folder or in temp. The rule is strict. Only a command that Ostra fully understands qualifies. The reason: an assignment or a wrapper can change what runs, a command named by a path can be a script that the agent wrote, and a dynamic word or glob can expand to an option that starts a program.

A command is read-only when all of these hold:

- It has no leading assignment, no wrapper, and no dynamic name.
- Its name has no `/`.
- Its name is in `READ_ONLY`: `ls`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `grep`, `rg`, `find`, `git`, `pwd`, `echo`, `printf`, `sort`, `uniq`, `diff`, `stat`, `file`, `which`, `tree`, `cd`, `true`, `test`, `[`, `basename`, `dirname`, `realpath`, and `readlink`.
- For the commands in `EXEC_CAPABLE` (`git`, `rg`, `sort`, `find`, `tree`, `file`, `uniq`), every argument is a static word and none is a glob. Their flags can start a program or write a file, so Ostra must know every word.
- It does not use a flag that starts a program or writes a file:
  - `find` without `-exec`, `-execdir`, `-delete`, `-fprint`, `-fprint0`, `-fprintf`, `-fls`, `-ok`, or `-okdir`
  - `rg` without `--pre`, `--pre-glob`, or `--hostname-bin`
  - `sort` without `--output`, `--compress-program`, or an `-o` cluster
  - `uniq` with at most one non-flag argument
  - `tree` without an `-o` or `-R` cluster
  - `file` without `--compile` or a `-C` cluster
  - `printf` without `-v`, which assigns a variable
  - `test` and `[` without `[`, `$`, or a backtick in an argument, because `test -v 'a[$(...)]'` evaluates its subscript

Long options match as GNU getopt reads them, including unique abbreviations. Thus `--out=x` counts as `--output`.

## Git write checks

Git needs its own checks because a git command can change the working tree, run a program from a repository's own configuration, and write the `.git` folder. Four rules cover git.

### Git write subcommands are write targets

`GIT_WRITE_SUBCOMMANDS` lists the subcommands that change the working tree: `checkout`, `switch`, `restore`, `reset`, `apply`, `am`, `stash`, `clean`, `rm`, `mv`, `merge`, `rebase`, `pull`, `cherry-pick`, `revert`, `commit`, and `add`. The parser records the directory of the command as a write target (`TargetSpec::GitTree`). The directory is the `-C` value, or the current directory. Layer 1 runs the write guards on that directory. Layer 2 treats the command as an edit, so it asks in `default` and `acceptEdits` and is denied in `plan`. A dynamic `-C`, `--git-dir`, or `--work-tree` value makes the target unresolved.

The list does not hold `push`, because `push` does not change the working tree. Add a deny rule for `Bash(git push *)` to refuse it.

### Git metadata changes only through git

The `git-metadata` guard refuses a direct write to any path with a `.git` component. It applies in every mode and under YOLO. The reason: files under `.git` (hooks, `fsmonitor`, a gitfile that points to another git directory) name programs that git runs later. A shell redirect into `.git/config` and a `cp` into `.git/hooks/` are both refused. A write to `.gitignore` is allowed. A `git commit` is allowed because the guard checks the paths that a command names, and git writes `.git` itself.

```rust
if target.components().any(|c| c.as_os_str() == ".git") {
    return Some(deny(
        GIT_METADATA,
        format!("Use git commands instead of writing \"{raw}\" directly: ..."),
    ));
}
```

### Read-only git forms

`git_read_only` allows a git command without asking when it only reads. It accepts leading options from `GIT_SAFE_GLOBAL` (`--no-pager`, `-P`, `--no-optional-locks`, `--literal-pathspecs`, `--no-replace-objects`) and `-C <dir>`. The options `-c`, `--config-env`, `--exec-path`, `--git-dir`, `--work-tree`, and `-p` are refused, because they choose programs, repositories, or a pager. The subcommands are in `GIT_READ`: `status`, `diff`, `log`, `show`, `rev-parse`, `ls-files`, and `blame`. The listing forms of `branch`, `tag`, `remote`, `describe`, and `config --get` also qualify. With a name, these commands create, rename, or delete. The options `--output`, `--ext-diff`, `--textconv`, and `--open-files-in-pager` are refused. A leading `GIT_*` assignment makes the command not read-only.

### Git runs unasked only inside the project

A read-only git command runs without asking only when its directory is inside the repo root. The directory is the current directory after any `cd`, or the `-C` value. If a dynamic `cd` makes the directory unknown, the command asks. The reason: git reads the config of the repository that it runs in, and that config can name programs. Inside the project, the `git-metadata` guard protects that config.

The [Sandbox](sandbox.md) page explains the separate git protection that the sandbox adds.

## Build streak and lesson gate

An agent that retries a failing build with small edits wastes time and money. The build streak counts consecutive build or test failures in one execution. It warns, then it refuses more build commands. The code in [`crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs`](crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs) ports three Ultracode hooks.

### Which commands count

`is_build_command` decides. The project commands `build` and `test` from `project.toml` come in `PolicyInputs.build_commands` and `PolicyInputs.test_commands`. A configured command becomes a matcher. A `{PLACEHOLDER}` token such as `{MODULE}` is a wildcard, and spaces are flexible. Thus `./mvnw test -pl {MODULE}` matches a concrete call. The first two words of a configured command also count, because agents change flags around the same tool.

When the project configures no command, `FALLBACK_BUILD` applies. It matches these forms:

- `./mvnw`, `mvn`, `./gradlew`, `gradle`, `tsc`, `cargo`, `dotnet`, `make`, and `pytest`
- `go build`, `go test`, and `go vet`
- `npm run <x>`, `npm test`, and `npm run-script`. It does not match `npm build`.
- `pnpm` and `yarn` with `test`, `run`, or `build`
- `uv run pytest`, `uv run mypy`, and `uv run ruff`
- `python -m pytest`, `python -m mypy`, and `python -m unittest`

### How a failure is detected

`failed_from` decides in this order:

1. If the outcome has an exit code, a non-zero code is a failure.
2. If the output holds an exit code in one of the `EXIT_CODE_PATTERNS`, a non-zero code is a failure.
3. If the call is an error that matches `INTERRUPTED`, there is no evidence either way. The streak does not change.
4. Any other error is a failure.
5. If the harness reports no results and the output is empty, there is no evidence either way.
6. If the output matches a marker from `FAILURE_MARKERS`, it is a failure. The markers include `BUILD FAILURE`, `Compilation failure`, `error TS<n>`, `npm ERR!`, `Traceback (most recent call last)`, and a count such as `3 failed`.
7. Otherwise the call passed.

The exit code wins over the output. A call with exit code 0 and the text `BUILD FAILURE` passed.

Two constants hold the text patterns of steps 2 and 3:

| Constant | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `EXIT_CODE_PATTERNS` | Three patterns: `Exit code N` at the start of a line, `exited with code N`, and `exit status N`. The two last forms ignore case. | Find an exit code in output text. The first pattern that matches gives `N`. |
| `INTERRUPTED` | `timed out`, `interrupted`, `canceled`, or `cancelled`, as whole words, ignoring case | Mark an error call as no evidence of failure |

### The thresholds

`Streak::record` changes the counter after each counted call.

| Consecutive failures | Constant | What Ostra does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | `RECALL_THRESHOLD` | Runs memory recall with the diagnostic signature as the query. A known fix arrives at attempt 2. |
| 3 | `WARN_THRESHOLD` | Appends a note to the tool result. The note tells the agent to state its root cause and not to retry a variation. If the same signature repeats in the last 12 results, the note says so. |
| 4 | none | Repeats the warning with the count of failures that remain. |
| 5 | `DENY_THRESHOLD` | The `build-streak` guard refuses every build or test command. The reason tells the agent to call its submit tool with status `stuck`. |

```rust
pub const RECALL_THRESHOLD: u32 = 2;
pub const WARN_THRESHOLD: u32 = 3;
pub const DENY_THRESHOLD: u32 = 5;
const MAX_HISTORY: usize = 12;
...
pub fn blocked(&self) -> bool {
    self.consecutive >= DENY_THRESHOLD
}
```

The `build-streak` reason starts with the correction and gives the reason: retrying is not the next step, because the agent does not yet have the information that the fix needs. It asks for what the agent made, the failing command, the diagnostic verbatim, the hypotheses that it ruled out, and the fact that it needs. It also forbids a retry under a different spelling. The gate refuses only build and test commands. Other commands, such as `cat`, still run. The gate applies in every mode, including YOLO.

### The diagnostic signature

`diagnostic_signature` makes a stable one-line fingerprint. It scans the output for the first line of 12 to 400 characters that matches `DIAGNOSTIC`, for example `cannot find symbol`, `AssertionError`, or `ModuleNotFoundError`. `normalize_diagnostic` then applies six patterns in this order. The signature needs at least 8 characters. Thus two failures that differ only in a path or a line number have the same signature.

| Constant | Pattern | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NORM_PREFIX` | A leading `ERROR`, `WARN`, `E`, or `FAIL`, with optional brackets and spaces, ignoring case | Removes the level prefix |
| `NORM_PATH` | `/` followed by letters, digits, `.`, `@`, `/`, `_`, or `-` | Replaces a path with `<path>` |
| `NORM_POS` | `[N,N]` or `[N:N]` | Removes a position |
| `NORM_LINE` | `:N` or `:N:N` | Removes a line number and a column |
| `NORM_VERSION` | A number with a digit and at least 2 more digits or dots | Replaces a version with `<v>` |
| `NORM_SPACE` | Any run of white space | Collapses it to one space |

After the six steps, the function trims the line and cuts it to 160 characters.

### Recovery and the lesson gate

A pass resets the counter to 0. A pass after at least 3 failures with a known signature is a verified recovery. Ostra then records a pending lesson and appends a note. The note tells the agent to record what fixed the failure with the `Memory` tool. The reason: the diagnostic recurs across sessions, and a recorded lesson stops the next run from deriving the fix again.

The `lesson-gate` guard then refuses three calls: a write to the declared report path, a `Report` call without a `reason`, and a `submit_*` call with status `ok`. A `submit_*` call with another status, such as `stuck`, passes. A successful `Memory` call clears the pending lessons. A successful `Report` call with a non-empty `reason` also clears them, so that a situational fix that teaches nothing does not block the run. The list of pending lessons keeps at most 12 entries.

### What happens when

- **A command is not a build command.** The call never changes the streak.
- **A build command is interrupted or times out.** The counter stays the same.
- **The streak is at 5 and the agent runs the build with other flags.** The command still matches `is_build_command`, so the guard refuses it.
- **A pass follows 1 or 2 failures.** The counter resets. Ostra records no lesson, because a plain pass is not a recovery.
- **A new execution starts.** The streak is 0, because the streak belongs to one `ExecutionPolicy`.

The [Storage](storage.md) page explains the lesson memory that recall reads.

## Containment signals and the pause after 3

A single refused call is an ordinary mistake. A pattern of refused calls that aim at secrets, Ostra's own files, git metadata, or the local network looks like an attempt to leave the sandbox. Rule P3 turns such a pattern into a pause. The code is in [`crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs).

### What counts as a signal

`classify` turns an execution delta into at most one `ContainmentSignal`. There are three kinds:

| Kind | Cause | Description line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Guard` | A layer 1 guard denies a tool call, and the guard is `secret-read`, `self-protection`, or `git-metadata` | the `<rule>` guard refused a tool call |
| `Egress` | The egress proxy refuses a destination that is loopback, private, or link-local | the sandbox refused a connection to the local address `<host>:<port>` |
| `Decoy` | A process opens a decoy credential file | a command opened the decoy credential file `<path>` |

The list `GUARDS` holds only the three guard IDs. The constants `SECRET_READ` (`secret-read`), `SELF_PROTECTION` (`self-protection`), and `GIT_METADATA` (`git-metadata`) in `containment.rs` hold the IDs. The guards use the same constants, so the ID that a guard denies with is the ID that `classify` matches. Other guards refuse ordinary mistakes, such as a write outside the scope of a phase. A permission rule that happens to be named `secret-read` is not a signal, because the layer must be `guard`. A refused public host is not a signal, because builds call telemetry hosts. It shows in the Activity view only. The [Sandbox](sandbox.md) page explains the egress proxy and the decoy files.

```rust
ExecutionDelta::Policy {
    decision: PolicyDecision::Deny { reason, rule },
    ..
} if rule.layer == "guard" && GUARDS.contains(&rule.rule.as_str()) => {
    Some(ContainmentSignal::Guard {
        rule: rule.rule.clone(),
        reason: reason.clone(),
    })
}
```

### How the third signal pauses the session

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["ExecutionDelta from an execution"] --> B{"classify"}
    B -->|"no signal"| C["Ignore"]
    B -->|"Guard, Egress, or Decoy"| D{"Signals already recorded for this execution"}
    D -->|"3 or more"| E["Record nothing"]
    D -->|"fewer than 3"| F["Append a ContainmentSignal event"]
    F --> G{"Count equals 3?"}
    G -->|"no"| H["Session continues"]
    G -->|"yes"| I["Pause the session"]
    I --> J["User continues: SessionResumed"]
```

The runner calls `classify` for each delta that an execution emits. `record_signal` appends a `SessionEvent::ContainmentSignal` event. It records at most `PAUSE_AFTER` signals for one execution, which is 3, so a retry loop cannot flood the log. When one execution holds 3 signals, the session pauses. The session view then shows: "Paused: read the `<agent>` execution's Activity, because it tripped 3 containment signals". The [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) page owns the event fold, the pause, and the resume.

### What happens when

- **One execution trips 1 or 2 signals.** The runner records them. The session continues.
- **Two executions trip 2 signals each.** The session does not pause, because the count is for each execution.
- **The session is already paused or finished when the third signal arrives.** The session does not pause again.
- **The user continues the session.** The pause ends. The recorded signals stay. That execution cannot record more signals, because it already holds 3.
- **A signal arrives and the event cannot be saved.** The runner logs an error and goes on.

## What the policy does not guarantee

The policy reduces the damage of a mistaken or hostile agent. It is not a complete boundary. Read these limits before you rely on it.

- **It is not a sandbox.** Guards check the paths that a tool call names. They cannot see what a process does after it starts. With tool enforcement off, which is the default, a script can write files and start processes. The [Sandbox](sandbox.md) bounds it.
- **It does not parse every command.** Nesting beyond 4 levels, a syntax error, and statements outside the command model make the result unparsed or unmodelled. Dynamic words and globs hide real targets. The parser does not model subshell scope, and its `cd` tracking is an approximation.
- **An ask is not a check.** When the user allows an unresolved or unparsed command, the real target was never checked.
- **PowerShell and cmd are opaque.** Layer 1 only scans their raw text for protected names.
- **A rule matches text.** An allow rule does not limit what the allowed program does. An invalid rule is ignored at run time, so an invalid deny rule refuses nothing.
- **Reads are open by default.** Layer 2 allows file tool reads in every mode. The `secret-read` guard covers only Ostra's own secrets, workspace databases, and process memory. To hide other files, add a `Read` deny rule or use the sandbox.
- **YOLO and bypass remove asks.** After that, only the guards and the deny rules remain.
- **Build detection is a heuristic.** The streak counts only commands that match the project commands or `FALLBACK_BUILD`, and it detects failures from exit codes and text markers.
- **Containment signals are narrow.** Only three guards, a refused local connection, and a decoy open count. A refused public connection does not count. The pause starts at the third signal of one execution, not before.
- **A tool with no canonical name is an unknown tool.** An `Other:<name>` call takes the mode default unless it is a known harness bookkeeping tool.
- **State is per execution.** The streak and the session allow rules end with the execution. Only the `always-in-workspace` answer saves a rule.

| Name | Value | File | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PAUSE_AFTER` | 3 | `crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs` | Containment signals of one execution that pause the session |
| `SECRET_READ` | `secret-read` | `crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs` | The ID of the secret read guard. `classify` matches it. |
| `SELF_PROTECTION` | `self-protection` | `crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs` | The ID of the self protection guard. `classify` matches it. |
| `GIT_METADATA` | `git-metadata` | `crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs` | The ID of the git metadata guard. `classify` matches it. |
| `GUARDS` | `secret-read`, `self-protection`, `git-metadata` | `crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs` | Guards whose denials count as signals |
| `RECALL_THRESHOLD` | 2 | `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs` | Consecutive failures that start a memory recall |
| `WARN_THRESHOLD` | 3 | `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs` | Consecutive failures that add a warning note |
| `DENY_THRESHOLD` | 5 | `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs` | Consecutive failures that refuse build and test commands |
| `MAX_HISTORY` | 12 | `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs` | Recent diagnostic signatures and pending lessons that Ostra keeps |
| `FALLBACK_BUILD` | One pattern, listed in [Which commands count](#which-commands-count) | `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs` | Build commands when the project configures none |
| `EXIT_CODE_PATTERNS` | 3 patterns | `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs` | Exit codes in output text |
| `INTERRUPTED` | `timed out`, `interrupted`, `canceled`, `cancelled` | `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs` | Errors that give no evidence of failure |
| `NORM_PREFIX`, `NORM_PATH`, `NORM_POS`, `NORM_LINE`, `NORM_VERSION`, `NORM_SPACE` | 6 patterns | `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs` | The steps of `normalize_diagnostic`. See [The diagnostic signature](#the-diagnostic-signature). |
| Signature length | 160 characters | `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs` | Maximum length of a normalized diagnostic |
| Diagnostic line | 12 to 400 characters | `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs` | Lines that `diagnostic_signature` considers |
| `MAX_DEPTH` | 4 | `crates/ostra-policy/src/bash.rs` | Nesting levels of `bash -c`, `eval`, and heredoc parsing |
| Ask text limit | 200 characters | `crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs` | Length of a command in an ask reason |
| `READ_ONLY` | 27 command names | `crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs` | Commands that can run without asking |
| `GIT_READ` | 7 subcommands | `crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs` | Git subcommands that only read |
| `GIT_SAFE_GLOBAL` | 5 options | `crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs` | Leading git options that a read-only command can carry |
| `EXEC_CAPABLE` | 7 command names | `crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs` | Commands whose words must all be static |
| `GIT_WRITE_SUBCOMMANDS` | 17 subcommands | `crates/ostra-policy/src/bash.rs` | Git subcommands that count as working tree writes |
| `KNOWN_TOOLS` | 29 tool names | `crates/ostra-policy/src/perms.rs` | Tool names that a permission rule can use |
