sections.title: Sandbox
sections.summary: How the kernel bounds agent commands: the profile, backend, and OS layers, bubblewrap and Seatbelt, the egress proxy, decoy files, git protection, the build cache, the settings, and the limits of the guarantee.
sections.body:
## The problem and the three layers

The policy layer judges each tool call by the paths that the call names. A shell command can hide a path, so the policy cannot bound a process after the process starts. The sandbox is the layer that the kernel enforces under the policy. This page explains the crate `ostra-sandbox`. It stops before the policy rules, which the [Policy engine](policy-engine.md) page owns.

The sandbox wraps three kinds of process:

- The commands of a native execution, which run through the Bash tool. See [Native executor loop](native-executor.md).
- A harness CLI and every command that the CLI starts. See [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).
- A program that Ostra starts for a project or workspace: a format command, a language server, a code provider, or a stdio MCP server. The [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) page owns the language servers and the code provider.

Without the sandbox, each of these processes runs with the full rights of the user. With the sandbox, the kernel enforces four rules:

- The host is read-only.
- Only the roots of the execution are writable.
- The data of Ostra and the credentials of the user are not reachable.
- The network leads out only through the egress proxy.

The crate has three layers. The layers keep each OS difference in one place.

| Layer | Files | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Profile` | `profile.rs` | Describes the boundary of one execution without naming a backend: mounts, environment, egress policy, and decoys. |
| `Backend` | `backend.rs`, `bwrap.rs`, `seatbelt.rs` | Renders a profile into a command. The code compiles on every OS, so tests check its output anywhere. |
| `sys` | `sys/` | Calls the kernel. Each OS implements the `Os` trait once, and `sys/mod.rs` chooses the implementation. |

Code outside a backend never matches on the backend to choose a behavior. It calls `Backend::enforcer`, so the quirks of a backend stay in the file of that backend.

### Diagram: from an execution to a sandboxed command

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["ExecContext and SandboxConfig"] --> B["Profile::for_execution or Profile::for_program"]
    B --> C["Profile::command calls Enforcer::wrap"]
    C --> D["Linux: bwrap runs ostra sandbox-init"]
    C --> E["macOS: sandbox-exec -p policy"]
    D --> F["The command runs inside the boundary"]
    E --> F
```

Windows and every other OS have no backend. The file `sys/other.rs` refuses each request, and the probe tells the user to run Ostra in WSL 2 or in Docker.

## Modes and the decision to sandbox

The sandbox mode decides what an execution does when a sandbox is or is not available. The function `decide` in `backend.rs` applies the mode. The enum `SandboxMode` has three values.

| Mode | A backend works | No backend works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `off` | Runs without a sandbox, with no warning. | Runs without a sandbox, with no warning. |
| `auto` | Runs in the sandbox. | Runs without a sandbox and warns. |
| `required` | Runs in the sandbox. | Refuses to start the execution and returns an error. |

The default mode is `required` on Linux and macOS. The default is `auto` on Windows. Windows has no backend, so mode `required` refuses every execution there.

```rust
pub fn decide(cfg: &SandboxConfig) -> Result<Decision, String> {
    match (cfg.mode, backend()) {
        (SandboxMode::Off, _) => Ok(Decision::Unsandboxed(None)),
        (_, Some(b)) => Ok(Decision::Sandboxed(b.clone())),
        (SandboxMode::Auto, None) => Ok(Decision::Unsandboxed(Some(unavailable_message()))),
        (SandboxMode::Required, None) => Err(format!(
            "The sandbox is required by the workspace settings or by `[sandbox] mode` in config.toml, but it is not available. {}",
            unavailable_message()
        )),
    }
}
```

The probe runs one time for each process. The static `PROBE` in `backend.rs` stores its result. Thus a user who installs `bwrap` after the server starts must restart the server. The function `unavailable_message` joins the reason of the probe with a fix. The fix is the constant `UNAVAILABLE` of the `Os` trait, which each OS defines in its own `sys` file:

| OS | What `UNAVAILABLE` tells the user |
| --- | --- |
| Linux (`sys/linux/mod.rs`) | Install bubblewrap (the `bwrap` command), or allow unprivileged user namespaces. |
| macOS (`sys/macos/mod.rs`) | Run Ostra outside any other sandbox, because macOS cannot nest them. |
| Windows (`sys/other.rs`) | Run Ostra inside WSL 2 or in Docker, because Ostra has no Windows sandbox yet. |
| Other OS (`sys/other.rs`) | Run Ostra on Linux or macOS. |

Each text also says that agent commands otherwise run with the full rights of the user. Each text ends with the way to choose mode `off` on purpose.

### How a workspace changes the mode

A workspace can replace the global mode and the global network choice. The method `SandboxConfig::for_workspace` in `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs` merges the two levels. A workspace adds its allowed hosts to the global list. A workspace never removes a global host or a built-in host. Ostra keeps the workspace values in the machine registry and never in `workspace.toml` (Rule A2). The [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) page explains why a folder file cannot set them.

### What the user sees

The function `status` in `status.rs` builds a `SandboxStatus` for the setup check and the console. The fields are:

- `mode` and `default_mode`.
- `available`, `backend`, and `active`.
- `message`, which holds the warning or the error.
- `gaps`, which names what the backend cannot enforce on this machine.
- `decoys`, `builtin_decoys`, and `builtin_hosts`.

At server start, `build` in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` checks the global `[sandbox]` table. An invalid value stops the server with the path of the value and a correction. After the check, the server reports the result in one of three ways:

- **A sandbox is active.** The server logs the backend name. If `gaps` is set, it also logs a warning with the gaps.
- **`sandbox.message` is `Some`.** This happens under mode `auto` or `required` when no backend works. The server logs a warning and prints a `WARNING` block on stderr. The block is there because mode `auto` still starts the server, and a log line is easy to miss.
- **The mode is `off`.** `decide` returns `Unsandboxed(None)`, so `message` is `None` and `active` is false. The server only calls `tracing::warn!` that the sandbox is off. It prints no block on stderr.

### What happens when

- **The mode is `required` and no backend works.** The execution does not start. The error holds the probe reason and the fix.
- **The mode is `auto` and no backend works.** The execution runs without a sandbox. A harness execution emits a `Status` delta that says the CLI runs without a sandbox. The function `first_warning` makes the log warning appear one time for each process (the static `WARNED`).
- **A setting changes while the server runs.** The next execution reads the new value. An execution that already runs keeps its boundary.
- **Ostra runs inside another sandbox on macOS.** The probe fails, because macOS cannot nest sandboxes.
- **Ostra runs in a container on Linux.** The probe fails when the default seccomp or AppArmor profile of the container blocks user namespaces. The message tells the user to allow them.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sandbox.mode` | `required` on Linux and macOS, `auto` on Windows | `[sandbox]` table of the global `config.toml` | At the next execution | `SandboxStatus` in the setup check and the console, and the server log | Set `"off"` to run without a sandbox on purpose. Set `"auto"` to allow a run without one, with a warning. |
| `sandbox_mode` | Not set, so the global value applies | Workspace settings, in the machine registry | At the next execution | `SandboxStatus` in the setup check and the console | Choose `Use the global setting` in the workspace settings to remove the override. |

## What a profile contains

The function `Profile::for_execution` in `profile.rs` builds the boundary of one agent execution. Each rule below gives a path one of four kinds: writable, read-only, hidden, or unchanged. A path that no rule names stays readable and read-only, because the base layer binds the whole host read-only.

### Writable paths

- The workspace root, the repo root, the session root, and the session dir of the execution.
- The `.git` dir of each repo. Ostra binds it onto itself, so no command can rename it away.
- The tool caches of the sandbox. See [the build cache](#build-cache-and-tool-caches).
- Each path in the extra writable list.
- A scratch dir that the sandbox mounts at `/tmp`. The function `new_scratch` makes it with owner-only rights.

### Read-only paths inside the writable ones

- The state files of Ostra: the session state dir, `workspace.toml`, the workspace database files (the main file and its `-wal`, `-shm`, and `-journal` files), the memory database files, the artifacts dir, and the books dir.
- The paths in `ctx.protected_paths`.
- The git paths that choose programs. See [Git protection](#git-protection).
- The files in the home folder that run code in later shells, logins, or builds. The constant `PERSISTENCE_IN_HOME` lists them. It holds shell start files such as `.bashrc` and `.zshrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.npmrc`, `.local/bin/`, `.cargo/bin/`, `.cargo/config.toml`, the autostart and systemd dirs, the macOS `Library/LaunchAgents/` dir, and the Windows startup dir. A trailing `/` in an entry marks a dir. The reason: an agent must not leave a program behind that runs when the user starts a shell.

Workspace artifacts and books are read-only for agents (Rules W1 and B5). An agent reads them and never writes them.

### Hidden paths

- The data dir of Ostra and the config dir of Ostra. When `OSTRA_CONFIG` places the config file in a shared dir, only the file is hidden.
- The sessions dir of the workspace, and the `harness` dir of the session, which holds the bridge tokens of other executions.
- `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, or `/run/user/<uid>` when the variable is not set. This dir holds the session bus.
- The file that `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` names, and the file that `XAUTHORITY` names. The [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md) page explains the master key.
- Each entry of `HOME_CREDENTIALS` in `crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`, except the sign-in file of the harness that runs. A harness keeps only its own sign-in file. The [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) page lists the data paths, the runtime folders, and the environment variables.
- Each path in the extra hidden list.
- The container engine sockets in `DOCKER_SOCKETS`. Whoever reaches a Docker socket can start a container that mounts the host, and a read-only file does not stop `connect`.

One exception exists. The `assets` dir inside the hidden data dir is revealed read-only, because agents read skills and references from it.

### Environment

The profile sets `TMPDIR=/tmp` and the cache variables. It removes each variable in `UNSET_VARS`: `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`, `DISPLAY`, `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, `XAUTHORITY`, `DOCKER_HOST`, and `GPG_AGENT_INFO`. These variables point a command at the desktop session, an agent, or a daemon socket.

### How the rules combine

The method `Profile::ordered` sorts every rule by path depth. A deeper rule overrides a shallower rule. When two rules name the same path, the more restrictive rule stays. The order of restriction is: home tmpfs, home entry, writable, read-only, hidden, link. Both backends use the same order, so the result is the same on Linux and macOS.

A read-only rule for a missing path needs a placeholder. Under bubblewrap, `placeholder` creates an empty file or dir, but only where the nearest mounted parent is a writable host dir. A `.json` placeholder holds `{}`. The placeholder stops an agent from creating the file. Ostra drops a read-only bind whose nearest parent is hidden, because the bind exposes the hidden parent again.

### Programs that Ostra starts

The function `Profile::for_program` builds the same boundary for a project program, with the given roots writable. The function `host_command` in `host.rs` wraps the program:

1. It reads the global config fresh and merges the workspace sandbox settings.
2. It removes the credential variables that Ostra holds and every variable that starts with `OSTRA_`.
3. It adds the git settings of `agent_env`, so a planted `.git/config` cannot start a program.
4. It calls `decide`. When no sandbox applies, it returns the program unchanged, with the environment changes from steps 2 and 3.
5. It finds the program in the folder or on `PATH` before it starts the sandbox, so a missing program reads as missing.

The struct `HostCommand` holds the result. Its `members` field kills what the program leaves running when the holder drops it.

### What happens when

- **A path is not UTF-8, or has a control character, and the backend is Seatbelt.** The wrap returns an error, because a path that ends its string early can rewrite the policy.
- **A listed path does not exist.** The profile skips a hidden or writable path that is missing. A read-only path gets a placeholder or a literal rule.
- **The mode is `off` for a program.** The program still runs without the credential variables and with the safe git settings.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sandbox.extra_writable` | Empty list | `[sandbox]` table of the global `config.toml` | At the next execution | The server refuses to start with an invalid entry | Remove the entry. |
| `sandbox.extra_hidden` | Empty list | `[sandbox]` table of the global `config.toml` | At the next execution | The server refuses to start with an invalid entry | Remove the entry. |

Each entry must be an absolute path or start with `~/`, and must hold no NUL byte. The meaning of a relative path depends on where an execution starts. Ostra checks this at server start with `validate::global`.

## Linux backend: bubblewrap, helper, and seccomp

On Linux, the `Bubblewrap` backend renders a profile as arguments for the `bwrap` binary. Each sandbox gets its own mount, pid, IPC, and network namespace. A helper, `ostra sandbox-init`, starts first inside the sandbox. The helper joins the loopback of the namespace to the sockets of Ostra and loads the seccomp filter. The [Ostra overview and first run](overview.md) page explains how the `ostra` command starts the server.

### The probe

The probe in `sys/linux/mod.rs` has two steps. First it looks for `bwrap` on `PATH`. Then it finds the helper binary with `helper()` and runs a trial sandbox: `--unshare-pid --unshare-net` with `sandbox-init --proxy /dev/null -- true`. The trial also proves that the helper can bind the loopback of a new network namespace.

The static `HELPER` in `bwrap.rs` is a `OnceLock<PathBuf>`. It holds the `ostra` binary that `set_helper` named at start. Only the first call of `set_helper` has an effect. If no name is set, `helper()` uses an `ostra` next to the running program or one dir above it. The second location finds `target/debug/ostra` from a test binary.

### The bwrap arguments

The function `Profile::args_with` in `bwrap.rs` writes the arguments in this order:

1. `--ro-bind / /`, `--dev /dev`, and `--proc /proc`.
2. `/tmp` as a bind of the scratch dir, or as an empty tmpfs when no scratch dir exists.
3. Each mount, sorted by depth. A hidden dir becomes a tmpfs. A hidden file becomes a read-only bind of `/dev/null`.
4. A read-only bind of each decoy file.
5. `--unsetenv` for each variable in `UNSET_VARS`, and `--setenv` for the profile environment.
6. `--unshare-pid` and `--unshare-ipc`.
7. `--unshare-net` when the network choice is not `host`, and a bind of each socket that leads out.
8. `--die-with-parent`, and `--new-session` when the profile asks for it.
9. `--chdir`, and a bind of each single writable file.

The `--new-session` option calls `setsid`, which blocks `TIOCSTI` input injection into the terminal that started Ostra. A PTY program turns it off, because the program needs its PTY as the controlling terminal.

A mount point cannot be renamed, but the dirs above it can. For example, the command `mv repo r && git init repo` leaves the protected `.git` under another name. Thus `Profile::plan` binds each dir between a writable bind and a mount inside it onto itself. This pins the dirs.

### The helper

The helper takes `[--proxy <socket>] [--forward <port>=<socket>]... -- <program> [args...]`. It uses std threads and no async runtime. It runs these steps:

1. It listens on `127.0.0.1:<port>` for each `--forward`, and on `[::1]` when the namespace has IPv6. Fixed ports come first, so the free port of the proxy cannot take one of them.
2. For `--proxy`, it listens on a free port of `127.0.0.1` and sets the proxy variables (`HTTP_PROXY` and the others) to that port.
3. It installs the seccomp filter when it has one thread, because a filter covers the calling thread and what it starts later.
4. It starts a thread for each listener. Each thread splices a connection to the Unix socket, with at most 256 open connections for each listener.
5. It starts the command, ignores the terminal signals (`SIGINT`, `SIGQUIT`, `SIGTERM`, `SIGHUP`, `SIGTSTP`, `SIGTTIN`, `SIGTTOU`), and waits.
6. It exits with the status of the command. If a signal ended the command, the helper raises the same signal and returns `128 + signal`.

The constant `FAILED` (125) is the exit status of a helper that cannot start the command. The programs `env` and `timeout` use the same value.

### The seccomp filter

The filter in `sys/linux/seccomp.rs` exists for `x86_64` and `aarch64` only. Inherited filters apply to every process that the command starts. Refusals return an error, so programs that probe for a feature fall back and do not die.

The filter starts with an architecture check. It loads the `arch` field of `seccomp_data`, which sits at `ARCH_OFFSET` (4). It compares the value with `ARCH`, the audit value of the CPU: `0xC000_003E` on `x86_64` and `0xC000_00B7` on `aarch64`. A different value kills the process. The syscall number sits at offset 0 (`NR`), and argument `i` has its low 32 bits at `16 + 8 * i`.

| Action | Calls |
| --- | --- |
| Kill the process | A call that comes from another architecture, such as 32-bit x86 on `x86_64`, because the numbers differ. |
| `ENOSYS` | A call with the `X32_SYSCALL_BIT` (`0x4000_0000`) set on `x86_64`, because x32 numbers reach the same calls under other numbers. |
| `EPERM` (`REFUSED`) | `bpf`, `userfaultfd`, `perf_event_open`, `keyctl`, `add_key`, `request_key`, `kexec_load`, `kexec_file_load`, `init_module`, `finit_module`, `delete_module`, `open_by_handle_at`. |
| `ENOSYS` (`MISSING`) | `clone3`, `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter`, `io_uring_register`. |
| `EPERM` for flags | `unshare` or `clone` with `CLONE_NEWUSER` in the first argument. |
| `EPERM` for terminal requests (`TTY_REFUSED`) | `ioctl` with `TIOCSTI` or `TIOCLINUX`, compared on the low 32 bits. |

The reasons come from the comments in the code. A new user namespace gives the command capabilities over fresh namespaces and mounts. The `ENOSYS` calls make libc and libuv fall back to older calls. The filter cannot read the flags of `clone3`, because they sit in memory. Thus glibc falls back to `clone`, whose flags the filter can read.

```rust
fn refuse_flags(p: &mut Vec<sock_filter>, call: libc::c_long, arg: u32, flags: u32) {
    p.push(jump(BPF_JMP | BPF_JEQ | BPF_K, call as u32, 0, 4));
    p.push(stmt(BPF_LD | BPF_W | BPF_ABS, arg_low(arg)));
    p.push(jump(BPF_JMP | BPF_JSET | BPF_K, flags, 0, 1));
    p.push(ret(errno(EPERM)));
    p.push(ret(SECCOMP_RET_ALLOW));
}
```

### What happens when

- **The CPU is not `x86_64` or `aarch64`.** No filter loads. The function `known_gaps` reports that agent commands can create user namespaces, and the server logs the gap.
- **`bwrap` is missing or cannot create a namespace.** The probe fails and the mode decides the result. See [the modes](#modes-and-the-decision-to-sandbox).
- **The helper binary is missing.** The wrap returns `The sandbox helper (the ostra binary) is missing.`
- **The socket path is too long.** The bind fails with a message that tells the user to keep the data dir path short, because a socket path has a limit of 107 bytes.
- **The host process dies.** `--die-with-parent` and the pid namespace end every process of the sandbox.

## macOS backend: Seatbelt and loopback rules

On macOS, the `Seatbelt` backend renders a profile as an SBPL policy for `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`. Seatbelt has no mount namespace. It only allows or denies the paths where they are. This causes five differences from bubblewrap.

| Topic | Bubblewrap | Seatbelt |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A hidden path | Looks empty. | Returns `EPERM`. |
| `/tmp` | Private, mounted from the scratch dir. | Denied. `TMPDIR` names the scratch dir, or the `tmp` dir of the cache when no scratch dir exists. `TMPPREFIX` is set for zsh. |
| Home folder of a harness | Overlaid with a tmpfs. | No overlay. The rest of the home stays read-only. |
| Loopback | One for each sandbox. | Shared with the host. The policy names the ports that the command can reach. |
| Process tracking | The pid namespace. | Mach service names. See below. |

### The probe

The constant `SANDBOX_EXEC` is `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`. Ostra calls it by absolute path, because the Homebrew prefix on `PATH` is writable by the user. The probe requires that the file is owned by root and that no other user can write it. Then it runs a trial policy, `(version 1)(allow default)`. If the trial fails with `sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted`, Ostra runs inside another sandbox and the message says so.

### The policy

The method `Profile::seatbelt` builds the policy in this order:

1. `SEATBELT_BASE`. It denies by default and allows what git, cargo, npm, go, pip, clang, and the four harness CLIs need. Those tools were measured. The keychain, the pasteboard, LaunchServices, Apple Events, the window server, and TCC stay denied, because each reaches something outside the sandbox. Terminals are denied, so a command cannot read from, write to, or inject input into another terminal.
2. An allow for two mach service names that no daemon registers. They mark the processes of the invocation.
3. A deny for `/private/tmp`, `/private/var/tmp`, and the user temp dir.
4. One rule for each mount, in the order of `Profile::ordered`. Seatbelt applies the last matching rule, so a deeper path overrides a shallower path.
5. A `file-read-metadata` allow for each dir above an allowed path, because reaching a path needs `stat` on each dir above it.
6. The terminal rule for a PTY program. The constant `TTY_PARAM` is `"TTY"`. It names the `sandbox-exec -D` parameter that holds the terminal device. The launcher passes `-D TTY=<path>` after it opens the PTY, and the policy allows `/dev/tty` and `(param TTY)` for read, write, and ioctl.
7. The network rules, which the next part describes.
8. The decoy rules. See [Decoy credential files](#decoy-credential-files).
9. A `file-write-unlink` deny for each writable dir above a protected path. This pins the dirs, so `mv .git .g` cannot carry `.git/config` away from its rule.

Seatbelt closes the read of the arguments and the startup environment of other processes. A process can read them with `sysctl(KERN_PROCARGS2)` when either `sysctl-read` covers `kern.procargs2` or `process-info-pidinfo` allows it. The base policy lists the allowed sysctls and denies `process-info*` before the same-sandbox allow. The function `scrub_startup_env` closes the same hole for Ostra itself. It moves the environment of the server off the stack and zeroes the original strings. Call it first in `main`, before any thread starts. Without this step, unsandboxed programs of the same user, such as agent commands under mode `off`, can read that environment.

### Loopback rules

Every Seatbelt sandbox shares the loopback of the host. When the network choice is not `host`, the policy controls the loopback with these rules, in this order:

1. `SEATBELT_LOOPBACK_LISTEN`: a command can listen on loopback, for dev servers and tests. The policy has no DNS resolver rule. The proxy resolves names, and a lookup can carry data out inside the name. The name `localhost` still resolves from `/etc/hosts`.
2. When the loopback choice is `open` and the network is `allowlist` or `public`, the command can connect to every port.
3. The command can connect to each loopback port from the allowed hosts list, for example `localhost:8317`.
4. The command can never connect to a blocked port, or to the port of the Ostra server. The server calls `set_server_port` at start and stores the port in `SERVER_PORT`. The reason: that port serves the API of the console.
5. The command can connect to the ports of its own proxy and forwards. These rules come last, so they win.

Under the `host` network, `Profile::seatbelt` takes the other branch. It replaces rules 1 to 5 with `SEATBELT_HOST_NETWORK`, which carries its own loopback listen rules. The constant allows all outbound IP, a listener on loopback, and the socket of the DNS resolver (`/private/var/run/mDNSResponder`). Other Unix sockets stay denied: the SSH agent, Docker, password managers, and IDEs.

On Linux the loopback choice changes nothing, because each sandbox has its own loopback. A blocked port on Linux only removes the port from the list of forwarded loopback ports.

### Process tracking with mach names

Seatbelt has no pid namespace and no `--die-with-parent`. A child that calls `setsid` or forks twice can outlive its shell. The struct `Members` in `members.rs` solves this. The policy of each invocation allows two mach names. One name is unique to the invocation. The other name (`dev.ostra.sandbox.d<hash of the data dir>`) is shared by every sandbox of the data dir. The kernel can tell, for any process, whether its policy allows a name (`sandbox_check`). A policy is inherited and cannot be dropped, so the name finds each descendant. Some system sandboxes allow every name. Thus a member must also be refused the `CANARY` name, `dev.ostra.sandbox.canary`.

The function `marked` in `sys/macos/mod.rs` calls `sandbox_check` with three numeric constants:

| Constant | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FILTER_NONE` | `0` | The filter type for a check with no filter. With `NO_REPORT`, it asks whether a process runs in any sandbox. |
| `FILTER_GLOBAL_NAME` | `2` | The filter type for a global mach name. With the operation `mach-lookup`, it asks whether a policy allows one name. |
| `NO_REPORT` | `0x4000_0000` | A flag that Ostra adds to the filter. It asks the kernel not to log the check as a refusal. |

The function keeps a process when it belongs to the user, runs in a sandbox, allows the marker name, and does not allow `CANARY`.

- `Members::kill` sends SIGKILL to each process with the own name, in up to 20 rounds with a 10 ms pause. The `Drop` of `Members` calls it.
- `kill_leftovers` does the same for the shared name. The server calls it at start, when no other server of the data dir runs. A restarted server thus finds the processes that an earlier server left.

### What happens when

- **Another sandbox already contains Ostra.** The probe fails and the mode decides.
- **A path is not valid UTF-8.** `sbpl_str` returns an error and the command does not start.
- **The workspace blocks a port.** No command of the workspace connects to that port.
- **The network choice is `none`.** The loopback `open` choice has no effect, because `none` reaches nothing. The proxy and forward ports of the invocation still work.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sandbox_loopback` | `open` | Workspace settings, in the machine registry | At the next execution | The workspace settings screen. It has no effect on Linux. | Set `listed` to allow only the loopback ports in the allowed hosts list. |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` | Empty list | Workspace settings, in the machine registry | At the next execution | The workspace settings screen | Remove a port from the list to allow it again. |

Each blocked port must be from 1 to 65535, and the list holds at most 64 ports (`MAX_BLOCKED_PORTS`). Each port is a rule in every sandbox policy. The save of the workspace settings refuses a list that breaks these rules.

## Network choices

The network choice decides what a sandboxed command can reach. Every choice except `host` gives the sandbox its own network namespace on Linux. In that namespace, loopback, the LAN, and the services of the host are out of reach. Traffic leaves only through the egress proxy. The default is `allowlist`.

| Choice | What the command reaches |
| --- | --- |
| `none` | Nothing. A harness CLI still reaches the model API and sign-in hosts of its own harness, and the hosts of its base URLs. |
| `allowlist` | The built-in package and source hosts, the model hosts of all four harnesses, and the allowed hosts. |
| `public` | Any public address, and the allowed hosts. Loopback, private, and link-local addresses stay refused. |
| `host` | The host network as it is, without a filter. This includes local services, the LAN, and the cloud metadata address. |

The allowed hosts list applies under `allowlist` and `public` only. Under `none`, a listed host is refused. Under `host`, no proxy runs and no filter applies.

### What happens when

- **The choice is `host`.** Bubblewrap does not call `--unshare-net`. The sandbox shares the network of the host.
- **The choice is `none` and a harness runs.** The harness adds its own model hosts and base URL hosts through `Profile::allow_hosts`. The proxy starts because it has somewhere to go.
- **The choice is `none` and a native command runs.** No proxy starts, and the namespace has no route out.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sandbox.network` | `allowlist` | `[sandbox]` table of the global `config.toml` | At the next execution | The Activity view shows each proxy decision. The setup check shows `builtin_hosts`. | Set `"none"` for the strictest choice. Set `"host"` to remove the filter. |
| `sandbox_network` | Not set, so the global value applies | Workspace settings, in the machine registry | At the next execution | The Activity view and the setup check | Choose the global setting in the workspace settings to remove the override. |

## Egress proxy: host rules and request handling

The egress proxy in `egress.rs` is the only way out of a private network. It sees the destination host and port of every connection. It lets through only what the policy allows. It connects to the address that it checked and never makes a second lookup.

### Where the proxy listens

- **Linux.** Each execution gets its own Unix socket in `<data dir>/egress`. The dir has mode 0700, and the data dir is hidden from every sandbox. The sandbox binds only its own socket. The helper listens on a loopback port inside the sandbox and splices each connection to that socket.
- **macOS.** Each execution gets its own port on `127.0.0.1`. The Seatbelt policy names this one port. Every request must carry a credential, because a sandbox whose workspace opens the loopback can reach the proxy ports of other executions. The proxy URL is `http://ostra:<credential>@127.0.0.1:<port>`. The user name is `PROXY_USER` and the password is a random UUID. The proxy compares the `Proxy-Authorization` value in constant time. Without a valid value, it answers `407` with a `Proxy-Authenticate` header. The reason for the challenge: git sends the credential only after it.

All proxies run on one shared Tokio runtime with two worker threads, named `ostra-egress`. When a `Listener` drops, it stops, ends its open connections, and removes its socket file. The server removes stale socket files at start with `remove_stale_sockets`, but only when no other server of the data dir runs.

The function `proxy_env` points the HTTP clients of a command at the proxy. It sets `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `ALL_PROXY` in upper case and lower case. It sets `NO_PROXY` to `localhost,127.0.0.1,::1`, and `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`. Loopback goes direct, so a loopback host in the allowed list works only as a forwarded port.

### Host rules

The struct `HostRule` parses one entry of the allowed hosts list. The accepted forms are `host`, `*.domain`, an IPv4 address, and `[v6]`. Each form takes an optional `:port`.

- Without a port, a rule allows ports 443 and 80.
- `*.domain` matches every name below `domain` and does not match `domain` itself.
- The parser rejects an entry that is empty, or has whitespace, `/`, `@`, `?`, or `#`. The proxy matches hosts and not URLs.
- A name has at most 253 characters. Each label has at most 63 characters, and holds letters, digits, `-`, and `_`.
- A rule for `localhost` or a loopback address must have a port. Clients skip the proxy for loopback, so the sandbox forwards only the ports that the user lists.
- An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address becomes the IPv4 address that it carries.

### Built-in hosts

The constant `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` holds 26 package registries and source hosts. Builds fetch from them under `allowlist`:

- Rust: `index.crates.io`, `static.crates.io`, `static.rust-lang.org`, `crates.io`.
- JavaScript: `registry.npmjs.org`, `registry.yarnpkg.com`, `repo.yarnpkg.com`.
- Python: `pypi.org`, `files.pythonhosted.org`.
- Go: `proxy.golang.org`, `sum.golang.org`.
- Source hosts: `github.com`, `codeload.github.com`, `objects.githubusercontent.com`, `raw.githubusercontent.com`, `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`.
- JVM and Android: `repo.maven.apache.org`, `repo1.maven.org`, `services.gradle.org`, `plugins.gradle.org`, `plugins-artifacts.gradle.org`, `dl.google.com`, `maven.google.com`.
- Ruby and .NET: `rubygems.org`, `index.rubygems.org`, `api.nuget.org`.

The function `model_hosts` lists the model API and sign-in hosts of each harness. A measured run of each CLI produced the lists.

| Harness | Hosts |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `api.anthropic.com`, `console.anthropic.com`, `platform.claude.com`, `claude.ai` |
| Codex | `api.openai.com`, `chatgpt.com`, `auth.openai.com` |
| Grok Build | `api.x.ai`, `auth.x.ai`, `accounts.x.ai`, `grok.com`, `cli-chat-proxy.grok.com` |
| Antigravity | `cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`, `daily-cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`, `generativelanguage.googleapis.com`, `oauth2.googleapis.com`, `www.googleapis.com`, `lh3.googleusercontent.com` |

A harness gets its own hosts under every network choice. The `allowlist` choice lets every command reach all of them, so a build or a test can call a model API.

### Trusted and built-in hosts

The struct `Policy` splits hosts into two groups, and the group decides how the proxy checks the address:

- **Trusted hosts.** The user chose them: the allowed hosts and the base URLs that a harness launch passes. They can resolve to any address, for example an internal mirror.
- **Built-in hosts.** The defaults and the model hosts. They must resolve to public addresses. Thus a DNS answer that points a built-in name at a private address does not reach the LAN.

Under `public`, every host that is not trusted gets the public-only check.

### How the proxy handles a request

The proxy accepts two request forms: `CONNECT host:port` for HTTPS, and an absolute `http://` URL for plain HTTP. It speaks HTTP/1.1 only. For plain HTTP, it rewrites the head to origin form, adds `Connection: close`, and removes `Proxy-*` headers and the old `Host`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` headers. It refuses folded header lines.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Request head arrives"] --> B{"Credential valid? Checked on macOS only"}
    B -- no --> R1["407 Proxy Authentication Required"]
    B -- yes --> C{"Head parses?"}
    C -- no --> R2["400 Bad Request"]
    C -- yes --> D{"Host and port allowed?"}
    D -- no --> R3["403 Forbidden with the reason"]
    D -- yes --> E{"Address public, or host trusted?"}
    E -- no --> R3
    E -- yes --> F["Connect directly or through the upstream proxy"]
    F -- fails --> R4["502 Bad Gateway"]
    F -- connects --> G{"CONNECT to a name: TLS server name equals host?"}
    G -- no --> R5["Close the tunnel and record a refusal"]
    G -- yes --> H["Copy bytes in both directions"]
```

The `resolve` method of `Policy` applies the address rules:

- A name that is local-only is refused without a lookup when the host is not trusted. Local-only names are `localhost`, names with no dot, and names that end in `.localhost`, `.local`, `.internal`, `.lan`, or `.home.arpa`. The reason: a lookup for these names goes out on the LAN, and on macOS a `.local` lookup uses multicast DNS and takes seconds to fail.
- A built-in or `public` host must resolve to at least one public address. The proxy connects only to the public addresses.
- The function `is_private` treats these as private: loopback, private ranges, link-local (the cloud metadata address included), CGNAT, unique-local, multicast, and reserved ranges. It also unwraps IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, and NAT64 forms of IPv6.

After a successful `CONNECT` to a host name, the proxy reads the TLS ClientHello and compares the server name (SNI) with the host. The reason: a CDN that routes by SNI can carry the tunnel to any site that it serves. These rules apply:

- A different server name closes the tunnel and records a refusal.
- A ClientHello that the proxy cannot read, or that is larger than `MAX_HELLO` (32 KiB), counts as invalid and closes the tunnel.
- A client that sends no TLS passes. The destination can speak first, for example an SSH banner.
- An IP address as the host skips the check.

### The upstream proxy

A machine that reaches the internet only through a corporate proxy sets an upstream proxy. The proxy must have the form `http://host:port`, with no path and no credentials. The egress proxy uses plain HTTP `CONNECT` to talk to it. The route depends on the destination:

- A trusted host on a private address connects directly, because an internal mirror is rarely behind the corporate proxy.
- Every other allowed destination goes through the upstream proxy. This includes names that do not resolve on this machine.
- A name that is local-only and not trusted never goes upstream, because that route reaches the network of the upstream proxy without a check.

The function `handle` in `egress.rs` reports an allowed `Decision` for the host before it uses the route. When `via_upstream` fails, the proxy adds no refusal and no second entry. The `502` text appears only in the output of the client command.

### What the proxy reports

The proxy reports a `Decision` for the first allowed connection and the first refusal of each host and port. A retry loop thus reports one time. The callback `OnDecision` runs on the proxy runtime and must not block. The function `report::egress` forwards each decision from a thread of its own as an `ExecutionDelta::Egress`. A refusal of a local destination (loopback, private, or link-local) also counts as a containment signal. The [Policy engine](policy-engine.md) page owns the pause after 3 signals. A refusal of a public host shows in the Activity view only, because builds call telemetry hosts.

Each refusal reason starts with the fix and names the setting. For example, a refused host gets the text `Add <host> to [sandbox] allowed_hosts in config.toml, or set [sandbox] network = "public"`. Under `none`, the text tells the user to choose `allowlist` first.

### What happens when

- **The head is longer than `MAX_HEAD` (8 KiB), or does not end in 30 seconds (`HEAD_TIMEOUT`).** The proxy answers `400` for a long head, and closes the connection after the timeout.
- **No address connects in 10 seconds (`CONNECT_TIMEOUT`).** The proxy tries each address in turn, then answers `502`. The Activity view already lists the host as allowed, because `handle` reports it before the connect.
- **More than 256 connections (`MAX_CONNECTIONS`) are open on one listener.** The proxy drops the new connection.
- **The accept call fails.** The proxy waits 50 ms before it tries again, because the cause is most often a lack of file descriptors.
- **The upstream proxy does not answer, or answers a status other than `200`.** The proxy answers `502` with the status. `handle` has already reported an allowed `Decision` for the host. When `via_upstream` fails, the proxy adds no refusal and no second entry. The `502` text appears only in the output of the client command.
- **A command is wrapped without a profile proxy.** The backend starts its own proxy, and decisions go to the log only.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sandbox.allowed_hosts` | Empty list | `[sandbox]` table of the global `config.toml` | At the next execution | The Activity view shows each allowed and refused host. | Remove the entry. |
| `sandbox_allowed_hosts` | Empty list | Workspace settings, in the machine registry | At the next execution | The Activity view, and the setup check for the built-in list | Remove the entry. A workspace cannot remove a global or built-in host. |
| `sandbox.upstream_proxy` | Not set | `[sandbox]` table of the global `config.toml` | At the next execution | The `502` text appears only in the output of the failed client command. The Activity view lists the host as allowed, because `handle` reports it before it uses the route. No refusal and no second entry follows. | Remove the value to connect directly. |

Each entry of the allowed lists must pass the host rule parser. A loopback entry needs a port, for example `127.0.0.1:8317`. The upstream proxy value must be `http://host:port`. The server refuses to start with an invalid global value, and the save of the workspace settings refuses an invalid workspace value.

## Decoy credential files

A decoy is a fake credential file at a path that an agent has no reason to read. When a process opens one, Ostra gets a containment signal (Rule P3). The kernel reports the open, so Ostra sees a Bash `cat` and a tool call in the same way. A decoy detects a read. It does not prevent the sandbox from showing the fake contents.

### The built-in decoys

The constant `HOME_DECOYS` lists four files under the home folder:

| Path | Kind | Fake content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `~/.ssh/id_rsa` | SSH key | An OpenSSH private key block of 5 lines, with 70 random base64 characters in each line. |
| `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` | SSH key | The same form. |
| `~/.git-credentials` | Git credentials | `https://git:<40 hex digits>@github.com`. |
| `~/.vault-token` | Vault token | `hvs.` and 24 random base64 characters. |

Two character tables in `decoy.rs` supply the random text. The constant `B64` holds the 64 base64 characters `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `+`, and `/`. The constant `HEX` holds the 16 characters `0123456789abcdef`. The function `contents` draws from `B64` for SSH keys and Vault tokens, and from `HEX` for git credentials and generic decoys.

Common tools do not open these files on their own. The exception is `ssh`, which reads its keys when it authenticates. Thus Ostra plants the SSH keys only where no SSH port is reachable. The function `Policy::reaches_port(22)` decides: it is true under `public` and `host`, and when a rule names port 22. In that case, `Profile::watch_decoys` filters the SSH key decoys out of the list. The file `~/.netrc` is not a decoy, because Python `requests` and Go module downloads read it on every fetch.

A workspace adds decoys. It cannot remove a built-in decoy. The function `wanted` returns the built-in list followed by the workspace entries. A workspace entry under `~/.ssh/` that starts with `id_` and does not end in `.pub` becomes an SSH key. Every other entry gets a generic content of 40 hex digits.

### Linux: a bound file and inotify

The function `Decoys::plant` writes each fake file into a private dir, `<data dir>/decoys/<16 hex digits>/<index>`. The backend binds each file read-only at its path in the sandbox. A decoy goes in one of two places. It goes where the tmpfs of a hidden dir can hold a new file. Or it goes over an existing file. Thus Ostra never writes to the real host path. A watcher on the host file uses inotify with `IN_OPEN`. The constant `HEAD` in `sys/linux/inotify.rs` is the size of the fixed `inotify_event` header. The reader uses it to split the bytes of one read into events.

- The watcher reports the first open of each decoy one time, with the path that the sandbox saw. Then it removes the watch.
- A `stat` or a directory listing is not an open.
- When the `Decoys` value drops, the watch ends first. Then the dir of fake files is removed.
- The server calls `remove_stale` at start to delete decoy dirs that an earlier server left.

### macOS: a refused read and the system log

Seatbelt cannot bind a file into the sandbox. A decoy is an existing file that the policy refuses to read. The rule is `(deny file-read-data (literal <path>) (with message <tag>))`, where the tag is `dev.ostra.decoy.` (`TAG_PREFIX`) and 16 random characters. Only `file-read-data` carries the message, so `stat` stays silent. A missing file raises no report, so only existing files become decoys.

Ostra reads the refusal from the system log with `log stream`. The predicate (`PREDICATE`) accepts only the kernel Sandbox extension, because any process can log text of its own. macOS shows the log to accounts in the `admin` group only. The constant `ADMIN_GID` in `sys/macos/log.rs` is `80`, the group ID of `admin`. The function `admin` checks the groups of the process for it.

- The server calls `watch_reports` at start. It waits up to 10 seconds until `log stream` is attached, so the first command of the first execution is watched. The static `READY` in `reader()` is a `OnceLock<bool>`. It stores the result of this start, so the reader starts one time for each process.
- If `log stream` exits, the reader starts it again after 1 second. If it exits before it attaches, the reader stops and decoys are not supported.
- When decoys are not supported, which is the case for a non-admin user, `Seatbelt::decoys` returns `Ok(None)` without a message. The execution runs without decoys.
- The warning `decoy files are not watched` appears only when `Decoys::refuse` returns an error, for example when the `log stream` reader fails to start. The server logs the warning and the execution runs without decoys.

### What happens when

- **A decoy path already holds a real file.** On Linux, the fake file covers it inside the sandbox only. The real file does not change.
- **A process opens a decoy.** Ostra emits an `ExecutionDelta::Decoy` through `report::decoys`. The signal counts toward the pause after 3 signals.
- **The user is not an admin on macOS.** `SandboxStatus.decoys` is false and no decoy is watched. The server logs no warning.
- **A workspace lists a sign-in file of a harness CLI.** The save refuses it, because a decoy there signs that CLI out in the sandbox.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sandbox_decoys` | Empty list | Workspace settings, in the machine registry | At the next execution | The Activity view shows a decoy open. `SandboxStatus.decoys` and `builtin_decoys` show the support and the built-in paths. | Remove the entry. A workspace cannot remove a built-in decoy. Decoys are absent in these cases: mode `off`, mode `auto` with no backend, a network choice that reaches port 22 (for the SSH key decoys), and on macOS a missing file or a non-admin user. |

Each entry must be a file path that starts with `~/`, with no empty, `.`, or `..` component, for example `~/.aws/credentials`. The list holds at most 32 entries (`MAX_WORKSPACE_DECOYS`), because each entry is a watch and a mount in every agent sandbox.

## Git protection

The `.git/config` file of a repository is writable by whoever controls the folder, an agent included. Git reads this file and starts the programs that it names: `core.fsmonitor`, `credential.helper`, hooks, and filter drivers. A program that an agent plants runs later on the host, outside the sandbox. Ostra has two defenses. One defense sets the profile read-only for the paths that choose programs. The other defense sets safe config for the git commands that Ostra runs.

### Read-only paths in each git dir

The constant `GIT_PROTECTED` in `git.rs` lists the paths: `config`, `config.worktree`, `hooks/`, and `info/`. The profile makes them read-only inside each repo. The method `Profile::protect_git` works in this way:

1. `git_repos` finds every work tree under the roots, at any depth. A work tree is a dir with a `.git` dir or a `.git` file.
2. A `.git` file becomes read-only, so it cannot name a planted git dir.
3. For a linked worktree, only `config.worktree` is protected. The main repo entry covers its other paths.
4. For other repos, each git dir (`git_dirs`) gets the protected paths. This includes each submodule git dir under `modules/`, up to 256 dirs, and `config.worktree` of each dir under `worktrees/`.
5. The dirs above these paths are pinned, so none of them can be renamed away.

The file `config.worktree` is read only with `extensions.worktreeConfig`, which `config` sets. Thus the empty placeholder that a missing file gets is harmless. The path `commondir` cannot be a placeholder, because git refuses to open a repository whose `commondir` is empty. The repair function covers it.

### Finding the repositories

The walk is breadth-first and bounded. It does not enter symlinks, `node_modules`, or a dir that holds a `CACHEDIR.TAG` file (Cargo tags `target/` with one). It stops after `GIT_WALK_DIRS` (20,000) dirs or `GIT_WALK_REPOS` (128) repos. When it stops, it logs a warning that repos below the stop point keep a writable `.git/config`. The caps bound the time of the walk and the number of mounts.

### Repair of a planted commondir

The function `repair_git_dirs` undoes what an agent can write inside `.git` to make git load the config of another repository. It runs these changes:

- It removes a `commondir` in the own git dir of a repository, because git never writes one there.
- It restores the `commondir` of a linked worktree to `../..` when it names something else.

The function returns the changed paths. The native executor, the harness executor, and the clone and pull code in the server call it. The runner calls it in the `CommandPurpose::Stage` arm of `perform_command`, so the staging command runs after the repair. The format command runs through `ostra_sandbox::host_command` and has no repair. For each changed path, the agent gets the text from `git_repair_note`: `Leave <path> to git: Ostra undid it, because a commondir makes git load another repository's config and run the programs it names.`

### Safe config for git commands that Ostra runs

The module `crates/ostra-core/src/git.rs` holds config overrides that switch off the programs that a repository config can name, for every git command that Ostra starts. The [Project files, Git dock, and cloning](project-files-and-git.md) page owns these overrides and the commands that use them.

### What happens when

- **A repo is deeper than the walk reaches.** Its `.git/config` stays writable and the log shows a warning.
- **A repo is added after the execution starts.** The profile does not protect it. The profile lists the repos when it is built.
- **An agent plants a `commondir`.** The next repair removes or restores it and tells the agent.

Git protection has no setting of its own. It applies whenever the sandbox applies.

## Build cache and tool caches

The sandbox gives agents their own tool caches, and the user caches stay read-only. The reason: builds on the host run what those caches hold, such as extracted crate sources, npm and pnpm stores, and Go build output. A writable shared cache lets one agent leave code for the next build of the user. A second reason concerns sessions. The downloads of one session must not feed the builds of a later session.

### Where the caches live

The base dir is `~/.cache/ostra/sandbox`. The environment variable `OSTRA_SANDBOX_CACHE` replaces it. Under the base dir:

- Agents in a session share one cache dir, `session-<session id>`, across all executions of that session. The function `session_cache` builds the path.
- An agent outside a session uses a dir that is keyed on the workspace root, or on the repo root when the workspace root is empty. The salt is `agents`.
- A program that Ostra starts uses a dir that is keyed on its first root, with an empty salt.

Only the runs outside a session and the programs use dirs keyed by path. The function `keyed_cache` builds those dirs.

The function `stable_hex` makes a key: 16 hex digits of SHA-256 over the salt, a NUL byte, and the path. Ostra does not use `DefaultHasher`, because its algorithm can change between Rust releases and move the names on disk.

The constant `CACHE_ENV` maps each tool variable to a sub dir of the cache:

| Variable | Sub dir |
| --- | --- |
| `CARGO_HOME` | `cargo` |
| `npm_config_cache` | `npm` |
| `npm_config_store_dir` | `pnpm-store` |
| `XDG_CACHE_HOME` | `xdg` |
| `GOMODCACHE` | `go-mod` |
| `GOCACHE` | `go-build` |
| `PIP_CACHE_DIR` | `pip` |
| `YARN_CACHE_FOLDER` | `yarn` |
| `UV_CACHE_DIR` | `uv` |
| `CLANG_MODULE_CACHE_PATH` | `clang-modules` |

macOS tools ignore `XDG_CACHE_HOME` and write under `~/Library/Caches`. That dir stays read-only for the same reason, so these tools get their own variables. The cache also has a private `tmp` sub dir. Under Seatbelt, `TMPDIR` points there when the profile has no scratch dir.

The constant `CARGO_SETTINGS` (`config.toml` and `config`) lists the cargo settings of the user. Ostra links them into the `CARGO_HOME` of the sandbox, so builds keep the same linker and registry settings. Credentials are not linked.

### When the caches are removed

- When a session ends, the engine calls `remove_session_cache`. It deletes the dir on a thread named `ostra-cache-remove`, because a cache can hold gigabytes.
- At server start, `sweep_session_caches` removes the caches of sessions that are `Completed` or `Failed` in a workspace that this data dir knows. This covers a removal that failed and a server that stopped first. It touches no other session, because other data dirs share the cache root.
- A failed removal logs a warning and does not stop the server.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to stop or change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_SANDBOX_CACHE` | `~/.cache/ostra/sandbox` | The environment of the Ostra server | After a restart of the server | The dirs in the cache base dir | Unset the variable to use the default. The cache itself has no off switch. |

## Limits and constants

The table lists each limit and constant of the sandbox crate with its value. The Linux, macOS, and decoy parts above give the reason for each one.

The sandbox crate does not own the language server limits. A language server runs as a program that `host_command` wraps, and the [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) page owns its limits. The `MAX_OPEN` below is the helper limit in `sys/linux/helper.rs`. It is a different constant from the language server limit of the same name.

| Name | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_BLOCKED_PORTS` | 64 | Blocked loopback ports for one workspace. |
| `MAX_WORKSPACE_DECOYS` | 32 | Decoys that one workspace adds. |
| `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | 26 hosts | Built-in package and source hosts under `allowlist`. |
| `MAX_HEAD` | 8 KiB | Size of a proxy request head. |
| `HEAD_TIMEOUT` | 30 seconds | Time for a request head, and for the first TLS bytes. |
| `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` | 10 seconds | Time for one connect, to an address or to the upstream proxy. |
| `MAX_CONNECTIONS` | 256 | Open connections on one proxy or splice listener. |
| `MAX_HELLO` | 32 KiB | Size of the TLS ClientHello that the proxy reads. |
| `PROXY_USER` | `ostra` | User name in the loopback proxy URL. |
| `MAX_OPEN` (helper) | 256 | Open connections for each listener of the helper. |
| `FAILED` | 125 | Exit status of a helper that cannot start the command. |
| `HELPER` | `OnceLock<PathBuf>` | Path of the `ostra` helper binary. `set_helper` fills it one time. |
| `UNAVAILABLE` | One text for each OS | The fix that `unavailable_message` adds to the probe reason. |
| `ARCH` | `0xC000_003E` on `x86_64`, `0xC000_00B7` on `aarch64` | Architecture value that the seccomp filter accepts. |
| `ARCH_OFFSET` | 4 | Byte offset of the `arch` field in `seccomp_data`. |
| `GIT_WALK_DIRS` | 20,000 | Dirs that the git repo walk reads. |
| `GIT_WALK_REPOS` | 128 | Repos that the git repo walk returns. |
| Git dirs of one repo | 256 | Git dirs, submodules included, that `git_dirs` returns. |
| `B64` | `A-Za-z0-9+/` | Characters for the random text of SSH key and Vault token decoys. |
| `HEX` | `0123456789abcdef` | Characters for the random text of git credential and generic decoys. |
| `HEAD` | Size of `inotify_event` | Fixed header of each inotify event that the decoy watcher reads. |
| `TAG_PREFIX` | `dev.ostra.decoy.` | Start of each Seatbelt decoy message. |
| `SANDBOX_EXEC` | `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` | Seatbelt front end. |
| `TTY_PARAM` | `TTY` | Name of the `sandbox-exec -D` parameter for the terminal device of a PTY program. |
| `CANARY` | `dev.ostra.sandbox.canary` | Mach name that every Ostra policy refuses. |
| `FILTER_NONE` | 0 | `sandbox_check` filter type that tests for any sandbox. |
| `FILTER_GLOBAL_NAME` | 2 | `sandbox_check` filter type that tests one global mach name. |
| `NO_REPORT` | `0x4000_0000` | Flag that stops `sandbox_check` from logging a refusal. |
| `ADMIN_GID` | 80 | Group ID of the macOS `admin` group, which `log stream` needs. |
| `READY` | `OnceLock<bool>` | Stored result of the one start of the `log stream` reader, with a 10 second wait. |
| Egress runtime | 2 worker threads | Threads for all proxies and splices. |
| Socket path | 107 bytes | Longest Unix socket path. |

The config overrides for git commands that Ostra starts have their own limits. See [Project files, Git dock, and cloning](project-files-and-git.md).

## What the sandbox does not guarantee

The sandbox lowers the damage that a command can do. It is not a promise that a command is safe.

- **It does nothing when it is off.** Under mode `off`, and under mode `auto` without a backend, commands run with the full rights of the user. Hidden artifacts, the data dir, and the sign-in files can then be read by a shell command that does not name them. The network choice does not apply.
- **It hides only what it lists.** The host is read-only and readable. A file that is not in `HOME_CREDENTIALS`, `DOCKER_SOCKETS`, or the extra hidden list stays readable. Add secrets of your own to the extra hidden list.
- **It does not protect the project files.** The roots are writable. An agent can change or delete any file in them, and also a build script, a Makefile, or a `package.json` that the user runs later on the host. The git protection covers only the paths that choose programs in git.
- **It filters by destination and not by content.** The proxy sees the host and the port. A command can send data to any allowed host, for example `github.com`. Under `public`, it can send data to any public address.
- **Network `host` has no filter.** The command reaches every local service, the LAN, and the cloud metadata address.
- **A trusted host can resolve to a private address.** The user chose it, so the proxy does not check the address.
- **The SNI check has limits.** It covers tunnels to a host name that carry TLS. It does not cover an IP address as the host, and it passes traffic that is not TLS.
- **Linux filter coverage depends on the CPU.** The seccomp filter exists for `x86_64` and `aarch64` only. On another CPU, a command can create user namespaces.
- **macOS shares the loopback.** Under the `open` choice, a command reaches every local server on loopback, except the blocked ports and the Ostra server. Block the ports of sensitive services.
- **A macOS hidden path shows that it exists.** The error is `EPERM` and not a missing file.
- **A decoy detects and does not prevent.** On Linux it hands out fake content. On macOS it needs an admin account and an existing file. Each decoy reports the first open only.
- **It is not a virtual machine.** The command shares the kernel of the host. The seccomp filter narrows the kernel surface, and it does not close it.

The [Policy engine](policy-engine.md) page explains the guards and permission rules that work together with the sandbox. The [Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) page lists the settings keys.
