sections.title: Browser sign-in and network binding
sections.summary: How a browser signs in with a one-time token and a cookie, how the server checks Host and Origin on each request, how the bind address and allowed hosts work, and what the sign-in does not guarantee.
sections.body:
## Why the server signs in browsers

Ostra runs shell commands and edits files for its agents. Any program that can send a request to the server can start that work. The server therefore refuses each request to `/api` and `/ws` that has no valid session cookie. The sign-in system has four parts:

- A one-time token that the server prints in a URL.
- An exchange that turns the token into a session cookie.
- Checks of the `Host`, `Origin`, and `Sec-Fetch-*` headers on each request.
- A bind address and a list of allowed host names that decide who can reach the server.

The code comments name two attacks that the header checks block: DNS rebinding (a host name that an attacker points at this machine) and requests from pages of other sites.

This page stops before secret storage. See [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md) for the master key and sealed secrets. See [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) for the other routes and the response headers. See [Ostra overview and first run](overview.md) for the start flags and the port.

The code lives in [`crates/ostra-server/src/auth.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/auth.rs). The `guard` middleware in [`crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs) applies the checks. The command line is in [`crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs).

## Follow one sign-in from the terminal to the browser

A sign-in has three terms. The token is the one-time value in the URL. The cookie is the browser cookie `ostra_session`. A sign-in is the record that the registry keeps for one cookie. The registry is the machine database. See [Storage: databases and lesson memory](storage.md) for it.

### Sign-in flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Server as ostra server
    participant Registry
    participant Browser
    Server->>Registry: mint_token writes auth:token:HASH
    Server->>User: print http://host/#token=TOKEN
    User->>Browser: open the URL
    Browser->>Server: GET / without the fragment
    Browser->>Server: POST /api/auth/exchange with the token in the body
    Server->>Registry: kv_replace marks the token as used
    Server->>Registry: store_record writes auth:cookie:HASH
    Server->>Browser: 204 and Set-Cookie ostra_session
    Browser->>Server: GET /api/... with the cookie
```

The steps run in this order:

1. The function `run` in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` writes `server.json` in the data directory and mints a token. It prints `Ostra is running on <address>. Open this URL to sign in:` and the URL.
2. The server opens the URL in the default browser. If the open fails, the server prints `Could not open a browser; copy the URL above.`
3. The web app reads the token from the fragment (`#token=`) in `web/src/auth.ts`. The browser never sends a fragment to a server.
4. The web app removes the fragment with `history.replaceState`. Then it posts `{"token": "..."}` to `/api/auth/exchange`.
5. The server answers `204 No Content` and sets the cookie. Each later request to `/api` and `/ws` carries the cookie.

### What the browser test asserts about the token

The test `tests/browser/specs/signin.spec.ts` asserts two facts after the sign-in. The address bar and `location.hash` hold no token. No request URL and no request header carries the token.

The test does not assert that the browser history is free of the token. The web app calls `history.replaceState` only after the page loads with `#token=` in the URL. The first navigation can therefore stay in the browser history. The test only logs the History rows and the profile files that hold the token, in `[pw report]` lines.

The one-time use makes a leftover token harmless. A replay of the token returns `401` with the text `already used`, and the test asserts this. See [One-time token](#one-time-token).

The web app also waits when the page is prerendered, because a prerendered page must not spend a token that the real visit needs. It keeps a set of tokens that it already sent, so a reload of the stripped URL does not send the token again. A `hashchange` event with a token reloads the page, so a link pasted into an open tab signs in.

If the browser has no cookie, the sign-in screen (`web/src/shell/SignIn.tsx`) accepts a pasted link or a bare hexadecimal token of at least 16 characters.

## One-time token

The token proves that the person who holds it can run `ostra` on the machine of the server. The function `mint_token` makes it from 32 random bytes, written as 64 hexadecimal characters. The registry stores only the SHA-256 hash of the token, under the key `auth:token:<hash>`, with the expiry time as its value. A reader of the registry therefore cannot rebuild a token.

The server accepts a token one time. The function `exchange` in `auth.rs` marks the token as used before it creates a cookie:

```rust
let claimed = self
    .registry
    .kv_replace(&key, &stored, format!("used:{}", now()).as_bytes())
    .unwrap_or(false);
if !claimed {
    return Err(ExchangeError::Used { seconds_ago: 0 });
}
...
let expires: u64 = stored.parse().map_err(|_| ExchangeError::Unknown)?;
if expires < now() {
    return Err(ExchangeError::Expired {
        seconds_ago: now() - expires,
    });
}
```

`kv_replace` changes the value only if it still equals the value that the server read. When two requests send the same token at the same time, only one wins. The other gets the error `Used`. The server keeps a used token in the registry, so a second request can say that the token was used and does not look like an unknown token.

### What happens when

Each refused token returns status `401` with a message. The log line `sign-in: refused (<kind>, ...)` names the kind. The message column quotes `ExchangeError::message` in `auth.rs`. `{n}` is the number of seconds.

| Case | Kind | Message of the response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The hash is not in the registry. | `unknown` | `This sign-in link was not issued by this server. Run `ostra url` on the machine running Ostra, as the same user.` |
| The token was used. | `used` | `This sign-in link was already used {n} s ago, so it cannot sign in again. Run `ostra url` for a new one.` |
| The token is older than 15 minutes. | `expired` | `This sign-in link expired; links last 15 minutes. Run `ostra url` for a new one.` |

- The server marks a token as used before it checks the expiry. A second attempt with an expired token therefore reports `used`.
- The body must be JSON with a `token` field and at most 64 KB. If it is not, the server answers `400` with the text `Send {"token": "..."}.`
- The server trims spaces from the token before it hashes the token.
- A restart of the server does not change a token, because the registry holds it. A token from an earlier run still works until it expires.

The registry holds the tokens. A second process can therefore mint a token for a server that already runs. See [Commands: url, sessions, and signout](#commands-url-sessions-and-signout).

## Session cookie

The cookie is the proof of sign-in on each later request. The function `exchange` makes a cookie value from 32 random bytes, written as 64 hexadecimal characters. It stores the record under `auth:cookie:<SHA-256 of the cookie>`. The server never stores the cookie itself.

Two constants in `auth.rs` name the cookie. `COOKIE` is the cookie name `ostra_session`, which the server sets and reads on each request. `COOKIE_KEY` is the registry key prefix `auth:cookie:`, and the server adds the SHA-256 hash of the cookie to it to find the record of a sign-in.

The server sends this header (`Auth::cookie_header`):

```text
ostra_session=<value>; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Path=/; Max-Age=2592000
```

- `HttpOnly` stops page scripts from reading the cookie.
- `SameSite=Strict` stops the browser from sending the cookie on a request that another site starts.
- `Max-Age=2592000` is 30 days. The constant is `COOKIE_TTL_SECS`.
- The server adds `; Secure` when the `Origin` header of the exchange starts with `https://`. This case is a TLS reverse proxy in front of Ostra. The code does not read `X-Forwarded-Proto`, because any client can send that header. A browser sets `Origin` itself.

The record of a sign-in holds these fields:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | `si_` and 16 random hexadecimal characters. The `id` is random and is not derived from the cookie, so a list of sign-ins does not leak a cookie. |
| `created` | The time of the exchange, in seconds. |
| `last_seen` | The last time a request used the cookie. The server writes it at most each 60 seconds (`SEEN_EVERY_SECS`), so an active tab does not write on each request. |
| `user_agent` | The `User-Agent` header, cut to 300 characters. |
| `ip` | The peer address of the exchange. |

A sign-in expires at `created` plus 30 days. A request does not extend it, and `last_seen` does not change the expiry. After 30 days the server refuses the cookie and deletes the record. Then you must sign in again with a new token.

Older servers stored only the creation time as a number. The function `parse_record` reads both forms, and the next read rewrites an old record with an `id`. Cookies from an older server keep working.

## Lifetimes, limits, and constants

No setting changes a value in this table. Each value is a constant in [`crates/ostra-server/src/auth.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/auth.rs) or in the handler for the exchange.

| Constant or limit | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `COOKIE` | `ostra_session` | The name of the session cookie. |
| `COOKIE_KEY` | `auth:cookie:` | The registry key prefix of a sign-in record. |
| `TOKEN_TTL_SECS` | 900 s (15 minutes) | The time in which a token can sign in. |
| `COOKIE_TTL_SECS` | 2,592,000 s (30 days) | The life of a sign-in and the `Max-Age` of the cookie. |
| `RECHECK` | 5 s | How long the server trusts a checked cookie before it reads the registry again. It also sets the interval at which an open WebSocket checks its sign-in. |
| `SEEN_EVERY_SECS` | 60 s | The shortest time between two writes of `last_seen` for one sign-in. |
| `MAX_FAILURES` | 5 | Failed exchanges that one address can make in the window. |
| `FAILURE_WINDOW` | 60 s | The window for the failure count. |
| Exchange body | 64 KB | The largest body that `/api/auth/exchange` reads. |
| `user_agent` length | 300 characters | The part of the `User-Agent` header that the server keeps. |
| Revoke channel | 64 messages | The size of the broadcast channel that tells open sockets about a revoke. |

The cache in `check_cookie` keeps, for each cookie hash, its expiry and the time of its last registry read. If the cache entry is younger than `RECHECK`, the server answers from the cache. Otherwise it reads the registry. The cache saves a registry read on each request. It also sets the delay of a revoke from another process. See [Revoke a sign-in](#revoke-a-sign-in).

## Failed exchanges and the failure limit

The server limits failed exchanges for each address. A token has 256 bits, so a guess cannot succeed. The comment in the code gives the real reason: the limit stops a guessing loop from filling the log and the registry.

The rules are:

- An address that fails 5 times (`MAX_FAILURES`) in 60 seconds (`FAILURE_WINDOW`) must wait. Each failure leaves the count after 60 seconds, so the window slides.
- During the wait, the server answers `429 Too Many Requests` with the text `Wait N s before trying another sign-in link...`. `N` is the time until the oldest failure leaves the window, and it is at least 1 second.
- A request that the limit refuses does not count as a new failure and does not use the token.
- A successful exchange removes the failures of that address.
- The limit does not apply to loopback addresses. The comment says why: if loopback failures counted, any local process can cause failures on purpose and lock the user out of signing in.
- The server reads the peer address of the TCP connection. It does not read a forwarded header. Behind a reverse proxy, the peer address is the address of the proxy.

The failure counts are in memory. A restart of the server clears them.

## Checks on each request

The `guard` middleware in `api.rs` runs on each request, before the handler. It refuses a request in this order:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Request"] --> B{"Host header in the allowed list?"}
    B -- no --> R1["421 This host is not allowed"]
    B -- yes --> C{"Path starts with /internal/?"}
    C -- yes --> E{"Local peer and no Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site?"}
    E -- no --> R3["403 Forbidden"]
    E -- yes --> S["Handler"]
    C -- no --> D{"Private host name in use and request on an IP name?"}
    D -- yes --> R2["307 redirect for a page, 421 for the API"]
    D -- no --> F{"Path is /api/ or /ws?"}
    F -- no --> S
    F -- yes --> G{"Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site, and Sec-Fetch-Dest allowed?"}
    G -- no --> R3
    G -- yes --> H{"Valid cookie, or path is /api/auth/exchange?"}
    H -- no --> R4["401 Unauthorized"]
    H -- yes --> S
```

A request that passes all checks goes to its handler. Each refusal also gets the security response headers, so a page on another site cannot put the refusal in a frame. See [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) for those headers.

### Host check

The server compares the `Host` header with its list of allowed hosts. The comparison is exact on the whole `host:port` text and ignores the case. A request with another host name, or with no `Host` header, gets status `421 Misdirected Request` and the message `This host is not allowed.` This check blocks DNS rebinding. A page at `http://attacker.example:7878` has its own host name, even if the name resolves to `127.0.0.1`. The test `tests/browser/specs/cross-origin.spec.ts` checks that such a host name gets `421` on every path.

The Host check applies to every path, also to the static files of the web app.

### Origin and fetch checks

These checks apply only to the paths under `/api/` and to `/ws`. A request is refused with `403` and `This origin is not allowed.` in these cases:

- The `Origin` header is present and is not `http://` or `https://` followed by an allowed host. A request with no `Origin` header passes this one check, but the cookie check still applies.
- The `Sec-Fetch-Site` header is `cross-site` or `same-site`. A page on another port of `localhost` is same-site with the app, so the browser sends the `SameSite=Strict` cookie. This header lets the server tell that page from the app itself.
- The `Sec-Fetch-Dest` header is present and is not `empty`, `websocket`, or `document`. The app calls the API with `fetch` (`empty`), with the socket (`websocket`), and with download links (`document`). An image, script, style, or frame request is page content, for example a Markdown image that an agent wrote. The server refuses it even with a valid cookie.

The server accepts `https://` origins because a TLS reverse proxy can sit in front of Ostra.

```rust
if !app.auth.allowed_origin(origin)
    || matches!(fetch_site, Some("cross-site" | "same-site"))
    || !dest_ok
{
    return Some(
        ApiErr::new(StatusCode::FORBIDDEN, "This origin is not allowed.").into_response(),
    );
}
```

### Cookie check

After the header checks, each `/api` request except `/api/auth/exchange` needs a valid cookie. The function `check_cookie` returns true when the registry holds a sign-in for the cookie hash that is younger than 30 days. A request without a valid cookie gets `401` and the message `Sign in with the URL the ostra command printed.` The server also writes a log line `unauthorized <path>: session cookie missing` or `sent but not recognized`. The line holds request facts such as `peer`, `host`, `origin`, and `sec-fetch-site`. It never holds a token or a cookie value.

The WebSocket upgrade passes the same checks. After the upgrade, the socket checks its cookie each 5 seconds. If the sign-in ends, the server closes the socket with code `4401` and the reason `Signed out`.

### Internal paths

The paths under `/internal/` serve the hook bridge and the MCP shim of harness executions. They have these rules:

- The server refuses a peer that is not an address of this machine, even when the server listens on every interface. The status is `403` and the message is `This endpoint accepts local connections only.`
- The server refuses a request that has an `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` header. A browser page on this machine is a local peer, and a browser always sends one of the two headers. The message is `This endpoint is for Ostra's harness bridge, not for web pages.`
- These paths use no cookie. They are exempt from the redirect to the private host name: `guard` applies the redirect only when the path does not start with `/internal/`.

See [Harness executors](harness-executors.md) for the bridge.

## Bind address and allowed hosts

The bind address decides which machines can connect to the server. A bind to a non-loopback address makes the server reachable from the network. By default the server listens on `127.0.0.1` only, so only programs on this machine can connect. The function `bind_addr` in `app.rs` finds the address in this order:

1. The flag `--bind`.
2. The setting `server.bind` in the global config.
3. `127.0.0.1`, when nothing is set.

The value is an IP address. The function trims spaces and square brackets. It also accepts `localhost` (`127.0.0.1`) and `all` or `*` (`0.0.0.0`). `0.0.0.0` and `::` listen on every interface. An address that does not parse stops the start with this error: "`<value>` is not an IP address to listen on (for example 127.0.0.1 or 0.0.0.0)".

### Allowed host list

The function `Access::hosts` builds the list of values that the `Host` header can have. The list always holds `127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>`, and `[::1]:<port>`. The bind address adds more entries:

| Bind address | Entries added |
| --- | --- |
| Loopback | None. |
| One non-loopback address | That address with the port. |
| `0.0.0.0` or `::` | The address of every interface of the machine, also bridge interfaces such as Docker, because a container or VM on the machine can connect through one. Also the host name of the machine and `<host name>.local`, with the port. |

The extra names add more entries. A name with a port (`box.lan:9000`) is one entry. A name without a port adds two entries: `name:<port>` and the bare `name`. The bare name is there because a reverse proxy on its default port sends the bare name. The server trims each name and makes it lowercase. In development mode, the list also holds `localhost:5173` and `127.0.0.1:5173`.

The Origin check uses the same list. The server removes `http://` or `https://` from the origin and compares the rest with the list. The port in the origin must match an entry.

### Sign-in URL host

The function `Access::url_host` picks the host of the printed URL. The function `Access::lan_addresses` gives it the candidate addresses:

- Bind to a loopback address: no address.
- Bind to one specific non-loopback address: only that address. No bridge filter and no link-local filter applies.
- Bind to `0.0.0.0` or `::`: the addresses of the interfaces of the machine, IPv4 first. The filter removes loopback addresses, bridge interfaces, and IPv6 link-local addresses. The filter applies only to these two binds.

If the bind address is not loopback and the list has an address, `url_host` is the first address with the port. Otherwise it is `127.0.0.1:<port>`.

For a loopback server with the private host name on, `Auth::new` replaces `url_host` with `<private name>:<port>`. See [Private host name for a loopback server](#private-host-name-for-a-loopback-server). The function `write_server_file` writes `auth.url_host` in `server.json`, and `ostra url` reads it. In the default case, `server.json` therefore holds the private name and the port, not `127.0.0.1:<port>`.

If the machine has more than one such address, the server prints `The link works once, from any address this machine has (...)`. A token is not tied to an address.

### What happens when the bind address is not loopback

The server prints a warning at start. The warning says that Ostra is reachable over plain HTTP, that anyone who reaches the port with a sign-in link can run commands as you, and that the traffic is not encrypted. It advises an SSH tunnel or a TLS reverse proxy with its host name added through `--allow-host`. It also says that push notifications need HTTPS or `localhost`. The warning ends with the command `ostra signout`.

For a reverse proxy, the proxy must send the `Host` header that the list holds. Add the public name of the proxy to the list. If the proxy uses TLS, the browser sends an `https://` origin, and the cookie gets the `Secure` attribute.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | When a change takes effect | What shows the state | How to change or stop it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--bind <address>` | Not set. The server uses `server.bind`, then `127.0.0.1`. | Command line only. | At the next start. | The line `Ostra is running on <address>` and the printed sign-in URL. | Start the server again without the flag, or with `--bind 127.0.0.1`. |
| `server.bind` | Not set. The server listens on `127.0.0.1`. | Section `[server]` of the global config. Run `ostra config` to print its path. | At the next start. | The same line. | Delete the key. The flag `--bind` overrides it. |
| `--allow-host <name>` | None. You can repeat the flag. | Command line only. | At the next start. | A request with that `Host` header gets no `421`. | Start the server again without the flag. |
| `server.allowed_hosts` | An empty list. | Section `[server]` of the global config. | At the next start. | The same. | Remove the name from the list. The server joins this list with the flag values. |

The server reads these values only when it starts. A change to the config file does not change a running server.

## Private host name for a loopback server

A cookie that the server sets on `127.0.0.1` goes to every other web server on the same machine, because a cookie is not tied to a port. By default, a server that listens on loopback therefore uses a private host name. The function `private_name` makes the name `ostra-<16 hexadecimal characters>.localhost` and stores it under the registry key `server:private_host`. The name is the same after a restart. Browsers resolve each `*.localhost` name to this machine. A cookie on this name is not sent to pages on `127.0.0.1` or on other names.

The rules are:

- The printed sign-in URL uses the private name, for example `http://ostra-0123456789abcdef.localhost:7878/#token=...`.
- A page request to `127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>`, or `[::1]:<port>` gets `307 Temporary Redirect` to the private name. The redirect keeps the path and the query. The browser keeps the fragment, so a token in the old URL still works.
- An API request to those names gets `421`. The message tells the client to open Ostra at `http://<name>/` and says that a sign-in on 127.0.0.1 shares its cookie with every other local port.
- The private name is in the allowed list.
- The server does not use the private name when it listens on a non-loopback address.
- Requests to paths under `/internal/` skip the redirect.

Some browsers do not resolve `*.localhost`. For such a browser, set `use_ip_host` to `true`. The cookie then reaches every other local port.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | When a change takes effect | What shows the state | How to change or stop it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `server.use_ip_host` | `false`. The server uses the private name. | Section `[server]` of the global config. | At the next start. | The host in the printed sign-in URL. | Set the key to `false` or delete it. |

## Commands: url, sessions, and signout

Three subcommands of `ostra` work on sign-ins. They open the registry directly, so `sessions` and `signout` also work when no server runs. The error message for an unknown token tells you to run `ostra url` as the same user that runs the server.

| Command | What it does | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra url` | Mints a fresh token and prints a sign-in URL for the running server. | `http://<url_host>/#token=<token>`. |
| `ostra sessions` | Lists each sign-in, oldest first. | One line for each sign-in: the id, `signed in`, `last seen` (UTC), the address, and the browser. The text is "No browser is signed in." when the list is empty. |
| `ostra sessions revoke <id>` | Removes the sign-in with that id. | "Revoked <id>. That browser is signed out within 5 seconds." For an unknown id the command fails with "No sign-in <id>. Run `ostra sessions` to list the current ones." |
| `ostra sessions revoke --all` | Removes every sign-in. | "Signed out <n> browsers. Run `ostra url` to sign in again." |
| `ostra signout` | The same as `ostra sessions revoke --all`. | The same text. |

The command `ostra url` reads `server.json` in the data directory. The server writes this file at start with the port, `url_host`, and its process ID. The server removes the file when it stops after Ctrl+C. If the file does not exist, the command fails with "No Ostra server is running. Start one with `ostra`." The command does not check that the process in the file still runs. After a crash, the file stays and the command prints a URL for a server that does not run.

### For the user

| Control | Default | Stored in | When a change takes effect | What shows the state | How to change or stop it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A sign-in | A new one for each exchange. It lasts 30 days. | The registry, key `auth:cookie:<hash>`. | A revoke from the browser takes effect at once. A revoke from the CLI takes effect in 5 seconds or less. | `ostra sessions`, and the sign-in tab of the settings screen (`web/src/screens/setup/SignInSessions.tsx`). | `ostra sessions revoke <id>`, `ostra sessions revoke --all`, `ostra signout`, or the buttons on the settings screen. |
| A token | 15 minutes, one use. | The registry, key `auth:token:<hash>`. | At once. | The result of the exchange in the log `server.log`. | Wait for the expiry. No command removes one token. |

If you cannot sign in, run `ostra url` on the machine that runs Ostra. If you lost a browser, run `ostra sessions` to list the sign-ins, and run `ostra signout` to remove them all.

## Revoke a sign-in

A revoke removes the registry record of the sign-in. The server refuses a cookie that has no record. Three paths end a sign-in:

- **The browser.** The settings screen calls `DELETE /api/auth/sessions/{id}` for one sign-in, `POST /api/auth/sessions/revoke-others` for all except the current one, and `POST /api/auth/signout` for the current one. The list comes from `GET /api/auth/sessions` and marks the current sign-in. The route for a missing id returns `404` with the text `No sign-in <id>.` and a note that the sign-in expired or is already revoked.
- **The CLI.** The commands `ostra sessions revoke` and `ostra signout` delete the records from a second process.
- **Expiry.** The server deletes a record that is older than 30 days when it reads the record.

A revoke through the running server takes effect at once. The server removes the cookie from its cache and sends the cookie hash on a broadcast channel. Each open WebSocket that has that cookie closes with code `4401`. A socket that missed a message because the channel was full checks the registry instead. A socket that opens during a revoke checks its cookie again after it subscribes, so no revoke is missed.

The running server does not see a revoke from the CLI, because the CLI is another process. The server trusts a cached cookie for 5 seconds (`RECHECK`). After that, it reads the registry and refuses the cookie. The WebSocket check runs at the same interval. A CLI revoke therefore takes effect in 5 seconds or less.

The sign-out route clears the cookie in the browser with `Max-Age=0`. A sign-out through the CLI cannot clear a cookie in a browser. The browser keeps the cookie, but the server refuses it.

When the server updates `last_seen`, it writes only over the row that it just read (`kv_replace`). A revoke that arrives at the same time is not undone.

## What the sign-in does not guarantee

The sign-in protects the server from other sites and from other machines that have no link. It does not guarantee these things:

- **No protection from the same OS user.** Any process that runs as your user can run `ostra url` or read the registry file and sign in. The registry file has mode `0600` on Unix, so other users cannot read it.
- **No encryption.** The server speaks plain HTTP. On a non-loopback address, anyone on the network path can read the cookie and the data of the session. Use an SSH tunnel or a TLS reverse proxy.
- **No protection for a link that someone else reads first.** The first browser to exchange a token gets the sign-in. The link is in the terminal output and in the address bar before the exchange.
- **No clean browser history.** The first navigation to the sign-in URL can stay in the browser history. The one-time use makes the leftover token harmless after the exchange.
- **No binding of a cookie to an address or a browser.** A stolen cookie works until you revoke it or it expires after 30 days. The `ip` and `user_agent` fields are for display only.
- **No levels of access.** Each valid cookie can use each `/api` route. There are no roles.
- **No limit on failures from loopback.** The failure limit skips loopback addresses. A local process can try tokens without a wait, but it cannot guess a 256-bit token.
- **No defense against a client that is not a browser.** The Host, Origin, and `Sec-Fetch-*` checks stop browsers. A program can send any header. The cookie is the only barrier for such a program.
- **A wider cookie reach on an IP host name.** When the server uses `127.0.0.1` as its host name, the cookie goes to every local port. `HttpOnly` stops scripts from reading it. `SameSite=Strict` and the `Sec-Fetch-Site` check stop requests from other local pages.
- **A delay for the CLI revoke.** It takes up to 5 seconds.

The sign-in does not seal secrets. See [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md). It also does not limit what an agent can do after you sign in. See [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) and [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

## Tests that pin these rules

- `tests/browser/specs/signin.spec.ts`: the address bar has no token after sign-in, and no request URL or header carries it. A replay of the token after sign-in gets `401` and the text `already used`. A page that opens in the background and then reloads makes one exchange with status `204`.
- `tests/browser/specs/cross-origin.spec.ts`: an attacker page on another localhost port and on another site sends form posts, `fetch` in each mode, a WebSocket, image and script tags, and top-level navigations. The server refuses each request, the page reads nothing, the WebSocket does not open, and the state of the server does not change. A rebinding host name on the port of the app gets `421` on every path. An image, script, or style request from the app origin to `/api` gets `403`, although the browser sends the cookie.
- Unit tests in `auth.rs`: one-time use, sign-ins that survive a restart, revoke at once, CLI revoke after `RECHECK`, old records, the failure limit and the loopback exception, the `Secure` attribute, the host and origin checks, the private name, and the hosts of a remote bind.

See [Testing and evals](testing.md) for how to run the browser tests.

code_refs.note: Token mint, exchange, cookie check, revoke, failure limit, and the allowed host and origin checks.
Bind address, extra hosts, and the lists that `hosts`, `lan_addresses`, and `url_host` build.
The three exchange errors with their message texts and kinds.
Writes `server.json` with the port, `auth.url_host`, and the process ID.
The middleware that checks Host, the private name redirect, Origin, fetch headers, and the cookie.
The handler for `/api/auth/exchange` with the failure limit and the cookie header.
The `url`, `sessions`, and `signout` subcommands and the flags `--bind` and `--allow-host`.
How the flag, the config, and the default give the bind address and the extra hosts.
The `[server]` settings: `port`, `bind`, `allowed_hosts`, and `use_ip_host`.
Browser test that the token leaves the address bar, appears in no request, and cannot be replayed.
Browser test that attacker pages and rebinding host names get no access.

sections.title: Secrets, credentials, and Web Push
sections.summary: How Ostra seals saved credentials with a master key, how provider and git credentials reach their users, and how Ostra encrypts and signs Web Push messages.
sections.body:
Ostra keeps secrets on a machine that also runs agent processes. Without protection, the registry file `registry.db` holds every API key, git token, and push key as plain text, and any process that reads the file reads the secrets. This page explains how Ostra seals those values and where the key lives. It also explains how credentials reach the model providers and git, and how Ostra sends Web Push messages. The page stops before sign-in. See [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md) for the sign-in token and the cookie.

The registry is the SQLite database of the machine. [Storage: databases and lesson memory](storage.md) owns its tables and migrations. This page owns only the sealing of its secret rows.

## Find the master key at start

The master key is a random 32-byte value. `master_key::unlock` loads it at start, before the server builds the providers and the notifier. Then it gives the registry a `Sealer` that uses the key. Until that step runs, each secret method of the registry returns `StoreError::Locked`.

`load_key` picks the key source in this order:

1. The file that `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` names. Ostra reads it, or creates it when it is missing.
2. The system keychain, unless the registry records that the key is in a file.
3. The file `master.key` in the data directory.

[Configuration reference](reference-configuration.md) owns the data directory, the variable `OSTRA_DATA_DIR`, and the other paths and variables.

### What the registry records

The registry records the chosen backend in the row `secrets:backend` (`BACKEND_KEY`). The value is `keychain` or `file`. Ostra does not write this record when `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` is set. The record has two effects:

- If the record says `file`, Ostra does not ask the keychain again.
- If the record says `keychain`, Ostra never replaces a missing or unreachable key silently.

### Decision flow of `load_key`

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["unlock starts"] --> B{"OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE set?"}
  B -- yes --> C["read or create that file"]
  C --> Z["key ready"]
  B -- no --> D{"recorded backend is file?"}
  D -- yes --> J["read or create data dir master.key"]
  D -- no --> E{"keychain get"}
  E -- "key found" --> K["record keychain"]
  K --> Z
  E -- "no entry" --> F["make key, set it, read it back"]
  F -- "same key" --> K
  F -- "not kept" --> J
  E -- unreachable --> G{"recorded backend is keychain?"}
  G -- yes --> H["stop start with an error"]
  G -- no --> J
  J --> L["record file"]
  L --> Z
```

### Keychain entry

The keychain service name is `SERVICE`, which is `ostra`. The account is `master-key` followed by the canonical path of the data directory. The code gives the reason: one entry for each data directory, so separate Ostra installs keep separate keys. The stored text is the key as 64 hexadecimal characters.

Each keychain call runs on its own thread. If the call does not finish in 10 seconds (`KEYCHAIN_TIMEOUT`), `with_timeout` abandons the thread and treats the keychain as unreachable. The reason is that a keychain call can block on an unlock prompt or on a dead D-Bus.

When Ostra makes a new key, it saves the key to the keychain and reads it back. If the keychain returns another value or no value, Ostra does not use the keychain. It uses the key file.

### Key file

`file_key` reads the key file. The file must hold 64 hexadecimal characters, which is the same text format as the keychain entry. These rules apply:

- If the file is missing, Ostra creates the parent folders and a new random key. It opens the file with `create_new` and mode `0600` on Unix, then calls `sync_all`.
- If the file exists with a wider mode on Unix, Ostra changes the mode to `0600`.
- If Ostra cannot change the mode, it logs a warning and continues. The code comment says that a read-only secret mount is already the choice of the operator.
- On Windows, the file keeps the access list that it inherits from the data directory under the profile of the user.

### Check that the key opens earlier data

`check_key` stores the row `secrets:check` (`CHECK_KEY`). Its value is the text `ostra` (`CHECK_PLAIN`), sealed with the current key. At each start, Ostra tries to open the row. Three cases exist:

- **The row opens to `ostra`.** The key is the same as before. `check_key` returns with `return Ok(())` and writes nothing.
- **The row is missing.** This is the first start. Ostra seals a new check value with the current key and stores it with `kv_set`.
- **The row exists but does not open.** Ostra logs a warning. Credentials that another key sealed cannot be read, so the user must enter them again in settings. Then Ostra seals a new check value with the current key and stores it with `kv_set`.

### What happens when

- **The first start finds a working keychain.** Ostra stores a new key in the keychain and records `keychain`. No `master.key` file exists.
- **The first start finds no usable keychain,** for example a server with no D-Bus. Ostra creates `master.key`, records `file`, and skips the keychain at each later start.
- **The record says `keychain` and the entry is missing.** Ostra logs a warning, makes a new key, and stores it. Saved credentials must be entered again.
- **The record says `keychain` and the keychain is unreachable.** Startup stops with the message that starts with `Unlock the system keychain and start Ostra again`. Ostra does not replace the old key, because a new key makes every saved credential unreadable. The message also names `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` as the way to move to a file.
- **The key file does not hold a valid key.** Startup stops with an error that names the file. The error says to restore the file, or to delete it and enter saved credentials again.
- **The key is lost or changed.** `secret_get` returns no value and logs a warning that names the row. `secret_scan` skips the row. The sealed bytes stay in the registry until the user saves a new value.

Caution: copy `master.key` to a safe place before you delete or replace it. A new key cannot open credentials that the old key sealed, and the user must enter them again.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` | Unset. Ostra uses the keychain, then `master.key` in the data directory. | Environment of the `ostra` process. The file holds 64 hexadecimal characters. | After a restart | The start log line `credentials are encrypted with the key in <path>` | Unset the variable and restart. Ostra then uses the keychain or `master.key`. |

Set `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` for a mounted secret, such as a Docker secret. The sandbox hides this file from agents. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

## Seal a registry row with AES-256-GCM

The `Sealer` in `crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs` encrypts each secret value before it reaches the database. It uses AES-256-GCM with the master key. Each seal uses a new random 12-byte nonce (`NONCE_LEN`). The row key is the associated data. Thus a sealed value cannot move to another row, because the tag check fails when the row key differs.

The stored bytes have this form: the prefix `enc:v1:`, then the standard base64 text of the nonce followed by the ciphertext and the tag.

```rust
pub fn seal(&self, row: &str, plain: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    let mut nonce = [0u8; NONCE_LEN];
    rand::fill(&mut nonce);
    let ct = self.cipher.encrypt(
        &Nonce::try_from(&nonce[..]).expect("12-byte nonce"),
        Payload { msg: plain, aad: row.as_bytes() },
    ).expect("AES-GCM encryption does not fail for small inputs");
    let mut body = nonce.to_vec();
    body.extend_from_slice(&ct);
    let mut out = PREFIX.to_vec();
    out.extend_from_slice(STANDARD.encode(body).as_bytes());
    out
}
```

### Which rows are secrets

`SECRET_KEYS` lists the registry keys whose values are credentials. An entry that ends with `:` matches each key that starts with it. Other entries match only the exact key. `is_secret_key` applies the rule.

| Entry | Match | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vapid_private` | Exact key | The VAPID private key for Web Push |
| `provider_credentials:` | Prefix | Saved provider credentials, one row for each provider |
| `git_credential:` | Prefix | Saved git credentials, one row for each credential |
| `mcp_oauth:` | Prefix | OAuth state of external MCP servers |
| `mcp_secret:` | Prefix | Saved secrets of external MCP servers |

[External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md) owns the MCP rows. Other rows of the `kv` table, such as the sign-in token rows, stay plain text. The tests check that `vapid_private_x` and `auth:token:abc` are not secrets.

### Registry methods

- `secret_set` seals the value and stores it. `secret_get` reads the row and opens it. `secret_scan` does the same for each row under a prefix.
- Each method uses a debug assertion that the key is in `SECRET_KEYS`.
- A registry without a sealer returns `StoreError::Locked`. `RegistryDb::open_in_memory` uses `Sealer::ephemeral`, a random key that lives for the life of the process.
- `Sealer::open` returns `OpenError::Undecryptable` for four cases: bad base64, a body shorter than the nonce, a wrong key, and altered or moved bytes. The registry logs a warning that names the row, and the caller sees no value.
- `Sealer::open` returns a value without the `enc:v1:` prefix unchanged. The reason is that registries written before encryption hold plain text until the migration runs.

### Migrate plain text at start

`seal_plaintext_secrets` runs after `check_key`. It seals each secret row that has no `enc:v1:` prefix with `kv_replace`, which changes the row only if the row still holds the old value.

Then it checks two conditions. If it sealed at least one row, or the flag `secrets_vacuumed` is missing, it runs `VACUUM` and `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`. The rewrite leaves no plain text in the file or in the write-ahead log. [Storage: databases and lesson memory](storage.md) owns the flag `SECRETS_VACUUMED` and the other registry migrations.

The code sets the flag after the rewrite, so a run that stopped between sealing and rewriting repeats the rewrite at the next start. If no row needed sealing and the flag exists, Ostra skips the rewrite. `RegistryDb::open` also sets `secure_delete` to `ON`, so freed pages are zeroed and a replaced plain credential does not stay in the file. Ostra logs the count when it sealed one row or more.

### What happens when

- **Two start-ups race on one row.** `kv_replace` lets one of them seal the row. The other counts no change.
- **A row holds JSON that does not parse.** The credential loaders log a warning and ignore the row.
- **A user deletes a credential.** `kv_delete` removes the row. No key is needed for a delete.

## Save provider credentials

The user enters provider keys in the browser. Ostra keeps them in the registry, not in `config.toml` and not in a response body. The type is `SavedCredentials` with the fields `base_url`, `api_key`, and `auth_token`. Ostra stores it as JSON in the sealed row `provider_credentials:<provider>`. Its `Debug` output prints `***` for the key and the token.

`PATCH /api/providers/{name}` accepts only `anthropic` and `openai`, and only when the provider exists in the global config. Other names return status 404 with the text `No provider {name} in the global config.` The handler runs these steps:

1. `credentials::load` reads the saved value.
2. `credentials::apply` merges the edit and validates the result.
3. `credentials::save` stores the result.
4. `Shared::reload_providers` rebuilds the provider clients from the global config and the saved values.

The next model call uses the new values without a restart.

### Merge and validation rules

For each field, an absent value keeps the saved value. An empty string, after the trim, clears the field. Any other text replaces it, after the trim. If the result has no field, `save` deletes the row instead of sealing an empty value.

The handler returns each problem with its field name in one invalid-request answer:

- `base_url` must parse as a URL with the scheme `http` or `https` and a host.
- `base_url` must not hold a user name, a password, or a query. The reason is that settings show the base URL, so a key in it is visible.
- `api_key` and `auth_token` must not hold a space or a control character. The reason is that Ostra sends them as an HTTP header.

### Where a value comes from

A saved value ranks below an environment variable. The function `lookup_key` in `crates/ostra-providers/src/lib.rs` uses this order for a key:

1. The environment variable that the provider entry names for the key.
2. The environment variable that the provider entry names for the token.
3. The saved `api_key`.
4. The saved `auth_token`.
5. The OS keychain entry. This step runs only when the provider entry sets `keychain_service`. Otherwise `lookup_key` returns before the keychain lookup. It reads the keychain with that service and the provider name.

`ProviderStatus.source` reports `env:NAME`, `saved`, `keychain`, `registered`, or `none`. [Model providers and pricing](providers-and-pricing.md) owns the provider calls.

### Keep credential variables from agents

`credential_env_names` returns each variable that holds a credential that Ostra must not pass to agent processes or MCP servers. The list has these parts:

- `DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV`: the five variables that the built-in providers read. They are `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `OPENAI_BASE_URL`.
- `BRIDGE_ENV`: `OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_URL`, and `OSTRA_HARNESS`. A child inherits them from Ostra only by accident, so Ostra drops them and sets them again.
- The variable names that each provider entry sets for the key, the token, and the base URL.
- The `oauth.client_secret_env` name of each MCP server.

The Bash tool, the sandbox, the harness launch, and the MCP launch remove these variables from the environment of the child. [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) owns the provider entries that name these variables.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Saved `base_url`, `api_key`, `auth_token` | None | Sealed row `provider_credentials:<provider>` in `registry.db` | At once, with no restart | The provider status in the setup screen and settings. Secrets show only as present. | Send an empty string for a field, or clear all fields. Then the row is deleted. |
| Environment variables of a provider | Set by the provider entry | The provider entry in `config.toml` | At the next start | `ProviderStatus.source` shows `env:NAME` | Unset the variable. |

Caution: use an `https://` base URL. The validation also accepts `http://`, and Ostra then sends the key without encryption on the network.

## Save git credentials

Git credentials let Ostra clone and pull private repositories and let the Git dock reach a remote. The code is in `crates/ostra-server/src/git.rs`. Credentials live in the registry next to the provider keys. They reach git only through the process environment and one-off `-c` options. They never land in the `.git/config` of a repository.

`SavedGitCredential` has the fields `label`, `host`, `kind`, `username`, and `secret`. Ostra stores it as JSON in the sealed row `git_credential:gc_<id>`. The id is `gc_` followed by a UUID version 7. The browser sees `GitCredentialView`, which has `has_secret` and no secret. The `Debug` output of the credential also omits the secret. A test checks that the secret is in neither the JSON view nor the debug text.

### Routes

| Route | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/git/credentials` | List the views |
| `POST /api/git/credentials` | Save a new credential |
| `PATCH /api/git/credentials/{id}` | Edit one credential. An absent field keeps its value. |
| `DELETE /api/git/credentials/{id}` | Delete one credential |

Each route returns the updated list of views. A patch or delete for an unknown id returns status 404 with `No such git credential.` [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) owns the route table.

### Validation rules

`apply` merges the edit with the saved value and lists every problem on its field:

- `kind` must be `https` or `ssh`.
- `host` is normalized. Ostra removes the scheme, a user name, and slashes at the ends, and it makes the host name lowercase. The result is a host name with an optional `:port` and an optional path prefix, such as `github.com` or `github.com/acme`.
- `username` must not hold a space or a control character.
- `secret` is required. On an edit, an empty secret keeps the saved one.
- An `https` secret must not hold a space or a line break.
- An `ssh` secret must hold `PRIVATE KEY-----`. A public key does not pass.
- A new `ssh` secret must not contain `ENCRYPTED`. The reason is that Ostra runs git with no terminal to ask for a passphrase.
- `label` defaults to the host.

### Choose the credential for a remote

`parse_remote` accepts `https://`, `http://`, `ssh://`, and the scp form `user@host:path`. It refuses local paths, `file://`, `ext::`, other schemes, text that starts with `-`, and text with spaces. It also refuses an `https` URL with a password. The reason is that git keeps the URL in the `.git/config` of the project, so the user must save the token as a git credential instead.

`credential_for` picks the credential. A credential matches a remote when all of these are true:

- The remote is not `http://` to a host other than `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `[::1]`. A saved token never goes over a network without TLS.
- The type fits: an `ssh` credential for an ssh remote, an `https` credential for an https remote.
- The host and path of the remote equal the credential host, or start with it followed by `/`.
- A credential host without a port matches the host on any port.

If more than one credential matches, the one with the longest host text wins. A clone request can name a credential by id. If the id does not exist, `clone_plan` returns `That git credential no longer exists. Choose another one.` If the type does not fit the URL, it returns `This URL needs an ssh credential. Choose another one, or change the URL.` or the same text with `an https`.

The pull and the Git dock commands that reach a remote call `remote_auth`. It reads the fetch URL, or the push URL for a push, and picks the matching credential.

## Give git a credential without leaking it

`GitAuth::new` builds the arguments and the environment for one git process. Every `GitAuth` sets `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, so a prompt fails and does not wait. On Windows it also sets `GCM_INTERACTIVE=never`, because the Credential Manager asks in a window, and a server with no user at the desktop waits forever. Stored credentials still answer.

### An https credential

Ostra gives git a token through an inline credential helper:

```rust
Some(c) if c.kind == GitCredentialKind::Https => {
    args.push("-c".into());
    args.push("credential.helper=".into());
    args.push("-c".into());
    args.push(r#"credential.helper=!f() { ... }; f"#.into());
    for pin in ["http.proxy=", "http.sslVerify=true"] { ... }
    envs.push(("OSTRA_GIT_HOST".into(), /* host without path */));
    envs.push(("OSTRA_GIT_USERNAME".into(), /* username or x-access-token */));
    envs.push(("OSTRA_GIT_PASSWORD".into(), c.secret.clone()));
}
```

The parts have these reasons:

- The first `credential.helper=` is empty. It drops the helpers of the user, so git does not copy the token into them after a successful fetch.
- The inline helper answers a `get` request only when the requested host equals `OSTRA_GIT_HOST`, with or without a port. The reason is that a remote rewritten by `url.*.insteadOf` in the repository config must never receive the token. A test checks that `evil.example` gets no answer.
- `http.proxy=` and `http.sslVerify=true` make the token go straight to the remote over verified TLS, whatever proxy or certificate setting the repository config names.
- The user name is the saved `username`, or `x-access-token` (`DEFAULT_TOKEN_USER`). GitHub and GitLab accept any user name with a personal access token.
- The token is in `OSTRA_GIT_PASSWORD` and not in the argument list.

### An ssh credential

Ostra writes the private key to a temporary folder `ostra-git-*` under the `tmp` folder of the data directory. It does not use the shared temp folder. The comment gives the reason: the data directory is owner-only and the sandbox hides it. The file `id` is created with `create_new` and mode `0600`, and it ends with one line break. Then Ostra sets `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` to this text, with the key path in single quotes:

`ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -i '<path>'`

`GitAuth` holds the temporary folder. Ostra deletes the folder and the key file when the `GitAuth` value ends.

### No credential

If no credential matches, Ostra sets `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` to `ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new`, but only when the environment has no `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`. Git can then use the ssh keys and agent of the user.

### Run git

`run_git` starts the git process and returns the last output lines. It does these steps:

1. If a folder is given, it removes a planted `commondir` from the git directories there with `repair_git_dirs`. The reason is that a planted `commondir` gives the command the config of another repository. That config can hold a credential helper or an SSH command that a push or a pull runs.
2. It adds the git config overrides of [Project files, Git dock, and cloning](project-files-and-git.md), which also owns the clone and pull timeouts.
3. It starts git with no stdin, with `LC_ALL=C`, and with `kill_on_drop`.
4. It reads stdout and stderr together and keeps the last 12 lines (`TAIL_LINES`).
5. It replaces the secret in the kept lines with `***`. `clone` does the same for each progress line that it sends to the browser.

### What happens when

- **Git is not installed.** The error says `Install git on the machine that runs Ostra, because cloning and pulling run the git command.`
- **Git runs longer than its timeout.** Ostra stops it and returns `git did not finish within N minutes and was stopped.`
- **The secret has fewer than 4 bytes.** Ostra does not redact it. `GitAuth::redact` tests `s.len() >= 4`, which counts bytes and not characters. A secret of 2 or 3 multi-byte characters has 4 bytes or more, so Ostra still redacts it.
- **A clone fails.** `clear_failed` removes the new folder, or empties a folder that existed before the clone.
- **The key file cannot be written.** The error says `Could not prepare the SSH key`.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Saved git credentials | None | Sealed rows `git_credential:<id>` in `registry.db` | At the next git command | The credential list shows label, host, type, user name, and `has_secret` | Edit or delete the credential in the git credentials form, or call the routes above. |
| The `credential` field of a clone request | The best match for the URL | The clone request | For that clone | The clone form and the progress lines | Choose another credential, or the form default. |

## Keep the VAPID keys and push subscriptions

Web Push needs a key pair so that a push service accepts messages from one application server. The pair is the VAPID key pair (voluntary application server identification) on the curve P-256. `vapid_keys` in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` runs at start:

1. It reads the sealed row `vapid_private`.
2. If the bytes parse as a P-256 secret key, it uses them.
3. Otherwise it makes a new pair with `VapidKeys::generate` and stores the private bytes with `secret_set`.

If the row cannot be opened, because the master key changed, Ostra makes a new pair and the public key changes. The `Notifier` is built with these keys and the contact subject `mailto:ostra@localhost`.

### Subscribe a browser

`GET /api/info` returns the public key in `ServerInfo.vapid_public_key`. It is the uncompressed point of 65 bytes in URL-safe base64 with no padding. The browser code `enablePush` in `web/src/lib/push.ts` runs these steps:

1. It asks for the notification permission.
2. It reads the public key from `GET /api/info`.
3. It registers the service worker `/sw.js`.
4. It calls `reg.pushManager.getSubscription()` to get an existing subscription of the browser.
5. If the browser has no subscription, it calls `pushManager.subscribe` with `userVisibleOnly: true` and the public key as `applicationServerKey`.
6. It sends the endpoint and the keys `p256dh` and `auth` to `POST /api/push/subscribe`.

The server returns status 400 with `Push endpoints must use https.` if the endpoint does not start with `https://`. Otherwise it stores the subscription in the table `push_subscriptions`. The endpoint is the primary key, so a second request with the same endpoint updates the keys. The upsert in `add_push_subscription` also sets `workspace_id` to the new value. The route always passes `None`, so a repeat request clears any workspace scope, and each workspace sends to the subscription. The sealing does not cover this table. `p256dh` and `auth` are plain text in `registry.db`.

`disablePush` calls `unsubscribe` in the browser only. It does not call the server. The server row stays until a send gets the answer 404 or 410. `remove_workspace` deletes the subscriptions that are scoped to that workspace.

### Send a notice

The runner builds a notice for a new gate, a finished or failed session, a blocked phase, and the third containment signal. [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) owns those rules. [REST and WebSocket API](server-api.md) shows where the notice enters the server.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Runner
  participant Services
  participant Registry
  participant Notifier
  participant PushService
  Runner->>Services: notify Notice
  Services->>Services: return if notifications.push is false
  Services->>Registry: list_push_subscriptions
  Registry-->>Services: subscriptions
  Services->>Notifier: send subscription and Notification
  Notifier->>PushService: POST endpoint with encrypted body
  PushService-->>Notifier: HTTP status
  Notifier-->>Services: SendOutcome
  Services->>Registry: remove_push_subscription on Gone
```

`Services::notify` in `crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs` runs these steps:

1. It returns at once if `notifications.push` is `false`. It reads the setting at each notice.
2. It starts a background task, so the runner does not wait.
3. The task lists the subscriptions and keeps those with no workspace or with this workspace.
4. It makes the `Notification` with the title, the body, and the tag of the notice. The URL is `/w/<workspace>` followed by the URL of the notice.
5. It calls `Notifier::send` for each subscription, one after the other.
6. On `SendOutcome::Gone`, it removes the subscription. On `Failed`, it logs a warning with the status and the message. On an `Err`, it logs `push error`.

Ostra does not retry a failed message. The code does not shorten the notice text before it encrypts. A notice with more than 3993 bytes of JSON fails with `NotifyError::TooLarge`, and the task logs a warning.

### For the user

| Setting | Default | Stored in | Takes effect | Shows the state | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `notifications.push` | `true` | `workspace.toml`, table `[notifications]` | At the next notice | The workspace settings editor. Push failures show as warnings in the server log. | Set it to `false`. The workspace creation form can also set it. |
| Browser subscription | None | Table `push_subscriptions` in `registry.db` | At once | The browser site settings for notifications | Block the site in the browser, or call `disablePush`. The server row stays until the push service answers 404 or 410. |

The setting `notifications.push` is for each workspace, and the subscription is for the machine. [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) owns the workspace settings file.

## Encrypt and sign a Web Push message

The crate `ostra-notify` implements Web Push without OpenSSL. It follows RFC 8291 for the message encryption, RFC 8188 for the `aes128gcm` content coding, and RFC 8292 for the VAPID authentication. The code is in `crates/ostra-notify/src/lib.rs`. The reason for the encryption is that the push service sees the message in transit, and only the browser must read it.

### Encrypt the body

`encrypt_with` builds the body from the plain text, the browser public key `p256dh`, the browser secret `auth`, a sender key, and a 16-byte salt. `encrypt` calls it with a new sender key and a new random salt for each message. These steps run in order:

1. If the plain text has more than 3993 bytes (`MAX_PLAINTEXT`), return `NotifyError::TooLarge`. Push services accept at most 4096 bytes of body, and the limit leaves room for the header and the tag.
2. Parse `p256dh` as an uncompressed SEC1 point. A bad value returns `NotifyError::Key`.
3. Compute the ECDH secret of the sender key and the browser key.
4. Derive a 32-byte input key with HKDF-SHA-256. The salt is the `auth` secret. The info is `WebPush: info`, a zero byte, the browser public key, and the sender public key.
5. Derive a 16-byte content key and a 12-byte nonce with HKDF-SHA-256. The salt is the random salt, and the infos are `Content-Encoding: aes128gcm` and `Content-Encoding: nonce`, each with a zero byte at the end.
6. Append the byte `0x02` to the plain text. It is the padding delimiter of the last record.
7. Encrypt with AES-128-GCM.
8. Write the body: the salt (16 bytes), the record size as a 32-bit number in network byte order, the key id length (1 byte, 65), the sender public key, and the ciphertext.

```rust
let mut key_info = b"WebPush: info\0".to_vec();
key_info.extend_from_slice(ua_public);
key_info.extend_from_slice(&as_public);
let mut ikm = [0u8; 32];
hkdf_expand(auth_secret, ecdh.raw_secret_bytes(), &key_info, &mut ikm)?;
let mut cek = [0u8; 16];
hkdf_expand(salt, &ikm, b"Content-Encoding: aes128gcm\0", &mut cek)?;
```

`RECORD_SIZE` is 4096. One record holds the whole message. The test `rfc8291_test_vector` checks the output against the example of RFC 8291 Appendix A. Its constants are `PLAINTEXT`, `AS_PRIVATE`, `AS_PUBLIC`, `UA_PRIVATE`, `UA_PUBLIC`, `SALT`, `AUTH`, and `EXPECTED`. `encrypt_with` takes the sender key and the salt as arguments for this reason. The test `round_trip_with_fresh_keys` decrypts a body that `encrypt` made. `b64_decode` accepts URL-safe base64 with or without padding, because browsers produce either.

### Sign the request with VAPID

`VapidKeys::jwt` makes an ES256 token for the origin of the push service. The header is `{"typ":"JWT","alg":"ES256"}`. The claims are `aud`, `exp`, and `sub`. The signature is a 64-byte ECDSA P-256 signature in URL-safe base64. `VapidKeys::authorization` returns `vapid t=<jwt>, k=<public key>`.

- `aud` is the origin of the endpoint: scheme, host, and port if given. `origin_of` returns `NotifyError::Endpoint` for a scheme other than `https` or `http`.
- `exp` is the current time plus 12 hours (`JWT_TTL`).
- `sub` is the subject `mailto:ostra@localhost`.

### Send the request

`Notifier::send` decodes the keys, encrypts the JSON of the `Notification`, and posts the body to the endpoint. The client timeout is 20 seconds. The request has these headers:

| Header | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `Authorization` | `vapid t=<jwt>, k=<public key>` |
| `Content-Encoding` | `aes128gcm` |
| `Content-Type` | `application/octet-stream` |
| `TTL` | `86400` seconds (`PUSH_TTL_SECS`, 24 hours) |
| `Urgency` | `high` |

The `Notification` has the fields `title`, `body`, `url`, and `tag`. Notifications with the same tag replace each other. The service worker `web/public/sw.js` shows the notification and opens the `url` when the user clicks it. [Ostra overview and first run](overview.md) describes the worker.

`send` maps the answer to `SendOutcome`:

| Answer | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Status 200 to 299 | `Delivered` |
| Status 404 or 410 | `Gone`. The caller removes the subscription. |
| Another status | `Failed` with the status and the first 500 characters of the answer body |
| Network error or timeout | `Failed` with no status and the error text |

The errors of `NotifyError` are `Key`, `TooLarge`, `Encrypt`, `Endpoint`, and `Json`. `send` returns them as `Err` before it sends anything.

## What this design does not guarantee

- **It does not protect a running Ostra.** The master key and the plain credentials are in the memory of the process. A git token is in the environment of each git process that uses it.
- **It does not protect against the key and the file together.** A reader that has the registry file and the master key can read every sealed row.
- **It does not recover a lost key.** Credentials that a lost key sealed cannot be opened. The user must enter them again.
- **It does not seal everything in the registry.** Only the keys of `SECRET_KEYS` are sealed. The push keys `p256dh` and `auth`, the workspace list, and the sign-in rows are plain text.
- **It does not stop an agent from reading the files if the sandbox is off.** The data directory has mode `0700` on Unix, and the sandbox and the policy hide it from agents. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md) and [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md).
- **It does not verify the host key of a new ssh host.** `StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new` accepts the key of a host that is not yet known.
- **It does not redact every leak.** Redaction replaces only the exact secret text, and only if the secret has 4 bytes or more. `GitAuth::redact` tests `s.len() >= 4`, which counts bytes, so a secret of 2 or 3 multi-byte characters is still redacted.
- **It does not force TLS for provider URLs.** A saved `http://` base URL is valid.

sections.title: REST and WebSocket API
sections.summary: The route groups of /api, the types that ts-rs exports to the console, the /ws channels and their limits, the nav search and activity routes, and the guard middleware.
sections.body:
## What the server API does

The console must read the state of Ostra, change it, and see changes when sessions run for minutes. Without one fixed contract, the Rust server and the TypeScript console drift apart. The server API gives that contract in three parts:

- REST routes under `/api`, which read state and start actions.
- One WebSocket at `/ws` for each browser tab, which pushes live updates.
- The `guard` middleware, which checks every request before a handler runs.

The router, the `guard` middleware, and the handlers live in [crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs). The request and response types live in [crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs](crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs). The socket lives in [crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs). The Sessions tree, the search, and the activity summary live in [crates/ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs), [crates/ostra-server/src/nav/search.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/nav/search.rs), and [crates/ostra-server/src/nav/activity.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/nav/activity.rs).

This page stops before the Files and Git routes. [Project files, Git dock, and cloning](project-files-and-git.md) explains them. The table in `## Route groups of /api` names the owner page of every other group.

### How the router is built

The function `router(app)` builds the `axum::Router` in this order:

1. It adds each route.
2. It merges `bridge::internal_routes()`, the routes under `/internal/` for harness executions.
3. It sets `assets::static_handler` as the fallback.
4. It adds `guard` as a layer.

Because the layer comes last, `guard` runs for every route, for the fallback, and for the internal routes. The function `run` in `app.rs` calls `axum::serve(listener, router.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<SocketAddr>())`. This wrapper gives `guard` the address of the peer.

The fallback returns status 404 for an unknown path under `api/`, `internal/`, or `assets/`. It also returns 404 for a root-level name with a file extension other than `.html`, such as `/favicon.ico`. Every other unknown path returns `index.html`, because the console has client routes such as `/w/<workspace>/settings`. An unknown `/api/` path still needs a valid cookie first, because `guard` runs before the fallback. [Ostra overview and first run](overview.md) explains the embedded web build.

## Route groups of /api

Each route maps to one handler function in [crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs). A handler reads the path, the query, or the JSON body. It calls the workspace runtime or the engine, then returns `Result<Json<T>, ApiErr>`. The JSON types come from `ostra-core`, and `## Request and response shapes from ts-rs` explains them. Some routes return status 204 with no body.

| Group | Routes | Shapes | Owner page |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Server info | `GET /api/info` | `ServerInfo` (version and VAPID public key) | This page |
| Sign-in | `POST /api/auth/exchange`, `GET /api/auth/sessions`, `DELETE /api/auth/sessions/{id}`, `POST /api/auth/sessions/revoke-others`, `POST /api/auth/signout` | `AuthExchange`, `SignInSession`, `RevokedSignIns` | [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md) |
| First run and machine | `GET /api/onboarding`, `POST /api/onboarding/complete`, `GET /api/environment`, `PATCH /api/providers/{name}`, `POST /api/harnesses/{harness}/setup` | `OnboardingState`, `EnvironmentStatus`, `ProviderStatus`, `HarnessSetupTerminal` | [Workspace, settings, and setup screens](web-workspace-and-setup.md) |
| Git credentials | `GET` and `POST /api/git/credentials`, `PATCH` and `DELETE /api/git/credentials/{id}` | `GitCredentialView` list | [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md) |
| Push | `POST /api/push/subscribe` | Status 204 | [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md) |
| Workspaces | `GET` and `POST /api/workspaces`, `POST /api/workspaces/validate`, `GET`, `PATCH`, and `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}`, `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/validate`, `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/settings/fix`, `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/approve`, `GET` and `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}/ui` | `WorkspaceSummary`, `WorkspaceDetail`, `ValidationIssue` list, `WorkspaceUiState` | [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) |
| Projects | `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects` (import), `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}`, `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/init`, `PUT /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/commands` | `ImportProject`, `WorkspaceDetail`, `SessionSummary`, `Commands` | [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) and [Project init and skills](init-and-skills.md) |
| Skills | `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/skills`, `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/skills/{name}`, `POST .../skills/{name}/adopt`, `GET .../projects/{key}/harness-skill` | `ProjectSkills`, `SkillDoc`, `SkillSave`, `SkillAdopt` | [Project init and skills](init-and-skills.md) |
| MCP servers | `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp`, `POST .../mcp/{name}/refresh`, `POST .../mcp/{name}/login`, `POST .../mcp/{name}/logout`, `GET /mcp/oauth/callback` | `McpServerStatus`, `McpLogin` | [External MCP servers](mcp-gateway.md) |
| Lesson memory | `GET`, `PATCH`, and `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/memory` | `Lesson`, `LessonEdit` | [Storage: databases and lesson memory](storage.md) |
| Sessions | `GET` and `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/sessions`, `GET /api/sessions/{id}`, `GET /api/sessions/{id}/events`, `POST /api/sessions/{id}/yolo`, `.../amend`, `.../pause`, `.../resume`, `.../stop`, `GET /api/sessions/{id}/diff` | `CreateSession`, `SessionSummary`, `SessionDetail`, `StoredEvent` list, `DiffFile` list | [Event log, runner, and limits](event-log-and-runner.md) |
