The prefix `/api/workspaces/{ws}` is shortened to `...` in some cells. Two paths sit outside `/api`. The MCP OAuth callback at `/mcp/oauth/callback` (the constant `crate::mcp::CALLBACK_PATH`) has no cookie check. The authorization server redirects the browser there, and the redirect is a cross-site navigation, so the browser does not send the `SameSite=Strict` cookie. The single-use `state` value authenticates the callback instead. The socket at `/ws` counts as an API path for `guard`.

### Find the workspace from an ID

A session, gate, execution, or decision ID has no workspace in its URL. The functions `ws_of_session`, `ws_of_gate`, `ws_of_execution`, and `ws_of_decision` ask each open workspace database in turn. They return the first workspace that holds the row. If no workspace holds it, the route returns 404 with a message such as `No session <id>.` The cost is one database lookup for each open workspace.

A route with `{ws}` in its path calls `ws(&app, &id)`. This function reads the map of open workspaces and returns 404 with `No workspace <id>.` when the ID is not there. The function `ws_of_execution` is public because [crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs) also uses it to read a stored terminal transcript.

### Work that blocks workspace removal

A removal must not run when a session starts. Each workspace runtime has a `work` lock (`RwLock<bool>`) for this rule. These groups show how a route uses it:

- **Takes the shared lock with `start_work`:** `POST .../projects/{key}/init`, `POST .../sessions`, `POST /api/executions/{id}/inspect`, and `POST .../ask`. The handler holds the lock until it returns, so a removal cannot pass its busy check in between. If the workspace is in removal, the route returns 404 with `No workspace <id>.`
- **Takes the exclusive lock with `try_write` (Rule W4):** `POST .../artifacts/move`, `DELETE .../artifacts`, and `DELETE .../docs/{book}`. No session starts between the busy check and the move or the removal. If a start holds the shared lock, the route returns 409 with `Try again in a moment, because work is starting in this workspace.`
- **Tries the shared lock with `try_read`:** `POST .../clone` and `POST .../projects/{key}/pull`. Both routes call the function `git::claim` in [crates/ostra-server/src/git.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/git.rs), through `git::clone` and `git::pull`. The function `claim` calls `w.work.try_read()`. The function `start_work` holds a shared read guard (`w.work.read()`), so a start does not make `claim` fail. The call `try_read` fails only while a writer holds the lock. The writers are `try_write` in `remove_project` and `retire`, the artifact move and delete routes, and the docs delete route. `claim` also fails when the `deleted` flag is true. In both cases `claim` returns `GitError::Busy`, and the route returns 409 through `git_err`. The text of `GitError::Busy` is the constant `STARTING`, which names starting work, but the cause is an exclusive holder or a removal. The pull route also returns 409 before it calls `git::pull` when a session works in the project.
- **Has its own busy check:** `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}` and `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}`. Live or starting work gives status 409. The test `live_or_starting_work_blocks_removing_a_project_or_the_workspace` pins this rule.
- **Takes no lock:** every route that the groups above do not name.

[Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) explains the removal itself.

### Request body limits

Axum limits a request body to 2 MB by default. Four routes set another limit or read a body with a cap:

| Route | Limit | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST .../uploads` | `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` plus 1024 bytes (25 MiB plus 1 KiB) | The route accepts files up to the upload cap. |
| `GET`, `POST`, `DELETE .../artifacts` | The artifact size cap plus 1024 bytes (25 MiB plus 1 KiB) | The route accepts files up to the artifact cap. [Workspace artifacts and uploads](artifacts-and-uploads.md) owns the cap. |
| `GET` and `PUT .../projects/{key}/file` | 8 times `TEXT_CAP` (8 MiB) | JSON escaping can double a text at the edit cap, which is past the 2 MB default. |
| `POST /api/auth/exchange` | 64 KiB, read by the handler | The body holds one token. |

### Downloads

The function `attachment(name, bytes)` builds each download response. It sets `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` and `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename*=UTF-8''<name>`. It percent-encodes each byte of the name except letters, digits, and the characters `-._~`. The RFC 5987 form keeps any character in a file name.

The route `GET /api/artifacts` opens a file only if it lies inside the sessions folder of an open workspace. `session_file` canonicalizes the path first. A path outside returns 403 with `Only files inside a session directory can be opened here.` The route sends no content for a file that is not UTF-8 text or is larger than `ARTIFACT_LIMIT` (4 MiB). It sets `binary` to true, and the console offers a download. [Workspace artifacts and uploads](artifacts-and-uploads.md) owns the other artifact rules.

### What happens when

- **A tab closes during a clone, a pull, or a Git dock command.** The handler runs the work in its own `tokio::spawn` task, so git does not stop halfway. This rule avoids a partial checkout.
- **A request needs the machine check and the check is old.** `create_workspace`, `validate_new_workspace`, and `get_workspace` call `refresh_env`. It detects the environment again when `env.stale()` is true.
- **A cost request has a bad `since` value.** `GET .../cost` returns 400. The message says that `since` must be an RFC 3339 time such as `2026-09-24T00:00:00Z`.
- **A push subscription has an endpoint that is not https.** `POST /api/push/subscribe` returns 400 with `Push endpoints must use https.`
- **A book ID has characters outside the allowed set.** The `docs/{book}` routes return 400. The test `workspace_books_are_listed_read_and_deleted` sends the ID `..%2Fx`.
- **A session diff names many files.** `GET /api/sessions/{id}/diff` returns at most 200 files. It skips each file that resolves outside the project, because an agent can leave a symlink that points out.
- **A memory list is long.** `GET .../memory` returns at most 500 lessons for each call. `PATCH` with no `id` records a new lesson with the source `user`.

## Error shape and status codes

Each error body has the shape `ApiError`: `error` (a message) and `issues` (a list of `ValidationIssue`, each with `path` and `message`). The list is empty unless the error names fields. The type `ApiErr` holds a status and a body, and it implements `IntoResponse`. Handlers build it with these constructors:

| Constructor | Status | Message and issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ApiErr::new(status, message)` | Any | The message, with no issues |
| `ApiErr::bad` | 400 | The message |
| `ApiErr::not_found` | 404 | The message |
| `ApiErr::conflict_on(field, message)` | 409 | The message, with one issue whose `path` is the request field that no longer matches the server state |
| `ApiErr::invalid(issues)` | 422 | `The settings have problems. Fix them and save again.` |
| `ApiErr::invalid_with(message, issues)` | 422 | The given message and issues |
| `ApiErr::invalid_request(issues, retry)` | 422 | With one issue, its message. With more, `Fix these problems and <retry> again:` and the messages joined by a space |

The constructor `invalid_request` puts the issues in the message too, for clients that show only `error`. The function `invalid_workspace` calls it with the text `create the workspace`.

The code maps lower-level errors to statuses in these places:

| --- | --- |

| `EngineError::Invalid` | 409 |
| `EngineError::Ended` | 409 |
| `EngineError::Store`, `StoreError` | 500 |

| `GitError::Git` | 502 |

## Request and response shapes from ts-rs

The server and the console must agree on each JSON shape. Hand-written copies of the types drift apart over time. Ostra writes the TypeScript types from the Rust types instead. Each type in `ostra-core` has `#[derive(TS)]` and `#[ts(export)]`. The crate `ts-rs` (version 12) writes one `.ts` file for each exported type.

The file [.cargo/config.toml](.cargo/config.toml) sets two environment variables for every cargo run:

- `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` is `web/src/api/gen`, relative to the repository. The generated files are in git, and the console imports them with lines such as `import type { Heading } from "../../api/gen/Heading"`.
- `TS_RS_LARGE_INT` is `number`. A 64-bit integer becomes the TypeScript type `number`.

The `ts-rs` tests write the files when they run. The test `export_bindings` in `crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs` is empty on purpose. It gives one stable command to regenerate the files: `cargo test -p ostra-core export_bindings`. The command `cargo test --workspace` writes them too.

> Run the export command after each change to an exported type. The console imports the committed files, so its types stay old until you regenerate them.

### Rules for the shapes

- A field uses its Rust name in `snake_case`, for example `active_sessions`.
- `ClientMsg` and `ServerMsg` use `#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "snake_case")]`. The `type` field names the variant, for example `session_event`.
- A plain enum such as `SearchKind` uses `rename_all = "snake_case"`.
- `#[serde(default)]` marks a request field that a client can leave out. `CreateSession` uses it for `options`, `projects`, `files`, and `uploads`.
- `#[ts(type = "string")]` forces a `PathBuf` to `string`, and `#[ts(type = "number")]` forces a `u64` such as `Artifact.size` to `number`.
- Other modules of `ostra-core` also export types. The console imports `Book`, `Effort`, and `Severity` from the same folder.

## The /ws socket and its channels

A console tab needs many live streams: the events of a session, the deltas of an execution, a terminal, and updates of a workspace. One connection for each stream multiplies the connections and the sign-in checks. The route `GET /ws` gives each tab one socket. The socket carries all streams, and a channel name tells which stream a message belongs to.

### Connect

The function `handler` in [crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs) reads the `Cookie` header and upgrades the connection. The upgrade passes `guard` first, so the origin, fetch, and cookie checks apply. `## Security middleware: guard and response headers` explains them. The handler sets `max_message_size` and `max_frame_size` to `MAX_MESSAGE` (1 MiB). Then `run` owns the socket until it ends.

The function `run` makes three subscriptions and then one cookie check:

1. `app.hub.subscribe()` subscribes to `app.hub`, the broadcast channel of engine notices.
2. `app.push.subscribe()` subscribes to `app.push`, the broadcast channel of messages that the server itself starts.
3. `app.auth.subscribe_revoked()` subscribes to the revoke channel of sign-ins.

After the three subscriptions, `run` checks the cookie once with `app.auth.check_cookie`. A revoke that happened between the upgrade and the subscription went to no one. A revoke removes the cookie before it broadcasts, so this check sees it.

### Channels

A socket receives no message until it subscribes to a channel. A channel is a text name. The server stores the name and does not check that the ID in it exists.

| Channel | Messages that it carries | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `session:<id>` | `session_event`, `session_updated` | Hub |
| `execution:<id>` | `execution_delta`, `execution_status` | Hub |
| `term:<execution>` | Binary terminal frames | PTY registry |
| `workspace:<id>` | `workspace_updated`, `session_updated`, `tree_patch`, `activity`, `project_fs_changed`, `git_progress` | Hub and push |
| `home` | `session_updated` of every workspace, `workspace_updated`, `harness_status` | Hub and push |

When a socket subscribes to `home`, the server first sends a `harness_status` message with the current harness list from the machine check. The server sends it again when a harness setup ends.

The diagram shows two paths. An engine notice goes through the hub. The Sessions tree update goes through the push channel after a tick.

The terminal bytes are not JSON. They use binary frames, and `### Terminal streaming` explains them.

### Terminal streaming

The channel `term:<execution>` streams the screen of a harness execution. When a socket subscribes, the server starts the task `stream_terminal` for it. The task runs this loop:

1. If the execution has no live PTY, it reads the stored transcript once and sends it as one frame. The transcript is read-only. A harness execution that ended has such a file.
2. It waits until the PTY registry inserts a PTY for the execution. This step covers a run whose PTY does not exist yet.
3. It sends the current screen as one frame, then each chunk that the PTY produces.
4. If the stream lags, it starts again from a fresh screen. If the PTY closes, it waits for another PTY.

A second `subscribe` to the same `term:` channel stops the old stream and starts a new one. This resends the screen. The function `frame(execution, bytes)` builds each binary frame:

```rust
fn frame(execution: &str, bytes: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    let id = execution.as_bytes();
    let n = id.len().min(255);
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(1 + n + bytes.len());
    out.push(n as u8);
    out.extend_from_slice(&id[..n]);
    out.extend_from_slice(bytes);
    out
}
```

The first byte is the length of the execution ID, at most 255. The ID follows, then the terminal bytes. A client reads the first byte, takes that many bytes as the ID, and treats the rest as terminal output. The test `terminal_streams_over_the_socket` checks that the first frame of a stream is a screen snapshot that starts with the reset sequence `ESC c`. [Harness executors](harness-executors.md) explains the PTY, the registry, and the transcript.

### Code hint requests

The Files editor sends `code_complete`, `code_signature`, and `code_navigate` when a user types. Each message carries the unsaved `text` of the file and a cursor position. Lines are 1-based. Columns are 0-based UTF-16 code units. The server answers with the same `id`, so the client can match the answer.

The socket keeps one task for each kind, under the keys `hint:complete`, `hint:signature`, and `hint:navigate`. A newer request of a kind aborts the older task. The older request then never gets an answer, because the cursor moved and its answer has no use. Answers wait in a queue of 8 (`HINT_QUEUE`) until the loop sends them. If the workspace is unknown, the answer has `result` null and `error` set to `No workspace <id>.` [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) explains how the server computes the hints.

### Socket limits

| Constant | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_MESSAGE` | 1 MiB | The largest client message and frame. Terminal pastes are the large ones. |
| `MAX_TERM_INPUT` | 64 KiB | The largest `data` of one `term_input`. One paste cannot fill the write queue of the PTY on its own. |
| `MAX_CHANNELS` | 256 | The most channels for one socket. |
| `TERM_QUEUE` | 64 | Binary frames that wait for one socket. A slow socket makes its PTY streams lag and resync. |
| `HINT_QUEUE` | 8 | Hint answers that wait for one socket. |
| `HINT_COMPLETE`, `HINT_SIGNATURE`, `HINT_NAVIGATE` | `hint:complete`, `hint:signature`, `hint:navigate` | The key of the one request in flight for each kind. |
| `pty::MAX_COLS`, `pty::MAX_ROWS` | 1000 and 500 | The range of `term_resize`. A zero or a larger value gets an error. |
| Hub capacity | 8192 | Notices that the broadcast channel `App.hub` holds for a slow socket. |
| Push capacity | 1024 | Messages that the broadcast channel `App.push` holds for a slow socket. |
| Close code | 4401 | The code of the close frame with the reason `Signed out`. |

### What happens when

- **A message is not valid JSON or has an unknown type.** The server sends `error` with `Unreadable message.` and keeps the socket open.
- **The browser sends a binary frame.** The server ignores it.
- **A message is larger than 1 MiB.** The library returns an error. The loop ends and the server closes the socket.
- **A socket subscribes to a new channel at 256 channels.** The server sends `error` with `Too many subscriptions on one connection. Unsubscribe from channels you no longer show.` A `subscribe` to a channel that the socket already has still works.
- **`term_input` is larger than 64 KiB.** The server sends `error` with `Terminal input is limited to 64 KiB per message. Paste in smaller parts.` The input does not reach the PTY.
- **`term_input` names an execution with no PTY.** The server ignores it and sends no reply.
- **A PTY write fails.** The server sends `error` with `The harness is not reading terminal input right now, so the input was dropped.`
- **`term_resize` has `cols` or `rows` of 0, `cols` above 1000, or `rows` above 500.** The server sends `error` with `Terminal size is out of range.`
- **A socket falls behind on the hub or the push channel.** The server sends `error` with `lagged`. The page fetches its REST snapshot again.
- **A terminal stream falls behind.** The stream sends a fresh screen and continues.
- **The sign-in ends.** The loop checks the cookie on the `RECHECK` interval and listens to the revoke channel. A revoke from this server closes the socket at once. A revoke from the command line, in another process, closes it within the recheck window. Both close with code 4401. [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md) owns the `RECHECK` value and the revoke rules.
- **The socket ends.** The `Drop` of `Streams` aborts every terminal and hint task of the socket, in every case.

## Sessions tree and live tree pushes

The Sessions tree in the console lists each session with its runs and artifacts. A running execution sends many deltas each second, and most deltas do not change the tree node. The struct `Nav` in [crates/ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs) marks nodes as dirty when a notice arrives, so the server does not rebuild a node for each delta. One ticker rebuilds the dirty nodes and pushes only the nodes that changed.

### The node

A `TreeSession` is one node. It holds the session ID, title, request, kind, status, `open_gates`, `cost_usd`, `updated_at`, a list of `TreeGroup` values, and a list of artifacts. A `TreeGroup` holds the runs of one agent on one project, with the key `<agent>:<project key>`. A `TreeRun` holds the execution ID, `run_label`, status, stream, and `summary`. A `tree_patch` message carries a whole node, and the console replaces the node with the same ID.

### Mark, rebuild, and push

1. `App::attach` starts one task for each workspace. The task reads each engine notice and calls `nav.observe(workspace, notice)`.
2. `observe` marks sessions and executions as dirty, as the table below shows.
3. The function `nav::run` ticks every `TREE_TICK` (250 ms). It uses `MissedTickBehavior::Delay`, so a slow flush delays the next tick and does not cause a burst. On each tick, it runs `flush` for every workspace inside `spawn_blocking`.
4. `flush` takes the dirty sets. It maps each dirty execution to its session, first through the cached nodes and then through the database.
5. `flush` rebuilds each dirty node with `engine.tree_session`, then calls `index_artifacts`. It compares the node with the cached node. If they differ, it stores the node and sends a `tree_patch` on `workspace:<id>`.
6. The loop ends when the `Weak<App>` cannot upgrade, which means the app is gone. If a flush fails, the loop logs `navigation flush failed` and continues.

| Notice | What `observe` marks |
| --- | --- |
| `Event` | The session and the activity summary |
| `SessionUpdated` | The session and the activity summary |
| `ExecutionStatus` | The execution and the activity summary |
| `Delta` of kind `ToolCall` or `Status` | The execution and the activity summary. These deltas change the summary line of the run. |
| `Delta` of another kind | Nothing |
| `ProjectsChanged` | Nothing |

The hub forwarder calls `nav.lagged(workspace)` when it misses notices. This marks every session as dirty, so the next tick rebuilds the whole tree. `App::delete_workspace` calls `nav.forget(id)` and drops the state of that workspace.

### Read the whole tree

The route `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/tree` calls `Nav::tree` inside `spawn_blocking`. The function lists the sessions from the database. It reuses a cached node for each session that is not dirty, and it rebuilds each other node. If the workspace is in the all-dirty state, it ignores the cache. A node that it builds for the first time, and that is not dirty, goes into the cache. A dirty node stays out of the cache, so the next tick still pushes it. The result is sorted by `updated_at`, newest first, then by ID. A session whose node fails to build is left out.

### Index artifacts for search

The function `index_artifacts` runs each time a node is built. For each artifact with an absolute path, it stores the file name and each Markdown heading in the workspace database, so that search finds the artifact. It skips a file when the stored label and modification time match. It reads the headings of a file up to 4 MiB and indexes a larger file by its label and file name only. If the store fails, the server logs `indexing <path> for search: <error>`. [Workspace artifacts and uploads](artifacts-and-uploads.md) owns the artifact rules.

### What happens when

- **Many deltas arrive in 250 ms.** The server rebuilds the node once at the next tick. A patch for one session goes out at most 4 times each second.
- **A rebuilt node equals the cached node.** The server sends no message.
- **The engine channel lags.** `lagged` marks everything dirty, and the next tick rebuilds every session.
- **A workspace never had a notice.** `flush` returns at once for it, because it has no state.
- **An agent writes an artifact.** The index catches up the next time the node is built, because agents write artifacts through their tools.

## Workspace search

A user looks for a thing by a few letters. The thing can be a session, a run, an artifact, a file, a project, a lesson, or a setting. The route `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/search?q=&limit=` returns one ranked list across all seven kinds. The code is in [crates/ostra-server/src/nav/search.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/nav/search.rs). The agent code tools use a separate usage search, and [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) explains it.

### How a query runs

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Q["GET search with q and limit"] --> E{"Query empty after trim?"}
  E -- yes --> R["recent: newest sessions"]
  E -- no --> S1["rank_static: projects and setting keys"]
  E -- no --> S2["rank_files: file name index of each project"]
  E -- no --> S3["blocking task: rank_tree, rank_text, rank_lessons"]
  S1 --> M["merge: sort, keep best hit per id, cut to limit"]
  S2 --> M
  S3 --> M
  R --> O["SearchResults"]
  M --> O
```

The function `search` clamps `limit` to the range 1 to 200. The default is 50. It makes a `Needle` from the query. The `Needle` trims the query, makes it lowercase, and splits it into words. If the query is empty, the route returns the newest sessions, ordered by `updated_at`. Their scores start at 1.0 and fall by 0.001 for each place.

For a query with text, the function starts the blocking task first. The task reads the Sessions tree and the databases, so it runs when the function awaits the file indexes. The function then merges all hits.

### Sources of hits

| Kind | Source | Match against | Score change | `id` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `session` | Full-text index of the workspace database (`search_text`, `TEXT_ROWS` is 200) | Title, and the request text at 0.95 | Plus 0.04, minus 0.0001 for each place in the index order | `session:<id>` |
| `execution` | Sessions tree | Agent, run label, and both together | Plus 0.02 | `exec:<id>` |
| `artifact` | Sessions tree, and the full-text index | Label, file name at 0.95, and headings at 0.95 | Plus 0.03 | `artifact:<absolute path>` |
| `file` | File name index of each project | Path, by `file_score` | None | `file:<project key>:<relative path>` |
| `project` | Project list | Key, and folder name at 0.9 | Plus 0.03 | `project:<key>` |
| `lesson` | Lesson memory of each project, `LESSONS_PER_PROJECT` is 20 | Lesson text, and area at 0.9 | Minus 0.0001 for each place | `lesson:<project key>:<lesson id>` |
| `setting` | The list of setting keys in `SETTING_KEYS` | Key, last part of the key at 0.95, and description at 0.85 | None | `setting:<dotted key>` |

The `setting` kind searches the setting keys and their descriptions only. [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) explains the settings files and the keys.

A factor such as 0.95 multiplies the score. The bonus values put a session above a run above a file when the match quality is equal. A score can pass 1.0 because of a bonus. Scores compare across kinds only inside one response.

A hit that the full-text index found by word prefix can be a match that the in-memory scorer cannot place. Such a hit gets the score `INDEX_ONLY` (0.45) before the bonus. For lessons, the search opens a project memory database only if its file exists. Opening a store creates its file, and a search must not write into a project.

The label of a session is its title. If the title is empty, the label is the request, cut by `clip`. The function `clip` calls `summary_line` and keeps 80 characters (`HINT_CHARS`).

### How the text score works

The function `Needle::text_score` returns the best match level that applies, minus a length penalty:

```rust
let base = if h == n {
    1.0                       // equal, ignoring case
} else if h.starts_with(n) {
    0.9                       // starts with the query
} else if find_at_word(h, n) {
    0.8                       // the query starts a word
} else if find(h, n).is_some() {
    0.65                      // the query is inside
} else if self.words.len() > 1 && /* every word is inside */ {
    0.55
} else if subsequence(h, n) {
    0.3                       // the letters appear in order
} else {
    return None;
};
Some(base - length_penalty(h.len(), n.len()))
```

The length penalty is `0.0005` for each extra byte of text, up to `0.05`. A shorter text ranks first among equal matches. The function `file_score` uses a different ladder for a project-relative path:

| Match | Base score |
| --- | --- |
| Exact file name | 1.0 |
| File name starts with the query | 0.88 |
| File name contains the query | 0.74 |
| Path contains the query | 0.6 |
| Letters in order inside the file name | 0.4 |
| Letters in order inside the path | 0.3 |

The length penalty applies to the whole path. The function `rank_files` keeps the best `limit` files of one project. It uses `select_nth_unstable_by` to avoid a full sort of a large index. A test ranks 50,000 paths and requires less than 50 ms for each query in a release build and less than 500 ms in a debug build.

The function `merge` sorts hits by score, highest first. It breaks a tie with the shorter label, then with the ID. It keeps the best hit for each `id`, so an artifact that came from two sources appears once. Then it cuts the list to `limit`.

### For the user

| Parameter | Default | Stored where | Takes effect | What shows the state | How to change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `q` | Empty | Not stored. The request carries it. | At once | `SearchResults.items` | Send another query. An empty query returns the newest sessions. |
| `limit` | 50 | Not stored. The request carries it. | At once | The length of `items` | Send a `limit` from 1 to 200. The server clamps any other value. |

### What happens when

- **A project has no file index.** `search` skips that project and returns the other hits.
- **A project has no lesson database.** The search skips it and creates no file.
- **The blocking task fails.** The route returns 500 with the error text.
- **A query has no match.** The route returns an empty `items` list.

## Workspace activity

The status bar and the workspace menu show what runs now, what waits for a person, and what the work cost. The route `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/activity` returns a `WorkspaceActivity` for this. The function `activity::build` in [crates/ostra-server/src/nav/activity.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/nav/activity.rs) makes it, and `Nav::flush` pushes it as an `activity` message.

The fields of `WorkspaceActivity` are:

- `running`: each running execution, oldest start first. It includes side-panel answers, which have no session. Each item has `id`, `session`, `agent`, `project`, `run_label`, `stream`, and `summary`. The label comes from `engine.run_labels` for the session. If that has no entry, the label is the stored `run_label`.
- `open_gates`: each gate with no answer, oldest first. Each item has `id`, `session`, `session_title`, `title`, `kind` (the payload kind, for example `plan_approval` or `permission`), and `opened_at`.
- `spend_today_usd` and `spend_week_usd`: the sum of `cost_usd` of the executions that started at or after the window start.
- `today_since` and `week_since`: the start of each window, in UTC.

### Spend windows

The function `windows(now)` finds the start of each window in the time zone of the server. The route calls it with `chrono::Local::now()`, so the windows follow the clock of the server and not the clock of the browser. The day window starts at local midnight today. The week window starts at local midnight six days earlier, so the week is today and the six days before it.

If a daylight saving change skips a midnight, the start moves to the first hour that exists. If that fails, the start is the current time. The test `windows_start_at_local_midnight` checks a zone east of UTC, a zone west of UTC, and a week that crosses a month end. A client can pass `week_since` as the `since` parameter of `GET .../cost`. The cost report then covers the same week. [Model providers and pricing](providers-and-pricing.md) explains the cost report.

### When the server pushes activity

Each notice that `observe` marks sets the activity-dirty flag. `flush` builds the summary only if the flag is set and at least `ACTIVITY_GAP` (500 ms) passed since the last build. So the server sends at most 2 `activity` messages each second for a workspace. It sends a message only if the new summary differs from the last one. If the build fails, the server drops that update and waits for the next notice, because the flag is already clear.

## How the engine calls back into the server

The engine does not know the server. It calls a `Services` trait, and `ServerServices` in [crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs) implements it for one workspace. [Architecture and crate map](architecture.md) explains the trait. The struct holds the shared state, the workspace root, and the workspace ID. A REST handler starts an engine call, and the engine uses `ServerServices` to reach settings, executors, judges, and push. Each method does this:

| Method | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `global()` | Returns the global config from the shared state. |
| `workspace()` | Reads `workspace.toml` and applies the folder-file approvals with `trust::effective`. If the file does not load, it uses `WorkspaceSettings::seeded("workspace")`. |
| `executor(kind)` | Returns the native executor, or asks the harness registry for a harness executor. A harness can be missing, so the result can be `None`. |
| `factory()` | Returns `AgentsFactory`, which builds each spawn. |
| `judge(route, system, user, schema, effort)` | Finds the provider for `route.model`, calls `ostra_providers::structured`, and returns the value with its usage. An error becomes a string. |
| `notify(notice)` | Does nothing if `notifications.push` is false. Otherwise it spawns a task that sends a Web Push message to each subscription. |
| `protected_paths()` | Returns the shared protected paths, `workspace.toml`, and the workspace database. |
| `command_approved(project, command)` | Checks the format command approval with `trust::format_approved`. |
| `add_allow_rule(rule)` | Adds a permission rule to the workspace settings and saves the workspace file. A save error is logged. |

The permission rules that `add_allow_rule` writes belong to the policy layer, and [Policy engine and containment](policy-engine.md) explains them.

The push task builds a `Notification` with the title, body, and tag of the notice. The URL is `/w/<workspace>` followed by the URL of the notice. It sends to each subscription that has no workspace or has this workspace. If the push service says that a subscription is gone, the task removes it. Other failures are logged as warnings. [Secrets, credentials, and Web Push](secrets-and-push.md) explains the encryption and the keys. [Judge calls and YOLO mode](judges-and-decisions.md) explains the judge calls. [Workspaces, settings, and routing](workspaces-and-settings.md) explains the folder-file approvals.

## Security middleware: guard and response headers

The server listens on a local port. A page on another site, a page on another local port, or content that an agent wrote into a Markdown file can send requests to it. The function `guard` in [crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs) checks each request before a handler runs. It also adds security headers to each response, also to a refusal. [Browser sign-in and network binding](browser-auth.md) owns the rules for the sign-in token, the cookie, the allowed hosts, and the failure limit. This part shows the order of the checks, the paths that each check covers, and the headers.

### Order of the checks

`guard` sets `api` to true when the path starts with `/api/` or is `/ws`. It then runs these steps:

1. **Host.** If the `Host` header is not in the allowed list, the answer is 421 with `This host is not allowed.`
2. **Private name.** If the server uses a private host name and the request came to an IP name, a page load gets a 307 redirect that keeps the path and the query. An API request gets 421. A path under `/internal/` skips this step.
3. **Refusal.** The function `refusal` checks the peer, the headers, and the cookie, in the order of the table below.
4. **Handler.** If no check refuses, the request goes on.
5. **Headers.** `secure_headers` adds the response headers to the answer.

The redirect keeps the `#token=` fragment of the sign-in link, because a browser keeps the fragment on a redirect. The API refusal tells the user to open Ostra at the private host name. The reason is that a sign-in on `127.0.0.1` shares its cookie with every other local port.

### Checks for each path class

| Path class | Peer and header checks | Cookie check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/api/auth/exchange` | Origin, `Sec-Fetch-Site`, and `Sec-Fetch-Dest` | No, because the cookie does not exist yet |
| Other `/api/` paths and `/ws` | Origin, `Sec-Fetch-Site`, and `Sec-Fetch-Dest` | Yes |
| `/internal/` paths | The peer must be a local address. A request with `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` is refused. | No. The bridge checks its own bearer token. |
| `/mcp/oauth/callback` and static files | None | No |

The header checks for `/api/` and `/ws` refuse a request with status 403 and `This origin is not allowed.` in these cases:

- The `Origin` header is present and is not an allowed origin.
- `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `cross-site` or `same-site`. A page on another port of `localhost` is same-site, so the browser sends the cookie. This header lets the server tell that page from the app.
- `Sec-Fetch-Dest` is present and is not `empty`, `websocket`, or `document`. The app uses `fetch`, the socket, and download links. An image, script, or frame request is page content that reaches the API, such as a Markdown image that an agent wrote.

The internal paths refuse a non-local peer with `This endpoint accepts local connections only.` They refuse a browser header with `This endpoint is for Ostra's harness bridge, not for web pages.` Harnesses always run on this machine, so the bridge refuses other peers even when the server listens on every interface. A browser page on this machine is a local peer, but it always sends `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site`. [Harness executors](harness-executors.md) explains the bridge.

A request without a valid cookie gets 401 with `Sign in with the URL the ostra command printed.` The server logs the facts of the request: peer, host, origin, the fetch headers, and the user agent. The log never holds a token or a cookie value.

### Response headers

| Header | Value | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; worker-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; font-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self' ws://<host> wss://<host>; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; frame-src 'none'; manifest-src 'self'` | Scripts run only from this origin. Images load only from this origin or from `data:`, because an injected agent can send data out through a Markdown image URL. |
| `Cache-Control` | `no-store` | The server sets it for API paths only. |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` | The browser does not guess the content type. |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `no-referrer` | The browser sends no referrer. |
| `X-Frame-Options` | `DENY` | A page elsewhere cannot frame the app or a refusal. |

The policy names `ws://<host>` and `wss://<host>` only after the host passes the allowlist. For a refused host, the policy has `connect-src 'self';` and names no host. The test `the_browser_boundary_refuses_page_content_and_other_sites` checks this rule.

### What the guard does not do

The guard checks who sends a request. It does not check which route the request calls. A signed-in browser can call every route in this page, because the handlers have no roles. Each file route enforces its own path rules, for example `session_file` for artifacts.

## Tests that pin these rules

The file [crates/ostra-server/tests/e2e.rs](crates/ostra-server/tests/e2e.rs) starts a real listener with a scripted model and uses cookie sign-in. These tests cover this page:

- `the_browser_boundary_refuses_page_content_and_other_sites`: the fetch headers, the origin, the host, the CSP, `Cache-Control`, `X-Frame-Options`, and the internal paths.
- `a_loopback_server_lives_at_its_private_name`: the 307 redirect, the 421 on `/api/auth/exchange` at an IP name, and the sign-in at the private name.
- `sign_in_sessions_are_listed_and_revoked`: the socket closes with code 4401 within 1 second of a browser revoke, and within the recheck window of a command-line revoke.
- `terminal_streams_over_the_socket`: a subscribe before the PTY exists, the first snapshot frame, the resize error, and the 64 KiB input error.
- `onboarding_flag_and_ui_state_round_trip`: the PATCH merge, the 413 for a state over 64 KiB, and the 400 for a body that is not an object.
- `the_bridge_socket_serves_only_harness_callbacks`: the bridge socket answers only the internal paths.
- `yolo_implement_session_end_to_end`: the `project_fs_changed`, `tree_patch`, and `activity` pushes, the tree route, one search hit of each kind, an empty query, the `limit` parameter, and the activity windows.
- `workspace_books_are_listed_read_and_deleted`: the docs routes, the 400 for a bad book ID, and the 404 for a missing book.

The unit tests in `nav/search.rs` pin the score order and the large-index time. The unit test in `nav/activity.rs` pins the windows. The unit test in `ws.rs` pins the frame layout.

## Constants and limits

This table lists the constants that this page owns. Two constants have owners on other pages, and the table links to them.

| Constant | Value | File | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ARTIFACT_LIMIT` | 4 MiB | `api.rs` | The largest session file that `GET /api/artifacts` returns as text. |
| `UI_STATE_MAX_BYTES` | 64 KiB | `ostra-core/src/api.rs` | The largest stored console layout document. |
| `SUMMARY_CHARS` | 120 | `ostra-core/src/api.rs` | The longest run summary line. |
| `MAX_MESSAGE` | 1 MiB | `ws.rs` | The largest client message and frame. |
| `MAX_TERM_INPUT` | 64 KiB | `ws.rs` | The largest `term_input` data. |
| `MAX_CHANNELS` | 256 | `ws.rs` | The most channels for one socket. |
| `TERM_QUEUE` | 64 | `ws.rs` | Binary frames that wait for one socket. |
| `HINT_QUEUE` | 8 | `ws.rs` | Hint answers that wait for one socket. |
| `TREE_TICK` | 250 ms | `nav/mod.rs` | The time between rebuilds of dirty tree nodes. |
| `ACTIVITY_GAP` | 500 ms | `nav/mod.rs` | The least time between two activity builds. |
| `ARTIFACT_INDEX_CAP` | 4 MiB | `nav/mod.rs` | The largest artifact that the search indexes by headings. [Workspace artifacts and uploads](artifacts-and-uploads.md) owns the artifact rules. |
| `DEFAULT_LIMIT` | 50 | `nav/search.rs` | The search result count when `limit` is absent. |
| `MAX_LIMIT` | 200 | `nav/search.rs` | The largest search result count. |
| `LESSONS_PER_PROJECT` | 20 | `nav/search.rs` | Lessons that the search reads from each project. |
| `HINT_CHARS` | 80 | `nav/search.rs` | The longest hint text of a hit. |
| `TEXT_ROWS` | 200 | `nav/search.rs` | Rows that the text index returns before the merge. |
| `INDEX_ONLY` | 0.45 | `nav/search.rs` | The score of a hit that only the text index placed. |

The usage search of the agent code tools has its own limits, and the search constants of this page do not change them. [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) owns that search.

Two routes set a body limit from an artifact or upload cap. Only `/api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts` uses `ostra_core::artifacts::MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` plus 1024 bytes. The `/api/workspaces/{ws}/uploads` route uses `ostra_engine::uploads::MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` plus 1024 bytes. [Workspace artifacts and uploads](artifacts-and-uploads.md) owns the other artifact caps.

sections.title: Project files, Git dock, and cloning
sections.summary: How the server reads project folders, files, diffs, and git state, how it tracks which execution wrote a file, how the Git dock, clone, and pull run git, and the config overrides and limits that protect every git command.
sections.body:
The Files view needs facts about a project folder: its tree, its text, its git state, and the session execution that last changed each file. The browser cannot read the disk, and an agent can write to the same folder at the same time. The server code in `crates/ostra-server/src/files` answers with capped reads, short caches, and git commands that start no program from the repository. This page also covers the folder picker, the Git dock commands, clone and pull, the git config overrides, and every cap and timeout. It stops before the editor UI, which [Project, Files, and dependency screens](web-project-screens.md) explains.

## Parts and routes

Eight source files hold this area. Each file has one job.

| File | Job |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/files/mod.rs` | The `Files` service: tree, text, index, diff, changes, save, mkdir, attribution, caches, and the live `project_fs_changed` messages |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/files/tree.rs` | Blocking disk code: path containment, listings with ignore flags, the file name walk, and capped reads |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/files/watch.rs` | `ToolWatch` and `Touch`: which files a write tool call changed |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/files/browse.rs` | The folder picker: `GET /api/fs` and `POST /api/fs/mkdir` |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/files/git.rs` | Read-only git facts: status, diff, and line counts |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/repo.rs` | The Git dock: status, branches, and the commands that change the checkout |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/git.rs` | Clone, pull, and `run_git`, the function that every non-automatic git command uses |
| `crates/ostra-core/src/git.rs` | The git config overrides |
